Vision Statement 
This Manual serves as the authoritative operational SOP for cyber-crime investigation in Uttar 
Pradesh. It integrates law, technology, digital forensics, policing practice, and judicial 
expectations into a single court-defensible investigative framework. The objective is to ensure 
that every cybercrime investigation conducted by UP Police: 
 
Survives legal scrutiny 
 
Produces admissible electronic evidence 
 
Ensures victim protection 
 
Targets organised networks, not merely surface offenders 
 
Leads to sustainable prosecution and conviction 
🎯 Core Objectives 
1. Standardization of cybercrime investigation across districts 
2. Elimination of procedural lapses causing acquittals 
3. Legally compliant search, seizure & digital evidence handling 
4. Institutional strengthening & training architecture 
5. Alignment with BNS, BNSS, BSA & DPDP Act framework 
📌 Applicability 
This SOP is mandatory for: 
 
All Cyber Crime Police Stations 
 
All District Police Units 
 
All Investigating Officers handling cyber-enabled offences 
 
Digital Forensic Laboratories (State level) 
[[PAGE 3]]
OPENING REMARK  
Cybercrime represents the most transformative shift in criminality faced by law enforcement in 
modern India. Unlike conventional crime, it is borderless, technology-enabled, rapidly scalable, 
and capable of targeting individuals, institutions, and the State simultaneously. In Uttar Pradesh 
one of the most populous and digitally expanding states cybercrime is no longer a specialized 
policing challenge; it is an everyday operational reality. 
The transition to digital governance, online financial systems, mobile penetration, social media 
expansion, and cloud-based infrastructure has strengthened economic growth and citizen 
empowerment. However, the same digital infrastructure has become an enabling environment for 
deception, impersonation, organized financial fraud, ransomware attacks, data breaches, child 
exploitation, misinformation campaigns, and attacks on critical systems. The investigative 
landscape has therefore fundamentally changed. 
Cybercrime investigation is not merely about technical expertise. It is fundamentally a legal 
exercise governed by statutory authority, procedural safeguards, evidentiary thresholds, and 
judicial scrutiny. A technically accurate investigation that violates procedural law is legally 
unsustainable. Courts do not convict on suspicion or technological complexity; they convict on 
legally admissible evidence collected through lawful process. 
This Manual has been prepared to address that exact challenge. 
It integrates substantive penal law under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, procedural safeguards 
under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, evidentiary standards under the Bharatiya 
Sakshya Adhiniyam, and sectoral obligations under the Information Technology Act, Digital 
Personal Data Protection Act, and allied legislation. It converts these legal frameworks into 
structured investigative workflows that are operationally executable by Investigating Officers at 
the district level. 
The purpose of this SOP is not to restrict investigative discretion, but to protect it by ensuring 
that every action taken by an Investigating Officer is legally defensible, proportionate, 
documented, and sustainable in court. It provides structured guidance on FIR registration, 
jurisdiction, digital crime scene management, forensic processes, financial tracing, 
[[PAGE 4]]
cryptocurrency analysis, intermediary coordination, admissibility standards, and courtroom 
This Manual is also institutional in character. It recognizes that cybercrime is organized, 
adaptive, and continuously evolving. Therefore, policing must also be structured, standardized, 
and continuously upgraded. Training, supervision, audit, and accountability are integral 
components of this framework. 
Every cybercrime investigation conducted in Uttar Pradesh must reflect professionalism, legality, 
technological awareness, and victim sensitivity. This SOP is the foundation upon which that 
standardization will be achieved. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
[[PAGE 5]]
CHAPTER 1 - CONCEPTUAL FOUNDATIONS OF 
CYBERCRIME: NATURE, EVOLUTION AND 
CLASSIFICATION 
1.1 Introduction: Understanding Cybercrime in the Contemporary Policing 
Context 
Cybercrime is no longer a specialised or peripheral form of criminal activity. It has become a 
routine and unavoidable component of everyday policing, cutting across territorial boundaries, 
social classes, and conventional crime categories. For the modern Investigating Officer, 
cybercrime is not merely crime involving computers; rather, it represents a fundamental 
transformation in how crime is committed, concealed, scaled, and monetised in a digitally 
connected society. 
Unlike traditional offences where the crime scene is physically visible and geographically fixed, 
cybercrime operates in an invisible, distributed, and dynamic environment commonly referred to 
as cyberspace. This environment consists of interconnected computers, mobile devices, servers, 
networks, applications, cloud infrastructure, and digital platforms that enable communication, 
commerce, governance, and social interaction. Cybercrime exploits this very infrastructure, often 
without physical contact between the offender and the victim, and frequently without immediate 
detection. 
From a law enforcement perspective, cybercrime disrupts long-established assumptions 
regarding jurisdiction, evidence, identity, and time. A single cyber offence may involve a victim 
located in one district, an accused operating from another State or country, financial proceeds 
routed through multiple intermediary accounts, and digital infrastructure hosted outside India. As 
a result, cybercrime investigation requires conceptual clarity at the outset, even before procedural 
and technical steps are initiated. 
This chapter provides that foundational clarity. It explains what cybercrime is, how it has 
evolved, how it typically operates, and how it is classified for policing purposes. A shared 
conceptual framework is essential to ensure that investigation does not become fragmented, 
[[PAGE 6]]
reactive, or limited to surface-level offenders, but instead targets the broader criminal ecosystem 
behind digital offences. 
1.2 Meaning and Definition of Cybercrime 
1.2.1 General Understanding of Cybercrime 
In general terms, cybercrime refers to unlawful acts in which computers, digital devices, 
networks, online platforms, or electronic data are used either as a tool, a target, or a facilitating 
environment for the commission of an offence. What distinguishes cybercrime from 
conventional crime is not the criminal intent—such as cheating, harassment, extortion, or theft—
but the medium through which that intent is executed. 
Cybercrime commonly manifests in the following forms: 
 
Deception and fraud conducted through online or electronic means 
 
Misuse of another person’s digital identity or credentials 
 
Harassment, stalking, or exploitation through digital communication platforms 
 
Unauthorised access to computer systems or data 
 
Disruption of digital services, infrastructure, or governance platforms 
Although cybercrime occurs in a virtual environment, the harm it causes is tangible and real. 
Victims suffer financial loss, psychological trauma, reputational damage, invasion of privacy, 
and erosion of trust in digital systems. These consequences directly impact public confidence in 
digital governance and law enforcement. 
1.2.2 Definitions by International Organizations 
International bodies have adopted broad, technology-neutral definitions of cybercrime to account 
for its constantly evolving nature.  
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime describes “cybercrime as criminal activity in 
which computers or computer networks are a tool, a target, or a place of criminal activity. This 
definition deliberately avoids restrictive categorization, recognizing that cybercrime adapts 
rapidly to technological change.” 
[[PAGE 7]]
The Council of Europe’s Convention on Cybercrime (Budapest Convention) focuses on 
“offences against the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of computer systems and data, as 
well as computer-related fraud and content-based offences. This framework highlights both 
technical system harm and victim-centric impact.” 
INTERPOL treat “cybercrime as an operational threat that intersects with organized crime, 
financial crime, and national security. From this perspective, cybercrime is viewed not as an 
isolated offence category, but as an enabler of wider criminal ecosystems.” 
1.2.3 Indian Legal and Policy Perspective 
In India, cybercrime is not defined through a single exhaustive statutory provision. Instead, cyber 
offences are addressed through a combination of specialized legislation and general penal law. 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 criminalizes unauthorized access, data damage, identity 
theft, cheating by personation using computer resources, violation of privacy, cyber terrorism, 
and related conduct. However, cyber-enabled offences are frequently prosecuted alongside 
general penal provisions dealing with cheating, forgery, criminal intimidation, sexual offences, 
defamation, and offences against the State. 
Statutory Transition Note (IPC to BNS): 
The substantive penal law governing criminal offences in India is now the Bharatiya Nyaya 
Sanhita, 2023, which has replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860. While judicial precedents 
developed under the IPC continue to guide interpretation, all offences committed after the 
commencement of the BNS must be registered, investigated, and prosecuted under the 
corresponding provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Accordingly, references in this 
SOP to traditional penal offences are to be understood as references to their corresponding 
provisions under the BNS. 
From a policing standpoint, cybercrime in India is best understood not as a separate legal silo, 
but as a method of committing recognised criminal offences through digital means. This 
approach ensures that substance prevails over form and prevents procedural delay caused by 
definitional confusion. 
1.2.4 Law Enforcement–Oriented Definition 
For the purposes of this Standard Operating Procedure, cybercrime may be understood as: 
[[PAGE 8]]
“Any unlawful act in which digital devices, networks, online platforms, or electronic data are 
used as the primary means to commit, facilitate, conceal, or benefit from the offence, resulting 
in harm to individuals, institutions, society, or the State.” 
This functional definition prioritizes investigative clarity over technical complexity. It enables 
Investigating Officers to quickly identify whether digital evidence, electronic intermediaries, or 
online platforms are involved, and therefore whether specialized procedures under this SOP must 
be followed. 
1.2.5 Procedural Law Context: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 
Cybercrime investigation is governed not only by substantive penal provisions but also by 
procedural law. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which has replaced the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1973, provides the procedural framework for registration of offences, 
investigation, search and seizure, arrest, jurisdiction, remand, and submission of police reports. 
For cybercrime cases, the BNSS is particularly significant due to its relevance to inter-
jurisdictional investigation, digital search and seizure, freezing of accounts, documentation of 
investigation steps, and lawful exercise of police powers. Investigating Officers must ensure that 
all procedural actions—especially those involving electronic devices, bank accounts, online 
platforms, and cross-district coordination—are carried out strictly in accordance with the BNSS 
to ensure legal sustainability. 
1.3 Scope and Nature of Cybercrime 
1.3.1 Scope of Cybercrime 
The scope of cybercrime expands with every increase in digital adoption. As banking, 
governance, healthcare, education, commerce, and social interaction move online, corresponding 
opportunities for criminal misuse also multiply. Cybercrime is no longer confined to urban or 
technologically sophisticated populations; it increasingly affects rural areas, first-time internet 
users, and small businesses. 
Cybercrime may involve: 
 
Individuals as victims or offenders 
[[PAGE 9]]
 
Private and public institutions 
 
Critical infrastructure and essential services 
 
Domestic as well as cross-border elements 
Cybercrime does not replace conventional crime; rather, it amplifies it. Fraud becomes faster, 
impersonation more convincing, harassment more persistent, and surveillance more intrusive 
when facilitated by digital tools. 
Data Protection Context: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 introduces a legal 
framework governing lawful processing and protection of digital personal data. While primarily 
regulatory in nature, cybercrime investigations frequently intersect with unlawful data access, 
misuse, leakage, or breach. Investigating Officers must therefore remain conscious of data 
protection considerations in cases involving identity theft, data breaches, and unauthorized 
disclosure of personal information. 
1.3.2 Nature of Cybercrime 
Certain characteristics distinguish cybercrime from traditional offences: 
 
Borderless operation: Physical location of the offender is often irrelevant, complicating 
jurisdiction and arrest. 
 
Speed and scale: A single offender can target hundreds or thousands of victims in a short 
time. 
 
Anonymity and obfuscation: Use of fake identities, proxy servers, and layered accounts 
conceals attribution. 
 
Evidence volatility: Digital evidence can be altered, deleted, or overwritten within 
minutes. 
 
Layered execution: Victim interaction, technical facilitation, and financial handling are 
often performed by different actors. 
Understanding these characteristics is essential for effective first response and early investigative 
decision-making. 
[[PAGE 10]]
1.3.3 Evidentiary Context: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 
Cybercrime investigation is inseparably linked with electronic and digital evidence. The 
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which has replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, 
expressly recognizes electronic and digital records as documentary evidence. Emails, call detail 
records, IP logs, server logs, device data, cloud records, platform data, and blockchain 
transactions are all admissible subject to compliance with legal requirements relating to 
authenticity and integrity. 
Given the fragile nature of digital evidence, improper handling at the initial stage—such as 
reliance on screenshots without metadata, unauthorized access to devices, or failure to maintain 
chain of custody—can render evidence inadmissible. Evidence preservation must therefore be 
treated as a legal obligation, not merely a technical exercise. 
1.4 Evolution of Cybercrime 
Cybercrime has evolved in parallel with technological development. Early cyber offences were 
largely experimental or individual-centric, involving simple hacking or misuse of systems. With 
the expansion of digital payments, social media, and online services, cybercrime shifted towards 
organised fraud, identity theft, and financial exploitation. 
In recent years, cybercrime has entered a more sophisticated phase marked by automation, use of 
artificial intelligence, deepfakes, cryptocurrency laundering, and cross-border coordination. This 
evolution demonstrates that cybercrime adapts faster than law and procedure, making continuous 
conceptual updating essential for effective policing. 
1.5 Modus Operandi of Cybercrime (Conceptual Overview) 
Despite diversity in offence types, cybercrimes commonly exhibit certain operational patterns: 
 
Exploitation of trust through impersonation or authority projection 
 
Creation of urgency or fear to bypass rational decision-making 
 
Abuse of digital identities, SIM cards, or accounts 
 
Separation of roles between victim contact, technical facilitation, and money handling 
 
Rapid monetisation and layering of proceeds 
[[PAGE 11]]
Understanding modus operandi at this conceptual level enables Investigating Officers to connect 
seemingly isolated complaints and identify organised structures. 
1.6 Classification of Cybercrime: A Law-Enforcement-Oriented Framework 
For the purposes of this SOP, cybercrime is classified based on the primary target and nature of 
harm rather than the technology used. This approach aligns with policing realities and supports 
investigation, supervision, and prioritisation. 
The major categories include: 
 
Cybercrimes against Individuals 
 
Cybercrimes against Property, Data, and Computer Systems 
 
Financial and Organised Cybercrime 
 
Social Media and Platform-Based Cybercrime 
 
Cybercrimes against the State and Society 
These categories are conceptual in nature. Detailed offence-wise treatment, legal mapping, and 
investigation procedures are provided in subsequent chapters. 
1.7 Purpose and Role of This SOP for Uttar Pradesh Police 
The increasing volume and complexity of cybercrime necessitate a standardised, structured, and 
legally sound response framework. This SOP is intended to provide Investigating Officers with 
conceptual clarity, procedural uniformity, and practical guidance from the moment a complaint is 
received. 
Cybercrime cases often fail not due to absence of law, but due to delayed action, improper 
handling of electronic evidence, or incorrect legal mapping at the initial stage. This SOP seeks to 
address these gaps while preserving investigative discretion. The ultimate objective is effective 
investigation, victim protection, and disruption of cybercrime networks. 
 
 
[[PAGE 12]]
CHAPTER 2 - CYBERCRIME TYPOLOGIES, MODUS 
OPERANDI & LEGAL MAPPING 
2.0 Introductory Note: Operationalizing Chapter 1 
Chapter 1 of this Standard Operating Procedure established the conceptual foundation of 
cybercrime, its nature, evolution, and classification. However, conceptual understanding alone 
does not translate into effective policing unless it is converted into a structured, legally accurate, 
and operational decision-making framework at the investigation stage. 
Field experience and judicial outcomes demonstrate that cybercrime cases most frequently fail 
not due to absence of substantive law, but due to: 
 
delayed registration of FIRs, 
 
incorrect or incomplete legal section mapping, 
 
improper handling of electronic evidence, and 
 
failure to exercise procedural powers at the initial stage. 
Chapter 2 operationalizes the conceptual framework of Chapter 1 by translating cybercrime 
categories into offence-wise investigative matrices. These matrices are designed to assist 
Investigating Officers in: 
 
identifying the correct offence category at the first point of contact, 
 
understanding common modus operandi, 
 
locating critical digital and financial evidence, and 
 
invoking the appropriate statutory provisions in a legally sustainable manner. 
2.1 Legal Architecture Governing Cybercrime Investigation 
Cybercrime investigation in India operates within a multi-statute legal architecture, which 
must be applied in a complementary—not isolated—manner. 
[[PAGE 13]]
2.1.1 Substantive Penal Law 
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) constitutes the primary penal law governing cyber-
enabled offences such as cheating, forgery, criminal intimidation, sexual offences, defamation, 
extortion, mischief, criminal breach of trust, conspiracy, and offences against the State. 
Cyber offences do not lose their criminal character merely because technology is used as the 
medium. Accordingly, general penal provisions under the BNS must be invoked wherever the 
ingredients of the offence are satisfied. 
2.1.2 Special Cyber Law 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 supplements the general penal law by criminalising 
specific technology-centric conduct, including: 
 
unauthorised access and data damage, 
 
identity theft and cheating by personation using computer resources, 
 
violation of privacy, 
 
publishing unlawful content, 
 
cyber terrorism, and 
 
intermediary obligations. 
IT Act provisions are supplementary in nature and must ordinarily be invoked alongside, not 
in substitution of, relevant BNS provisions. 
2.1.3 Procedural Law 
All procedural actions in cybercrime cases are governed by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha 
Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). This includes: 
 
registration of FIRs, 
 
exercise of search and seizure powers, 
 
freezing of bank accounts and digital assets, 
 
recording of statements, 
[[PAGE 14]]
 
inter-jurisdictional investigation, and 
 
submission of police reports. 
Investigating Officers must ensure that procedural legality under BNSS is strictly adhered to, as 
procedural lapses in cybercrime cases are often irreversible. 
2.1.4 Evidence Law 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) governs admissibility of electronic and digital 
evidence. Electronic records are admissible subject to proof of authenticity, integrity, and chain 
of custody. 
Screenshots, forwarded messages, and secondary digital material cannot be treated as primary 
evidence unless corroborated by metadata, platform records, or device-level extraction. 
2.1.5 Ancillary Statutes (Case-Specific Application) 
Depending on the nature of the offence, the following statutes may also be attracted: 
 
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 – identity misuse, data breach cases 
 
Telecommunications Act, 2023 – SIM misuse, caller ID spoofing 
 
Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 – organised cyber fraud involving 
laundering of proceeds 
Invocation of ancillary statutes must be reasoned, recorded, and case-specific, not mechanical. 
2.2 Structure of Chapter 2 
Each cybercrime category in this chapter is presented in a uniform operational structure: 
1. Conceptual Explanation 
2. Expanded Investigative Table (with legally corrected statutory mapping) 
3. Typical Real-Life Reporting Pattern 
4. Standard Investigation Flow 
5. Common Investigation Failures 
[[PAGE 15]]
6. Supervisory Review Checkpoints 
This structure is intended to ensure uniformity of investigation across districts and facilitate 
supervisory oversight. 
2.3 Cybercrimes Against Individuals 
2.3.1 Conceptual Explanation 
Cybercrimes against individuals are offences in which the primary victim is a natural person and 
the harm suffered is personal in character. Such harm may be financial, psychological, 
reputational, bodily, or identity-based. These offences frequently rely more on manipulation of 
human behaviour than on sophisticated technical exploitation, making them both widespread and 
difficult to prevent through technology alone. 
From a policing perspective, cybercrimes against individuals require immediate legal and 
procedural intervention. Delay in FIR registration, failure to preserve volatile digital evidence, 
or incorrect legal mapping at the initial stage often results in irreversible loss of evidence and 
weak prosecution. Victims in this category commonly include senior citizens, women, minors, 
and first-time internet users, necessitating both legal precision and victim-sensitive handling.

 In all offences listed below, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) provisions constitute 
the primary penal offences. 
 Information Technology Act, 2000 provisions are supplementary and must not be

2.3.3 Typical Real-Life Reporting Patterns 
Cybercrimes against individuals are usually reported in the following manner: 
[[PAGE 18]]
 
Victims approach the police after financial loss has already occurred or harassment has 
continued for some time. 
 
In fraud cases, reporting is often delayed due to embarrassment, confusion, or false hope 
of recovery. 
 
In harassment or sexual offence cases, victims frequently present screenshots or 
forwarded messages without original metadata. 
 
Victims may have already interacted with banks, platforms, or intermediaries before 
approaching police, sometimes resulting in partial loss of evidence. 
Understanding these patterns assists Investigating Officers in identifying evidentiary gaps at the 
very first interaction. 
2.3.4 Standard Investigation Flow 
The following step-by-step investigation flow must be followed in cybercrimes against 
individuals: 
1. Register FIR immediately; jurisdictional issues must not delay registration. 
2. Identify whether the offence involves both cyber and financial components. 
3. Issue immediate account freezing requests to banks and payment intermediaries. 
4. Issue data preservation notices to platforms, telecom service providers, and banks. 
5. Secure the victim’s device in its original condition; forensic cloning must be done only by 
trained personnel. 
6. Obtain CDRs, IP logs, platform account data, and transaction trails through lawful 
channels. 
7. Analyse mule accounts and determine whether conspiracy or organised elements exist. 
8. Assess applicability of PMLA only where laundering indicators are present and record 
reasons in the case diary. 
[[PAGE 19]]
2.3.5 Common Investigation Failures (Observed by Courts) 
Supervisory experience and judicial scrutiny reveal the following frequent lapses: 
 
Informal counselling or compromise without formal legal action. 
 
Delay in freezing accounts beyond the initial transaction window. 
 
Failure to issue data preservation notices before seeking takedown. 
 
Treating screenshots as primary evidence without metadata corroboration. 
 
Mechanical addition of IT Act sections without invoking primary BNS offences. 
Such lapses often result in weak charge-sheets or adverse judicial observations. 
2.3.6 Supervisory Review Checkpoints 
Supervisory officers must conduct structured review at early stages of investigation. The 
following checkpoints are mandatory: 
 
FIR registered promptly without jurisdictional delay. 
 
Correct BNS + IT Act section mapping at FIR stage. 
 
Timely initiation of financial preservation measures. 
 
Issuance and follow-up of data preservation requests. 
 
Forensically sound handling of victim devices. 
 
Proper identification and treatment of mule accounts. 
 
Recorded reasoning for invoking or not invoking DPDP Act / PMLA. 
Early supervisory intervention prevents procedural defects that cannot be cured at later stages. 
2.4 Cybercrimes Against Property, Data & Computer Systems 
2.4.1 Conceptual Explanation 
Cybercrimes against property, data, and computer systems are offences where the primary 
target is a computer resource, digital asset, or data, rather than a natural person. The harm is 
directed at the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of systems and information. These 
[[PAGE 20]]
offences frequently remain undetected for extended periods and are often discovered incidentally 
through service disruption, audits, or ransom demands. 
From a policing perspective, this category demands technical restraint, early supervisory 
control, and strict evidence discipline. Improper handling—such as rebooting systems, internal 
remediation before forensic capture, or unauthorised access by untrained personnel—can 
permanently destroy critical evidence and fatally weaken prosecution. 
2.4.2 Consolidated Investigative Table: Cybercrimes Against Property, Data & Systems 
 In all system-based cybercrimes, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) provisions 
constitute the primary penal offences. 
 Information Technology Act, 2000 provisions are supplementary and must be invoked 
alongside, not independently.

2.4.3 Typical Real-Life Detection & Reporting Patterns 
Cybercrimes against systems are commonly detected in the following manner: 
 
Organisations report system slowdown, service disruption, or data unavailability. 
 
In many cases, internal IT teams attempt remediation before informing police. 
 
Evidence is frequently partially destroyed due to premature patching, reinstallation, or 
malware removal. 
 
Reporting may be delayed due to reputational concerns or misunderstanding of 
criminality. 
These patterns explain why early police intervention is critical. 
2.4.4 Standard Investigation Flow 
The following mandatory investigation flow must be followed in system-based cybercrimes: 
1. Direct complainant to immediately halt all remediation activity. 
2. Isolate affected systems from the network without powering them down. 
3. Secure forensic images, volatile memory, logs, and backups using authorised personnel. 
4. Identify whether the intrusion is internal, external, or hybrid. 
5. Preserve ransom communications, malware samples, and encrypted data in original form. 
6. Coordinate with CERT-In for indicators of compromise and technical guidance. 
[[PAGE 23]]
7. Assess applicability of DPDP Act in data breach cases and document findings. 
8. Where ransom or laundering indicators exist, evaluate PMLA applicability and record 
reasons. 
2.4.5 Common Investigation Failures (Judicially Noted) 
Courts and supervisory reviews have repeatedly noted the following failures: 
 
Allowing internal IT teams to “clean” systems before forensic capture. 
 
Failure to document ransomware communications and payment demands. 
 
Treating system intrusions as civil or contractual disputes. 
 
Absence of supervisory oversight during critical technical decisions. 
Such lapses often result in loss of attribution and weak evidentiary value. 
2.4.6 Supervisory Review Checkpoints (Strict Control Model) 
In system-based cybercrimes, direct supervisory control is mandatory. Supervisors must 
ensure: 
 
No system reboot, reinstallation, or patching occurred prior to forensic imaging. 
 
Chain of custody and isolation steps are properly documented. 
 
Written preservation instructions were issued to the complainant organisation. 
 
DPDP Act breach implications are assessed and recorded. 
 
Ransom communications and digital artefacts are preserved in original form. 
 
Forensic analysis is conducted only through authorised laboratories. 
Failure at these checkpoints must be immediately corrected and documented, as later 
rectification is often impossible. 
[[PAGE 24]]
2.5 Financial & Organised Cybercrime 
2.5.1 Conceptual Explanation 
Financial and organized cybercrime comprises cyber-enabled offences committed for direct or 
indirect monetary gain, often through structured roles, repetition, and concealment of 
proceeds. Unlike isolated individual frauds, these offences display indicators of organization 
such as recruitment of mule accounts, scripted victim engagement, technological facilitation, and 
systematic laundering of proceeds. 
From a policing perspective, the critical error in such cases is treating them as standalone 
complaints. Failure to identify repetition, financial layering, or control structures leads to 
premature charge-sheets against mule account holders while principal offenders remain 
untouched. Early financial intelligence, linkage analysis, and supervisory oversight are 
therefore essential. 
2.5.2 Consolidated Investigative Table: Financial & Organized Cybercrime 
 In all organized financial cybercrimes, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) provisions 
constitute the primary offences. 
 Information Technology Act, 2000 provisions are supplementary. 
 Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) must be invoked only upon 
reasoned satisfaction of laundering indicators.

2.5.3 Typical Real-Life Detection & Reporting Patterns 
Financial and organised cybercrime is commonly detected through: 
 
Multiple FIRs across districts with similar modus operandi. 
 
Rapid fund movement through newly opened or low-KYC accounts. 
 
Victims unknown to each other but linked by identical scripts, links, or caller 
behaviour. 
 
Discovery of cryptocurrency use to obscure money trails. 
Early recognition of these patterns is crucial to prevent fragmentation. 
2.5.4 Standard Financial Investigation Flow 
The following mandatory investigation flow must be followed: 
1. Collate FIRs to identify repetition, common scripts, and shared financial nodes. 
2. Freeze all linked accounts, not merely the first beneficiary account. 
3. Conduct backward and forward transaction analysis to identify controllers. 
4. Analyse IP access, device fingerprints, and login behaviour to establish control. 
[[PAGE 27]]
5. In crypto cases, trace wallets beyond the first hop and seek exchange-level KYC. 
6. Assess laundering indicators (layering, integration) and record reasons for invoking or 
not invoking PMLA. 
7. Consider need for inter-agency coordination where thresholds are crossed. 
2.5.5 Common Investigation Failures (Judicial & Supervisory Observations) 
The following failures frequently weaken organised cybercrime prosecutions: 
 
Treating each complaint as a standalone offence. 
 
Filing charge-sheets against mule account holders without conspiracy analysis. 
 
Ignoring cryptocurrency trails due to technical unfamiliarity. 
 
Mechanical invocation of PMLA without documenting laundering indicators. 
 
Failure to document proceeds-of-crime analysis in the case diary. 
Such lapses result in loss of jurisdictional advantage and dilution of the case. 
2.5.6 Supervisory Review Checkpoints (PMLA-Conscious Model) 
Supervisory officers must ensure the following checkpoints are satisfied: 
 
Verification of repetition and financial layering across cases. 
 
Examination of conspiracy and organised crime indicators. 
 
Documentation of proceeds of crime and laundering process. 
 
Legal sustainability of account freezing orders and timely renewals. 
 
Adequate tracing of crypto wallets and exchange disclosures. 
 
Written reasons for invoking or not invoking PMLA. 
Active supervisory oversight at this stage is decisive for successful prosecution. 
 
[[PAGE 28]]
2.6 Social Media & Platform-Based Cybercrime 
2.6.1 Conceptual Explanation 
Social media and platform-based cybercrime refers to offences where online platforms act as 
the primary medium, facilitator, or amplifier of criminal conduct. The speed, scale, and 
persistence of digital platforms significantly magnify harm, often within hours of first 
publication. 
These offences frequently involve identity misuse, harassment, sexual exploitation, fraud, 
misinformation, and coordinated campaigns. From a policing perspective, the defining risk is 
loss of volatile platform data due to takedown, account deletion, or routine data-retention 
expiry. Therefore, preservation must always precede takedown. 
2.6.2 Consolidated Investigative Table: Social Media & Platform-Based Cybercrime 
Platform policies do not override criminal law.

2.6.3 Typical Reporting Patterns 
 
Victims approach police after content has already spread. 
 
Platforms may remove content due to policy violations before police preservation. 
 
Initial evidence often limited to screenshots or forwarded links. 
 
Original uploader and coordinated amplifiers are frequently confused. 
[[PAGE 30]]
2.6.4 Standard Investigation Flow (Platform Cases) 
1. Register FIR promptly; free-speech concerns do not bar investigation of cognisable 
offences. 
2. Issue immediate data preservation requests to the platform. 
3. Capture URLs, account IDs, timestamps, hashes, and engagement metrics. 
4. Seek platform disclosure of account creation data and IP access logs. 
5. Issue takedown requests only after preservation is secured. 
6. Assess whether platform activity links to financial gain or organised conduct. 
2.6.5 Supervisory Review Checkpoints 
 
Preservation issued before or with takedown. 
 
Accurate section mapping under BNS + IT Act. 
 
Evidence integrity beyond screenshots. 
 
Identification of original uploader vs re-sharers. 
 
Assessment of escalation into organised or financial cybercrime. 
 
2.7 Cybercrimes Against the State & CII 
2.7.1 Conceptual Explanation 
Cybercrimes against the State and Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) are offences that 
threaten sovereignty, public order, governance systems, essential services, or national 
security. Harm in such cases is collective and systemic, with potential cascading effects across 
society. 
District police officers often act as first responders, even when specialised agencies later 
assume control. Early-stage errors—such as unauthorised access, delayed isolation, or informal 
information sharing—can irreversibly compromise attribution and national response. 
[[PAGE 31]]

Treat every suspected CII incident as a national-security event until ruled otherwise.

2.7.3 Typical Detection Patterns 
 
Sudden unavailability or defacement of government websites. 
 
Alerts from CERT-In or internal IT teams. 
 
Unusual traffic spikes or unauthorised administrative access. 
2.7.4 Standard First-Responder Investigation Flow (State/CII) 
1. Treat incident as national-security related until assessment is complete. 
2. Isolate affected systems without powering down. 
3. Preserve logs, backups, and volatile memory through authorised teams. 
4. Inform supervisory officers and initiate formal escalation. 
5. Coordinate with CERT-In / NCIIPC as applicable. 
6. Avoid public disclosure or informal media interaction. 
7. Document every action taken during first response. 
2.7.5 Supervisory Review Checkpoints (Escalation-Control Model) 
 
Verification of immediate isolation and evidence preservation. 
 
Determination whether system qualifies as “protected system”. 
 
Timely escalation to State and national authorities. 
 
Compliance with secrecy and confidentiality requirements. 
 
Assessment of need for specialised agency takeover. 
2.8 Unified Glossary of Technical & Legal Terms 
This glossary standardises technical and legal terminology used across Parts A–E of Chapter 2. 
Definitions are operational, not academic, and are intended to ensure uniform understanding 
[[PAGE 33]]
among Investigating Officers and supervisory staff during registration, investigation, and 
prosecution of cybercrime cases. 
Term 
Operational Definition (For Police Use) 
Account Freezing 
Temporary restriction on operation of a bank account, wallet, or 
payment instrument to prevent dissipation of suspected proceeds of 
crime under BNSS powers. 
Blockchain Analysis 
Examination of public distributed ledger data to trace movement of 
cryptocurrency across wallet addresses, transactions, and exchanges. 
Chain of Custody 
Documented process recording seizure, handling, storage, transfer, 
and examination of evidence to ensure integrity and admissibility. 
Critical Information 
Infrastructure (CII) 
Computer resources whose incapacity or destruction would have a 
debilitating impact on national security, economy, public health, or 
safety. 
Data Preservation 
Request 
Legal direction issued to intermediaries, telecom service providers, 
banks, or platforms to retain specified data for investigation. 
Information of probative value stored, processed, or transmitted in 
digital form, including logs, messages, metadata, device data, and 
cloud records. 
Forensic Imaging 
Bit-by-bit duplication of a digital storage device or system for 
analysis without altering original data. 
Hash Value 
Cryptographic identifier used to verify integrity of digital files and 
confirm that evidence has not been altered. 
Intermediary 
Any entity that hosts, stores, transmits, or facilitates online 
communication or content, including social media platforms and 
service providers. 
Mule Account 
Bank or payment account used to receive and transfer illicit funds on 
[[PAGE 34]]
behalf of controllers or organised cybercrime networks. 
Proceeds of Crime 
Property or value derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, from 
criminal activity, including cyber-enabled offences. 
Protected System 
Computer system notified under law as requiring enhanced security 
due to its importance to the State or public interest. 
Malware that encrypts data or systems and demands payment for 
restoration or non-disclosure. 
Screenshots 
Visual captures of on-screen content; treated as secondary evidence 
unless supported by metadata or platform records. 
SIM Swap 
Fraudulent transfer of a victim’s mobile number to a new SIM card 
to intercept communications or access accounts. 
Takedown Request 
Legal request directing removal or disabling of access to unlawful 
online content, issued after evidence preservation. 
Volatile Data 
Digital information (such as RAM or live logs) that is lost upon 
system shutdown or restart.

CHAPTER 3 – LEGAL FRAMEWORK FOR CYBERCRIME 
INVESTIGATION 
3.1 Introduction: Legal Framework as the Foundation of Cybercrime 
Cybercrime investigation is fundamentally a legal exercise, not merely a technical or forensic 
one. While cyber offences are committed through sophisticated technologies, networks, and 
digital platforms, the authority to investigate them arises solely from law. Every investigative 
action—whether accessing digital data, seizing electronic devices, invoking coercive powers, or 
relying upon electronic records—derives its legitimacy from statutory provisions and judicial 
interpretation. In the absence of legal compliance, even the most technically accurate 
investigation risks invalidation at the threshold stage of judicial scrutiny.[1] 
Unlike conventional crimes, cyber offences often involve intangible conduct, cross-
jurisdictional elements, and data stored across multiple systems and locations. This complexity 
frequently tempts investigators to prioritise speed and technical efficiency over procedural 
discipline. However, Indian courts have repeatedly emphasised that technological complexity 
does not dilute legal safeguards. On the contrary, cybercrime investigations attract heightened 
scrutiny precisely because they involve intrusive access to personal data, digital 
communications, financial systems, and informational privacy.[2] 
The legal framework governing cybercrime investigation in India is not contained in a single 
statute. Instead, it operates through an interlinked system of substantive criminal law, procedural 
law, evidence law, and sector-specific regulatory enactments. Investigating Officers must 
therefore navigate a composite legal environment where powers, duties, and limitations arise 
from multiple enactments operating simultaneously.[3] 
[[PAGE 43]]
At the level of substantive criminality, cyber offences are addressed primarily under the 
Information Technology Act, 2000, which criminalises unauthorised access to computer 
resources, data interference, identity theft, online fraud, privacy violations, and cyber terrorism. 
Simultaneously, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 governs cyber-enabled manifestations of 
traditional crimes such as cheating, forgery, criminal intimidation, sexual exploitation, 
conspiracy, and organised crime, irrespective of the medium used. Effective investigation 
depends upon correctly identifying whether the gravamen of the offence lies in technology 
misuse, human conduct, or a combination of both.[4] 
Procedural authority for investigation flows exclusively from the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha 
Sanhita, 2023. All actions relating to registration of offences, investigation, search, seizure, 
arrest, summons, custody, and jurisdiction must conform to this statute unless a special law 
expressly provides otherwise. The digital nature of an offence does not create new procedural 
powers; it merely alters the context in which existing powers are exercised. Courts have 
consistently held that procedural safeguards apply with equal, if not greater, force in cybercrime 
cases due to their intrusive potential.[5] 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 governs the legal recognition and evaluation of 
digital evidence. Electronic records, metadata, logs, call records, server data, and digital 
communications acquire evidentiary value only when they satisfy statutory requirements of 
relevance, authenticity, and reliability. The existence of digital material alone does not make it 
evidence in the eyes of law. Improperly collected or inadequately supported electronic material is 
treated as legally non-existent, irrespective of its technical accuracy.[6] 
Beyond these core criminal statutes, cybercrime investigation frequently intersects with sectoral 
and regulatory laws. Financial cyber offences trigger the application of the Prevention of 
Money-Laundering Act, 2002. Investigations involving telecommunications infrastructure are 
governed by the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and allied regulatory frameworks. Platform-
based offences require engagement with the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines 
and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. Processing of personal data during investigation 
must align with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Each of these enactments 
introduces additional legal thresholds and compliance obligations, non-observance of which 
may undermine investigation outcomes.[7] 
[[PAGE 44]]
A recurring theme in judicial decisions relating to cybercrime is that investigative failure is 
rarely technological. Most cyber prosecutions fail due to legal infirmities such as incorrect 
invocation of statutory provisions, unlawful searches, routine or unjustified arrests, excessive 
freezing of accounts, jurisdictional errors, or defective handling of electronic evidence. Courts 
have consistently refused to condone illegality on the ground that the offence was serious, 
complex, or digitally sophisticated.[8] 
It is therefore imperative for Investigating Officers to appreciate that legal thresholds precede 
investigative action. Necessity, proportionality, authorisation, and documentation are not 
procedural formalities; they are conditions precedent to the lawful exercise of power. Evidence 
law validates content only after procedural law legitimises collection. Sectoral exemptions 
facilitate investigation only within the boundaries of statutory purpose. Data protection 
exemptions do not override constitutional or procedural safeguards.[9] 
Doctrinal Continuity Note (Mandatory SOP Clarification): 
Although the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, and Bharatiya 
Sakshya Adhiniyam have replaced the IPC, CrPC, and Evidence Act respectively, the 
foundational principles governing criminal liability, procedural safeguards, and evidentiary 
admissibility remain structurally continuous. Judicial interpretations rendered under the repealed 
enactments continue to guide the application of the new codes unless expressly displaced by 
statutory text. Investigating Officers shall therefore treat settled jurisprudence under the earlier 
laws as interpretive guidance for applying corresponding provisions under the new criminal law 
framework.[10] 
This chapter is designed to function as the legal backbone of the SOP. It does not prescribe 
operational steps or investigative techniques. Instead, it equips Investigating Officers with a 
structured understanding of what powers exist, when they may be invoked, and where legal 
boundaries operate. Mastery of this framework is essential to ensure that cybercrime 
investigations are not only effective at the technical level but also sustainable in court.[11] 
The sections that follow map the statutory architecture, offence provisions, procedural powers, 
evidentiary rules, sectoral interfaces, judicial precedents, jurisdictional principles, and legally 
recognised risk zones that collectively shape cybercrime investigation in India. This legal 
[[PAGE 45]]
grounding is indispensable for the lawful execution of investigative functions addressed in 
subsequent chapters of this manual.[12] 
3.2 Architecture of Cybercrime Laws in India 
Cybercrime investigation in India operates within a multi-layered legal architecture, rather 
than a single consolidated cyber code. This architecture reflects the complexity of digital 
offending, where a single act may simultaneously involve unauthorised access to computer 
systems, deception of individuals, financial diversion, invasion of privacy, and cross-border data 
flows. For Investigating Officers, understanding this architecture is essential to ensure that 
investigative action is legally anchored, procedurally valid, and judicially sustainable.[1] 
At the core of this framework lies the Information Technology Act, 2000, which functions as 
the principal special statute addressing offences that are inherently digital in nature. The IT Act 
criminalises unauthorised access, data interference, identity theft, online cheating, privacy 
violations, publication of prohibited content, and cyber terrorism. It also creates statutory duties 
for intermediaries and service providers. Where the computer resource itself is the object or 
instrument of the offence, the IT Act provides the primary substantive foundation.[2] 
Operating alongside the IT Act is the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which governs cyber-
enabled manifestations of traditional criminal conduct. Many cybercrime complaints reveal 
conduct that is fundamentally deceptive, coercive, exploitative, or conspiratorial, even though 
executed through digital means. In such cases, offences such as cheating, forgery, criminal 
intimidation, sexual exploitation, criminal conspiracy, and organised crime derive their 
criminality from general penal law. The use of the internet or digital platforms does not displace 
penal provisions; it merely alters the modality of commission.[3] 
From an investigative standpoint, it is crucial to appreciate that the IT Act and the BNS are not 
mutually exclusive. Courts have consistently recognised that where a special offence under the 
IT Act is attracted, it must be invoked; however, this does not preclude simultaneous application 
of appropriate penal provisions where the factual ingredients are satisfied. Failure to invoke 
either regime correctly often results in under-charging or over-charging, both of which weaken 
prosecution.[4] 
[[PAGE 46]]
Procedural authority for cybercrime investigation flows exclusively from the Bharatiya Nagarik 
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. All police powers relating to registration of offences, commencement 
of investigation, search, seizure, arrest, summons, custody, and jurisdiction are exercised under 
BNSS unless expressly excluded by a special statute. The digital nature of an offence does not 
confer any additional procedural power upon investigators. On the contrary, courts have 
emphasised that procedural safeguards assume greater significance in cyber investigations 
due to their intrusive potential into personal data, communications, and financial records.[5] 
The evidentiary dimension of cybercrime investigation is governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya 
Adhiniyam, 2023. This statute provides the legal basis for recognising electronic records as 
documents and evidence. Emails, messages, server logs, call data records, metadata, cloud-stored 
information, and digital media can function as evidence only when statutory conditions relating 
to relevance, authenticity, and reliability are satisfied. The mere existence of digital material does 
not confer evidentiary value unless legally recognised.[6] 
Cybercrime investigations frequently extend beyond core criminal statutes and intersect with 
sectoral and regulatory enactments. Financial cyber offences often generate proceeds of crime, 
attracting the application of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002. Investigations 
involving telecom infrastructure, subscriber information, or communication data must comply 
with the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and allied regulatory frameworks. Platform-based 
offences require engagement with the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and 
Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, which impose preservation and cooperation 
obligations on intermediaries.[7] 
A significant recent addition to the legal architecture is the Digital Personal Data Protection 
Act, 2023. While the DPDP Act recognises investigation and prosecution as lawful purposes for 
data processing, it simultaneously introduces statutory limits on collection, use, disclosure, and 
retention of personal data. Investigating Officers must therefore ensure that data processing 
during investigation is traceable to statutory authority and confined to investigative 
necessity, failing which such data may attract constitutional and statutory challenge.[8] 
Hierarchy Principle for Investigating Officers: 
While special statutes such as the Information Technology Act create specific cyber offences, 
procedural law under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita governs the manner of 
[[PAGE 47]]
investigation in all cases, unless expressly excluded. No substantive cyber offence provision 
authorises bypassing procedural safeguards relating to search, seizure, arrest, jurisdiction, or 
judicial oversight.[9] 
Judicial precedents have repeatedly clarified that cybercrime law is not a collection of isolated 
provisions but a coherent legal system. Investigative action taken under one statute inevitably 
interacts with obligations and limitations under others. Courts examine cyber investigations 
holistically, assessing whether statutory powers were exercised in a coordinated, proportionate, 
and legally defensible manner.[10] 
From an administrative perspective, this architectural understanding enables Investigating 
Officers to: 
 
Select appropriate charging provisions 
 
Exercise procedural powers within lawful bounds 
 
Anticipate evidentiary challenges at trial 
 
Avoid jurisdictional and sectoral conflicts 
From a judicial perspective, it demonstrates that the investigation was conducted with legal 
awareness rather than mechanical enforcement.[11] 
Accordingly, cybercrime investigation must proceed not by isolating individual statutes, but by 
applying the legal framework as an integrated system, where each law performs a defined 
function and no provision is invoked in disregard of another.[12] 
3.2.1 Transition Mapping: Legacy Criminal Law to New Criminal Laws in Cybercrime 
Context 
The transition from the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the 
Indian Evidence Act, 1872 to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik 
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) represents 
a structural reform rather than a substantive disruption. For cybercrime investigation, continuity 
of judicial interpretation is preserved, while statutory numbering, drafting language, and 
procedural emphases have evolved. 
[[PAGE 48]]
Investigating Officers must consciously translate legacy offence-thinking into the new statutory 
framework to avoid charging errors, jurisdictional confusion, and drafting inconsistencies. Courts 
have clarified that mere renumbering does not alter the essential ingredients of offences, and 
legacy jurisprudence remains applicable unless expressly displaced.

Investigating Officers shall avoid referencing IPC or Evidence Act provisions in FIRs, case
