doctrinally. 
3.3 Information Technology Act, 2000: Core Substantive Cyber Offences 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 constitutes the primary substantive statute governing 
offences where the computer resource, digital data, or electronic identity is central to the 
commission of the crime. The Act was enacted to address forms of wrongdoing that could not be 
adequately captured by traditional penal provisions, particularly those involving unauthorised 
[[PAGE 49]]
access, manipulation of data, misuse of digital credentials, and electronic publication of 
prohibited content.[1] 
From an investigative perspective, the IT Act serves two critical functions. First, it defines 
technology-specific criminal conduct. Second, it supplies a legal framework that distinguishes 
between civil contraventions and criminal offences in digital environments. Investigating 
Officers must therefore exercise precision while invoking IT Act provisions, as courts have 
repeatedly cautioned against mechanical or excessive application of cyber sections without 
factual alignment.[2] 
Primary Charging Rule under the IT Act (SOP Principle): 
Where the gravamen of the offence lies in unauthorised access to computer resources, 
interference with data or systems, digital identity misuse, or electronic privacy violation, the IT 
Act shall constitute the primary charging statute. Where the gravamen lies in deception, 
coercion, exploitation, or inducement of a human victim, appropriate provisions of the Bharatiya 
Nyaya Sanhita must be applied concurrently, not in substitution.[3] 
3.3.1 Section 65 – Tampering with Computer Source Documents 
Section 65 criminalises the intentional concealment, destruction, or alteration of computer 
source code where such code is required to be maintained by law. This provision is frequently 
misunderstood and over-applied. Courts have clarified that Section 65 does not criminalise every 
deletion or modification of software files; it applies only where maintenance of source code is 
legally mandated, such as in licensed software, regulated systems, or statutory compliance 
environments.[4] 
An employee of a regulated fintech company deliberately alters backend source code to conceal 
unauthorised transaction routing. Even in the absence of immediate financial loss, Section 65 is 
attracted because the alteration targets legally required source code.[5] 
Judicial interpretation has emphasised that the prosecution must establish both legal obligation 
to maintain the source code and intentional tampering. Absence of either ingredient defeats 
the charge.[6] 
[[PAGE 50]]
3.3.2 Section 66 – Computer-Related Offences 
Section 66 converts acts enumerated under Section 43 into criminal offences when committed 
dishonestly or fraudulently. This provision forms the backbone of most cybercrime 
prosecutions involving hacking, unauthorised access, malware insertion, denial-of-service 
attacks, or data destruction.[7] 
However, courts have repeatedly underscored that mens rea is the decisive element. Mere 
unauthorised access, without dishonest or fraudulent intent, may attract civil liability under 
Section 43 but does not automatically constitute a criminal offence under Section 66. 
Mandatory Mens Rea Clarification (SOP Standard): 
Technical access or system interaction, by itself, does not attract criminal liability under Section 
66. Investigating Officers must establish dishonest or fraudulent intent through surrounding 
circumstances, conduct, or consequence.[8] 
An intern accesses a restricted server directory without permission but causes no harm and 
derives no gain. While administrative or civil consequences may follow, criminal prosecution 
under Section 66 would be unsustainable absent evidence of dishonest intent.[9] 
Courts have cautioned that criminalising technical irregularities without intent risks misuse 
of cyber law and dilution of prosecutorial credibility.[10] 
3.3.3 Sections 66B, 66C, and 66D – Identity Theft and Online Cheating 
Sections 66B to 66D address offences relating to digital identity misuse and electronic 
deception, which constitute a significant proportion of reported cybercrime cases. 
 
Section 66B criminalises dishonest receipt or retention of stolen computer resources or 
communication devices. 
 
Section 66C addresses identity theft, including misuse of passwords, OTPs, biometric 
identifiers, or digital signatures. 
 
Section 66D criminalises cheating by personation using computer resources.[11] 
[[PAGE 51]]
Using a victim’s OTP to fraudulently transfer funds attracts Section 66C (identity theft) read with 
Section 66D (cheating by personation), in addition to appropriate penal provisions relating to 
cheating.[12] 
In Sharat Babu Digumarti v. Government (NCT of Delhi), the Supreme Court clarified that where 
a special offence under the IT Act squarely applies, prosecution must proceed under the IT Act 
rather than mechanically invoking general penal provisions.[13] 
This principle reinforces the special-law primacy of Sections 66B–66D in identity-based cyber 
frauds. 
3.3.4 Section 66E – Violation of Privacy 
Section 66E criminalises the intentional capture, publication, or transmission of images of a 
person’s private areas without consent. This provision protects informational and bodily 
privacy in digital environments and operates independently of obscenity thresholds.[14] 
Secretly recording an individual through a mobile phone camera in a private space and 
circulating the recording through messaging platforms attracts Section 66E irrespective of 
whether the content is obscene.[15] 
Courts have interpreted Section 66E in light of the constitutional right to privacy, recognising 
that digital voyeurism and non-consensual sharing cause harm beyond reputational injury.[16] 
3.3.5 Section 66F – Cyber Terrorism 
Section 66F addresses acts committed through computer resources that threaten the sovereignty, 
integrity, security, or defence of India, or disrupt critical information infrastructure. This 
provision carries severe penal consequences and must therefore be invoked with extreme 
restraint.[17] 
Restricted Invocation Warning (Non-Negotiable SOP Rule): 
Section 66F shall be invoked only where the factual matrix demonstrates a clear nexus with 
national security or critical infrastructure. Routine cyber frauds, data breaches, or hacking 
incidents do not qualify merely because of scale or sophistication.[18] 
[[PAGE 52]]
Courts have consistently frowned upon casual invocation of national security provisions in 
ordinary cybercrime cases, observing that such overreach undermines both investigation and 
prosecution.[19] 
3.3.6 Sections 67, 67A, and 67B – Obscene, Sexually Explicit, and Child Sexual Abuse 
Material 
These provisions criminalise publication or transmission of prohibited content in electronic form. 
 
Section 67 addresses obscene material. 
 
Section 67A covers sexually explicit content. 
 
Section 67B specifically targets child sexual abuse material (CSAM).[20] 
CSAM offences are treated with zero tolerance, and courts have adopted an expansive 
interpretation to ensure child protection. Viewing, storing, transmitting, or facilitating access to 
such material attracts criminal liability, even in the absence of commercial motive.[21] 
Temporary storage of CSAM in cache memory or cloud backups may constitute possession if 
knowledge and access are established.[22] 
3.3.7 Section 67C – Preservation and Retention of Information 
Section 67C imposes a statutory obligation on intermediaries to preserve and retain 
information for investigation. This provision provides the legal foundation for data preservation 
requests.[23] 
However, Section 67C does not dispense with procedural or evidentiary requirements. 
Preservation facilitates investigation; it does not by itself authorise disclosure or prove 
admissibility.[24] 
3.3.8 Relationship Between IT Act Offences and Penal Law 
The IT Act supplements, but does not replace, general criminal law. Courts have repeatedly 
emphasised that special-law primacy operates only where the offence is squarely covered. 
Where additional elements of deception, coercion, conspiracy, or exploitation exist, penal 
provisions must be invoked concurrently.[25] 
[[PAGE 53]]
Incorrect isolation of IT Act offences often results in: 
 
Under-charging 
 
Weak sentencing outcomes 
 
Failure to capture human culpability 
Conversely, indiscriminate invocation leads to over-criminalisation and judicial dilution.[26] 
3.3.9 Investigative Significance of IT Act Compliance 
For Investigating Officers, correct application of IT Act provisions ensures: 
 
Precise charge framing 
 
Reduced overlap confusion with penal law 
 
Stronger evidentiary foundation 
 
Greater judicial confidence in investigation 
Cybercrime investigation under the IT Act demands legal accuracy equal to technical 
competence. The sustainability of prosecution depends not on the number of sections invoked, 
but on the correctness of their application.[27] 
3.4 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Cyber-Enabled Penal Offences 
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) governs offences where the core criminality lies in 
human conduct, even though the offence is committed, facilitated, or amplified through digital 
means. Unlike the Information Technology Act, which targets misuse of computer resources and 
electronic systems, the BNS addresses deception, coercion, exploitation, intimidation, 
conspiracy, and organised criminal behaviour that merely adopts cyberspace as a medium.[1] 
From an investigative standpoint, this distinction is critical. Courts have consistently held that 
the use of technology does not neutralise penal liability. An offence does not cease to be 
cheating, forgery, intimidation, or sexual exploitation merely because it is executed through 
email, messaging platforms, or online portals. Failure to invoke appropriate BNS provisions in 
cyber-enabled crimes often results in under-charging, inadequate sentencing, and incomplete 
attribution of criminal intent.[2] 
[[PAGE 54]]
At the same time, indiscriminate addition of penal provisions without analysing the factual 
ingredients attracts judicial criticism. Sustainable cybercrime prosecution requires careful 
alignment between factual conduct and penal elements, rather than mechanical invocation of 
sections.[3] 
3.4.1 Cheating and Fraud Committed Through Digital Means 
Cheating under the BNS is attracted where deception dishonestly induces a person to deliver 
property, part with money, or act to their detriment. The mode of deception—physical or 
digital—is legally immaterial. Online impersonation, phishing emails, fake investment portals, 
fraudulent customer-care calls, and spoofed communications are contemporary manifestations of 
the same offence.[4] 
An accused creates a fake government recruitment website and induces applicants to pay 
registration fees online. Although the interaction is entirely digital, the offence is fundamentally 
one of cheating, attracting BNS provisions in addition to relevant IT Act sections.[5] 
Courts have repeatedly held that digital deception culminating in delivery of property 
completes the offence, irrespective of whether the accused and victim ever meet physically.[6] 
SOP Decision Principle: 
Where dishonest inducement and delivery of property are established, BNS cheating provisions 
must be invoked even if IT Act sections are also attracted.[7] 
3.4.2 Forgery and Use of Forged Electronic Records 
The BNS recognises that electronic records are documents, and their falsification attracts 
forgery provisions in the same manner as physical documents. Fabrication or alteration of emails, 
digital certificates, PDFs, online contracts, e-stamps, or electronically generated records may 
constitute forgery if accompanied by intent to deceive.[8] 
Boundary Clarification (Non-Negotiable): 
Digital alteration by itself does not constitute forgery. Criminal liability arises only where 
alteration is accompanied by intent to deceive or cause wrongful gain or loss.[9] 
[[PAGE 55]]
Manipulating a digitally generated bank statement to inflate account balance for securing a loan 
constitutes forgery, regardless of the absence of a physical document.[10] 
Judicial precedents have consistently affirmed that electronic records fall squarely within the 
concept of “documents” and are equally capable of being forged.[11] 
3.4.3 Criminal Intimidation and Online Threats 
Criminal intimidation under the BNS extends to threats conveyed through emails, social media 
platforms, messaging applications, or anonymous digital accounts. The absence of physical 
proximity does not dilute the offence; what matters is whether the threat is intended to cause 
alarm or compel action or omission.[12] 
Sending repeated messages threatening reputational harm unless money is paid constitutes 
criminal intimidation, even if the accused operates anonymously from another jurisdiction.[13] 
Courts have emphasised that digital anonymity cannot be used as a shield against penal 
liability where the threatening intent and effect are established.[14] 
3.4.4 Sexual Offences Facilitated Through Cyberspace 
The BNS addresses sexual offences where digital platforms are used to initiate, facilitate, 
coerce, or aggravate sexual exploitation. Online grooming, sextortion, coercive sharing of 
intimate material, and digital harassment often involve a combination of BNS provisions and IT 
Act sections.[15] 
An accused befriends a victim through social media, obtains private images through deception, 
and later uses those images to coerce sexual acts or silence. While transmission of content may 
attract IT Act provisions, the substantive sexual offence is governed by the BNS.[16] 
Courts have recognised that cyber-facilitated sexual offences often produce deeper 
psychological harm and must be addressed with full penal rigour.[17] 
[[PAGE 56]]
3.4.5 Criminal Conspiracy in Cybercrime 
Cybercrime frequently involves distributed roles—phishers, data harvesters, mule recruiters, 
account operators, and laundering facilitators. Where two or more persons agree to commit an 
illegal act or a legal act by illegal means, criminal conspiracy provisions under the BNS are 
attracted.[18] 
Direct evidence of conspiracy is rare. Courts permit inference of conspiracy from coordinated 
digital conduct, financial trails, communication patterns, and role-based participation.[19] 
Multiple individuals operating different parts of an online scam ecosystem may be charged with 
conspiracy even if each performs a limited role.[20] 
3.4.6 Abetment and Digital Facilitation 
Abetment provisions under the BNS apply where a person intentionally aids, instigates, or 
facilitates a cyber offence. Digital facilitation—such as knowingly providing bank accounts, 
SIM cards, servers, or technical assistance—may attract liability even without direct victim 
interaction.[21] 
Providing mule bank accounts with knowledge that they will be used for online fraud constitutes 
abetment, notwithstanding the absence of direct communication with victims.[22] 
Courts have clarified that passive facilitation combined with knowledge is sufficient to attract 
abetment liability.[23] 
3.4.7 Organised and Repeat Cybercrime 
The BNS contains provisions addressing organised and habitual criminal conduct. Where cyber 
offences are executed systematically, across multiple victims or jurisdictions, enhanced penal 
provisions may apply.[24] 
Investigating Officers must carefully document patterns of conduct, recurrence, and 
coordination, as courts require clear factual demonstration before invoking enhanced penal 
consequences.[25] 
[[PAGE 57]]
3.4.8 Relationship Between BNS and the IT Act 
The BNS and IT Act operate in tandem, not in competition. The IT Act addresses the misuse of 
technology; the BNS addresses the misuse of human intent. Correct prosecution strategy requires 
identifying what is criminalised because it is digital and what is criminalised because it is 
deceitful, coercive, or exploitative.[26] 
SOP Charging Guidance: 
Failure to invoke appropriate BNS provisions results in under-charging and weak sentencing 
outcomes. Conversely, indiscriminate invocation without factual alignment results in judicial 
dilution. Investigating Officers must align penal provisions with the nature of conduct, not 
merely the digital medium used.[27] 
3.4.9 Investigative Significance of BNS in Cybercrime 
From an administrative perspective, the BNS ensures that cybercrime investigations: 
 
Capture human culpability beyond technical misuse 
 
Address victim harm comprehensively 
 
Enable proportionate sentencing 
From a judicial perspective, correct invocation of BNS provisions demonstrates that the 
investigation recognises cyberspace as a medium, not a mitigating factor.[28] 
Cybercrime investigation that relies exclusively on technical offences without addressing 
underlying penal conduct risks producing legally incomplete prosecutions.[29] 
3.5 Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023: Procedural Powers of 
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) constitutes the exclusive source of 
procedural authority for cybercrime investigation. Irrespective of the digital or technical nature 
of an offence, every investigative action—registration of offence, commencement of 
investigation, search, seizure, arrest, summons, custody, and determination of jurisdiction—must 
conform to BNSS unless a special statute expressly provides otherwise.[1] 
[[PAGE 58]]
A recurring misconception in cyber investigations is that technological complexity or urgency 
creates expanded police powers. Courts have consistently rejected this assumption. The BNSS 
does not recognise a separate category of “digital urgency” that dilutes procedural safeguards. 
On the contrary, cybercrime investigations attract heightened procedural scrutiny because they 
often involve deep intrusion into personal devices, private communications, financial data, and 
digital identity.[2] 
From an SOP perspective, BNSS performs a dual function. Administratively, it empowers 
Investigating Officers to act. Judicially, it constrains discretion by requiring necessity, 
proportionality, and recorded satisfaction before coercive powers are exercised.[3] 
3.5.1 Mandatory Videography of Search and Seizure under Section 105 BNSS 
One of the most consequential procedural reforms under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha 
Sanhita, 2023 is Section 105, which mandates videography of search and seizure operations. 
This provision assumes exceptional significance in cybercrime investigations, where seizure of 
electronic devices and digital storage media forms the evidentiary backbone of prosecution. 
Scope and Applicability of Section 105 BNSS 
Section 105 BNSS requires that: 
 
Search and seizure operations shall be videographed, and 
 
The videographic record shall form part of the case record 
In cybercrime investigations, this requirement applies with full force to: 
 
Seizure of mobile phones, laptops, tablets 
 
Seizure of servers, storage devices, hard drives 
 
On-site digital search operations 
Seizure of a mobile phone suspected to contain incriminating WhatsApp chats or transaction 
records must be videographed from the point of discovery to sealing. 
[[PAGE 59]]
Rationale in Cybercrime Context 
Courts have consistently held that digital devices contain vast amounts of personal and third-
party data unrelated to the offence. Videography under Section 105 BNSS: 
 
Establishes transparency of seizure 
 
Prevents allegations of data planting or tampering 
 
Protects Investigating Officers from personal allegations 
 
Strengthens evidentiary credibility 
Consequences of Non-Compliance 
Failure to comply with Section 105 BNSS may result in: 
 
Judicial doubt regarding integrity of seized devices 
 
Adverse inference against the prosecution 
 
Exclusion or dilution of evidentiary value 
 
Departmental accountability in serious cases 
Non-Negotiable SOP Rule: 
In cybercrime cases, absence of videography during device seizure is not a technical lapse 
but a substantive procedural defect. 
Practical SOP Guidance 
Investigating Officers shall ensure: 
 
Videography begins before physical handling of the device 
 
Device condition, power status, and sealing are recorded 
 
The videographic record is preserved and indexed 
This requirement is mandatory, not discretionary, and applies irrespective of offence severity. 
[[PAGE 60]]
3.5.2 Power to Register and Investigate Cyber Offences 
BNSS authorises police officers to register and investigate cognizable offences without prior 
court approval. A significant number of cyber offences under the IT Act and BNS fall within this 
category. However, cognizability does not confer unrestricted authority. The power to investigate 
is conditioned upon lawful registration, jurisdictional nexus, and adherence to statutory 
procedure.[4] 
Upon receipt of a complaint disclosing large-scale online fraud, the Investigating Officer may 
commence investigation immediately. However, accessing unrelated digital accounts or devices 
without relevance exceeds procedural authority.[5] 
Courts have emphasised that investigation is a process regulated by law, not an unfettered 
search for incriminating material.[6] 
3.5.3 Search Powers in the Digital Context 
BNSS empowers search where there exists reasonable suspicion that evidence relating to an 
offence is located at a particular place or in the possession of a person. In cybercrime cases, this 
power extends to electronic devices, storage media, and digital repositories.[7] 
However, digital searches differ qualitatively from physical searches. A single device may 
contain vast quantities of personal, professional, and third-party data unrelated to the offence. 
Courts have therefore insisted upon narrow tailoring of search scope and strict adherence to 
statutory thresholds.[8] 
Judicially Recognised Principle: 
Discovery of incriminating material does not retrospectively legitimise an unlawful search.[9] 
Seizing and examining an entire office network when allegations relate to a single system may be 
held disproportionate unless necessity is clearly recorded.[10] 
[[PAGE 61]]
3.5.4 Seizure of Electronic Devices and Digital Property 
BNSS permits seizure of property suspected to be connected with an offence. Electronic devices 
qualify as property for this purpose. However, seizure must be evidence-oriented, not punitive 
or speculative.[11] 
Courts have cautioned against: 
 
Blanket seizure of all devices 
 
Indefinite retention without review 
 
Seizure causing disproportionate hardship 
Seizing a person’s primary business laptop without considering data extraction alternatives may 
be held excessive if investigation objectives can be achieved otherwise.[12] 
Procedural proportionality is central to sustaining such seizures during judicial review.[13] 
3.5.5 Arrest Powers in Cybercrime Investigations 
Arrest under BNSS is a coercive measure of last resort, not a routine investigative tool. 
Cybercrime cases typically rely on documentary and digital evidence rather than physical 
confrontation, reducing the necessity of arrest in many situations.[14] 
Arrest Exception Rule (Non-Negotiable SOP Standard): 
In cyber and economic offences, arrest is an exception and not the rule. Arrest shall be effected 
only where statutory necessity—such as prevention of further offence, risk of evidence 
tampering, or non-cooperation—is demonstrably satisfied and recorded.[15] 
Arresting an accused in an online fraud case solely to compel cooperation, without satisfying 
statutory criteria, has been repeatedly deprecated by courts.[16] 
Illegal or unjustified arrest often results in bail as a matter of right and weakens the prosecution 
irreversibly.[17] 
[[PAGE 62]]
3.5.6 Power to Summon and Examine Persons 
BNSS empowers Investigating Officers to summon persons acquainted with the facts of the case. 
In cyber investigations, this includes victims, witnesses, service providers, platform 
representatives, and financial intermediaries.[18] 
However, courts have cautioned against misuse of summons as a coercive or punitive device. 
Summons must be issued for legitimate investigative purposes and within reasonable limits.[19] 
Repeated summoning of platform employees without specific queries or factual necessity may 
attract judicial intervention.[20] 
3.5.7 Jurisdiction in Cybercrime Investigation 
BNSS recognises jurisdiction based on: 
 
Place of commission of offence 
 
Place where consequence ensues 
 
Place where part of the offence occurs 
Cyber offences frequently involve multiple jurisdictions, including cross-border elements. 
Courts have accepted consequence-based jurisdiction in cyber cases, provided the nexus is 
demonstrable and recorded.[21] 
Where a phishing email sent from another State causes financial loss to a local victim, the local 
police station may assume jurisdiction based on the place of consequence.[22] 
Failure to articulate jurisdictional basis invites transfer or quashing of proceedings.[23] 
3.5.8 Procedural Safeguards and Judicial Oversight 
BNSS embeds safeguards such as: 
 
Recording of reasons 
 
Production before magistrate 
 
Time limits on detention 
[[PAGE 63]]
 
Judicial scrutiny of coercive action 
In cybercrime cases, these safeguards assume heightened importance because procedural 
illegality often contaminates digital evidence irreversibly.[24] 
Courts have consistently held that procedural compliance legitimises investigation, while 
procedural violation undermines even strong evidence.[25] 
3.5.9 Failure to Record Satisfaction as an Independent Risk 
A critical but often overlooked risk zone is failure to record satisfaction regarding necessity, 
proportionality, or jurisdiction. Courts treat absence of recorded reasoning as a substantive 
defect, not a curable irregularity.[26] 
Unrecorded satisfaction is itself a procedural illegality, even where power otherwise exists.[27] 
3.5.10 Investigative Significance of BNSS Compliance 
From an administrative perspective, BNSS compliance: 
 
Protects Investigating Officers from allegations of overreach 
 
Ensures continuity of investigation 
 
Reduces pre-trial litigation 
From a judicial perspective, it demonstrates legal awareness and restraint, which courts 
consistently reward.[28] 
Cybercrime investigations succeed not merely through technical expertise but through 
procedural discipline. BNSS therefore operates as the procedural backbone upon which all 
cyber investigations must rest.[29] 
3.6 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023: Legal Recognition of Digital 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) governs the legal recognition, evaluation, and 
judicial treatment of evidence in criminal proceedings, including cybercrime cases. In 
investigations involving digital environments, evidence is predominantly electronic in nature; 
[[PAGE 64]]
however, technological existence does not translate into legal evidence by default. The BSA 
determines whether a digital artefact can be treated as evidence at all, before questions of proof, 
weight, or credibility arise.[1] 
Courts have consistently reiterated that cybercrime investigations fail not because digital 
material is unavailable, but because investigators confuse technical extraction with legal 
recognition. Digital files, logs, messages, or recordings may appear incriminating, yet remain 
legally irrelevant if they do not satisfy the statutory conditions prescribed by evidence law.[2] 
From an SOP perspective, the BSA performs a gatekeeping function. Administratively, it informs 
Investigating Officers what categories of digital material may be relied upon. Judicially, it filters 
out material that is unreliable, unlawfully obtained, or incapable of legal proof.[3] 
3.6.1 Section 63 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023: Four-Condition Framework for 
Admissibility of Electronic Evidence 
One of the most critical reforms introduced by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) 
is the re-articulation of the law governing admissibility of electronic evidence under Section 63. 
While this provision replaces the much-litigated Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, its 
objective is not dilution but clarification and operational simplification. 
Courts have consistently observed that electronic evidence is rejected not because it is unreliable 
in substance, but because Investigating Officers fail to satisfy foundational admissibility 
conditions. Section 63 BSA codifies these foundations into a principle-based framework, 
which must be internalised at the investigation stage itself. 
3.6.2 The Four Mandatory Conditions Under Section 63 BSA 
For an electronic record to be admissible and relied upon by a court, the prosecution must be able 
to demonstrate compliance with four cumulative conditions. These conditions operate as legal 
thresholds, not discretionary factors. 
Condition I – Lawful Source Identification 
The prosecution must establish: 
 
What electronic record is relied upon, and 
 
From where and how it was obtained 
[[PAGE 65]]
This requires clear identification of: 
 
The device, server, platform, or system 
 
The authority under which access was obtained 
A WhatsApp chat relied upon in prosecution must be traced to a specific device or platform 
account, obtained through lawful search, seizure, or requisition. 
SOP Rule: 
Electronic evidence of unknown or undocumented origin is legally fragile and vulnerable to 
exclusion. 
Condition II – Reliability of the Computer Resource 
Section 63 BSA requires that the computer or digital system from which the electronic record is 
derived must be shown to be functioning reliably at the relevant time. 
This does not require proof of technical perfection. Courts look for: 
 
Normal operational use 
 
Absence of known malfunction affecting the record 
A transaction log generated by a routinely used banking server is presumed reliable unless 
evidence of system malfunction is shown. 
Operational Clarification: 
Investigating Officers are not expected to certify software integrity but must avoid reliance on 
demonstrably compromised or manipulated systems. 
Condition III – Integrity of the Electronic Record 
Integrity refers to assurance that the electronic record: 
 
Has not been altered, edited, or manipulated 
 
Remains the same as when originally created or stored 
Courts examine whether: 
[[PAGE 66]]
 
Access was controlled 
 
Handling was documented 
 
No unexplained gaps exist in custody 
A video file copied multiple times without documentation raises integrity concerns even if 
content appears authentic. 
SOP Rule: 
Integrity is preserved through documentation, not technical jargon. 
Condition IV – Lawful Production and Attribution 
Finally, the electronic record must be lawfully produced before the court and attributed to a 
relevant person, device, or transaction. 
This involves: 
 
Demonstrating relevance 
 
Linking the record to the accused or offence 
 
Ensuring production follows procedural law 
A payment confirmation email must be linked to the accused’s account, device, or transaction 
trail—not merely produced in isolation. 
3.6.3 Section 63 BSA vs Section 65B Evidence Act: Operational Shift 
The BSA intentionally moves away from the certificate-centric rigidity of the old Section 65B 
regime. Courts now focus on substantive compliance with admissibility principles, rather than 
ritualistic certification. 
Comparative Clarification Table 
Aspect 
Section 65B (Old) 
Section 63 BSA (New)

Important SOP Warning: 
Section 63 BSA does not eliminate the need for careful documentation. It replaces blind 
formalism with responsible legal demonstration. 
Common Investigative Errors to Avoid 
Courts have rejected electronic evidence where: 
 
Source was not identified 
 
Device seizure was illegal 
 
Data extraction was undocumented 
 
Records were selectively produced 
These failures are investigative, not forensic. 
Integration with BNSS and DPDP Act 
Compliance with Section 63 BSA is inseparable from: 
 
Procedural legality under BNSS (lawful search, seizure, requisition), and 
 
Purpose limitation under DPDP Act (data relevance and proportionality) 
Electronic evidence obtained in violation of either regime remains vulnerable, irrespective of 
apparent authenticity. 
SOP-Level Operational Guidance 
Investigating Officers shall ensure that for every electronic record relied upon: 
1. Source is identified and lawful 
2. System reliability is not in doubt 
3. Integrity is documented 
[[PAGE 68]]
4. Attribution is demonstrable 
Failure at any one stage risks evidentiary exclusion. 
3.6.4 Electronic Records as “Documents” and Evidence 
The BSA expressly recognises electronic records as documents, capable of constituting 
documentary evidence. Emails, text messages, call data records, server logs, metadata, cloud-
stored files, social media communications, and digitally generated records fall within this 
definition.[4] 
This statutory recognition resolves earlier ambiguity surrounding the status of electronic 
material. Courts have held that intangible form does not diminish evidentiary value; what 
matters is whether the record can be shown to be authentic, relevant, and reliable.[5] 
WhatsApp messages retrieved from a device or server qualify as documentary evidence once 
legally recognised, regardless of whether they are printed or viewed electronically in court.[6] 
However, recognition as a document does not automatically confer probative value. Electronic 
records must still satisfy foundational evidentiary requirements.[7] 
3.6.5 Recognition Versus Proof: A Critical Distinction 
A recurring error in cybercrime investigations is conflating recognition of electronic records 
with proof of their contents. The BSA draws a clear distinction between the two. 
Recognition of an electronic record as evidence does not dispense with statutory requirements 
relating to proof, authenticity, and admissibility. Investigating Officers must not assume that 
once a digital artefact is recognised, it will necessarily be accepted by the court.[8] 
Courts have repeatedly excluded electronic material where authenticity or source integrity could 
not be established, even though the content appeared incriminating.[9] 
3.6.6 Authenticity and Reliability as Core Thresholds 
Under the BSA, authenticity and reliability constitute the central thresholds for digital 
evidence. Courts examine whether the electronic record: 
[[PAGE 69]]
 
Originated from a reliable source 
 
Has remained free from tampering or manipulation 
 
Can be attributed to a particular device, account, or individual 
The law is not concerned with technological sophistication but with legal trustworthiness.[10] 
A screen recording of an online transaction may appear genuine, but if the source device, time-
stamp, or continuity cannot be established, courts may treat it as unreliable.[11] 
3.6.7 Presumptions Relating to Electronic Evidence 
The BSA incorporates statutory presumptions relating to electronic records, intended to assist 
courts where foundational requirements are satisfied. These presumptions are conditional, not 
automatic.[12] 
Investigating Officers must appreciate that presumptions: 
 
Support lawful evidence 
 
Do not cure illegal collection 
 
Do not override procedural defects 
Courts have consistently held that presumptions cannot legitimise unlawfully obtained 
material.[13] 
3.6.8 Continuity of Judicial Principles on Electronic Evidence 
Although the BSA has replaced the Indian Evidence Act, judicial interpretation developed under 
the earlier framework continues to guide courts, particularly in relation to electronic evidence. 
Principles articulated in decisions such as Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer and Arjun Panditrao 
Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal continue to inform judicial reasoning on authenticity, 
admissibility, and procedural compliance.[14] 
Doctrinal Application Principle: 
Judicial standards developed under earlier evidence law remain applicable to the BSA unless 
expressly displaced by statutory text.[15] 
[[PAGE 70]]
3.6.9 Relationship Between Evidence Law and Procedural Law 
The BSA does not operate in isolation. Legal recognition of digital evidence is inseparable from 
procedural legality under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Evidence obtained 
through illegal search, unauthorised access, or coercive misuse of power remains vulnerable 
regardless of its relevance.[16] 
Personal data extracted from a device without lawful search authority may satisfy technical 
authenticity but fail legal admissibility due to procedural illegality.[17] 
Courts have consistently held that evidence law validates content only after procedural law 
legitimises collection.[18] 
3.6.10 Digital Evidence and Rights of the Accused 
Judicial precedents recognise that electronic records relied upon by the prosecution must be 
accessible to the accused for effective defence. Denial of access to relied-upon digital material 
has been held to violate principles of fair trial.[19] 
Investigating Officers must therefore ensure that digital evidence is: 
 
Properly documented 
 
Securely preserved 
 
Capable of judicial production 
Electronic evidence is not merely case property; it often contains sensitive personal data, 
demanding careful handling.[20] 
3.6.11 Investigative Significance of BSA Compliance 
From an administrative perspective, compliance with the BSA ensures that investigative effort 
translates into courtroom utility. From a judicial perspective, it demonstrates respect for 
evidentiary discipline and fair trial standards.[21] 
Failure to comply with evidence law results in: 
 
Exclusion of crucial material 
[[PAGE 71]]
 
Weakening of prosecution narrative 
 
Acquittals despite substantive wrongdoing 
Cybercrime investigation therefore demands legal literacy equal to technical expertise.[22] 
3.6.12 Scope Limitation of This Section 
This section addresses legal recognition and foundational principles governing digital 
evidence. Detailed procedural requirements relating to certification, chain of custody, forensic 
extraction, and proof mechanisms are addressed separately in Chapter 19. Investigating Officers 
must avoid conflating recognition with admissibility at the investigation stage.[23] 
3.7 Sectoral and Allied Laws Impacting Cybercrime Investigation 
(PMLA, Telecommunications Act, Intermediary Rules) 
Cybercrime investigations rarely remain confined to core criminal statutes. In practice, they 
intersect with sectoral and regulatory laws governing finance, telecommunications 
infrastructure, and digital platforms. These allied laws do not substitute the Information 
Technology Act, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or the 
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. Instead, they supplement investigative authority in defined 
domains, while simultaneously imposing additional statutory thresholds and safeguards.[1] 
From an administrative perspective, sectoral laws enable investigators to trace financial flows, 
access regulated communication data, and secure platform-held evidence. From a judicial 
perspective, these laws act as legal filters, ensuring that investigative actions affecting sensitive 
domains—money, communications, and personal data—are exercised within legislatively 
prescribed limits. Courts routinely examine whether investigators correctly identified the 
applicable sectoral framework before acting.[2] 
3.7.1 Telecommunications Act, 2023: Requisition, Metadata, and Interception in 
Cybercrime Investigation 
The enactment of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 marks a decisive departure from the 
colonial-era Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, particularly in its treatment of digital communications, 
metadata, and lawful interception. For cybercrime investigation, this transition is not merely 
[[PAGE 72]]
legislative but operationally transformative, as telecom data often constitutes the first 
corroborative layer linking a digital offence to an individual or device. 
Investigating Officers must therefore recalibrate investigative practice to align with the rights-
oriented, technology-aware framework introduced by the Telecommunications Act, 2023. 
Continued reliance on assumptions derived from the Telegraph Act era exposes investigations to 
legal challenge and evidentiary vulnerability. 
From Telegraph Act to Telecommunications Act: Structural Shift 
Under the Telegraph Act, interception and requisition powers were executive-centric and 
technologically limited. The Telecommunications Act, 2023 recognises modern communication 
ecosystems and introduces clear statutory differentiation between categories of telecom data.

SOP Clarification: 
Investigating Officers shall not rely on legacy interception assumptions while dealing with

Distinction Between Subscriber Information, Metadata, and Content 
A recurring operational error in cybercrime investigations is failure to distinguish between 
categories of telecom data, each governed by different legal thresholds.

Obtaining Call Data Records (CDRs) to establish contact between accused and victim involves

Requisition of Telecom Metadata in Cybercrime Cases 
Metadata plays a crucial role in: 
 
Establishing identity linkage 
 
Corroborating device usage 
 
Tracing movement and coordination 
However, metadata is regulated personal data, not general investigative material. 
Non-Negotiable SOP Rule: 
Requisition of telecom metadata must:

Be offence-specific 
 
Be proportionate in scope and duration 
 
Be supported by recorded justification 
Bulk or exploratory requisitions without nexus to the offence have been judicially questioned. 
[[PAGE 74]]
Interception and Monitoring: Heightened Legal Threshold 
Interception under the Telecommunications Act, 2023 is treated as a grave intrusion into 
privacy and is therefore subject to heightened safeguards. Investigating Officers must appreciate 
 
Interception ≠ metadata access 
 
Interception is not a routine investigative tool 
 
Emergency does not eliminate procedural compliance 
Courts have consistently held that unauthorised interception vitiates both legality and 
admissibility, regardless of evidentiary value. 
Cybercrime investigation urgency does not justify informal interception or bypass of statutory 
safeguards. 
Impact on Cybercrime Investigation Strategy 
The Telecommunications Act, 2023 reshapes investigative sequencing in cybercrime cases. Best 
practice now requires: 
1. Initial reliance on metadata and subscriber information 
2. Escalation to interception only where strictly necessary 
3. Documentation of necessity and proportionality at every stage 
This graduated approach aligns investigative efficiency with constitutional compliance. 
Judicial Sensitivity to Telecom Evidence 
Courts increasingly scrutinise: 
 
Source of telecom data 
 
Authority under which it was obtained 
 
Scope and duration of requisition 
 
Compliance with statutory safeguards 
[[PAGE 75]]
Failure to demonstrate lawful requisition has resulted in dilution or exclusion of telecom-based 
evidence in several cases. 
Investigative Significance 
From an administrative perspective, correct application of the Telecommunications Act, 2023: 
 
Enhances evidentiary reliability 
 
Prevents privacy-based litigation 
 
Shields Investigating Officers from personal allegations 
From a judicial perspective, it demonstrates measured exercise of intrusive power, which 
courts consistently favour. 
3.7.2 Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) 
The Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 becomes relevant where cyber offences 
generate, conceal, possess, transfer, or project proceeds of crime. Large-scale online frauds, 
phishing syndicates, investment scams, ransomware attacks, and mule-account networks 
frequently involve systematic laundering of illicit digital proceeds.[3] 
Under the PMLA, money-laundering is treated as a distinct and continuing offence, independent 
of the scheduled offence that generated the proceeds. Consequently, cybercrime investigations 
often proceed on parallel tracks: 
(i) investigation of the predicate cyber offence under IT Act/BNS, and 
(ii) financial investigation relating to proceeds of crime under PMLA.[4] 
Funds obtained through phishing are routed through multiple bank accounts, prepaid 
instruments, and wallets to obscure origin. While cheating and identity theft are investigated 
under IT Act and BNS, the act of layering and projecting those funds attracts PMLA 
provisions.[5] 
The Supreme Court has clarified that PMLA proceedings are independent and may continue 
irrespective of the status of prosecution for the scheduled offence, subject to statutory 
safeguards.[6] 
[[PAGE 76]]
Threshold for Invoking PMLA in Cybercrime 
Mechanical invocation of PMLA merely because money is involved has been judicially 
deprecated. Courts require demonstrable linkage between the cyber offence and laundering 
activity.[7] 
SOP Threshold Principle: 
PMLA shall be invoked only where there is material indicating generation of proceeds of crime 
and subsequent activity aimed at concealment, layering, or projection as untainted property.[8] 
Judicial Caution: 
Absence of laundering elements reduces PMLA invocation to punitive overreach and exposes 
investigation to judicial correction.[9] 
Coordination Between Police Investigation and PMLA Authorities 
While police investigate the scheduled offence, designated authorities under the PMLA exercise 
powers relating to attachment, seizure, and confiscation. Investigating Officers must coordinate 
with such authorities without jurisdictional overreach.[10] 
Courts have emphasised that: 
 
Police powers under BNSS cannot be substituted for PMLA attachment powers 
 
Financial attachment must follow PMLA procedure 
 
Parallel action must remain legally distinct[11] 
Failure to maintain this separation often results in procedural challenges and delay.[12] 
3.7.3 Telecommunications Act, 2023 and Telecom-Related Evidence 
The Telecommunications Act, 2023 governs access to telecom infrastructure, subscriber 
information, traffic data, and communication records. In cybercrime investigations, telecom 
evidence—subscriber details, call data records, IP-SIM linkage, routing data—often forms a 
crucial evidentiary chain.[13] 
However, telecom data is regulated data, not general investigative material. Access to such data 
must conform strictly to statutory and regulatory frameworks.[14] 
[[PAGE 77]]
Tracing a fraudulent call requires lawful access to subscriber and routing information held by 
telecom service providers. Such access must comply with telecom law safeguards, not merely 
general investigative power.[15] 
Courts have consistently held that telecom data obtained outside statutory authority is 
vulnerable to exclusion, irrespective of relevance.[16] 
Interception, Monitoring, and Metadata Distinction 
Investigating Officers must distinguish between: 
 
Subscriber information and historical metadata, and 
 
Interception or real-time monitoring of communications 
Interception attracts heightened legal thresholds, judicial oversight, and procedural 
safeguards.[17] 
Unauthorised interception or informal access to communication content violates statutory 
safeguards and constitutional privacy guarantees.[18] 
3.7.4 Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) 
Rules, 2021 
The Intermediary Rules impose statutory duties on social media platforms, online marketplaces, 
messaging services, and hosting providers to: 
 
Preserve specified information 
 
Cooperate with lawful investigations 
 
Appoint compliance and grievance officers 
These obligations facilitate investigation but do not create independent investigative 
powers.[19] 
[[PAGE 78]]
A platform may be legally required to preserve account data upon lawful request, but disclosure 
must still comply with procedural and evidentiary law.[20] 
3.7.4.1 Safe Harbour and Limits of Intermediary Liability 
Judicial interpretation has consistently recognised that intermediaries enjoy conditional safe 
harbour. They are not treated as accused persons by default unless there is evidence of active 
participation, knowledge, or facilitation of the offence.[21] 
 Safe Harbour Principle (Mandatory SOP Guidance): 
Intermediaries are custodians of evidence, not offenders by default. Cooperation 
obligations facilitate investigation but do not negate safe harbour absent statutory 
grounds.[22] Overreach against intermediaries without factual or legal basis has 
repeatedly attracted judicial censure.[23] 
3.7.4.2 Investigative Significance of Sectoral Law Compliance 
From an administrative perspective, correct invocation of sectoral laws enables: 
 
Effective tracing of illicit financial flows 
 
Lawful access to regulated telecom evidence 
 
Preservation of platform-held digital data 
From a judicial perspective, it demonstrates that the investigation respected domain-specific 
statutory limits, strengthening evidentiary sustainability.[24] 
Failure to integrate sectoral laws appropriately results in: 
 
Suppression of evidence 
 
Jurisdictional conflict 
 
Prolonged litigation and adverse orders[25] 
Cybercrime investigation must therefore treat sectoral statutes as supporting legal frameworks, 
invoked with precision, restraint, and statutory awareness.[26] 
[[PAGE 79]]
3.8 Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: Investigation Interface 
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) establishes the statutory framework 
governing collection, processing, storage, and disclosure of personal data in India. In cybercrime 
investigations, personal data—financial details, communication records, identifiers, location 
data, and device information—constitutes the primary evidentiary material. The DPDP Act 
therefore directly interfaces with investigative practice, not as a barrier, but as a regulatory 
discipline on the manner of investigation.[1] 
Contrary to initial perception, the DPDP Act does not prohibit law enforcement access to 
personal data. Instead, it conditions such access upon legality, purpose limitation, and 
proportionality. Courts have increasingly examined whether investigative agencies complied 
with data-protection principles while exercising statutory powers, particularly where large 
volumes of personal or third-party data are involved.[2] 
From an SOP perspective, the DPDP Act performs a balancing function. Administratively, it 
enables lawful processing of personal data for investigation and prosecution. Judicially, it 
imposes boundaries that prevent excessive or indiscriminate intrusion into informational 
privacy.[3] 
3.8.1 Lawful Basis for Processing Personal Data During Investigation 
The DPDP Act expressly recognises prevention, detection, investigation, and prosecution of 
offences as lawful purposes for processing personal data without consent of the data principal. 
This recognition is essential for effective cybercrime investigation, where consent-based access 
is impractical or impossible.[4] 
However, the existence of a lawful purpose does not create unfettered authority. Investigative 
processing must still be: 
 
Anchored in statutory power 
 
Confined to investigative necessity 
 
Proportionate to the offence under inquiry 
[[PAGE 80]]
Accessing bank transaction data to trace proceeds of an online fraud is lawful. Harvesting 
unrelated personal data of all account holders without relevance exceeds statutory purpose.[5] 
3.8.2 Purpose Limitation and Data Minimisation 
A central principle of the DPDP Act is purpose limitation. Personal data may be processed only 
to the extent necessary to achieve the specific investigative objective for which it is collected.[6] 
In cybercrime cases, digital devices and accounts often contain extensive personal and third-
party data unrelated to the offence. Courts have cautioned that investigative convenience cannot 
justify indiscriminate data extraction.[7] 
SOP Operational Principle: 
Investigating Officers shall collect and process only such personal data as is reasonably 
connected to the offence under investigation. Over-collection exposes the investigation to legal 
challenge and evidentiary exclusion.[8] 
3.8.3 Interaction Between DPDP Act and Procedural Law 
The DPDP Act does not operate independently of criminal procedure. Lawful data processing 
under the DPDP Act presupposes lawful exercise of procedural powers under the Bharatiya 
Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Data obtained through unlawful search, unauthorised access, or 
procedural violation remains vulnerable notwithstanding DPDP exemptions.[9] 
DPDP exemptions do not override constitutional safeguards or procedural illegality. Compliance 
with data-protection law cannot cure defects arising from illegal search or seizure.[10] 
Personal data extracted from a mobile device without lawful search authority may violate both 
procedural law and data-protection principles, rendering such material susceptible to 
exclusion.[11] 
[[PAGE 81]]
3.8.4 Processing of Third-Party and Incidental Data 
Cyber investigations frequently involve incidental access to third-party personal data, such as 
contacts, communications, or transaction histories of individuals not accused of any offence. The 
DPDP Act requires heightened caution in such situations.[12] 
Investigating Officers must ensure that: 
 
Third-party data is accessed only where unavoidable 
 
Such data is not unnecessarily retained 
 
Disclosure is limited to investigative or judicial necessity 
Courts have shown increasing sensitivity to collateral intrusion into third-party privacy, 
particularly where individuals are not suspects.[13] 
3.8.5 Retention and Storage of Personal Data 
The DPDP Act mandates that personal data shall not be retained beyond the period necessary for 
the purpose for which it was processed. In the investigative context, this principle translates into 
reviewable retention, not indefinite storage.[14] 
Retaining cloned device data indefinitely after completion of forensic examination, without 
documented necessity, may violate data-protection principles.[15] 
Investigating Officers must therefore periodically review retention of personal data and ensure 
secure storage, access control, and eventual disposal in accordance with law.[16] 
3.8.6 Disclosure of Personal Data During Investigation and Trial 
Disclosure of personal data during investigation or trial must be: 
 
Legally authorised 
 
Purpose-specific 
 
Limited to what is necessary for judicial proceedings 
Uncontrolled dissemination of personal data through charge-sheets, annexures, or open-court 
records may attract legal scrutiny.[17] 
[[PAGE 82]]
Courts have emphasised that open justice does not imply unrestricted exposure of personal 
data, particularly in sensitive cybercrime cases.[18] 
3.8.7 DPDP Act and Rights of the Accused 
The DPDP Act indirectly reinforces fair-trial rights by requiring transparency and 
accountability in data processing. Accused persons are entitled to challenge: 
 
Unlawful collection of personal data 
 
Excessive data retention 
 
Use of data beyond investigative purpose 
Such challenges are increasingly being raised in cybercrime proceedings.[19] 
3.8.8 Investigative Significance of DPDP Compliance 
From an administrative perspective, DPDP compliance: 
 
Protects Investigating Officers from allegations of privacy violation 
 
Enhances institutional credibility 
 
Reduces constitutional litigation 
From a judicial perspective, it demonstrates proportionality and restraint, strengthening 
confidence in the investigation.[20] 
Failure to integrate DPDP principles may result in: 
 
Suppression of evidence 
 
Constitutional challenges 
 
Judicial directives limiting investigative scope[21] 
3.8.9 Scope Limitation of This Section 
This section addresses the legal interface between data-protection law and cybercrime 
investigation. Operational procedures relating to forensic extraction, access controls, 
anonymisation, and secure handling are addressed in subsequent SOP chapters. Investigating 
[[PAGE 83]]
Officers must avoid treating DPDP compliance as a post-investigation formality; it is an integral 
legal requirement.[22] 
3.9 Judicial Precedents Shaping Cybercrime Investigations 
Judicial precedents occupy a central position in cybercrime investigation. Unlike conventional 
crimes, where statutory provisions often provide relatively settled operational clarity, cybercrime 
law has evolved primarily through judicial interpretation. Courts have progressively articulated 
principles governing investigation, evidence, arrest, jurisdiction, privacy, and proportionality in 
response to the unique challenges posed by digital offences.[1] 
For Investigating Officers, judicial precedents perform a dual function. Administratively, they 
operate as binding constraints on investigative discretion. Judicially, they serve as benchmarks 
against which the legality of investigative conduct is assessed. Failure to internalise settled 
precedent often results in quashing of proceedings, exclusion of evidence, or adverse 
observations against investigating agencies.[2] 
It is therefore essential to appreciate that precedents do not create investigative power; they 
regulate the manner in which statutory power is exercised. Courts repeatedly emphasise that 
cybercrime investigation must remain law-led, not tool-led or urgency-led.[3] 
3.9.1 Precedents on Registration of FIR and Abuse of Process 
One of the most frequently invoked judicial principles in cybercrime litigation arises from State 
of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal. The Supreme Court delineated categories of cases where criminal 
proceedings may be quashed, including situations involving abuse of process, absence of prima 
facie offence, or mala fide invocation of law.[4] 
In cybercrime investigations, this precedent assumes heightened relevance due to: 
 
Over-criminalisation of civil or contractual disputes 
 
Mechanical registration of FIRs based on technical allegations 
 
Addition of penal provisions without factual foundation 
Courts routinely apply Bhajan Lal principles to scrutinise whether cyber complaints disclose 
genuine criminality or merely commercial disagreement dressed as cyber offence.[5] 
[[PAGE 84]]
SOP Implication: 
Investigating Officers must ensure that registration of FIR is grounded in disclosure of statutory 
ingredients, not merely technological allegations or transactional disputes.[6] 
3.9.2 Precedents Governing Arrest in Cyber and Economic Offences 
The Supreme Court in Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar laid down binding guidelines restricting 
routine arrest in offences punishable up to seven years. Although originally delivered in the 
context of IPC offences, the principle has been consistently applied to economic and cyber 
offences.[7] 
Courts have repeatedly held that arrest in cybercrime cases: 
 
Must not be used as a tool for coercion or recovery 
 
Requires demonstrable necessity 
 
Must be supported by recorded satisfaction 
Failure to comply with Arnesh Kumar guidelines has resulted in personal liability warnings and 
disciplinary directions in several cases.[8] 
Arresting an accused in an online fraud case solely because of non-cooperation, without 
assessing necessity under procedural law, is routinely struck down.[9] 
3.9.3 Precedents on Search, Seizure, and Procedural Illegality 
Judicial scrutiny of cybercrime investigations often focuses on search and seizure legality, 
particularly in relation to electronic devices. In State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh, the Supreme 
Court clarified that procedural safeguards are not technicalities but substantive protections, and 
that discovery of incriminating material does not cure illegal search.[10] 
This principle has been repeatedly applied to digital searches, where: 
 
Entire devices are seized without necessity 
 
Scope of search is disproportionate 
 
Procedural requirements are bypassed due to urgency 
[[PAGE 85]]
Courts have emphasised that digital search intrudes far deeper into personal life than physical 
search, necessitating strict adherence to procedure.[11] 
3.9.4 Precedents on Electronic Evidence and Admissibility 
Judicial interpretation of electronic evidence has been among the most significant contributions 
to cyber law. In Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer, the Supreme Court clarified that electronic records 
are admissible only when statutory requirements relating to authenticity are satisfied. This 
position was reaffirmed and elaborated in Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao 
Gorantyal.[12] 
Although these decisions were rendered under the Indian Evidence Act, courts continue to rely 
upon their reasoning under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, particularly with respect to: 
 
Source integrity 
 
Authenticity 
 
Prevention of manipulation 
SOP Implication: 
Investigating Officers must treat electronic evidence as legally fragile, requiring meticulous 
procedural compliance from collection to production.[13] 
3.9.5 Precedents on Privacy and Informational Autonomy 
The constitutional recognition of privacy in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India has profoundly 
reshaped cybercrime investigation. Courts now examine whether investigative actions involving 
data access, device seizure, surveillance, or platform requests satisfy the tests of legality, 
necessity, and proportionality.[14] 
In cybercrime cases, privacy jurisprudence has been invoked to challenge: 
 
Indiscriminate device cloning 
 
Excessive data extraction 
 
Unregulated access to communication records 
Courts have clarified that seriousness of offence does not dispense with privacy safeguards.[15] 
[[PAGE 86]]
3.9.6 Precedents on Interception and Communication Surveillance 
In People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India, the Supreme Court laid down safeguards 
governing interception of communications. Although delivered prior to widespread digital 
communication, its principles continue to govern interception under information technology and 
telecom laws.[16] 
Courts distinguish between: 
 
Lawful access to subscriber or historical metadata, and 
 
Real-time interception or monitoring of communication content 
Unauthorised interception has been treated as a serious violation of statutory and constitutional 
safeguards.[17] 
3.9.7 Precedents on Intermediary Liability and Platform Cooperation 
Judicial interpretation of intermediary liability has evolved through cases such as Shreya 
Singhal v. Union of India & Avnish Bajaj v. State (NCT of Delhi). Courts have consistently 
held that intermediaries are not criminally liable by default and enjoy conditional safe harbour, 
subject to statutory compliance.[18] 
In cybercrime investigations, courts scrutinise whether: 
 
Intermediaries were treated as evidence custodians or accused 
 
Cooperation requests were lawful and specific 
 
Platform obligations were confused with investigative powers 
Overreach against intermediaries has frequently attracted judicial correction.[19] 
3.9.8 Precedents on Jurisdiction in Cybercrime 
Jurisdictional disputes are common in cybercrime cases. In K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan 
Balan, the Supreme Court recognised that jurisdiction may arise where consequence of offence 
ensues. This principle has been applied in cyber cases involving online fraud, defamation, and 
harassment.[20] 
[[PAGE 87]]
However, courts require a demonstrable nexus between the offence and the forum jurisdiction. 
Mere online accessibility is insufficient to assume jurisdiction.[21] 
3.9.9 Precedents on Fair Trial and Disclosure of Digital Evidence 
Courts have repeatedly held that denial of access to relied-upon electronic material violates 
principles of fair trial. In Gopalakrishna v. State of Kerala, the Supreme Court emphasised the 
accused’s right to access material relied upon by the prosecution.[22] 
In cybercrime cases, this principle extends to: 
 
Digital records 
 
Forensic reports 
 
Extracted data relied upon for prosecution 
Failure to disclose relied-upon digital material has resulted in adverse judicial orders.[23] 
3.9.10 Investigative Significance of Judicial Precedents 
From an administrative perspective, judicial precedents: 
 
Guide lawful exercise of discretion 
 
Protect Investigating Officers from personal liability 
 
Reduce pre-trial litigation 
From a judicial perspective, adherence to precedent reflects institutional discipline and 
constitutional sensitivity.[24] 
Cybercrime investigation conducted in disregard of settled judicial principles is unlikely to 
survive judicial scrutiny, irrespective of technical evidence strength.[25] 
Judicial precedents therefore function as the interpretive spine of cybercrime law, translating 
statutory text into enforceable limits on investigative power.[26] 
3.10 Jurisdictional Reach of Cybercrime Laws 
Jurisdiction in cybercrime investigation presents unique legal challenges due to the borderless 
nature of digital activity. Unlike conventional offences, cyber offences are often committed 
[[PAGE 88]]
across multiple locations simultaneously—where the offender operates from one place, servers 
are located in another, victims reside elsewhere, and financial consequences are felt in multiple 
jurisdictions. Determining lawful jurisdiction is therefore not a mere administrative formality but 
a substantive legal requirement that directly impacts the validity of investigation and 
prosecution.[1] 
Indian criminal law does not treat cyberspace as a separate territorial domain. Instead, 
jurisdiction in cybercrime cases is determined by applying established principles of criminal 
jurisdiction to digital conduct. Courts have consistently emphasised that digital complexity does 
not dispense with jurisdictional discipline. Investigating Officers must be able to demonstrate 
a clear legal nexus between the offence and the territorial jurisdiction assumed.[2] 
3.10.1 Statutory Basis of Jurisdiction in Cybercrime 
Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, jurisdiction may be assumed where: 
 
The offence is committed wholly or partly 
 
The consequence of the offence ensues 
 
Any act forming part of the offence occurs 
These principles apply equally to cyber offences, notwithstanding the virtual mode of 
commission.[3] 
Additionally, the Information Technology Act, 2000 contains express provisions extending its 
applicability to offences committed outside India, provided the computer resource affected is 
located in India. This statutory extension recognises the transnational character of cyber offences 
but does not eliminate the requirement of demonstrating a nexus.[4] 
3.10.2 International Legal Cooperation in Cybercrime Investigation 
(MLAT, Foreign Data, and Multilateral Frameworks) 
Cybercrime investigation increasingly involves cross-border digital infrastructure. Emails, 
social media accounts, cloud servers, payment gateways, and messaging platforms relied upon 
by offenders are frequently hosted outside India. Consequently, effective cybercrime 
[[PAGE 89]]
investigation cannot remain territorially insular; it must integrate international legal 
cooperation mechanisms to lawfully access evidence located abroad.[1] 
Courts have consistently emphasised that extra-territorial jurisdiction does not imply extra-
legal investigation. While Indian law may extend to offences impacting India, evidence 
collection beyond national borders must conform to international legal processes, failing which 
such material becomes vulnerable to challenge.[2] 
 Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs): Core Framework 
Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties constitute the primary legal mechanism through which Indian 
authorities seek assistance from foreign States in criminal investigations. MLATs operate on the 
principle of reciprocity and sovereign consent, enabling lawful access to evidence located in 
foreign jurisdictions.[3] 
In cybercrime cases, MLAT requests are commonly used to obtain: 
 
Subscriber information from foreign platforms 
 
Account activity logs 
 
Content data where legally permissible 
 
Preservation of volatile electronic evidence 
SOP Clarification: 
Direct requests to foreign service providers, bypassing MLAT channels, do not substitute lawful 
international assistance unless expressly permitted by law or treaty.[4] 
 MLAT Workflow in Cybercrime Investigation 
The MLAT process involves multiple stages, each requiring precision and legal clarity: 
1. Identification of foreign-located evidence 
2. Preparation of a detailed and offence-specific request 
3. Routing through designated central authorities 
4. Compliance with foreign jurisdiction’s legal standards 
[[PAGE 90]]
Delays are inherent in MLAT processes; however, courts have held that procedural patience is 
not a defect where legal compliance is necessary.[5] 
Operational Note: 
Investigating Officers must draft MLAT requests with specificity, avoiding fishing expeditions or 
vague data demands, which are frequently rejected by foreign authorities.[6] 
 Preservation Requests and Volatile Digital Evidence 
Given the volatile nature of digital evidence, timely data preservation requests play a critical 
role. Preservation requests seek to prevent deletion or alteration of data pending formal legal 
process.[7] 
Such requests: 
 
Do not authorise disclosure 
 
Temporarily freeze data 
 
Support subsequent MLAT or court orders 
Preservation does not equal production. Investigating Officers must still follow formal legal 
processes for data access.[8] 
 Budapest Convention on Cybercrime: Contextual Relevance 
The Budapest Convention on Cybercrime represents the most significant multilateral 
instrument addressing cyber offences and international cooperation. Although India is not a 
signatory, its procedural standards and cooperation models influence international cybercrime 
practice.[9] 
Many foreign service providers and States align their cooperation frameworks with Budapest 
Convention principles, particularly regarding: 
 
Expedited data preservation 
 
Trans-border access safeguards 
 
Standardised request formats 
[[PAGE 91]]
Investigating Officers must remain cognisant of Budapest-aligned practices when engaging with 
foreign jurisdictions, without misrepresenting India’s treaty status.[10] 
 Role of I4C and Central Agencies 
The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) functions as a national coordination hub for 
cybercrime investigation, capacity-building, and international liaison. In complex cross-border 
cases, coordination with I4C and central agencies enhances efficiency and legal coherence.[11] 
I4C facilitates: 
 
Standardised formats 
 
Inter-agency coordination 
 
Capacity-building on foreign evidence handling 
Administrative Principle: 
State-level cyber units must leverage national coordination mechanisms rather than pursuing 
fragmented international outreach.[12] 
 
 Extra-Territorial Jurisdiction vs Enforcement Reality 
While Indian law recognises extra-territorial jurisdiction where offences impact India, courts 
have cautioned against confusing jurisdiction with enforceability. Evidence located abroad 
requires foreign cooperation, irrespective of statutory reach.[13] 
Courts assess whether: 
 
Investigators attempted lawful international cooperation 
 
Shortcuts were avoided 
 
Due process was respected 
Failure to pursue lawful cooperation may weaken prosecution even where substantive 
jurisdiction exists.[14] 
[[PAGE 92]]
 Investigative Significance of International Cooperation 
From an administrative perspective, effective international cooperation: 
 
Strengthens evidentiary chains 
 
Reduces admissibility challenges 
 
Enhances conviction sustainability 
From a judicial perspective, it demonstrates respect for international law and procedural 
propriety, which courts consistently favour.[15] 
Cross-border cybercrime investigation therefore requires strategic patience, legal precision, and 
institutional coordination, not unilateral action.[16] 
 Place of Commission and Place of Consequence 
Courts have repeatedly recognised that in cybercrime cases, place of consequence assumes 
particular importance. Financial loss, reputational harm, psychological injury, or disruption of 
services occurring within a jurisdiction may confer territorial competence, even if the offender 
operates remotely.[5] 
A phishing email sent from another State induces a victim residing locally to transfer funds from 
a local bank account. The local police station may assume jurisdiction based on the place where 
financial loss occurred.[6] 
However, mere accessibility of digital content within a jurisdiction is insufficient. Courts require 
actual or intended impact within the territorial limits.[7] 
 
3.10.3 Jurisdiction Based on Location of Computer Resource 
The IT Act recognises jurisdiction based on the location of the computer resource affected by 
the offence. Servers, data centres, or digital infrastructure situated within India may establish 
jurisdiction even where the offender is physically located abroad.[8] 
[[PAGE 93]]
Unauthorised access to a cloud server located in India from a foreign country attracts Indian 
jurisdiction under the IT Act, subject to procedural compliance.[9] 
Investigating Officers must be cautious in asserting server-based jurisdiction and ensure that the 
location of the computer resource is factually established and documented.[10] 
3.10.4 Multiple Jurisdictions and Concurrent Authority 
Cybercrime cases frequently attract concurrent jurisdiction of multiple police stations or States. 
Courts have recognised that more than one jurisdiction may be legally competent, provided each 
satisfies statutory criteria.[11] 
However, parallel investigations without coordination often result in: 
 
Conflicting proceedings 
 
Duplication of effort 
 
Jurisdictional disputes 
SOP Administrative Principle: 
Where multiple jurisdictions are competent, investigative coordination and lawful transfer 
mechanisms must be utilised to prevent procedural conflict.[12] 
3.10.5 Cross-Border Cybercrime and Extra-Territorial Reach 
Many cyber offences involve foreign actors, offshore servers, or international financial channels. 
Indian law recognises extra-territorial jurisdiction in such cases where statutory conditions are 
met.[13] 
However, exercise of extra-territorial jurisdiction requires: 
 
Clear statutory basis 
 
Demonstrable nexus with India 
 
Compliance with international cooperation mechanisms 
Courts have cautioned against asserting jurisdiction in a vacuum, without addressing 
enforcement feasibility or legal reciprocity.[14] 
[[PAGE 94]]
3.10.6 Jurisdictional Recording and Documentation 
Judicial scrutiny of cybercrime cases frequently turns on whether the Investigating Officer 
recorded reasons for assuming jurisdiction. Absence of documented reasoning is treated as a 
substantive defect rather than a curable irregularity.[15] 
Mandatory SOP Requirement: 
Investigating Officers shall record the factual and legal basis of jurisdiction at the earliest stage 
of investigation. Jurisdictional satisfaction must be demonstrable from the case record.[16] 
3.10.7 Jurisdictional Errors as a Legal Risk Zone 
Common jurisdictional errors include: 
 
Assuming jurisdiction solely based on online accessibility 
 
Ignoring location of victim or consequence 
 
Failure to document server location or data nexus 
 
Parallel investigations without coordination 
Courts have consistently quashed proceedings where jurisdiction was assumed mechanically or 
without legal foundation.[17] 
3.10.8 Investigative Significance of Jurisdictional Compliance 
From an administrative perspective, correct jurisdictional determination: 
 
Prevents transfer delays 
 
Avoids duplication of investigation 
 
Ensures continuity of prosecution 
From a judicial perspective, it demonstrates legal consciousness and procedural discipline, 
strengthening the credibility of investigation.[18] 
Cybercrime investigation must therefore treat jurisdiction not as a technical obstacle but as a 
foundational legal requirement. Failure to establish and document jurisdiction undermines 
investigation at inception, regardless of the strength of evidence subsequently collected.[19] 
[[PAGE 95]]
3.11 Legal Risk Zones in Cybercrime Investigation 
Cybercrime investigation operates in a legally sensitive environment where procedural excess, 
statutory misapplication, or evidentiary shortcuts can irreversibly damage prosecution. Unlike 
traditional crimes, cyber investigations often involve early and deep intrusion into digital 
devices, personal data, financial systems, and online identities. Courts therefore scrutinise cyber 
investigations with heightened intensity, particularly at the pre-trial stage.[1] 
A “legal risk zone” refers to a recurring point in investigation where statutory power is most 
likely to be misused, misunderstood, or over-extended, leading to judicial correction. 
Identification of these zones is essential for SOP compliance, officer protection, and 
sustainability of prosecution.[2] 
3.11.1 Over-Charging and Mechanical Addition of Sections 
One of the most common risk zones in cybercrime investigation is mechanical over-charging. 
Investigating Officers frequently add multiple IT Act and penal provisions without analysing 
whether factual ingredients are independently satisfied.[3] 
Courts have repeatedly held that multiplicity of sections does not strengthen a case; rather, it 
invites judicial dilution and quashing where over-inclusion reflects non-application of mind.[4] 
Adding cyber terrorism or organised crime provisions in a routine online fraud case, without 
satisfying statutory thresholds, exposes the investigation to immediate judicial challenge.[5] 
Each invoked section must be supported by a factual matrix demonstrating all statutory 
ingredients. Convenience or deterrence cannot substitute legal necessity.[6] 
3.11.2 Under-Charging and Failure to Invoke Penal Law 
Conversely, another risk zone arises from under-charging, particularly where investigations rely 
exclusively on IT Act provisions while ignoring substantive penal offences. This often results in 
inadequate sentencing and incomplete attribution of criminal intent.[7] 
[[PAGE 96]]
Courts have criticised investigations that treat cybercrime as a purely technical offence while 
ignoring deception, coercion, conspiracy, or exploitation underlying the digital conduct.[8] 
Charging only unauthorised access provisions in an online investment scam, while omitting 
cheating and conspiracy provisions, weakens prosecution despite strong evidence.[9] 
3.11.3 Unlawful Search and Excessive Digital Seizure 
Digital search and seizure represents one of the most litigated risk zones. Investigators often 
seize entire devices or networks without recording necessity, proportionality, or relevance.[10] 
Courts have consistently held that discovery of incriminating digital material does not cure 
illegal search. Digital searches intrude far deeper into personal life than physical searches, 
attracting stricter scrutiny.[11] 
Search scope must be narrowly tailored, purpose-specific, and supported by recorded reasoning. 
Blanket or exploratory digital searches are legally vulnerable.[12] 
3.11.4 Routine or Coercive Arrest in Cybercrime Cases
