Routine arrest in cyber and economic offences remains a major legal risk zone. Courts have 
repeatedly emphasised that arrest must not be used as a tool for coercion, recovery, or signalling 
seriousness.[13] 
Illegal or unnecessary arrest often results in: 
 
Bail as a matter of right 
 
Adverse judicial observations 
 
Loss of prosecutorial credibility 
Arresting an accused solely to compel cooperation in a digital fraud case, without demonstrating 
statutory necessity, has been repeatedly deprecated.[14] 
[[PAGE 97]]
Arrest must satisfy statutory necessity and be supported by recorded reasons. Absence of 
justification renders arrest legally indefensible.[15] 
3.11.5 Improper Freezing of Bank Accounts and Digital Assets 
Another frequent risk zone is excessive or indefinite freezing of bank accounts, wallets, or digital 
assets. Courts have held that freezing must be proportionate, evidence-linked, and subject to 
review.[16] 
Freezing accounts unrelated to the offence, or freezing amounts far exceeding alleged loss, has 
been treated as punitive overreach.[17] 
Freezing orders must be offence-specific, proportionate, and periodically reviewed. Indefinite 
freezing without justification invites judicial intervention.[18] 
3.11.6 Mishandling of Digital Evidence 
Improper handling of digital evidence—such as failure to preserve integrity, inadequate 
documentation, or unauthorised access—constitutes a critical risk zone. Courts have excluded 
otherwise relevant evidence due to procedural contamination.[19] 
Accessing or copying device data without lawful authority or documentation may compromise 
evidentiary integrity irreversibly.[20] 
Digital evidence must be collected, preserved, and handled strictly in accordance with 
procedural and evidentiary law.[21] 
3.11.7 Jurisdictional Assumptions Without Nexus 
Assuming jurisdiction solely based on online accessibility or complainant convenience is a 
recurring risk zone. Courts require a demonstrable nexus between the offence and territorial 
jurisdiction.[22] 
[[PAGE 98]]
Failure to record jurisdictional reasoning has resulted in quashing or transfer of proceedings at 
early stages.[23] 
Jurisdiction must be legally established and documented at inception. Convenience cannot 
substitute statutory nexus.[24] 
3.11.8 Overreach Against Intermediaries and Service Providers 
Treating intermediaries or service providers as accused by default, rather than evidence 
custodians, exposes investigations to judicial correction. Courts have consistently upheld 
conditional safe harbour principles.[25] 
Issuing coercive notices or registering cases against platforms without evidence of active 
participation has attracted judicial censure.[26] 
Intermediaries shall be engaged as evidence custodians unless statutory grounds for liability are 
established.[27] 
3.11.9 Data Protection Non-Compliance 
With the advent of data-protection law, indiscriminate collection, retention, or disclosure of 
personal data has emerged as a new legal risk zone. Courts increasingly assess proportionality 
and purpose limitation.[28] 
Failure to integrate data-protection principles exposes investigations to constitutional 
challenge.[29] 
Personal data must be collected and retained strictly for investigative necessity, with documented 
justification.[30] 
[[PAGE 99]]
3.11.10 Failure to Record Legal Satisfaction 
A pervasive and often fatal risk zone is failure to record legal satisfaction regarding necessity, 
proportionality, jurisdiction, or statutory thresholds. Courts treat absence of recorded reasoning 
as a substantive defect, not a curable irregularity.[31] 
Mandatory SOP Warning: 
Unrecorded satisfaction is itself a procedural illegality, even where statutory power otherwise 
exists.[32] 
3.11.11 Investigative Significance of Risk-Zone Awareness 
From an administrative perspective, awareness of legal risk zones: 
 
Protects Investigating Officers from adverse judicial findings 
 
Reduces pre-trial litigation 
 
Enhances institutional credibility 
From a judicial perspective, it demonstrates legal maturity and constitutional sensitivity.[33] 
Cybercrime investigation succeeds not merely by gathering evidence, but by avoiding legally 
fatal missteps. Conscious navigation of legal risk zones is therefore essential for sustainable 
prosecution.[34] 
3.12 Conclusion: Law as the Backbone of Sustainable Cyber Prosecution 
Cybercrime investigation is sustainable only when it is law-led. This chapter has demonstrated 
that cyber policing is not defined by technological capability, speed of response, or volume of 
data collected, but by legally disciplined exercise of statutory power. In the absence of such 
discipline, even technically flawless investigations are vulnerable to judicial invalidation.[1] 
The Indian legal framework governing cybercrime investigation operates as an integrated 
system, not a collection of isolated statutes. The Information Technology Act defines technology-
centric criminality; the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita captures cyber-enabled human wrongdoing; the 
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita regulates investigative power; the Bharatiya Sakshya 
Adhiniyam determines evidentiary legitimacy; and sectoral enactments regulate finance, 
[[PAGE 100]]
platforms, communications, and personal data. Sustainable prosecution depends upon 
coordinated invocation of these laws, not selective reliance on any single statute.[2] 
Judicial precedents have transformed statutory text into operational guardrails. Courts have 
clarified where investigative power begins, where it ends, and the consequences of crossing 
those limits. Recurrent failures—over-charging, unlawful search, routine arrest, excessive 
freezing, jurisdictional assumptions, mishandling of digital evidence, and data-protection non-
compliance—are not accidental. They are predictable outcomes of investigations conducted 
without adequate legal grounding.[3] 
For Investigating Officers, the central lesson of this chapter is unambiguous: legal thresholds 
precede investigative action. Necessity, proportionality, authorisation, jurisdictional nexus, and 
recorded satisfaction are not procedural formalities; they are conditions precedent to lawful 
investigation. Evidence law validates content only after procedural law legitimises collection. 
Sectoral exemptions facilitate investigation only within statutory purpose. Data-protection 
exemptions do not override constitutional or procedural safeguards.[4] 
From an administrative perspective, adherence to the legal framework: 
 
Protects Investigating Officers from adverse judicial findings 
 
Reduces pre-trial litigation and supervisory intervention 
 
Enhances institutional credibility and public confidence 
From a judicial perspective, legally disciplined investigation signals constitutional sensitivity, 
restraint, and professionalism, which courts consistently reward with deference to investigative 
outcomes.[5] 
This chapter therefore functions as the legal backbone of the SOP. It equips Investigating 
Officers to decide what powers exist, when they may be invoked, and how far they extend, before 
any operational step is taken. It is designed not merely to secure convictions, but to ensure that 
prosecutions are legally durable, resistant to challenge, and capable of surviving appellate 
scrutiny.[6] 
The succeeding chapters transition from legal foundation to procedural execution. Chapter 4 
addresses registration of FIRs and initiation of cybercrime investigation, applying the legal 
[[PAGE 101]]
principles articulated in this chapter to the first actionable stage of cyber policing. The 
effectiveness of all subsequent SOP chapters depends upon faithful adherence to the legal 
framework established herein.[7] 
 
CHAPTER 4 - JURISDICTION, FIR REGISTRATION & CASE 
INITIATION IN CYBERCRIME CASES 
4.1 Conceptual Positioning of Chapter 4 
This Chapter operationalises the legal framework articulated in Chapter 3 and converts abstract 
statutory powers into a disciplined, step-wise process for lawful initiation of cybercrime 
investigations. It governs the most sensitive phase of cyber policing: deciding where, when, and 
how criminal law is set into motion. Errors at this stage do not remain curable procedural 
defects; they often metastasize into fatal infirmities that contaminate search, seizure, arrest, and 
prosecution, even where digital evidence otherwise exists [1]. 
Cybercrime, unlike conventional offences, rarely conforms to territorial neatness. Victims, 
accused persons, devices, servers, intermediaries, and financial rails frequently span multiple 
police jurisdictions, states, and countries. This borderless architecture has historically led to two 
institutional failures: (a) refusal to register FIRs on jurisdictional pretexts, and (b) mechanical 
registration without jurisdictional reasoning, both of which courts have repeatedly deprecated 
[2]. Chapter 4 therefore establishes a jurisdiction-first but victim-centric SOP, harmonising the 
Information Technology Act, 2000, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), and 
binding judicial precedents. 
This Chapter consciously separates three distinct decision points which are often confused in 
practice: 
(i) competence to receive information, 
(ii) duty to register FIR, and 
(iii) authority to investigate. 
Failure to distinguish these stages has historically resulted in illegal burking of cybercrime 
[[PAGE 102]]
complaints, especially in cases involving financial frauds, social media offences, and cross-
border digital harm [3]. 
PART I – JURISDICTION & COMPETENCE IN CYBERCRIME CASES 
4.2 Jurisdiction in the Digital Environment: From Territory to Consequence 
Classical criminal procedure was designed for territorially anchored offences. Cybercrime 
dismantles this assumption by enabling criminal acts to be committed through keystrokes, 
scripts, or automated processes that may originate in one place, transit through multiple 
infrastructures, and culminate in harm elsewhere. Recognising this, Indian cyber law deliberately 
expands jurisdictional reach beyond physical presence [4]. 
Section 75 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 gives the Act explicit extra-territorial 
application, providing that offences or contraventions committed outside India are punishable if 
the act involves a computer resource located in India [5]. This provision is technologically 
neutral and deliberately broad, ensuring that the location of the computer resource—not the 
offender—is the jurisdictional anchor. In cybercrime cases, this may include servers, victim 
devices, payment gateways, cloud infrastructure, or intermediary systems located within India. 
Simultaneously, Section 173(1) of the BNSS, 2023 imposes a mandatory duty to record 
information relating to a cognizable offence, irrespective of whether the offence appears to have 
been committed within the territorial jurisdiction of the police station [6]. This provision marks a 
decisive legislative shift away from territorial gatekeeping and squarely places victim access to 
justice above administrative convenience. 
Read together, Section 75 of the IT Act and Section 173(1) BNSS dismantle the traditional 
excuse of “lack of jurisdiction” at the complaint stage. Jurisdiction is no longer a threshold 
barrier to FIR registration; it is a question to be resolved after information is recorded and 
evidence is preserved [7]. 
4.3 Virtual vs. Physical Jurisdiction: Reconciling Dual Realities 
Cybercrime investigations operate simultaneously in two planes: the virtual plane (networks, 
platforms, IP routing, data flows) and the physical plane (victim location, police station limits, 
[[PAGE 103]]
court jurisdiction). This duality has generated confusion among field officers accustomed to 
physical crime scenes [8]. 
The correct legal position is that virtual acts create physical consequences, and criminal law 
attaches jurisdiction to either. Section 199 of the BNSS (corresponding to settled CrPC 
principles) recognises that an offence may be tried where the act is done or where its 
consequence ensues. In cybercrime, the “act” may be distributed, automated, or anonymised, but 
the consequence financial loss, reputational harm, psychological injury manifests at the victim’s 
location [9]. 
Accordingly, jurisdiction may legitimately arise at: 
 
the place where the victim resides or carries on business, 
 
the place where the victim’s device was accessed or compromised, 
 
the place where financial loss was suffered, 
 
the place where the affected computer resource is located. 
This approach aligns with victim-centric justice and prevents procedural paralysis in digitally 
mediated crimes [10]. 
4.4 The “Keyboard Rule” of Cyber Jurisdiction 
For operational clarity, this SOP adopts what may be termed the “Keyboard Rule”—a 
functional doctrine derived from judicial reasoning rather than statutory text. Under this rule, 
jurisdiction may be asserted at any location where the effect of a keystroke is legally cognizable 
[11]. 
In practical terms, an Investigating Officer may assume competence if: 
 
the victim clicked, received, viewed, or acted upon digital content within the police 
station limits, 
 
a fraudulent transaction was authorised from within the jurisdiction, 
 
access credentials were compromised on a device located within the jurisdiction, 
 
psychological harm from online abuse manifested within the jurisdiction. 
[[PAGE 104]]
This doctrine ensures that cyber offenders do not exploit technological opacity to defeat 
jurisdiction and that victims are not forced to chase distant police stations for redress [12]. 
4.5 Jurisdiction vs. Investigation Authority 
A recurring institutional error is conflating jurisdiction to register an FIR with authority to 
conduct the entire investigation. The former is mandatory; the latter is transferable. Registration 
of an FIR does not irrevocably bind the police station to investigate the case to its conclusion 
Under BNSS, investigation may be lawfully transferred to the competent police station after FIR 
registration, either administratively or through judicial direction. What is impermissible is refusal 
to register the FIR at the threshold. Courts have repeatedly clarified that jurisdictional doubts 
cannot defeat the statutory duty to record information disclosing a cognizable offence [14]. 
This SOP therefore mandates a register-first, resolve-jurisdiction-later approach, particularly in 
cybercrime cases where digital evidence is volatile and delay may result in irreversible loss [15]. 
4.6 Decision Matrix for Investigating Officers (Textual SOP) 
Every cybercrime complaint received at a police station or cyber crime unit shall be assessed 
using the following decision logic: 
Step 1: Does the information disclose a cognizable offence under the IT Act, BNS, or allied 
laws? 
 
If No: Record as per law and take appropriate non-cognizable action. 
 
If Yes: Proceed to Step 2. 
Step 2: Does the offence appear to have a clear territorial nexus with this police station? 
 
If Yes: Register a Regular FIR immediately. 
 
If No or Doubtful: Proceed to Step 3. 
Step 3: Is the offence cognizable and time-sensitive (risk of evidence loss)? 
 
If Yes: Register a Zero FIR without delay. 
 
If No: Seek supervisory guidance but do not refuse registration. 
[[PAGE 105]]
This matrix is non-negotiable and deviation without recorded reasons shall invite supervisory 
scrutiny [16]. 
4.7 Supervisory Accountability in Jurisdictional Decisions 
Given the legal complexity of cyber jurisdiction, supervisory officers must actively oversee FIR 
registration decisions. SHO-level officers and Cyber Crime Unit heads shall review jurisdictional 
reasoning in all cyber FIRs within 24 hours of registration [17]. 
Failure to register FIRs on jurisdictional grounds, or directing complainants to other police 
stations without recording information, constitutes a breach of statutory duty and may attract 
disciplinary as well as penal consequences under applicable provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya 
Sanhita [18]. 
PART II – ZERO FIR: STANDARD OPERATING PROCEDURE IN 
CYBERCRIME CASES 
4.8 Zero FIR: Conceptual Foundation and Legal Character 
Zero FIR is not an administrative innovation or discretionary courtesy extended by the police; it 
is a statutorily compelled legal mechanism evolved to prevent denial of justice at the threshold 
stage of criminal law. In cybercrime cases, where territorial boundaries are routinely blurred by 
digital infrastructure, Zero FIR operates as a jurisdiction-neutral ignition point that preserves 
victim rights and volatile electronic evidence simultaneously [19]. 
A Zero FIR is an FIR registered by a police station without assigning a regular FIR number of 
that station, usually marked with serial number “0”, when the offence is cognizable but appears 
to have been committed outside the station’s territorial jurisdiction. Its legal validity is identical 
to that of a regular FIR; the only distinction lies in its temporary character pending transfer to the 
competent police station [20]. 
The Supreme Court and the Ministry of Home Affairs have repeatedly clarified that Zero FIR is 
not a diluted or provisional FIR. Once registered, it sets the criminal law in motion with full legal 
force, authorising lawful investigation steps such as evidence preservation, platform intimation, 
and supervisory reporting [21]. 
[[PAGE 106]]
4.9 Mandatory Nature of Zero FIR in Cybercrime Complaints 
Cybercrime complaints frequently involve cross-border elements: servers located in another 
state, payment gateways headquartered elsewhere, social media platforms operating from outside 
India, or accused persons using anonymisation tools. These features cannot be allowed to defeat 
the statutory duty of FIR registration [22]. 
Section 173(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 imposes an unequivocal 
obligation on every officer in charge of a police station to record information relating to the 
commission of a cognizable offence, irrespective of territorial jurisdiction. This provision 
statutorily absorbs and strengthens the judicial mandate laid down in Lalita Kumari v. 
Government of Uttar Pradesh [23]. 
The Ministry of Home Affairs, through multiple advisories, has expressly directed that refusal to 
register Zero FIR on jurisdictional grounds amounts to burking of crime and undermines rule of 
law. Cybercrime units are specifically instructed to prioritise registration over jurisdictional 
perfection, particularly where delay may lead to loss of electronic evidence [24]. 
Accordingly, in cybercrime cases, Zero FIR is not optional; it is mandatory wherever jurisdiction 
is doubtful but the offence is cognizable. 
4.10 Penal Consequences for Refusal or Delay in Zero FIR Registration 
The refusal to register a Zero FIR, or deliberate delay under the pretext of jurisdictional 
clarification, is not a mere procedural lapse. It attracts potential penal liability. Under the 
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, a public servant who knowingly disobeys a direction of law with 
intent to cause injury commits a punishable offence [25]. 
Section 199(c) of the BNS (corresponding to public servant disobedience) may be attracted 
where an officer refuses to register a Zero FIR despite clear disclosure of a cognizable cyber 
offence. Courts have consistently held that administrative convenience or workload cannot 
justify non-registration [26]. 
In addition to penal exposure, such refusal invites departmental action, adverse judicial remarks, 
and supervisory accountability. This SOP therefore treats Zero FIR registration as a non-
negotiable duty, deviation from which must be explained contemporaneously in writing [27]. 
[[PAGE 107]]
4.11 Scope of Zero FIR in Cybercrime Context 
Zero FIR is particularly critical in cybercrime cases involving: 
 
Online financial frauds where transactions route through multiple states, 
 
Social media offences where platforms are headquartered elsewhere, 
 
Identity theft and impersonation using foreign servers, 
 
Cryptocurrency-related frauds involving decentralised networks, 
 
Online sexual offences where victim protection requires immediate action. 
In all such cases, the receiving police station or cyber crime unit shall register a Zero FIR 
immediately upon disclosure of a cognizable offence, without directing the complainant to 
another jurisdiction [28]. 
4.12 Step-by-Step SOP for Registration of Zero FIR 
The following procedure shall be strictly followed by all police stations and cyber crime units in 
Uttar Pradesh: 
 Step 1: Receipt of Information 
Information may be received orally, in writing, electronically, or through NCRP 
integration. The mode of receipt does not dilute the duty to register FIR if cognizable 
offence is disclosed [29]. 
 Step 2: Recording of Zero FIR 
The FIR shall be recorded in the prescribed FIR register, clearly marked as “Zero FIR”, 
with complete particulars of the complainant, incident, and preliminary digital facts. 
Jurisdictional doubts, if any, shall be recorded narratively but shall not delay registration 
[30]. 
 Step 3: Immediate Preservation Actions 
Where necessary, the IO may initiate urgent evidence preservation measures, such as 
intimation to banks, intermediaries, or platforms, strictly limited to preservation and not 
substantive investigation [31]. 
 Step 4: GD Entry 
A General Diary entry shall be made recording the registration of Zero FIR, reasons for 
[[PAGE 108]]
treating it as Zero FIR, and immediate steps taken. This entry serves as a safeguard 
against later allegations of manipulation or post-facto justification [32]. 
4.13 Transfer Protocol: Zero FIR to Competent Police Station 
Zero FIR is inherently transitional. Once registered, it must be transferred to the police station 
having territorial jurisdiction for further investigation. However, such transfer must be orderly, 
documented, and complete [33]. 
Transfer shall include: 
 
Certified copy of Zero FIR, 
 
Complete Case Diary entries till date, 
 
All seized material or preserved digital evidence, 
 
Copies of correspondence with banks, intermediaries, or service providers, 
 
A forwarding note explaining jurisdictional basis for transfer. 
The transfer must be effected without undue delay, ordinarily within 48 hours, unless 
preservation actions necessitate brief retention [34]. 
4.14 Chain of Custody During Transfer 
In cybercrime cases, transfer of Zero FIR often coincides with transfer of electronic evidence. It 
is imperative that chain of custody is maintained uninterrupted. All handovers shall be 
documented with time, date, officer identity, and description of material transferred [35]. 
Any break or ambiguity in custody during this stage may fatally weaken the prosecution at trial, 
particularly where defence challenges authenticity of electronic records [36]. 
4.15 Supervisory Oversight of Zero FIR Transfers 
Supervisory officers shall review all Zero FIR transfers to ensure: 
 
FIR was not delayed, 
 
Transfer reasons are legally sound, 
 
Evidence preservation was not compromised, 
[[PAGE 109]]
 
Victim was not made to shuttle between police stations. 
Failure in supervisory oversight at this stage reflects systemic negligence and may attract 
institutional criticism during judicial review [37]. 
4.16 Victim-Centric Obligations Post Zero FIR 
The complainant shall be informed in writing about: 
 
Registration of Zero FIR, 
 
Proposed transfer to competent police station, 
 
Details of receiving police station. 
This transparency reinforces victim confidence and prevents allegations of suppression or 
abandonment of complaint [38]. 
PART III – PRELIMINARY ENQUIRY (PE) IN CYBERCRIME CASES: 
THE BNSS SHIFT 
4.17 Preliminary Enquiry in Cybercrime: Purpose and Misuse History 
Preliminary Enquiry (PE) has historically been one of the most misunderstood and misused 
instruments in Indian criminal procedure. Intended as a narrow exception to mandatory FIR 
registration, it was frequently employed as a shield for delay, dilution, or outright refusal to 
register complaints, particularly in complex or high-value offences [39]. Cybercrime 
investigations suffered disproportionately from this misuse, as technical complexity was often 
mistaken for legal ambiguity. 
Courts have consistently clarified that PE is not an alternative to FIR registration, nor a 
discretionary filtering mechanism to assess truthfulness or evidentiary sufficiency. Its sole 
purpose is to ascertain whether the information received discloses the commission of a 
cognizable offence, and nothing beyond that [40]. Any use of PE to test credibility, demand 
proof, or await expert opinion has been judicially condemned. 
With the enactment of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, the legislature has 
recalibrated the PE regime by statutorily defining its scope, duration, and accountability, 
particularly relevant for cybercrime cases where complexity and delay often coexist [41]. 
[[PAGE 110]]
4.18 The BNSS Departure from Lalita Kumari: The 14-Day Rule 
Under the earlier CrPC regime, guided by Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh, PE—
where permissible—was ordinarily to be completed within seven days [42]. While this timeline 
was effective for conventional disputes, it proved inadequate for technologically layered cyber 
offences where basic verification of digital facts itself may require coordination with banks, 
platforms, or intermediaries. 
Section 173(3) of the BNSS, 2023 introduces a statutory 14-day window for conducting PE in 
cases where the alleged offence is punishable with imprisonment of three to seven years. This 
category squarely includes several cybercrime-related offences such as cheating, identity theft, 
certain frauds, and technology-facilitated deception under the IT Act and the BNS [43]. 
This extension is not a dilution of victim rights; rather, it is a recognition of technological 
realities. However, the extension is conditional, not automatic. PE remains an exception, not 
the rule, and may be invoked only in legally permissible categories [44]. 
4.19 Cyber-Specific Categories Justifying Preliminary Enquiry 
In cybercrime policing, PE may be justified in limited, clearly definable scenarios where 
immediate registration of FIR without minimal verification risks either criminalising civil 
disputes or misclassifying technical incidents. This SOP recognises the following cyber-specific 
categories where PE may be lawfully undertaken: 
 Commercial and Business Email Compromise (BEC) Disputes 
Where allegations arise from complex commercial transactions, email spoofing, or 
vendor impersonation involving contractual relationships, a short PE may be necessary to 
distinguish criminal deception from civil breach [45]. 
 Abnormal Delay in Reporting Cyber Offences 
Cyber offences are often discovered belatedly. However, where reporting is delayed 
substantially and no explanation is apparent, PE may be used to ascertain whether 
criminality still subsists or whether evidence has irretrievably dissipated [46]. 
 Source Verification in High-Value or Complex Crypto Frauds 
In cryptocurrency-related complaints involving decentralised platforms, PE may be 
[[PAGE 111]]
required to identify whether the alleged activity constitutes fraud, market risk, or user 
negligence, without venturing into merits [47]. 
 Platform-Based Content Offences with Ambiguous Criminality 
Complaints relating to online content, parody, or speech where criminal intent is unclear 
may justify PE to determine whether statutory thresholds are met [48]. 
These categories are illustrative, not exhaustive. However, PE shall never be conducted merely 
because the offence is technical or unfamiliar [49]. 
4.20 Impermissible Grounds for Preliminary Enquiry 
The following grounds shall never justify PE in cybercrime cases: 
 
Lack of technical expertise at the police station, 
 
Absence of immediate documentary proof, 
 
Requirement of forensic confirmation, 
 
Pending opinion of senior officers, 
 
Anticipated jurisdictional transfer. 
Invocation of PE on these grounds amounts to illegal delay and may attract judicial censure [50]. 
4.21 Mandatory Documentation: General Diary Discipline 
To prevent misuse of PE, this SOP mandates strict documentation discipline. Every initiation 
and closure of PE must be recorded through a General Diary (GD) entry, specifying: 
 
Date and time of commencement of PE, 
 
Legal justification for invoking PE, 
 
Scope of enquiry (limited to disclosure of cognizable offence), 
 
Date and time of closure, 
 
Outcome: FIR registered or complaint closed with reasons. 
Failure to record GD entries renders the PE vulnerable to being characterised as an attempt to 
burke crime [51]. 
[[PAGE 112]]
If PE results in closure, a brief written communication must be supplied to the complainant, 
explaining reasons for non-registration, as mandated by judicial precedent [52]. 
4.22 PE and Evidence Preservation 
A common misconception is that PE prohibits any investigative action. This is incorrect. While 
substantive investigation is barred, evidence preservation is not. In cybercrime cases, PE must 
coexist with minimal preservation steps to prevent loss of volatile data [53]. 
Accordingly, during PE, IOs may: 
 
Advise complainants on preserving devices and accounts, 
 
Issue limited preservation requests to banks or platforms, 
 
Secure publicly available digital artefacts. 
However, coercive actions such as search, seizure, or interrogation are impermissible at the PE 
stage [54]. 
4.23 Time Discipline and Supervisory Review 
The 14-day period under BNSS is a hard outer limit, not a flexible guideline. Any delay beyond 
this period must be explained in writing and reviewed by supervisory officers. Silence or inertia 
will be construed against the investigating agency [55]. 
Supervisory officers shall periodically review all pending PEs to ensure they do not morph into 
de facto investigations without FIR registration. This oversight is critical in cybercrime units 
handling high complaint volumes [56]. 
4.24 Conversion of PE into FIR 
Where PE discloses the commission of a cognizable cyber offence, FIR registration shall be 
immediate and automatic. No fresh complaint or additional approval is required. The FIR shall 
reference the PE GD entries to maintain continuity and transparency [57]. 
Delay between PE conclusion and FIR registration is impermissible and may invalidate 
subsequent investigative steps [58]. 
[[PAGE 113]]
PART IV – FIR DRAFTING & SECTION SELECTION MATRIX IN 
CYBERCRIME CASES 
4.25 FIR in Cybercrime: From Procedural Trigger to Prosecutorial Anchor 
In cybercrime investigations, the First Information Report (FIR) performs a function far more 
consequential than merely setting criminal law into motion. It is the foundational prosecutorial 
document upon which the legality of every subsequent coercive act—search, seizure, arrest, 
forensic extraction, and finally chargesheet—will be judged. Courts have repeatedly emphasised 
that defects at the FIR stage do not remain confined to initiation; they propagate downstream and 
may ultimately vitiate the entire prosecution [59]. 
Unlike conventional crimes, cyber offences often lack immediate physical manifestation. Digital 
acts may be invisible, automated, or remotely executed, making the FIR the first structured 
articulation of digital harm, attribution, and legal suspicion. An FIR that fails to narrate the 
digital pathway of the offence risks being characterised as speculative or mechanical, even if 
strong evidence is later recovered [60]. 
This SOP therefore treats FIR drafting in cybercrime cases not as a clerical formality but as a 
deliberate legal exercise, requiring clarity, precision, and foresight of trial-stage scrutiny. 
4.26 The “Special vs. General” Rule in Section Selection 
One of the most frequent and damaging errors in cyber-FIRs is indiscriminate invocation of 
penal provisions without regard to legislative hierarchy. The Supreme Court, in Sharat Babu 
Digumarti v. Government of NCT of Delhi, clarified that where a special statute occupies the 
field, offences should ordinarily be examined within that statutory framework rather than 
mechanically resorting to general penal provisions [61]. 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 is a special law governing offences committed using 
computer resources. Where the factual ingredients of an offence squarely fall within IT Act 
provisions—such as identity theft, cheating by personation using computer resources, 
unauthorised access, or violation of privacy—those sections should be invoked consciously and 
specifically [62]. 
[[PAGE 114]]
However, the IT Act does not exclude the application of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. In 
many cybercrime cases, the digital act constitutes the means, while the harm attracts general 
penal offences such as cheating, criminal breach of trust, intimidation, or sexual exploitation. In 
such cases, careful and reasoned dual invocation of IT Act and BNS provisions may be legally 
appropriate [63]. 
What is impermissible is casual duplication without articulation of how each provision is 
attracted. Courts have deprecated FIRs that merely list sections without factual linkage, 
describing such drafting as non-application of mind [64]. 
4.27 Principles Governing Section Selection in Cyber FIRs 
The following principles shall guide section selection: 
 Technology-Specific Conduct → IT Act First 
Where the gravamen of the offence lies in misuse of a computer resource, the IT Act must 
be examined as the primary statute [65]. 
 Harm-Based Consequences → BNS Supplement 
Where digital conduct results in deception, loss, intimidation, or sexual harm, 
corresponding BNS provisions may be added with reasons [66]. 
 Avoid Overloading 
Excessive section invocation weakens rather than strengthens prosecution by creating 
internal inconsistencies [67]. 
 Narrative Justification 
Every invoked section must be supported by factual narration within the FIR, not merely 
listed at the end [68]. 
4.28 Essential Fields Checklist for Cybercrime FIRs 
To ensure legal sufficiency and evidentiary continuity, every cybercrime FIR must, as far as 
information permits at initiation stage, clearly record the following essential fields: 
[[PAGE 115]]
 Identity Markers of the Suspect 
Instead of generic expressions such as “unknown person”, FIRs should record available 
digital identifiers such as: 
o Username or handle, 
o Profile URL, 
o Email address or phone number used, 
o Wallet address or transaction ID (where applicable). 
Recording partial identifiers demonstrates investigative application of mind and assists later 
attribution [69]. 
 (b) Temporal Precision 
The FIR must distinguish between: 
o Date and time of the cyber act (transaction, access, communication), 
o Date and time of discovery by the victim, 
o Date and time of reporting to police. 
This distinction is crucial in addressing delay-related challenges and limitation arguments [70]. 
 (c) Technical Identifiers 
Where available at the initial stage, FIRs should record: 
o IP addresses, 
o URLs or domain names, 
o IMEI or device identifiers, 
o Hash values (if immediately available). 
Absence of these details is not fatal, but their presence strengthens early evidentiary linkage [71]. 
[[PAGE 116]]
4.29 FIR Drafting Discipline 
Cyber FIRs frequently fail due to mechanical reproduction of statutory language without factual 
grounding. Courts have consistently held that FIRs are not expected to prove the case, but they 
must disclose prima facie commission of a cognizable offence through factual narration [72]. 
The FIR narrative should therefore: 
 
Describe the digital sequence of events chronologically, 
 
Explain how the victim interacted with the digital medium, 
 
Articulate the harm suffered, 
 
Link the digital act to legal injury. 
Overuse of technical jargon without explanation is discouraged, as it may confuse judicial 
officers unfamiliar with digital architecture [73]. 
4.30 Standard Drafting Templates for Common Cyber Offences 
To promote consistency and legal clarity, the following illustrative drafting templates may be 
used, with necessary factual customisation: 
 Phishing / Fraudulent Link Cases: 
“The complainant states that on [date], at approximately [time], they received a message 
containing a hyperlink hosted at [URL], purporting to be from a legitimate service. Upon 
clicking the link and entering credentials, unauthorised transactions were effected from 
the complainant’s account, resulting in wrongful loss…” [74] 
 
 Social Media Impersonation: 
“The complainant reports that an unknown person created a social media profile bearing 
their name and photographs at [profile URL], and used the same to communicate with 
third parties, causing reputational harm and deception…” [75] 
These templates are guides, not substitutes for application of mind. 
[[PAGE 117]]
4.31 FIR and Future Coercive Actions: Laying the Legal Foundation 
Search, seizure, and arrest derive their legal legitimacy from the FIR. Courts scrutinise whether 
the FIR disclosed sufficient grounds to justify subsequent intrusion into privacy and liberty [76]. 
FIRs that are vague, overbroad, or internally inconsistent invite adverse inference when coercive 
actions are challenged under constitutional remedies. 
Accordingly, FIR drafting must anticipate: 
 
Search warrant scrutiny, 
 
Arrest justification, 
 
Forensic admissibility, 
 
Chargesheet coherence. 
An FIR drafted with investigative convenience but without prosecutorial foresight often 
collapses at trial [77]. 
4.32 Supervisory Vetting of Cyber FIRs 
Given the complexity of cyber offences, supervisory review of FIRs is indispensable. Senior 
officers shall vet cyber FIRs for: 
 
Correct section selection, 
 
Jurisdictional reasoning, 
 
Narrative coherence, 
 
Evidentiary orientation. 
Such vetting is not interference but institutional quality control, ensuring that investigations are 
legally defensible from inception [78]. 
 
[[PAGE 118]]
PART V – HANDLING DELAYS, E-COMPLAINTS & NCRP 
INTEGRATION IN CYBERCRIME CASES 
4.33 Delay in Cybercrime Reporting: Understanding the “Discovery Doctrine” 
Delay in reporting is an endemic feature of cybercrime, not an aberration. Unlike conventional 
offences where harm is immediately perceptible, cyber offences often remain latent, concealed 
within transaction statements, platform dashboards, or system logs that are accessed only 
periodically. Courts have increasingly recognised that in cybercrime, the time of discovery 
frequently diverges from the time of commission, and that this divergence must be judicially 
accommodated rather than mechanically penalised [79]. 
This SOP adopts the Discovery Doctrine as an operational principle: the clock for assessing 
delay in cybercrime cases must be understood with reference to when the victim reasonably 
became aware of the offence, not merely when the digital act occurred. This approach aligns 
with judicial reasoning that treats cyber offences as continuing or concealed wrongs until 
discovery [80]. 
Accordingly, delay per se does not invalidate an FIR in cybercrime cases. What is required is 
transparent explanation, not instantaneous reporting. 
4.34 Recording and Condonation of Delay in Cyber FIRs 
Where delay exists between the date of occurrence and the date of reporting, the FIR must 
explicitly narrate the reasons for such delay. Silence on delay often invites adverse inference, 
whereas explanation neutralises suspicion [81]. 
Common cyber-specific grounds for delay include: 
 
Time taken to obtain bank statements or transaction confirmations, 
 
Delay in platform responses or account access, 
 
Gradual discovery of unauthorised access or data misuse, 
 
Initial belief that the incident was technical error rather than criminal act. 
The FIR narrative should therefore include a sentence to the effect that: 
“The delay in reporting occurred due to the time taken by the complainant to obtain necessary 
[[PAGE 119]]
transaction records / logs / platform confirmations, and the offence came to light upon such 
verification.” [82] 
This articulation safeguards the prosecution from later arguments that the complaint is an 
afterthought or embellishment. 
4.35 Delay and Preliminary Enquiry: Avoiding Conflation 
Delay alone does not automatically justify Preliminary Enquiry. While abnormal delay may be 
one of the permissible categories for PE, the presence of delay cannot be used as a blanket 
justification to defer FIR registration where cognizable offence is otherwise disclosed [83]. 
Investigating Officers must therefore distinguish between: 
 
Explained delay, which requires no PE, and 
 
Unexplained or suspicious delay, which may justify limited PE strictly within BNSS 
parameters. 
Conflation of these categories leads to illegal postponement of FIRs and has been judicially 
deprecated [84]. 
4.36 Electronic Complaints and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (NCRP) 
The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (NCRP) has been established to facilitate online 
reporting of cybercrime complaints, recognising the digital-native nature of such offences. 
However, it is legally settled that NCRP complaints are not FIRs by themselves. They are 
information inputs that must be assessed and converted into FIRs where cognizable offences are 
disclosed [85]. 
This SOP clarifies that NCRP exists to supplement, not supplant, statutory FIR registration 
under BNSS. Police stations and cyber crime units remain legally responsible for evaluating 
NCRP complaints and taking appropriate action under criminal procedure [86]. 
4.37 SOP for Conversion of NCRP Complaints into FIRs 
The following standard procedure shall be followed upon receipt of an NCRP complaint: 
[[PAGE 120]]
 Step 1: Acknowledgement and Scrutiny 
The complaint shall be acknowledged electronically and examined to determine whether 
it discloses a cognizable offence [87]. 
 Step 2: Jurisdictional Assessment 
Jurisdiction shall be assessed using the principles laid down in Part I of this Chapter. 
Jurisdictional doubt shall not delay registration [88]. 
 Step 3: FIR Registration 
Where cognizable offence is disclosed, FIR shall be registered forthwith, either as a 
regular FIR or Zero FIR, as applicable. The FIR shall reference the NCRP complaint ID 
for traceability [89]. 
 Step 4: GD Entry 
A General Diary entry shall record the receipt of NCRP complaint, decision taken, and 
FIR number generated, ensuring auditability [90]. 
4.38 Anonymous NCRP Complaints: Special Handling 
Certain NCRP categories permit anonymous reporting, particularly in cases involving child 
sexual abuse material or sexually explicit content. While anonymity complicates attribution, it 
does not dilute the duty to act where cognizable offence is disclosed [91]. 
In such cases: 
 
FIR may be registered suo motu based on information received, 
 
Investigation shall proceed without insisting on complainant identity, 
 
Victim protection and evidence preservation shall be prioritised. 
Courts have recognised that insistence on identity disclosure in such cases may deter reporting 
and undermine public interest [92]. 
4.39 Evidentiary Value of NCRP Submissions 
Attachments uploaded on NCRP, such as screenshots, URLs, or transaction details, form part of 
the initial information. While they are not automatically admissible evidence, they serve as leads 
requiring preservation and verification [93]. 
[[PAGE 121]]
Investigating Officers must therefore promptly secure original sources of such material to 
prevent later evidentiary challenges arising from reliance on secondary copies alone. 
4.40 Supervisory Monitoring of E-Complaint Conversion 
Supervisory officers shall periodically review NCRP complaint handling to ensure: 
 
Timely conversion into FIRs where required, 
 
No systemic delays or backlogs, 
 
No selective registration. 
Failure to convert cognizable NCRP complaints into FIRs reflects institutional inertia and may 
attract judicial scrutiny during writ proceedings [94].
