CHAPTER 5 - DIGITAL CRIME SCENE MANAGEMENT 
(PHYSICAL & VIRTUAL) 
5.1 Conceptual Foundation of Digital Crime Scene Management 
The transformation of crime through digitalisation has fundamentally altered the evidentiary 
landscape of criminal investigations. In contemporary policing, crimes are no longer confined to 
physical acts occurring at visible locations; instead, they frequently manifest through electronic 
interactions, remote access, automated processes, and platform-mediated conduct. As a result, 
digital artefacts now constitute primary evidence rather than mere corroborative material [1]. 
A digital crime scene is not limited to a physical space containing electronic devices. It extends 
to virtual environments, including cloud infrastructures, online platforms, financial systems, 
communication services, and data repositories controlled by third parties. These environments 
collectively form an evidentiary ecosystem where actions leave traces that are intangible, 
volatile, and often transient [2]. 
Unlike traditional physical crime scenes, where evidence degradation is gradual and observable, 
digital crime scenes are inherently fragile. Routine actions—such as powering on a device, 
connecting it to a network, or allowing background processes to execute—may permanently alter 
or destroy crucial evidence without leaving visible signs of interference. This characteristic 
demands a higher standard of restraint, documentation, and technical awareness from 
investigating officers at the earliest stage [3]. 
Digital crime scene management therefore represents a legal–forensic discipline, not a purely 
technical exercise. The manner in which digital evidence is identified, secured, preserved, and 
documented directly determines its admissibility under evidentiary law and its credibility during 
trial. Courts increasingly scrutinise first-responder conduct in cybercrime cases, and deficiencies 
at this stage are frequently exploited during cross-examination to challenge authenticity, chain of 
custody, and investigative fairness [4]. 
5.2 Position of Chapter 5 within the SOP Architecture 
This Chapter is intentionally placed after Chapter 4 (Jurisdiction, FIR Registration & Case 
Initiation) and before coercive and investigative chapters. The sequencing is deliberate. 
[[PAGE 127]]
 
Chapter 4 answers when and how criminal law is activated 
 
Chapter 5 answers how evidence is protected at the moment of first contact 
 
Subsequent chapters address search, seizure, forensic examination, and prosecution 
Digital crime scene management functions as the procedural firewall between lawful initiation 
and lawful investigation. Any failure at this stage contaminates every subsequent step, regardless 
of the strength of forensic analysis or confessional material [5]. 
This Chapter applies to: 
 
Police stations 
 
Cyber Crime Units 
 
District Cyber Cells 
 
First responders assisting specialised teams 
and governs both physical and virtual crime scenes, including hybrid environments where 
conventional and digital evidence coexist. 
5.3 Objectives and Operational Scope 
The objectives of this Chapter are fourfold: 
1. To provide a standardised, legally defensible framework for securing and managing 
digital crime scenes. 
2. To equip Investigating Officers with clear first-responder protocols that minimise 
evidentiary risk. 
3. To prevent contamination, spoliation, and unauthorised access to digital evidence. 
4. To ensure that digital evidence withstands scrutiny under BNSS, IT Act, and evidentiary 
jurisprudence. 
The scope of this Chapter covers: 
 
Standalone digital devices 
[[PAGE 128]]
 
Networked and enterprise systems 
 
Live and powered-off systems 
 
Cloud-only and platform-controlled evidence 
 
IoT and embedded devices 
 
Hybrid crime scenes 
This Chapter does not authorise forensic examination; it governs pre-forensic preservation and 
documentation only. 
5.4 Digital Crime Scene: Classification and Typology 
For operational clarity, digital crime scenes are classified into three categories: 
 Physical Digital Crime Scene 
A tangible location where digital devices or systems are physically present and accessible, such 
as residences, offices, data centres, cyber cafés, or institutional premises [6]. 
 Virtual (Cloud-Based) Crime Scene 
An evidentiary environment existing entirely on remote systems or platforms, including social 
media accounts, cloud storage, SaaS applications, payment gateways, and online dashboards [7]. 
 Hybrid Crime Scene 
A combination of physical devices and virtual environments, such as a mobile phone accessing 
cloud-hosted accounts or a workstation connected to enterprise servers. 
Each category presents distinct risks and requires differentiated handling, but documentation 
discipline and legal compliance remain constant across all types. 
5.5 Role and Responsibility of the First Responder 
In digital investigations, the first responder is often the most consequential actor. Actions 
taken—or consciously avoided—during the first minutes of contact can preserve or permanently 
destroy evidence. 
[[PAGE 129]]
The first responder shall be responsible for: 
 
Securing the digital crime scene 
 
Preventing unauthorised interaction with devices or systems 
 
Identifying potential digital evidence sources 
 
Documenting original conditions accurately 
 
Coordinating with cyber units and forensic experts 
The first responder shall not: 
 
Explore files, applications, or accounts 
 
Test passwords or credentials 
 
Power devices on or off without justification 
 
Attempt “preliminary verification” of content 
Courts treat first-responder conduct as a reflection of investigative integrity, and unexplained 
deviations are frequently construed against the prosecution [8]. 
5.6 Core Principles Governing Digital Crime Scene Management 
All actions under this Chapter shall be guided by the following non-negotiable principles: 
 Preservation over exploration 
 Documentation over assumption 
 Restraint over speed 
 Legality over convenience 
These principles ensure that digital evidence remains authentic, verifiable, and admissible, and 
that officers are protected from allegations of manipulation or negligence. 
[[PAGE 130]]
5.7 Transition to Operational Procedures 
Having established the conceptual and legal foundation, the following sections of this Chapter 
will prescribe step-by-step operational SOPs for: 
 Securing physical digital crime scenes 
 Handling powered-on and powered-off devices 
 Managing live systems and volatile data 
 Preserving virtual and cloud-based evidence 
 Preventing contamination and spoliation 
 Documentation, photography, seizure memos, and chain of custody 
 IO quick checklists and decision matrices 
Each section will combine theory + field usability, ensuring that officers can both understand 
why a procedure exists and how to apply it under operational pressure. 
5.8 Securing Physical Digital Crime Scenes 
A physical digital crime scene refers to any tangible location where digital devices, electronic 
systems, or data-bearing infrastructure connected with an offence are found. Such locations may 
include private residences, offices, commercial establishments, server rooms, cyber cafés, 
educational institutions, financial entities, or any premises where computers, mobile devices, 
storage media, network equipment, or surveillance systems are used. 
In cybercrime investigations, physical digital crime scenes are rarely limited to a single device. 
They often constitute hybrid environments, where conventional physical evidence coexists with 
fragile and volatile digital evidence. Securing such scenes is therefore a time-sensitive and 
legally significant responsibility of the first responder, and errors at this stage are frequently 
irreparable. 
Unlike conventional physical evidence, digital evidence can be altered or destroyed 
instantaneously through routine actions such as powering on a system, connecting it to a 
network, or permitting automated background processes to run. Accordingly, the objective of 
[[PAGE 131]]
securing a physical digital crime scene is not exploration or verification, but preservation, 
isolation, and documentation. 
5.8.1 Immediate Scene Control and Isolation 
Upon arrival at a suspected physical digital crime scene, the first responder shall immediately 
assume control of the premises. 
The following actions are mandatory: 
 
Secure the location to prevent unauthorised entry or movement. 
 
Restrict access strictly to essential police personnel. 
 
Prevent occupants, employees, family members, or staff from interacting with any 
electronic device or system. 
 
Establish a controlled perimeter where necessary, using physical barriers or officer 
supervision. 
 
Record the identity, role, and presence of all persons found at the scene. 
It is a common but critical error to permit occupants to “shut down systems”, “log out accounts”, 
or “secure data”. Such actions, though often presented as protective, frequently result in loss of 
volatile data, alteration of logs, or destruction of encryption keys. The first responder must 
assertively prevent such interaction, while maintaining professional restraint. 
5.8.2 Identification of Digital Evidence Sources 
After securing access control, the first responder shall conduct a systematic visual survey of the 
scene to identify potential sources of digital evidence. 
This survey shall be observational only and must not involve operating or manipulating devices. 
Potential sources include, but are not limited to: 
 
Desktop computers, laptops, and workstations 
 
Mobile phones, tablets, smart watches, and wearable devices 
 
External storage media such as USB drives, external hard disks, memory cards 
[[PAGE 132]]
 
Servers, Network Attached Storage (NAS), and backup units 
 
Routers, switches, modems, firewalls, and CCTV/DVR systems 
 
Smart devices and IoT equipment such as biometric systems, access controls, smart TVs, 
or home automation hubs 
Each identified device or system shall be mentally mapped to its location, apparent function, 
and connectivity, but left in its existing state unless immediate action is justified to prevent 
evidence loss. 
5.8.3 Preservation of Original State 
The foundational rule of digital crime scene management is preservation of the original state. 
 
Devices shall not be powered on or powered off at the scene without clear legal and 
forensic justification. 
 
No application, file, folder, email, or account shall be opened or explored. 
 
No peripheral device (USB, keyboard, storage media) shall be connected to any system. 
 
No passwords, PINs, biometric inputs, or credentials shall be tested casually or 
experimentally. 
Even minimal interaction can alter timestamps, system logs, or metadata, which defence counsel 
frequently exploit to allege evidence manipulation. Officers must therefore prioritise restraint 
over curiosity. 
5.8.4 Network and Connectivity Safeguards 
Network connectivity presents a significant risk at physical digital crime scenes, as it enables: 
 
Remote tampering or deletion of data 
 
Activation of remote wipe or encryption mechanisms 
 
Ongoing commission of offences through connected systems 
[[PAGE 133]]
Where legally permissible and technically justified, the first responder may take limited steps to 
prevent unauthorised remote access, subject to documentation. 
Preferred practices include: 
 
Physical disconnection of Ethernet cables rather than software-based network changes. 
 
Isolation of mobile devices using signal-blocking methods where available. 
 
Avoidance of configuration changes to routers or network equipment. 
Any action affecting connectivity must be documented with time, method, and rationale, as 
network isolation is often questioned during trial. 
5.8.5 Coordination with Cyber Units and Forensic Experts 
Physical digital crime scenes frequently involve technical complexity beyond the training of 
general duty officers. Early coordination is therefore essential. 
The first responder shall: 
 
Inform the designated cyber crime unit or district cyber cell immediately upon identifying 
digital evidence. 
 
Seek guidance before shutting down, disconnecting, or seizing critical systems such as 
servers or enterprise workstations. 
 
Facilitate timely arrival or remote consultation of forensic experts where available. 
This coordination ensures that decisions taken at the scene are technically sound, legally 
defensible, and institutionally supported. 
5.8.6 Legal Authority and Procedural Compliance 
Securing a digital crime scene does not dispense with legal safeguards. All actions must be 
grounded in lawful authority and proportionality. 
Investigating officers shall ensure that: 
 
Search and seizure actions are supported by lawful authority as required. 
[[PAGE 134]]
 
Any interference with devices or systems is necessary for evidence preservation or harm 
prevention. 
 
Rights relating to privacy and procedural fairness are respected. 
Courts have repeatedly emphasised that illegality at the evidence collection stage cannot be 
cured by subsequent forensic accuracy. Therefore, lawful restraint is a prosecutorial asset, not 
an investigative weakness. 
5.8.7 Documentation of Scene Securing Actions 
Every step taken to secure a physical digital crime scene must be contemporaneously 
Documentation shall include: 
 
Time of arrival and scene control 
 
Access restrictions imposed 
 
Devices and systems identified 
 
Actions taken and actions consciously avoided 
 
Reasons for any deviation from standard procedure 
This documentation forms the foundation of later case diaries, seizure memos, and court 
testimony. In judicial scrutiny, what is not documented is presumed not to have occurred. 
5.8.8 Defence Resilience and Evidentiary Value 
Securing a physical digital crime scene is not merely an operational task; it is a defence-
resilience measure. 
Most challenges to digital evidence arise not from forensic reports but from allegations that: 
 
Devices were accessed improperly 
 
Systems were altered at the scene 
 
Evidence was planted or manipulated 
 
Chain of custody was compromised from inception 
[[PAGE 135]]
Strict adherence to scene-securing SOPs significantly reduces the credibility of such challenges 
and strengthens the prosecution narrative. 
5.8.9 Operational Principle 
The officer at the scene must always remember: 
In digital investigations, doing less—lawfully and deliberately—often preserves more. 
Accordingly, restraint, documentation, and legal compliance are the most effective tools 
available to the first responder at a physical digital crime scene. 
5.9 Handling Digital Devices at the Crime Scene 
Digital devices encountered at a crime scene are not merely containers of information; they are 
dynamic evidentiary environments whose state, configuration, and interaction history directly 
affect evidentiary value. Improper handling at the scene can irreversibly alter data, corrupt 
metadata, destroy volatile information, or render electronic evidence legally inadmissible. This 
section prescribes mandatory standard operating procedures for handling digital devices at 
the scene, focusing on forensic integrity, legal compliance, and defence resilience. 
The procedures below apply to all digital devices, irrespective of ownership, value, or apparent 
relevance, until a reasoned assessment is completed and documented. 
5.9.1 Governing Principles for Device Handling 
All handling of digital devices at the scene shall be guided by the following principles: 
1. Preserve the device in the condition in which it is found to the maximum extent 
possible. 
2. Minimise interaction to avoid alteration of data, metadata, or system logs. 
3. Document every observation and action contemporaneously. 
4. Act only under lawful authority and proportional necessity. 
5. Respect privacy and data protection safeguards, particularly where devices may 
contain third-party or unrelated personal data. 
[[PAGE 136]]
No exploratory or confirmatory examination shall be conducted by untrained personnel or 
without proper authorisation. The scene is not the place for verification; it is the place for 
preservation. 
5.9.2 Categories of Digital Devices Covered 
The SOPs in this section apply to, but are not limited to, the following categories: 
 
Desktop computers and workstations 
 
Laptop computers and portable systems 
 
Servers and networked storage devices 
 
Mobile phones, tablets, and wearable devices 
 
Routers, modems, switches, and firewalls 
 
CCTV systems, DVRs/NVRs, and access control units 
 
Internet of Things (IoT) devices such as smart TVs, smart locks, biometric systems, voice 
assistants, and automation hubs 
Each category may present distinct technical risks, but the legal obligation of restraint and 
documentation remains uniform. 
5.9.3 Handling Powered-On Devices (Live Systems) 
A powered-on device, also referred to as a live system, may contain volatile data such as running 
processes, encryption keys, unsaved files, active sessions, and live network connections. Such 
data is lost upon shutdown or reboot and may be critical to establishing intent, attribution, or 
chronology. 
 
Do not switch off, reboot, lock, or log into the device unless expressly justified and 
 
Do not interact with open applications, files, browsers, or messaging platforms. 
 
Observe and record visible indicators only, including: 
[[PAGE 137]]
o Screen display and open applications 
o Logged-in user profile (if visible) 
o System date and time as displayed 
o Network indicators (Wi-Fi, Ethernet, mobile data icons) 
 
Photograph the screen and device clearly before any further action. 
 
Prevent unauthorised access by physically securing the device. 
 
Isolate network connectivity only when necessary to prevent remote interference, and 
document the method used. 
Correct Handling Example: 
A powered-on laptop displaying an active financial dashboard is photographed, network-isolated 
through physical cable removal, and left untouched pending forensic examination. 
Incorrect Handling Example: 
An officer closes applications “to see what else is running”, altering session data and 
timestamps, later leading to defence allegations of evidence manipulation. 
5.9.4 Handling Powered-Off Devices 
A powered-off device generally preserves stored data in a relatively stable condition and should 
be kept so unless expert guidance indicates otherwise. 
 
Do not power on the device at the scene. 
 
Do not connect chargers, power cables, or external peripherals. 
 
Do not attempt to unlock, test credentials, or bypass security features. 
 
Remove external storage media (USB drives, memory cards) only if it can be done 
safely and documented. 
 
Label, seal, and package the device in its powered-off state for forensic examination. 
[[PAGE 138]]
Correct Handling Example: 
A switched-off desktop CPU is seized, labelled, sealed, and transported for forensic imaging 
without being powered on. 
Incorrect Handling Example: 
Powering on a seized mobile phone “to check contents”, triggering encryption or remote wipe 
mechanisms. 
5.9.5 Mobile Devices: Special Precautions 
Mobile phones and tablets pose unique risks due to constant network connectivity, encryption, 
and remote management features. 
Mandatory Precautions: 
 
Avoid interaction with the screen, applications, or notifications. 
 
If the device is powered on, photograph the screen state immediately. 
 
Prevent network connectivity using shielding methods where available. 
 
Do not allow the device to auto-lock through inactivity if avoidable without interaction. 
 
Package mobile devices individually using protective and signal-blocking materials. 
Mobile devices are frequently the subject of intense defence scrutiny; meticulous handling and 
documentation are therefore essential. 
5.9.6 Routers, Servers, and Network Equipment 
Network devices often contain configuration data, access logs, and traffic records critical to 
cybercrime investigations. 
 
Do not reset, reboot, or reconfigure network equipment. 
 
Document: 
o Indicator lights and status 
o Connected cables and ports 
[[PAGE 139]]
o Apparent network topology as observed 
 
Servers supporting live operations shall not be seized or shut down without coordination, 
due to risk of data loss and service disruption. 
 
Seek immediate guidance from cyber units or forensic experts before any action. 
Incorrect Practice: 
Unplugging a router without documentation, resulting in loss of volatile logs and raising 
allegations of evidence destruction. 
5.9.7 IoT and Embedded Devices 
IoT and embedded systems may store limited but highly probative data, such as access logs, 
timestamps, or sensor activity. 
 
Identify all smart and connected devices in the environment. 
 
Avoid interaction via mobile applications, voice commands, or remote interfaces. 
 
Photograph device placement, indicators, and connectivity. 
 
Preserve hubs or controllers linked to such devices. 
Even small embedded devices may become pivotal in reconstructing events and timelines. 
5.9.8 Labeling, Packaging, and Transport 
Proper labeling and packaging protect both evidence integrity and officer credibility. 
 Labeling: 
o Use tamper-evident labels indicating case number, device ID, date, time, and officer 
details. 
 Packaging: 
o Use anti-static packaging for computers and storage media. 
o Use shielding materials for mobile and wireless devices. 
[[PAGE 140]]
o Package each device separately unless technically inseparable. 
 Transport: 
o Transport devices promptly to secure storage or forensic facilities. 
o Avoid exposure to heat, moisture, magnetic fields, or physical shock. 
o Maintain uninterrupted chain of custody documentation. 
5.9.9 Privacy and Data Protection Considerations 
While handling digital devices, officers shall ensure that: 
 
Access is limited strictly to investigative necessity. 
 
Personal data unrelated to the offence is not accessed, copied, or disclosed. 
 
Devices are secured to prevent leakage or misuse of data. 
Failure to observe privacy safeguards may result in legal challenges, exclusion of evidence, or 
departmental liability, irrespective of investigative intent. 
5.9.10 Evidentiary Integrity and Court Readiness 
Courts frequently assess digital evidence not only on technical merit but on how devices were 
handled at the scene. Defence challenges commonly target: 
 
Unauthorised access 
 
Device operation without justification 
 
Incomplete documentation 
 
Breaks in chain of custody 
Strict adherence to this section ensures that digital devices remain authentic, verifiable, and 
admissible, and that investigating officers can confidently defend their actions during cross-
examination. 
At the digital crime scene, preservation is an action; restraint is a skill. 
[[PAGE 141]]
Officers must therefore act with deliberation, discipline, and accountability when handling digital 
devices at the scene. 
5.10 Virtual and Cloud-Only Crime Scenes 
A virtual or cloud-only crime scene exists where relevant digital evidence is hosted on remote 
systems and online platforms, and no physical device is immediately accessible to the 
investigating officer. In such cases, the “scene” comprises digitally mediated environments—
accounts, platforms, dashboards, logs, and data repositories—controlled wholly or substantially 
by third-party service providers. 
Virtual crime scenes are now routine in offences involving online financial fraud, identity theft, 
impersonation, data theft, cyberstalking, platform-based abuse, and technology-enabled cheating. 
These environments are characterised by high volatility, automated retention limits, and 
jurisdictional complexity, making prompt, accurate, and lawful action essential. 
The absence of a physical device does not diminish evidentiary value; rather, it heightens the 
importance of documentation, preservation, and procedural discipline. 
5.10.1 What Constitutes a Virtual Crime Scene 
A virtual crime scene may include, inter alia: 
 
Social media accounts, pages, posts, messages, profiles, and metadata 
 
Email accounts and web-based communication platforms 
 
Cloud storage services (documents, images, backups, logs) 
 
Online banking portals, payment gateways, and digital wallets 
 
Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) dashboards and user consoles 
 
E-commerce accounts, transaction histories, and order records 
 
Collaboration tools, forums, and messaging applications 
Such environments may be controlled by intermediaries located outside the territorial jurisdiction 
of the investigating agency, and often outside India. Control, access, and retention policies are 
governed by provider terms and applicable law, not by police custody. 
[[PAGE 142]]
5.10.2 Immediate Documentation of Virtual Evidence 
Because virtual evidence can be altered or removed without notice, immediate documentation 
is the first and most critical preservation step. 
SOP Procedure: 
 
Record the initial discovery of the virtual crime scene with: 
o Date and time 
o Source of information (complaint, NCRP, open-source, referral) 
o Manner of access (publicly accessible, victim-provided access, lawful access) 
 
Capture screenshots or screen recordings of relevant content, including: 
o Webpages, profiles, posts, messages, transaction details 
o URLs, usernames, account identifiers, visible timestamps 
 
Ensure screenshots clearly display: 
o Full browser address bar 
o Page identifiers and account context 
Screenshots and recordings are preliminary preservation measures. They do not substitute for 
lawful acquisition from the service provider, but they establish contemporaneous existence and 
context. 
Incorrect Practice: 
Relying on verbal descriptions or memory, resulting in evidentiary gaps when content is later 
removed. 
5.10.3 Issuing Preservation Requests 
Virtual crime scenes are uniquely susceptible to spoliation through deletion, whether by suspects, 
automated retention policies, or platform moderation. 
[[PAGE 143]]
 
Issue preservation requests without delay to the relevant service provider or 
intermediary. 
 
Clearly specify: 
o Accounts, identifiers, or URLs involved 
o Categories of data to be preserved (content, logs, metadata) 
o Relevant date and time range 
 
Maintain written records of: 
o Time and mode of issuance 
o Recipient details 
o Acknowledgement or response received 
Preservation requests are time-critical and must precede formal legal processes for data 
acquisition wherever feasible. 
Field Example: 
In a social media impersonation case, prompt preservation prevents deletion of the fake profile 
and associated access logs. 
5.10.4 Lawful Access and Acquisition: Limits at the Scene Stage 
Investigating officers shall clearly distinguish between documentation, preservation, and 
acquisition. 
At the digital crime scene stage: 
 
Officers may document publicly visible or lawfully accessible content. 
 
Officers shall not: 
o Attempt unauthorised access to accounts 
o Use victim credentials without legal basis 
o Circumvent security measures 
[[PAGE 144]]
o Engage with suspects through the platform 
Data acquisition must follow lawful procedures, appropriate authorisation, and prescribed 
formats. Any deviation risks evidentiary exclusion and allegations of illegal access. 
5.10.5 Coordination with Service Providers and Intermediaries 
Virtual crime scenes are often controlled by third-party intermediaries. 
 
Identify the correct legal compliance or law-enforcement contact point of the provider. 
 
Use prescribed formats and channels for preservation and data requests. 
 
Ensure requests are specific, proportionate, and legally authorised. 
 
Track response timelines and escalate delays through supervisory channels. 
Informal communication or vague requests frequently result in incomplete responses or later 
evidentiary challenges. 
5.10.6 Jurisdictional and Cross-Border Considerations 
Virtual crime scenes may involve: 
 
Data stored outside India 
 
Providers subject to foreign legal regimes 
 
Cross-border data access restrictions 
 
Document jurisdictional limitations at the earliest stage. 
 
Use established legal cooperation mechanisms where required. 
 
Avoid direct access attempts exceeding lawful authority. 
 
Record all efforts made, responses received, and constraints encountered. 
Courts recognise jurisdictional complexity but expect demonstrable diligence and lawful effort, 
not inaction. 
[[PAGE 145]]
5.10.7 Privacy and Data Protection Safeguards 
While documenting and preserving virtual evidence, officers shall ensure that: 
 
Data collected is strictly relevant to the offence. 
 
Personal data unrelated to the investigation is not unnecessarily captured or disclosed. 
 
Access and handling comply with statutory data protection obligations. 
 
Collected material is stored securely to prevent leakage or misuse. 
Failure to observe these safeguards may result in privacy-based challenges, even where criminal 
conduct is otherwise established. 
5.10.8 Case-Based Illustrations 
 Online Financial Fraud: 
Upon receipt of complaint, officers immediately capture screenshots of the fraudulent 
website, payment interface, and transaction prompts, followed by preservation requests to 
the hosting provider and payment gateway. 
 Social Media Impersonation: 
A fake profile is documented with full screenshots showing URLs, profile identifiers, and 
visible connections. Preservation requests ensure retention of account creation data and 
IP logs. 
These actions establish existence, context, and continuity pending lawful acquisition. 
5.10.9 Evidentiary Reliability and Prosecution Readiness 
Virtual crime scenes demand swift yet restrained action. Delay, incomplete documentation, or 
unauthorised access commonly results in: 
 
Loss of evidence through deletion 
 
Defence claims of fabrication or manipulation 
 
Challenges to authenticity and continuity 
Properly managed virtual crime scenes: 
 
Preserve evidence against spoliation 
[[PAGE 146]]
 
Establish contemporaneous authenticity 
 
Support admissibility of electronic records 
 
Strengthen prosecution despite absence of physical devices 
 
In virtual crime scenes, evidence exists by permission of the platform and survives by speed of 
documentation. 
Investigating officers must therefore act promptly, lawfully, and with disciplined restraint when 
managing virtual and cloud-only crime scenes. 
5.11 Live System Risk Assessment and Decision-Making 
A live system is any digital device or environment that is powered on, logged in, network-
connected, or otherwise operational at the time of police contact. Live systems present a paradox 
in cybercrime investigations: they may contain high-value volatile evidence, yet any interaction 
carries a substantial risk of alteration, loss, or legal contamination. This section prescribes a 
structured decision-making framework to guide officers in determining whether to maintain, 
isolate, or transition a live system to a stable state, without compromising evidentiary integrity or 
legality. 
Live system handling is not routine; it is an exceptional scenario requiring heightened restraint, 
documentation, and, where feasible, expert guidance. 
5.11.1 Why Live Systems Are High-Risk Evidence 
Live systems may contain volatile artefacts that disappear upon shutdown or disconnection, 
including: 
 
Active user sessions and authentication states 
 
Running processes and memory-resident malware 
 
Unsaved documents or transaction states 
 
Encryption keys stored in volatile memory 
[[PAGE 147]]
 
Network connections and real-time communications 
At the same time, live systems are subject to: 
 
Automatic system processes that alter logs and timestamps 
 
Remote access, remote wipe, or encryption triggers 
 
Background synchronisation with cloud services 
Courts have recognised that live system evidence is inherently fragile and have scrutinised police 
handling to ensure that any interference was necessary, proportionate, and well-documented. 
Unjustified interaction is often characterised as investigative overreach. 
5.11.2 The Decision Imperative: Act, Isolate, or Preserve 
Upon encountering a live system, the Investigating Officer must immediately undertake a risk-
benefit assessment, documented contemporaneously, to decide among three options: 
1. Preserve in Live State (do not interact) 
2. Isolate Without Interaction (prevent remote access) 
3. Transition to Stable State (shutdown or controlled action) 
This decision shall not be driven by curiosity, convenience, or time pressure, but by evidentiary 
necessity and legal proportionality. 
5.11.3 Factors Governing Live System Decisions 
The following factors shall be assessed and recorded before any decision is taken: 
 Nature of the Alleged Offence 
Offences involving active fraud, ongoing data exfiltration, or live coordination may 
justify greater urgency, whereas historical offences usually do not. 
 Risk of Remote Interference 
Indicators such as active internet connectivity, known remote access tools, or prior 
attempts at deletion increase the risk of spoliation. 
[[PAGE 148]]
 Presence of Volatile Evidence 
Visible running processes, open dashboards, or active transactions may contain evidence 
that cannot be recovered post-shutdown. 
 Availability of Technical Expertise 
Absence of trained cyber personnel weighs strongly against any active manipulation of 
the system. 
 Legal Authority and Necessity 
Any action must be defensible under existing legal authority and demonstrably 
necessary to prevent evidence loss or harm. 
Failure to assess these factors renders subsequent actions vulnerable to challenge. 
5.11.4 Option I: Preservation in Live State (Preferred Default) 
The default and preferred approach is to preserve the system in its live state without interaction. 
 
Do not touch the keyboard, mouse, or screen. 
 
Photograph the system, including: 
o Screen display and open applications 
o Network indicators 
 
Secure the area to prevent unauthorised interaction. 
 
Document observations only. 
This approach preserves both volatile and non-volatile data while minimising risk of alteration. It 
is particularly appropriate where expert assistance is en route or where the evidentiary value of 
volatile data is uncertain. 
5.11.5 Option II: Isolation Without Interaction 
Where there is a credible risk of remote interference, the officer may isolate the system without 
interacting with software or applications. 
[[PAGE 149]]
 Permissible Isolation Measures: 
o Physically disconnect network cables. 
o Disable external connectivity through non-intrusive means. 
o Shield wireless signals where equipment is available. 
 Mandatory Documentation: 
o Time and method of isolation 
o Reason for believing remote interference was imminent 
o Visible system state before and after isolation 
Isolation must be minimal and reversible, avoiding configuration changes or system commands. 
5.11.6 Option III: Transition to Stable State (Exceptional Measure) 
Transitioning a live system to a powered-off or stable state is an exceptional measure and shall 
be undertaken only when: 
 
There is a high likelihood of imminent evidence destruction, or 
 
Continued operation poses immediate harm, or 
 
Expert guidance directs controlled shutdown. 
 
Do not shut down a system merely for convenience. 
 
Where shutdown is unavoidable, document: 
o Justification for shutdown 
o Method used (power removal, controlled shutdown, etc.) 
o System state immediately prior to action 
 
Ensure supervisory awareness as soon as practicable. 
[[PAGE 150]]
Unjustified shutdowns have been a recurring basis for defence allegations of deliberate evidence 
destruction. 
5.11.7 Live Systems in Enterprise and Institutional Environments 
Live systems in offices, data centres, or institutional settings require additional caution. 
 
Avoid disruption of essential services or business continuity. 
 
Coordinate with authorised technical personnel. 
 
Prefer preservation and documentation over seizure. 
 
Record organisational roles, access controls, and system ownership. 
Institutional systems often involve third-party data and legal obligations beyond the immediate 
offence. 
5.11.8 Live Virtual Environments and Dashboards 
Live systems may also exist as logged-in dashboards or sessions on web platforms or cloud 
services. 
 
Do not navigate or explore content. 
 
Document visible information using screenshots. 
 
Log out or close sessions only if advised and justified. 
 
Preserve session context through documentation, not interaction. 
Use of victim credentials without legal basis is strictly prohibited. 
5.11.9 Documentation and Case Diary Integration 
Every live system decision shall be reflected in: 
 
Scene documentation 
 
Case diary entries 
[[PAGE 151]]
 
Supervisory review notes 
The documentation must clearly demonstrate that: 
 
A reasoned assessment was conducted 
 
The least intrusive option was chosen 
 
Actions taken were necessary and proportionate 
In judicial review, reasoned restraint is often treated as evidence of investigative fairness. 
5.11.10 Defence Resilience and Judicial Scrutiny 
Live system handling is a frequent focal point of defence cross-examination. Common 
challenges include allegations that: 
 
Officers accessed data unlawfully 
 
Systems were altered to create evidence 
 
Volatile data was selectively preserved 
Strict adherence to this section ensures that officers can confidently explain what was done, 
what was avoided, and why. 
In live systems, restraint is not inaction—it is informed decision-making. 
Officers must therefore balance urgency with legality, and preservation with proportionality, 
when managing live digital environments. 
5.12 Documentation, Photography, and Scene Recording Standards 
Documentation is the spinal column of digital crime scene management. In cybercrime cases, 
courts rarely witness the original crime scene; they encounter it only through records prepared by 
investigating officers. Consequently, the credibility of digital evidence depends not merely on 
forensic output, but on the accuracy, completeness, and neutrality of scene documentation. 
This section prescribes mandatory standards for documenting digital crime scenes, including 
written records, photography, and contemporaneous scene recording. The objective is to ensure 
[[PAGE 152]]
that the investigation narrative remains verifiable, transparent, and resistant to defence 
allegations of manipulation or afterthought. 
5.12.1 Purpose and Evidentiary Value of Documentation 
Documentation serves multiple legal functions: 
 
It establishes the original condition of devices and environments. 
 
It explains why certain actions were taken and others avoided. 
 
It links the scene to subsequent seizure, forensic analysis, and testimony. 
 
It protects officers from allegations of misconduct or evidence fabrication. 
Courts have repeatedly held that where digital evidence is challenged, contemporaneous 
documentation carries greater probative value than retrospective explanations. Silence or 
ambiguity in records is often interpreted against the investigating agency. 
5.12.2 Written Scene Documentation: Mandatory Elements 
Every digital crime scene—physical, virtual, or hybrid—shall be documented in writing at the 
earliest opportunity. The documentation may form part of the case diary, scene memo, or a 
dedicated digital crime scene record, but must contain the following elements: 
1. Date and Time 
o Time of arrival at the scene 
o Time when scene control was established 
o Time of departure 
2. Location Description 
o Exact address or virtual location 
o Nature of premises (residential, commercial, institutional) 
o Access points and layout (brief description) 
3. Personnel Present 
[[PAGE 153]]
o Names, ranks, and roles of police personnel 
o Presence of occupants, staff, or third parties 
o Arrival and departure times where relevant 
4. Scene Condition 
o State of access control 
o Presence of powered-on or powered-off devices 
o Network connectivity indicators 
5. Actions Taken 
o Securing measures 
o Isolation steps 
o Documentation actions 
6. Actions Deliberately Avoided 
o Non-access of devices 
o Non-exploration of content 
o Non-shutdown of systems 
Recording actions avoided is as important as recording actions taken; it demonstrates restraint 
and compliance with SOP. 
5.12.3 Neutral and Objective Language 
All documentation shall be drafted in neutral, descriptive language, avoiding assumptions, 
conclusions, or speculative statements. 
Acceptable Language: 
“The laptop was found powered on, displaying an open spreadsheet application.” 
Unacceptable Language: 
“The laptop was being used by the accused to commit fraud.” 
[[PAGE 154]]
At the scene stage, officers document what is observed, not what is inferred. Conclusions belong 
to the investigation and prosecution stages, not scene documentation. 
5.12.4 Photography Standards: General Principles 
Photography is an essential tool for preserving the visual state of a digital crime scene. 
Photographs provide an objective reference point that supports written documentation and later 
General Principles: 
 
Photographs shall be taken before any handling or movement of devices. 
 
Use official equipment wherever possible. 
 
Ensure images are clear, well-lit, and unambiguous. 
 
Do not edit, crop, or annotate original photographs. 
All photographs shall be treated as evidentiary material and handled accordingly. 
5.12.5 What Must Be Photographed at a Digital Crime Scene 
The following shall be photographed as applicable: 
 
Overall scene view showing device placement and surroundings 
 
Individual devices from multiple angles 
 
Screens of powered-on devices showing: 
o Open applications 
o Logged-in profiles (if visible) 
 
Network equipment with connected cables and indicator lights 
 
Serial numbers, asset tags, and identifying marks 
 
External storage media and peripherals 
[[PAGE 155]]
Where virtual crime scenes are involved, screenshots shall capture: 
 
Full browser window with address bar 
 
Account identifiers and URLs 
 
Visible timestamps 
5.12.6 Sequence and Integrity of Photographic Evidence 
Photographs shall follow a logical sequence, moving from general to specific: 
1. Scene overview 
2. Device context 
3. Device details 
4. Screen or interface details 
This sequence assists courts in reconstructing the scene spatially and temporally. Random or 
disordered images reduce evidentiary clarity and may weaken credibility. 
Photographic integrity must be preserved: 
 
Original files shall be retained. 
 
Metadata shall not be altered. 
 
Transfers shall be documented. 
5.12.7 Video Recording: Use and Limitations 
Video recording may be used where it assists in capturing dynamic or complex scenes, such as 
multiple connected devices or live system displays. 
 
Use video sparingly and purposefully. 
 
Avoid commentary or narration during recording. 
 
Do not interact with devices while recording unless justified. 
[[PAGE 156]]
 
Clearly identify start and end points of recording. 
Video is a supplementary tool; it does not replace detailed written documentation. 
5.12.8 Documentation of Virtual Crime Scenes 
Virtual crime scenes require equivalent documentation standards adapted to digital 
environments. 
Mandatory Documentation Includes: 
 
URLs and platform names 
 
Account identifiers and usernames 
 
Date and time of access 
 
Method of access (public view, victim-provided) 
Screenshots shall be cross-referenced in written records, ensuring traceability between visual and 
narrative evidence. 
5.12.9 Documentation Errors to Avoid 
Common documentation failures that weaken prosecutions include: 
 
Missing timestamps 
 
Generic descriptions (“computer”, “mobile”) without identifiers 
 
Failure to record device state (on/off) 
 
Post-facto reconstruction of events 
 
Use of informal or speculative language 
Officers must recognise that documentation errors are often irreparable and cannot be cured by 
later testimony. 
5.12.10 Integration with Case Diary and Supervisory Review 
All scene documentation shall be integrated into the case diary at the earliest stage. Supervisory 
officers shall review documentation for: 
[[PAGE 157]]
 
Completeness 
 
Neutrality 
 
SOP compliance 
 
Evidentiary sufficiency 
Supervisory oversight at this stage prevents downstream legal vulnerabilities and reinforces 
institutional accountability. 
In digital investigations, documentation is not paperwork—it is evidence. 
Officers must therefore approach documentation with the same seriousness as evidence seizure 
or forensic analysis. 
5.13 Prevention of Contamination, Spoliation, and Evidence Tampering 
Digital evidence is uniquely vulnerable to contamination, spoliation, and unauthorised 
alteration, often without visible indicators. In cybercrime investigations, such compromise 
frequently occurs not through deliberate misconduct, but through well-intentioned but 
uninformed actions taken at the earliest stages. This section establishes mandatory safeguards to 
prevent evidentiary degradation and to ensure that digital material remains authentic, reliable, 
and legally admissible. 
Contamination refers to unintended alteration or introduction of data. Spoliation refers to loss or 
destruction of evidence, whether intentional or accidental. Evidence tampering involves 
unauthorised or improper modification. Each of these risks undermines prosecutorial integrity 
and exposes the investigation to judicial challenge. 
 
5.13.1 Sources of Contamination in Digital Crime Scenes 
Digital contamination most commonly arises from: 
 
Unauthorised access to devices or accounts 
[[PAGE 158]]
 
Powering on or interacting with systems without justification 
 
Automatic system processes triggered by user interaction 
 
Network connectivity allowing remote alteration or deletion 
 
Use of non-forensic tools or personal devices 
 
Inadequate documentation masking inadvertent changes 
Unlike physical contamination, digital contamination may leave no obvious trace yet materially 
alter evidentiary value. 
 
5.13.2 Spoliation Risks Unique to Digital Evidence 
Spoliation in digital contexts may occur through: 
 
Automatic log rotation and data overwriting 
 
Platform retention policies deleting data after fixed periods 
 
Remote wipe or encryption commands 
 
Device battery depletion causing shutdown and data loss 
 
Routine system updates or synchronisation 
These risks make speed and documentation essential. Delay, even if well-intentioned, often 
results in irreversible loss. 
 
5.13.3 Mandatory Preventive Measures at the Scene 
The following preventive measures shall be strictly observed at all digital crime scenes: 
 
Restrict access to authorised personnel only. 
 
Prevent occupants or third parties from interacting with devices. 
 
Avoid powering devices on or off unless justified. 
[[PAGE 159]]
 
Isolate network connectivity where necessary to prevent remote access. 
 
Use protective packaging and signal-blocking materials for mobile devices. 
 
Maintain physical security of the scene and devices at all times. 
These measures apply equally to physical devices and virtual environments. 
 
5.13.4 Handling Human Interaction Risks 
Human interaction is the most frequent source of digital contamination. Officers must therefore 
manage people at the scene with clarity and authority. 
 
Politely but firmly instruct all persons not to touch or operate devices. 
 
Document any prior interaction reported by occupants before police arrival. 
 
Prevent “helpful” actions such as closing applications or logging out accounts. 
 
Record any unavoidable interaction and the reasons for it. 
Courts recognise that pre-arrival contamination may occur, but expect police to prevent further 
compromise once present. 
 
5.13.5 Preventing Spoliation in Virtual Crime Scenes 
Virtual evidence is particularly susceptible to spoliation due to third-party control. 
Mandatory Measures: 
 
Immediate documentation of visible content. 
 
Prompt issuance of preservation requests to service providers. 
 
Recording provider responses and retention timelines. 
 
Avoidance of unauthorised access or content interaction. 
[[PAGE 160]]
Failure to issue timely preservation requests is a recurring cause of evidentiary loss and judicial 
criticism. 
 
5.13.6 Evidence Handling During Transport and Storage 
Contamination and spoliation risks extend beyond the scene. 
 
Package each device separately and securely. 
 
Use tamper-evident seals. 
 
Maintain controlled storage with restricted access. 
 
Avoid unnecessary handling or movement of devices. 
 
Document every transfer in the chain of custody. 
Improper storage conditions or undocumented access may render otherwise valid evidence 
unreliable. 
 
5.13.7 Documentation as a Preventive Tool 
Documentation itself functions as a safeguard against contamination allegations. 
Officers shall document: 
 
Device state at discovery 
 
Actions taken and avoided 
 
Access restrictions imposed 
 
Preservation measures initiated 
 
Transfers and custody changes 
[[PAGE 161]]
Where contamination is alleged, detailed documentation often determines whether the court 
accepts or rejects such claims. 
 
5.13.8 Supervisory Responsibility and Accountability 
Supervisory officers bear a critical responsibility in preventing contamination and spoliation. 
They shall: 
 
Review scene documentation promptly. 
 
Ensure compliance with SOPs. 
 
Direct corrective measures where deficiencies are observed. 
 
Record supervisory review in the case diary. 
Institutional accountability strengthens prosecutorial credibility and protects individual officers. 
 
5.13.9 Consequences of Non-Compliance 
Failure to prevent contamination or spoliation may result in: 
 
Exclusion of evidence 
 
Adverse judicial inference 
 
Collapse of prosecution case 
 
Departmental or legal liability 
Courts have repeatedly held that investigative lapses affecting evidence integrity cannot be cured 
by later forensic excellence. 
 
Digital evidence is most often lost not by criminals, but by carelessness. 
[[PAGE 162]]
Investigating officers must therefore treat prevention of contamination and spoliation as a core 
investigative duty, not a peripheral concern. 
5.14 Chain of Custody in Digital Evidence 
The chain of custody is the documentary and procedural record that establishes the identity, 
integrity, and continuity of evidence from the moment it is discovered until its production 
before the court. In digital investigations, chain of custody is not a mere administrative formality; 
it is the principal safeguard against allegations of fabrication, substitution, or tampering. 
Courts routinely treat defects in chain of custody as substantive infirmities, particularly where 
electronic evidence is involved. Unlike physical exhibits, digital evidence can be duplicated, 
altered, or deleted without visible markers. Consequently, the prosecution’s ability to prove that 
the evidence examined, analysed, and produced is the same evidence originally secured 
depends almost entirely on chain-of-custody compliance. 
 
5.14.1 Concept and Legal Significance 
Chain of custody refers to the unbroken, documented sequence of control, transfer, analysis, 
and storage of digital evidence. It answers three fundamental judicial questions: 
1. What was seized or preserved? 
2. Who handled it, when, where, and why? 
3. Was its integrity preserved throughout? 
In the absence of clear answers, courts may either exclude the evidence or attach diminished 
probative value to it, irrespective of its technical contents. 
 
5.14.2 When Chain of Custody Begins 
In digital investigations, chain of custody begins at the moment of first police contact with the 
evidence, not at the time of formal seizure or forensic examination. 
Accordingly, chain-of-custody obligations arise when: 
[[PAGE 163]]
 
A device is first identified at the scene, 
 
A virtual account is first documented or preserved, 
 
A storage medium is first secured, 
 
A platform preservation request is first issued. 
Failure to record early-stage custody creates gaps that defence counsel routinely exploit. 
 
5.14.3 Core Elements of Digital Chain of Custody 
Every chain-of-custody record shall capture, at a minimum, the following elements: 
 
Unique Identification 
o Case number 
o Evidence ID 
o Device or account description 
 
Condition at Acquisition 
o Powered-on or powered-off state 
o Visible damage or alteration 
o Network connectivity status 
 
Custodian Details 
o Name, rank, and designation of the officer 
o Date and time of custody commencement 
 
Transfer Records 
o Date, time, and purpose of each transfer 
o Identity of receiving and handing-over officers 
o Location of transfer 
[[PAGE 164]]
 
Storage and Security 
o Storage location 
o Access restrictions 
o Seal numbers and condition 
 
Final Disposition 
o Forensic examination details 
o Court production 
o Return, retention, or disposal as per law 
Each entry must be chronological, legible, and contemporaneous. 
 
5.14.4 Chain of Custody for Physical Digital Devices 
For physical devices such as computers, mobile phones, and storage media, the following SOP 
shall be observed: 
 
Assign a unique evidence number immediately upon securing the device. 
 
Record the device description with: 
o Make, model, colour 
o Serial number or IMEI (if visible without powering on) 
 
Seal the device using tamper-evident material. 
 
Record seal number and condition at each transfer. 
 
Limit handling to authorised personnel only. 
 
Document every instance the seal is opened and resealed, including purpose and 
authorisation. 
[[PAGE 165]]
Unexplained seal damage or undocumented access is frequently interpreted as evidence 
tampering. 
 
5.14.5 Chain of Custody for Virtual and Cloud-Based Evidence 
Virtual evidence requires a modified but equally rigorous chain-of-custody framework. 
 
Assign a unique evidence identifier to each virtual account, dataset, or platform source. 
 
Document: 
o URLs, account IDs, and platform names 
o Date and time of initial documentation 
o Preservation request details 
 
Maintain records of: 
o Provider acknowledgements 
o Data received, including format and scope 
o Hash values or integrity markers where applicable 
 
Control access to downloaded datasets and logs. 
 
Document every instance of access, copying, or analysis. 
The fact that data originates from a third party does not dilute the duty to maintain custody 
records once it enters police control. 
 
5.14.6 Hash Values and Integrity Verification 
Where digital evidence is copied, imaged, or extracted, hash values function as integrity 
fingerprints. 
[[PAGE 166]]
 
Generate hash values at the earliest appropriate stage. 
 
Record hash values in custody documentation. 
 
Re-verify hashes upon transfer or analysis where feasible. 
 
Document any discrepancy immediately with explanation. 
Hash mismatches, if unexplained, can undermine confidence in the evidence and the 
 
5.14.7 Access Control and Audit Trails 
Digital evidence shall be stored in controlled environments with restricted access. 
Mandatory Practices: 
 
Maintain access logs for evidence storage areas. 
 
Restrict access to authorised officers and forensic personnel. 
 
Prohibit informal or unsupervised examination. 
 
Document all access, even for inspection or verification. 
Courts increasingly expect auditability, particularly in cases involving sensitive personal or 
financial data. 
 
5.14.8 Supervisory Oversight of Chain of Custody 
Supervisory officers play a critical role in maintaining custody integrity. 
They shall: 
 
Periodically review custody records for completeness. 
 
Verify seal conditions and access logs. 
[[PAGE 167]]
 
Address discrepancies immediately. 
 
Record supervisory checks in the case diary. 
Supervisory neglect at this stage often results in institutional criticism during trial. 
 
5.14.9 Common Chain-of-Custody Errors to Avoid 
Officers must avoid the following recurring errors: 
 
Delayed assignment of evidence identifiers 
 
Incomplete or retrospective entries 
 
Shared custody without documentation 
 
Informal access for “checking” or “previewing” 
 
Failure to record virtual evidence handling 
Such lapses are difficult, and often impossible, to cure later. 
 
5.14.10 Evidentiary and Trial-Stage Implications 
During trial, the chain of custody is tested through: 
 
Cross-examination of investigating officers 
 
Scrutiny of custody records 
 
Comparison of seals, hashes, and logs 
A well-maintained chain of custody enables officers to answer confidently and consistently. 
Conversely, gaps or inconsistencies often overshadow even strong forensic findings. 
 
In digital evidence, custody is credibility. 
[[PAGE 168]]
Every officer handling digital evidence must therefore treat chain-of-custody compliance as a 
core investigative obligation, inseparable from evidence preservation and analysis. 
5.15 Coordination with Forensic Laboratories and Transition from Scene to Analysis 
The transition from crime scene management to forensic analysis marks a decisive shift in a 
cybercrime investigation. This transition must be deliberate, documented, and legally 
coherent. Forensic laboratories do not cure defects arising from improper scene handling; they 
merely analyse what is lawfully and correctly preserved. Accordingly, effective coordination 
with forensic laboratories begins at the scene itself, not after seizure. 
This section prescribes standard operating procedures to ensure that digital evidence moves from 
the scene to forensic examination without loss of integrity, legality, or evidentiary value. 
 
5.15.1 Purpose of Early Forensic Coordination 
Early coordination with forensic laboratories serves four critical purposes: 
1. Preservation of Evidence Integrity – ensuring that evidence is received in a condition 
suitable for analysis. 
2. Correct Scoping of Examination – preventing overbroad or irrelevant forensic requests. 
3. Judicial Defensibility – demonstrating that forensic analysis was guided by investigative 
necessity, not fishing expeditions. 
4. Efficiency and Timeliness – reducing rework, delays, and evidentiary gaps. 
Courts have increasingly scrutinised whether forensic analysis was purpose-driven and 
proportionate, rather than exploratory or speculative. 
 
5.15.2 When Forensic Coordination Must Begin 
Forensic coordination shall begin as soon as digital evidence is identified, and not merely after 
its physical seizure. 
[[PAGE 169]]
Early coordination is mandatory where: 
 
Live systems are encountered with volatile data risks, 
 
Enterprise or institutional systems are involved, 
 
Large datasets or multiple devices are seized, 
 
Encryption, proprietary software, or specialised hardware is suspected, 
 
Cross-border or platform-based evidence is anticipated. 
Delayed coordination often results in irreversible data loss or legally questionable extraction 
practices. 
 
5.15.3 Defining the Scope of Forensic Examination 
Before forwarding any device or dataset for forensic examination, the Investigating Officer shall 
define the scope of examination clearly and in writing. 
The scope shall specify: 
 
Nature of the alleged offence, 
 
Relevant time period, 
 
Categories of data sought (communications, transactions, logs, files), 
 
Specific questions the forensic analysis is intended to answer. 
Open-ended requests such as “examine the device fully” are discouraged, as they invite privacy 
challenges and judicial criticism for lack of proportionality. 
 
5.15.4 Preparation of Forensic Referral Documentation 
Every transfer of digital evidence to a forensic laboratory shall be accompanied by a complete 
and accurate referral package, including: 
 
Copy of FIR and relevant sections invoked, 
[[PAGE 170]]
 
Brief factual synopsis of the case, 
 
Chain-of-custody records, 
 
Scene documentation and photographs (where relevant), 
 
Description of the device or data submitted, 
 
Specific forensic questions to be addressed, 
 
Any legal limitations or court directions applicable. 
Incomplete or vague referral documentation is a recurring cause of delayed or inconclusive 
forensic reports. 
 
5.15.5 Legal Authority and Compliance 
Forensic examination must always be grounded in lawful authority. 
Investigating Officers shall ensure that: 
 
Seizure and examination are authorised under applicable law, 
 
Any court orders or warrants are complied with, 
 
Examination does not exceed the scope of legal authority, 
 
Privacy and data protection obligations are respected. 
Forensic laboratories are not substitutes for judicial authorisation; unlawful referrals expose both 
the investigation and the examining agency to legal risk. 
 
5.15.6 Transfer Protocol to Forensic Laboratories 
The physical and digital transfer of evidence to forensic laboratories shall follow strict protocol: 
 
Verify seal integrity before dispatch. 
 
Document date, time, and mode of transfer. 
[[PAGE 171]]
 
Use secure transport and authorised personnel. 
 
Obtain acknowledgment of receipt from the laboratory. 
 
Record any observations regarding condition or anomalies. 
For virtual evidence, secure transmission methods shall be used, and access credentials shall be 
handled with heightened security. 
 
5.15.7 Interaction During Forensic Examination 
Once evidence is submitted, Investigating Officers shall maintain professional but non-
intrusive interaction with forensic personnel. 
Permissible interaction includes: 
 
Clarifying forensic questions, 
 
Providing contextual information, 
 
Responding to lawful queries from the laboratory. 
Impermissible interaction includes: 
 
Directing or influencing forensic conclusions, 
 
Requesting examination beyond authorised scope, 
 
Informal access to evidence during analysis. 
Forensic independence enhances evidentiary credibility. 
 
5.15.8 Receipt and Integration of Forensic Reports 
Upon receipt of forensic reports, the Investigating Officer shall: 
 
Verify that the report corresponds to the submitted evidence, 
 
Cross-check identifiers, hashes, and descriptions, 
[[PAGE 172]]
 
Integrate findings with the case diary, 
 
Assess whether additional clarification or supplementary examination is required. 
Any discrepancy between the evidence submitted and the report received must be addressed 
immediately and documented. 
 
5.15.9 Supervisory Review and Accountability 
Supervisory officers shall review forensic coordination at two stages: 
 
Pre-examination – to ensure lawful scope and necessity, 
 
Post-examination – to ensure proper integration and understanding. 
Supervisory oversight at this stage prevents overreach, delays, and misinterpretation of technical 
findings. 
 
5.15.10 Transition to Investigative and Coercive Stages 
Completion of forensic coordination marks the formal transition from scene management to 
investigation and, where justified, coercive action. 
Officers must ensure that: 
 
Scene management SOPs are fully complied with, 
 
Chain of custody remains intact, 
 
Forensic findings are contextualised, not overstated, 
 
Subsequent actions are legally justified by evidence, not assumption. 
A disciplined transition preserves the credibility of the entire investigative process. 
 
[[PAGE 173]]
Forensics does not rescue poor procedure; it amplifies good procedure. 
Investigating Officers must therefore treat coordination with forensic laboratories as an 
extension of crime scene discipline, not as a separate or corrective phase. 
5.16 IO Quick Checklists, Decision Matrices, and Scene Exit Protocol 
This section consolidates the procedural requirements of Chapter 5 into actionable checklists, 
decision matrices, and a structured scene exit protocol. It is designed to support Investigating 
Officers (IOs) and first responders operating under time pressure, uncertainty, and judicial 
accountability. These tools do not replace the substantive SOP; they operationalise it. 
5.16.1 Digital Crime Scene – First Responder Quick Checklist 
Upon arrival at any suspected digital crime scene, the IO shall mentally and operationally verify 
the following: 
A. Scene Control 
 
☐ Assumed control of the scene 
 
☐ Restricted unauthorised access 
 
☐ Identified and documented all persons present 
B. Device State Awareness 
 
☐ Identified powered-on vs powered-off devices 
 
☐ Avoided interaction with devices 
 
☐ Prevented occupants from “helpful” interference 
C. Initial Documentation 
 
☐ Recorded date, time, and location 
 
☐ Photographed overall scene and devices 
 
☐ Noted visible screen states (if any) 
[[PAGE 174]]
Failure to complete these steps before handling devices increases contamination risk and 
weakens evidentiary credibility. 
 
5.16.2 Device Handling Decision Matrix (At the Scene) 
Use the following matrix to guide immediate decisions: 
Device State 
Immediate Action 
Prohibited Action 
Powered-Off 
Preserve as is, label & seal 
Powering on 
Powered-On 
Document, isolate if needed Exploring content 
Mobile Device 
Shield signals, photograph 
Unlocking 
Server / Enterprise Document & coordinate 
Unilateral shutdown 
IoT Device 
Photograph & identify hub 
Remote access 
Golden Rule: If unsure, preserve and escalate. 
5.16.3 Live System Risk Assessment – One-Page Guide 
Before any decision affecting a live system, confirm: 
 
☐ Is there imminent risk of remote deletion? 
 
☐ Is volatile evidence clearly visible? 
 
☐ Is expert guidance available? 
 
☐ Is legal authority established? 
If any answer is “No”, default to preservation without interaction and document reasons. 
5.16.4 Virtual Crime Scene Handling – Quick SOP 
For platform-based or cloud-only evidence: 
 
☐ Capture screenshots with full URLs and timestamps 
 
☐ Document access method (public / victim-provided) 
 
☐ Issue preservation request immediately 
[[PAGE 175]]
 
☐ Record provider details and response 
 
☐ Avoid unauthorised access or engagement 
Reminder: Documentation preserves existence; providers preserve data. 
5.16.5 Documentation & Photography – Minimum Standards 
Before leaving the scene, ensure: 
 
☐ Written scene notes completed 
 
☐ All devices photographed from multiple angles 
 
☐ Screen states captured (if applicable) 
 
☐ Serial numbers / identifiers recorded 
 
☐ Actions taken and avoided documented 
What is not documented will be presumed not to have occurred. 
5.16.6 Chain of Custody – Exit Verification 
Before evidence leaves the scene: 
 
☐ Evidence IDs assigned 
 
☐ Devices labelled and sealed 
 
☐ Seal numbers recorded 
 
☐ Custodian identified 
 
☐ Transfer purpose documented 
Any break at this stage creates permanent evidentiary vulnerability. 
5.16.7 Scene Exit Protocol (Mandatory) 
The IO shall not formally exit a digital crime scene until the following steps are completed: 
[[PAGE 176]]
1. Final Scene Review 
o Reconfirm no device or evidence source is overlooked. 
o Verify access control remains effective until exit. 
2. Documentation Closure 
o Complete scene notes. 
o Cross-check photographs and recordings. 
3. Evidence Security 
o Ensure all seized items are sealed and secured. 
o Confirm custody records are updated. 
4. Supervisory Intimation 
o Inform supervisory officer of actions taken. 
o Record supervisory communication where required. 
5. Victim / Occupant Communication 
o Inform relevant persons of next procedural steps. 
o Avoid disclosure of investigative strategy. 
Leaving a scene without structured closure often results in later contradictions and credibility 
issues. 
5.16.8 Common Errors Identified in Judicial Scrutiny 
Courts have frequently criticised investigations for: 
 
Scene documentation prepared later at the police station 
 
Inconsistent descriptions of device state 
 
Missing or unclear photographs 
 
Informal device handling “for verification” 
[[PAGE 177]]
 
Unexplained gaps in custody 
These errors are avoidable through disciplined use of this section. 
5.16.9 Supervisory Use of Chapter 5 Tools 
Supervisory officers shall use Section 5.16 as a review and audit framework to assess: 
 
Compliance with scene management SOPs 
 
Quality of documentation 
 
Integrity of custody 
 
Readiness for forensic transition 
Early supervisory correction prevents downstream legal damage. 
Operational Closure Principle 
A digital crime scene is not closed when officers leave; it is closed when the record speaks for 
itself. 
Investigating Officers must therefore ensure that any independent reviewer—court, 
prosecutor, or defence—can reconstruct the scene solely from the documentation created.

These annexures convert Chapter 5 into: 
 
a field checklist, 




A digital crime scene well managed rarely collapses in court. 
A poorly managed one almost always does. 
 
 
PART I – CONCEPTUAL, CONSTITUTIONAL & STATUTORY FRAMEWORK 
 
6.1 Positioning of Chapter 6 within the Cybercrime SOP 
Chapter 6 marks a decisive transition in the cybercrime investigation workflow. Until Chapter 
5, the SOP governs non-coercive actions—jurisdictional assessment, FIR registration, 
preliminary enquiry, and digital crime scene management. Chapter 6 is the first chapter that deals 
with coercive State power: search, seizure, and arrest. 
This positioning is intentional and legally necessary. Courts have consistently held that coercive 
powers cannot be exercised in isolation; they must be rooted in lawful initiation, evidentiary 
[[PAGE 185]]
preservation, and documented necessity. When search, seizure, or arrest precede these 
foundations, the entire investigation becomes vulnerable to constitutional challenge [1]. 
In cybercrime cases, this risk is magnified. Digital evidence is pervasive, private, and often 
unrelated to the alleged offence. Devices and accounts may contain years of personal, financial, 
medical, or third-party data. Accordingly, cyber searches and seizures represent one of the 
most intrusive exercises of State power in modern policing [2]. 
This Chapter therefore treats search, seizure, and arrest not as investigative conveniences, but 
as exceptional powers constrained by constitutional morality, statutory discipline, and 
judicial oversight. 
 
6.2 Search, Seizure and Arrest as Coercive Powers 
Search, seizure, and arrest are not routine procedural steps; they are coercive intrusions into 
personal liberty, privacy, and property. 
 
Search intrudes upon privacy and informational autonomy. 
 
Seizure deprives a person of possession and control. 
 
Arrest restrains bodily liberty and dignity. 
Indian constitutional jurisprudence recognises that such powers, though necessary for law 
enforcement, must be narrowly exercised, proportionate, and justified by necessity, not 
suspicion alone [3]. 
In cybercrime investigations, these intrusions often extend beyond the accused: 
 
seizure of shared computers, 
 
access to family members’ devices, 
 
collection of third-party communications, 
 
platform-level data affecting multiple users. 
Courts have therefore repeatedly warned against mechanical or overbroad coercive action, 
particularly in technology-driven offences [4]. 
 
6.3 Constitutional Foundations Governing Coercive Action 
6.3.1 Article 21 – Due Process and Fairness 
[[PAGE 186]]
Article 21 of the Constitution mandates that no person shall be deprived of life or personal 
liberty except according to procedure established by law. Judicial interpretation has long 
settled that such procedure must be just, fair, and reasonable, not arbitrary or excessive [5]. 
In cybercrime cases, courts examine: 
 
whether coercive action was necessary, 
 
whether less intrusive alternatives were considered, 
 
whether procedural safeguards were followed. 
A search or arrest that technically complies with statute but violates fairness principles may still 
be struck down [6]. 
 
6.3.2 Article 20(3) – Protection Against Self-Incrimination 
Cyber investigations frequently involve digital credentials, passwords, biometrics, and 
encryption keys. Courts have drawn a careful distinction between: 
 
compelled testimonial acts, which are prohibited, and 
 
lawful collection of material evidence, which is permitted. 
Improper compulsion during search or arrest—such as forcing disclosure of passwords without 
legal basis—has repeatedly resulted in exclusion of evidence and adverse judicial remarks [7]. 
 
6.3.3 Article 22 – Arrest Safeguards 
Arrest is subject to constitutional safeguards, including: 
 
communication of grounds of arrest, 
 
right to legal counsel, 
 
production before a magistrate within stipulated time. 
Cybercrime arrests, particularly in financial and online offences, have been scrutinised where 
arrest appeared to be used as a tool of pressure rather than necessity [8]. 
 
6.4 Statutory Shift: From CrPC to BNSS 
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 represents a structural re-calibration of 
criminal procedure. While many core principles remain, BNSS reflects judicial experience of 
misuse, especially in: 
[[PAGE 187]]
 
indiscriminate arrests, 
 
overbroad searches, 
 
poorly documented seizures. 
BNSS strengthens: 
 
documentation requirements, 
 
supervisory accountability, 
 
necessity-based coercive action. 
This Chapter is aligned entirely with the BNSS framework, not legacy CrPC assumptions [9]. 
 
6.5 Cybercrime and the Problem of Over-Seizure 
One of the most criticised practices in cybercrime policing is over-seizure. 
Examples repeatedly noted by courts include: 
 
seizure of entire offices for a single email account, 
 
seizure of all family devices for one accused user, 
 
seizure of servers where copying would suffice, 
 
prolonged retention of devices unrelated to the offence. 
Courts have emphasised that seizure is not synonymous with investigation. Where data can be 
preserved, imaged, or obtained lawfully from intermediaries, physical seizure may be 
disproportionate [10]. 
This SOP therefore adopts the principle that “seize only what is necessary, and only when 
necessary.” 
 
6.6 Search in Cybercrime: Beyond Physical Spaces 
Cybercrime search is not confined to physical premises. It may extend to: 
 
digital devices, 
 
cloud accounts, 
 
online platforms, 
 
virtual workspaces, 
[[PAGE 188]]
 
remote servers. 
However, courts have consistently warned that digital search is not boundless search. Each 
layer of access must be legally justified and specifically scoped [11]. 
A search warrant for a device does not automatically authorise: 
 
exploration of all accounts, 
 
access to unrelated cloud storage, 
 
analysis beyond the offence period. 
This Chapter therefore treats scope limitation as a constitutional requirement, not an 
administrative preference. 
 
6.7 Arrest in Cybercrime: Not a Default Tool 
Arrest in cybercrime cases has been a subject of repeated judicial concern. The Supreme Court 
has clarified that arrest is not mandatory merely because an offence is cognizable [12]. 
In cybercrime, particularly: 
 
financial frauds, 
 
online cheating, 
 
platform-based offences, 
arrest often occurs: 
 
before evidence consolidation, 
 
without arrest necessity analysis, 
 
as a means of recovery or pressure. 
Such practices have been explicitly deprecated. Courts have reiterated that arrest must satisfy a 
necessity test, not merely an investigative desire [13]. 
 
6.8 Relationship of Chapter 6 with Chapter 23 
Chapter 23 (Case Initiation, Coercive Action & Prosecution Workflow) establishes a sequencing 
discipline: 
FIR → lawful enquiry → evidence preservation → coercive action → prosecution. 
Chapter 6 operationalises this sequencing at the coercive stage. It ensures that: 
[[PAGE 189]]
 
search is not used to compensate for weak FIRs, 
 
seizure does not substitute evidence analysis, 
 
arrest does not precede investigative justification. 
This alignment ensures institutional coherence, not compartmentalised policing. 
 
6.9 Guiding Principles for Chapter 6 
All actions under this Chapter shall be governed by the following principles: 
1. Necessity over convenience 
2. Proportionality over volume 
3. Documentation over discretion 
4. Supervisory accountability over individual impulse 
5. Trial-stage defensibility over immediate impact 
These principles are not aspirational; they are derived directly from constitutional and judicial 
standards. 
 
6.10 Transition to Operational Doctrine 
Having established the constitutional and statutory foundation, the subsequent parts of Chapter 6 
will prescribe precise operational SOPs for: 
 
search of physical and digital spaces, 
 
seizure of devices, data, and accounts, 
 
arrest decision-making under BNSS, 
 
cyber-specific coercive action workflows, 
 
supervisory controls and documentation discipline. 
Each subsequent part will integrate case law interpretation, BNSS provisions, and cyber-
specific realities, ensuring that coercive power is exercised lawfully, sparingly, and effectively.
