PART II – SEARCH & SEIZURE OF DIGITAL EVIDENCE: LEGAL FRAMEWORK, 
SCOPE & SAFEGUARDS 
 
6.11 Concept of “Search” in Cybercrime Investigations 
In cybercrime investigations, the meaning of “search” has expanded far beyond its classical 
understanding as a physical intrusion into premises. A search may now occur without physical 
entry, without visible force, and sometimes without the knowledge of the person affected. Courts 
have therefore repeatedly emphasised that digital searches demand stricter legal discipline, 
not looser interpretation [14]. 
A cyber search may include: 
 
examination of digital devices, 
 
access to data stored on local storage, 
 
access to cloud-hosted accounts, 
 
retrieval of logs, metadata, or backups, 
 
access to online platforms through lawful process. 
[[PAGE 191]]
Each of these actions constitutes a search in the constitutional sense, because each intrudes into 
informational privacy. The fact that data is intangible or remotely stored does not dilute the 
constitutional protection attached to it [15]. 
 
6.12 Search as a Privacy Intrusion: Post-Puttaswamy Position 
After the Supreme Court’s recognition of the right to privacy as a fundamental right, any State 
action involving access to personal data must satisfy the tests of: 
1. legality, 
2. legitimate State aim, 
3. proportionality, and 
4. procedural safeguards [16]. 
Cyber searches often involve: 
 
personal communications, 
 
financial records, 
 
browsing histories, 
 
health or location data, 
 
third-party information. 
Courts have clarified that overbroad or exploratory digital searches violate privacy, even 
where the investigation itself is lawful. Consequently, cyber search must be purpose-limited 
and offence-specific, not device-wide by default [17]. 
 
6.13 Statutory Authority for Search under BNSS 
Under the BNSS framework, search powers are derived from statutory provisions that broadly 
mirror earlier CrPC powers but are now interpreted through stricter constitutional lenses. 
Search may be conducted: 
 
pursuant to a search warrant issued by a competent court, or 
 
without warrant in exceptional circumstances expressly recognised by law. 
However, BNSS reinforces that warrantless search is the exception, not the rule, particularly 
where privacy-intensive digital evidence is involved [18]. 
[[PAGE 192]]
In cybercrime cases, the default presumption shall be: 
Search digital data through judicial authorisation unless delay would defeat the purpose of 
 
6.14 Search Warrants in Cybercrime Cases 
6.14.1 Necessity of Specificity 
Courts have repeatedly held that search warrants for digital evidence must not be vague or 
omnibus. A warrant authorising “search of all digital devices” without specifying: 
 
offence, 
 
time period, 
 
type of data sought, 
has been criticised as unconstitutional fishing [19]. 
Accordingly, applications for search warrants in cybercrime cases shall: 
 
specify the alleged offence, 
 
identify devices, accounts, or platforms sought, 
 
define the data category (communications, transactions, logs), 
 
restrict the temporal scope. 
This discipline protects both the investigation and the officer executing the warrant. 
 
6.14.2 Search of Devices vs Search of Data 
A critical distinction often missed in practice is the difference between: 
 
search of a device, and 
 
search of data contained in or accessible through that device. 
A warrant to seize a laptop does not automatically authorise: 
 
examination of all cloud accounts logged into the device, 
 
access to historical backups, 
 
analysis of unrelated user profiles. 
[[PAGE 193]]
Courts have emphasised that each layer of access requires legal justification [20]. 
Investigating Officers must therefore treat device access and data access as legally distinct acts. 
 
6.15 Warrantless Searches: Exceptional, Not Routine 
Warrantless search powers exist to meet emergencies, not to bypass judicial oversight. 
Courts have recognised warrantless searches only where: 
 
delay would lead to destruction of evidence, 
 
immediate action is necessary to prevent serious harm, 
 
statutory conditions are strictly satisfied. 
In cybercrime cases, warrantless searches are often unjustifiably invoked on grounds of 
“technical urgency” or “risk of deletion”. Courts have cautioned that mere possibility of 
deletion does not automatically justify bypassing a warrant, especially where preservation 
mechanisms exist [21]. 
Accordingly, officers must record: 
 
why a warrant could not be obtained, 
 
what imminent risk existed, 
 
why less intrusive measures were insufficient. 
Absence of such recording has repeatedly resulted in courts disbelieving claims of urgency. 
 
6.16 Search of Premises Involving Digital Evidence 
When physical premises are searched for digital evidence, officers must remember that: 
 
the premises belong to a person, 
 
devices may belong to multiple users, 
 
data may belong to third parties. 
Courts have deprecated “carpet searches” where officers indiscriminately access all devices 
found at the premises [22]. 
The correct approach is: 
 
identify devices reasonably connected to the offence, 
 
document the basis of such connection, 
[[PAGE 194]]
 
avoid accessing unrelated systems. 
A family residence is not transformed into a digital free-for-all merely because one member is 
under investigation. 
 
6.17 Search of Cloud and Platform-Based Data 
Cloud and platform data pose unique legal challenges because: 
 
the data is not physically located at the premises, 
 
it is controlled by intermediaries, 
 
it may be stored outside India. 
Courts have clarified that search powers over physical premises do not automatically extend 
to remote cloud data, unless specifically authorised [23]. 
 
access to cloud data shall ordinarily be obtained through lawful requests to service 
providers, 
 
direct access using seized credentials without authorisation is impermissible, 
 
preservation requests should precede acquisition. 
Improper access to cloud data has been treated as illegal search, even where the underlying 
investigation was lawful. 
 
6.18 Seizure in Cybercrime: Conceptual Clarification 
Seizure is the act by which the State assumes control over property or data to the exclusion of 
its possessor. In cybercrime cases, seizure may occur in multiple forms: 
 
physical seizure of devices, 
 
logical seizure of data through copying, 
 
constructive seizure through preservation orders. 
Courts have clarified that seizure need not always mean physical removal. Where investigative 
objectives can be achieved through copying or preservation, physical seizure may be 
disproportionate [24]. 
This Chapter adopts a least-intrusive seizure principle, consistent with constitutional 
proportionality. 
[[PAGE 195]]
 
6.19 Physical Seizure of Digital Devices 
Physical seizure of digital devices shall be resorted to only where: 
 
the device itself is an instrumentality of offence, 
 
on-device data cannot be preserved otherwise, 
 
there is risk of tampering or concealment, 
 
forensic integrity demands custody. 
Courts have criticised routine seizure of: 
 
entire offices, 
 
servers supporting multiple users, 
 
devices unrelated to the offence period. 
Investigating Officers must therefore record why seizure was necessary, not merely that it was 
possible [25]. 
 
6.20 Seizure vs Copying of Data 
In many cybercrime cases, investigative needs are met by: 
 
forensic imaging, 
 
data copying, 
 
extraction under supervision. 
Courts have recognised that copying data may sufficiently preserve evidence while 
minimising intrusion, especially where business continuity or third-party rights are involved 
[26]. 
This SOP therefore mandates that: 
 
copying shall be preferred where feasible, 
 
seizure shall be justified where copying is inadequate. 
Failure to consider this alternative has led to judicial observations of arbitrariness. 
 
6.21 Seizure of Servers and Enterprise Systems 
[[PAGE 196]]
Seizure of servers and enterprise systems carries heightened legal risk because: 
 
they often host data of multiple users, 
 
disruption may affect innocent parties, 
 
excessive seizure may violate proportionality. 
Courts have repeatedly cautioned against seizing servers where: 
 
targeted data extraction is feasible, 
 
logs can be preserved remotely, 
 
service continuity is critical [27]. 
 
seizure of servers shall be a measure of last resort, 
 
supervisory approval shall ordinarily precede such action, 
 
reasons shall be recorded in writing. 
 
6.22 Documentation Requirements during Search and Seizure 
Every cyber search and seizure must be accompanied by meticulous documentation, including: 
 
legal authority relied upon, 
 
scope of search, 
 
devices/data accessed, 
 
actions taken and avoided, 
 
items seized or copied. 
Courts have repeatedly held that absence of documentation creates presumption of illegality, 
even where officers later claim good faith [28]. 
 
6.23 Judicial Scrutiny Patterns in Cyber Searches 
Judicial scrutiny of cyber searches typically focuses on: 
 
scope creep beyond the warrant, 
 
lack of necessity recording, 
[[PAGE 197]]
 
over-seizure of devices, 
 
unauthorised access to accounts, 
 
poor chain of custody linkage. 
This Chapter is drafted precisely to ensure that Investigating Officers anticipate these questions 
at the time of action, not during cross-examination. 
 
6.24 Relationship of Search & Seizure with Arrest 
Courts have emphasised that: 
 
search and seizure do not automatically justify arrest, 
 
seizure cannot be used to coerce confessions, 
 
arrest must independently satisfy statutory tests. 
Investigating Officers must therefore resist the tendency to treat search, seizure, and arrest as a 
single coercive package. Each power has its own legal threshold [29]. 
 
6.25 Transition to Arrest Doctrine 
Having examined the legal contours of search and seizure, the next part will address arrest in 
cybercrime cases, including: 
 
BNSS arrest framework, 
 
necessity test, 
 
Supreme Court arrest jurisprudence, 
 
cyber-specific misuse patterns, 
 
documentation and supervisory controls.

PART III – CYBER-SPECIFIC SEIZURE PROTOCOLS (DEVICES, DATA, CLOUD & 
ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS) 
 
6.26 Conceptual Reframing of “Seizure” in Cybercrime 
In cybercrime investigations, seizure must be understood as control over evidentiary material, 
not merely physical possession. Unlike traditional crimes, where the object seized is often the 
instrumentality or proceeds of the offence, cybercrime evidence is frequently data-centric, 
replicated across systems, and embedded within larger digital ecosystems. 
Courts have clarified that the purpose of seizure is evidentiary preservation, not punitive 
deprivation. Where seizure exceeds this purpose, it risks being characterised as arbitrary or 
disproportionate [30]. Accordingly, cyber-specific seizure requires a graduated and calibrated 
approach, rather than default physical confiscation. 
 
6.27 Forms of Seizure Recognised in Cybercrime 
Cybercrime investigations may involve one or more of the following forms of seizure: 
1. Physical Seizure – Taking custody of a device or storage medium. 
2. Logical Seizure – Copying, imaging, or extracting data while leaving the device with the 
owner. 
3. Constructive Seizure – Restricting access through preservation orders, freezing, or 
access control without physical removal. 
[[PAGE 199]]
Courts have recognised that constructive and logical seizure may satisfy investigative 
necessity while better protecting constitutional rights, especially in commercial or shared 
environments [31]. 
 
6.28 Principle of Least Intrusive Seizure 
This SOP adopts the principle that: 
Seizure must intrude no further than is strictly necessary to preserve evidence and advance 
Investigating Officers shall therefore assess: 
 
whether physical custody is essential, 
 
whether data can be preserved without removal, 
 
whether third-party rights will be affected, 
 
whether seizure will disrupt lawful activity. 
Failure to consider these factors has led courts to conclude that seizure was punitive rather than 
investigative [32]. 
 
6.29 Seizure of Personal Digital Devices 
6.29.1 Mobile Phones, Laptops, and Personal Computers 
Personal devices often contain: 
 
intimate communications, 
 
financial information, 
 
professional data, 
 
third-party material unrelated to the offence. 
Courts have cautioned that blanket seizure of personal devices without offence linkage is 
constitutionally suspect [33]. 
 
Seizure shall be limited to devices reasonably connected to the alleged offence. 
 
The basis of such connection shall be documented. 
 
Where feasible, data extraction shall be preferred over prolonged seizure. 
[[PAGE 200]]
Prolonged retention of personal devices without justification has attracted adverse judicial 
comment. 
 
6.29.2 Shared and Family Devices 
In many cybercrime cases, devices are shared among family members or colleagues. Seizing 
such devices impacts innocent users. 
Courts have held that collective inconvenience cannot be justified by individual suspicion 
[34]. Investigating Officers must therefore: 
 
identify user profiles where possible, 
 
consider selective data extraction, 
 
record reasons where seizure of shared devices is unavoidable. 
 
6.30 Seizure of Storage Media and Backups 
External hard disks, USB drives, memory cards, and backup systems may contain historical or 
redundant data. 
SOP guidance: 
 
Identify relevance to offence period. 
 
Avoid seizing entire backup repositories where targeted extraction suffices. 
 
Document storage structure and relevance. 
Courts have questioned seizure of entire archival systems without demonstrating relevance [35]. 
 
6.31 Seizure of Enterprise Systems and Office Infrastructure 
6.31.1 Distinct Risks in Enterprise Seizure 
Enterprise systems host: 
 
data of multiple users, 
 
proprietary business information, 
 
regulated or sensitive third-party data. 
Courts have repeatedly emphasised that enterprise seizure carries heightened proportionality 
obligations [36]. 
[[PAGE 201]]
 
6.31.2 Servers and Centralised Systems 
Seizure of servers should be treated as exceptional. 
Investigating Officers shall: 
 
assess whether logs, databases, or snapshots can be preserved remotely, 
 
consult technical experts before action, 
 
obtain supervisory approval where practicable. 
Courts have deprecated seizure of live servers where copying or preservation could meet 
investigative needs [37]. 
 
6.31.3 Business Continuity Considerations 
Courts have recognised that disruption of lawful business activity without necessity may violate 
constitutional guarantees [38]. 
 
seizure plans shall account for business continuity, 
 
downtime risks shall be assessed, 
 
reasons for overriding continuity shall be recorded. 
 
6.32 Seizure of Cloud-Based Data 
Cloud data presents unique challenges: 
 
physical location is irrelevant, 
 
control lies with service providers, 
 
data may span jurisdictions. 
Courts have clarified that seizure of a device does not equate to seizure of cloud data [39]. 
SOP mandates: 
 
preservation requests as first response, 
 
lawful acquisition through service providers, 
 
avoidance of credential-based access without authority. 
[[PAGE 202]]
Improper access to cloud accounts using seized credentials has been held to violate privacy and 
procedural safeguards. 
 
6.33 Seizure of Social Media and Platform Accounts 
Accounts on social media or digital platforms are not “objects” in the traditional sense. 
Courts have held that: 
 
freezing or disabling accounts constitutes a form of seizure, 
 
such action must be legally authorised and proportionate [40]. 
Investigating Officers shall: 
 
prefer preservation over disabling, 
 
avoid account takeover without authority, 
 
document all platform communications. 
 
6.34 Seizure of Cryptocurrency and Digital Assets 
Seizure of cryptocurrency involves: 
 
wallets, 
 
private keys, 
 
exchange accounts. 
Courts have cautioned that loss of access keys may permanently destroy asset value, thereby 
defeating evidentiary and recovery objectives [41]. 
SOP guidance: 
 
secure access credentials lawfully, 
 
coordinate with specialised units, 
 
avoid unilateral actions without technical understanding. 
 
6.35 Documentation and Seizure Memo Discipline 
Every cyber seizure shall be accompanied by: 
 
precise description of item or data seized, 
[[PAGE 203]]
 
method of seizure (physical/logical/constructive), 
 
reasons for choosing that method, 
 
safeguards adopted. 
Courts have repeatedly held that vague seizure memos weaken evidentiary value and credibility 
[42]. 
 
6.36 Linkage with Chain of Custody (Chapter 5) 
Seizure marks the formal entry point of evidence into police custody. Accordingly: 
 
chain of custody shall commence immediately, 
 
identifiers shall be assigned at seizure stage, 
 
custody continuity shall be maintained without gaps. 
Any inconsistency between seizure documentation and custody records is treated as a serious 
infirmity [43]. 
 
6.37 Judicial Patterns of Criticism in Cyber Seizure 
Courts have commonly criticised: 
 
indiscriminate seizure of devices, 
 
failure to consider copying alternatives, 
 
prolonged retention without review, 
 
seizure affecting unrelated parties. 
This Part is structured precisely to avoid these recurring pitfalls. 
 
6.38 Supervisory Oversight in Cyber Seizure 
Supervisory officers shall: 
 
review seizure necessity, 
 
verify proportionality, 
 
ensure documentation sufficiency. 
[[PAGE 204]]
Cyber-specific seizures, particularly of enterprise systems or cloud data, shall ordinarily involve 
supervisory consultation. 
 
6.39 Transition to Arrest Doctrine 
Seizure alone does not justify arrest. The next Part will address: 
 
arrest powers under BNSS, 
 
necessity-based arrest doctrine, 
 
Supreme Court jurisprudence, 
 
cybercrime-specific misuse of arrest, 
 
documentation and accountability. 
 
End of Chapter 6 – Part III

Control)

Proceed with Chapter 6 – Part IV 
Below is CHAPTER 6 – PART IV, drafted in the same disciplined, BNSS-aligned, court-
conscious SOP style, integrating binding Supreme Court jurisprudence and cyber-specific arrest 
risks.

[[PAGE 205]]
PART IV – ARREST IN CYBERCRIME CASES: NECESSITY, PROPORTIONALITY & 
JUDICIAL CONTROL 
 
6.40 Arrest as an Exceptional Coercive Power 
Arrest represents the most intrusive coercive power available to the State. It restrains bodily 
liberty, exposes the individual to stigma, and triggers a cascade of legal consequences. Courts 
have consistently held that arrest is not an investigative tool, but a procedural necessity to be 
used sparingly [44]. 
In cybercrime cases, this caution assumes greater significance. Many cyber offences are: 
 
document-centric, 
 
transaction-based, 
 
dependent on electronic trails, 
 
investigable without custodial interrogation. 
Accordingly, arrest must be justified independently of search and seizure, and never treated as 
a default or symbolic step. 
 
6.41 Statutory Framework for Arrest under BNSS 
The BNSS codifies arrest powers while embedding judicially evolved safeguards. The statutory 
scheme reflects the Supreme Court’s long-standing concern over unnecessary arrests, 
particularly in offences punishable with moderate sentences. 
Under BNSS, arrest must satisfy: 
 
statutory thresholds, 
 
necessity-based reasoning, 
 
documentation requirements, 
 
supervisory accountability. 
The shift from a power-centric to a reason-centric arrest framework is central to BNSS and is 
fully adopted in this SOP [45]. 
 
6.42 The “Necessity Test” for Arrest 
[[PAGE 206]]
The Supreme Court has clarified that arrest is not mandatory in every cognizable offence. 
Instead, arrest must pass a necessity test, examining whether custody is required for one or more 
legitimate purposes [46]. 
The recognised grounds include: 
 
preventing further offence, 
 
preventing tampering with evidence, 
 
preventing intimidation of witnesses, 
 
ensuring presence of the accused in investigation or trial. 
In cybercrime cases, Investigating Officers must record which of these grounds apply, and 
why non-custodial measures would be insufficient. 
 
6.43 Arrest and Punishment Thresholds in Cybercrime 
A significant proportion of cyber offences fall within punishment ranges where arrest misuse has 
been judicially criticised. Courts have emphasised that punishment severity does not 
automatically justify arrest, especially where investigation is evidence-driven [47]. 
For offences involving: 
 
online cheating, 
 
digital impersonation, 
 
platform-based fraud, 
 
unauthorised access, 
courts have repeatedly insisted on reasoned arrest decisions, not mechanical custody. 
 
6.44 Arnesh Kumar Doctrine and Its Application to Cybercrime 
The Supreme Court’s ruling in Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar fundamentally altered arrest 
jurisprudence by mandating that arrest must be preceded by application of mind and written 
justification [48]. 
Cybercrime investigations frequently attract Arnesh Kumar scrutiny because: 
 
evidence is largely digital, 
 
accused are often traceable, 
[[PAGE 207]]
 
cooperation can be secured without custody. 
Non-compliance with Arnesh Kumar guidelines has resulted in: 
 
quashing of arrest, 
 
grant of anticipatory bail, 
 
departmental observations against police officers. 
This SOP mandates strict adherence to Arnesh Kumar principles in cybercrime cases. 
 
6.45 Arrest as a Tool of Recovery or Pressure: Judicial Prohibition 
Courts have unequivocally held that arrest cannot be used to recover money, extract 
confessions, or compel settlements [49]. 
In cyber financial fraud cases, arrest is often prematurely resorted to: 
 
to compel refund, 
 
to force disclosure of credentials, 
 
to demonstrate “action taken”. 
Such practices have been expressly condemned. Arrest for recovery purposes has been treated as 
abuse of power, not law enforcement. 
 
6.46 Custodial Interrogation in Cybercrime: Limits 
Courts have clarified that custodial interrogation is not inherently superior to non-custodial 
questioning, especially in cyber offences where: 
 
data trails exist, 
 
logs and records are preserved, 
 
platform responses provide attribution. 
Investigating Officers must therefore record why custodial interrogation is indispensable, and 
why questioning under notice or summons would be inadequate [50]. 
 
6.47 Arrest and Digital Evidence: Inadmissibility Risks 
Improper arrest practices frequently contaminate digital evidence cases by: 
[[PAGE 208]]
 
coercing disclosure of passwords, 
 
compelling access to accounts, 
 
extracting statements under duress. 
Courts have excluded or disbelieved evidence obtained through custodial compulsion, 
particularly where Article 20(3) protections are implicated [51]. 
This SOP therefore mandates that arrest shall not be used as a shortcut to obtain digital access. 
 
6.48 Notice of Appearance and Non-Custodial Measures 
BNSS reinforces the use of notice of appearance as a preferred alternative to arrest where 
investigation can proceed without custody. 
In cybercrime cases, notice-based cooperation is often sufficient because: 
 
accused are digitally traceable, 
 
documentary evidence predominates, 
 
risk of absconding is low. 
Courts have favourably viewed investigations that prioritise notice over arrest, treating them as 
indicators of procedural fairness [52]. 
 
6.49 Arrest in Platform-Based and Multi-Accused Cybercrime 
Cybercrime cases often involve: 
 
multiple actors, 
 
layered roles (creator, facilitator, mule), 
 
platform intermediaries. 
Courts have cautioned against indiscriminate arrests of all persons connected with digital 
transactions without role differentiation [53]. 
Investigating Officers must: 
 
assess individual role, 
 
record role-specific necessity, 
 
avoid collective arrest strategies. 
[[PAGE 209]]
 
6.50 Arrest of Technical Personnel and Intermediary Staff 
In cases involving platforms, fintechs, or IT services, arrest of technical staff has attracted sharp 
judicial criticism where: 
 
there is no mens rea, 
 
actions were routine or automated, 
 
liability is regulatory or civil in nature. 
Courts have emphasised that technical association is not criminal culpability [54]. Arrest of 
such persons requires heightened scrutiny and supervisory oversight. 
 
6.51 Documentation Requirements for Arrest Decisions 
Every arrest in a cybercrime case must be supported by: 
 
written reasons satisfying necessity test, 
 
reference to statutory provisions, 
 
linkage to investigation needs, 
 
consideration of alternatives. 
Absence of such documentation has led courts to infer arbitrariness, even where arrest power 
existed [55]. 
 
6.52 Supervisory Control over Arrest Decisions 
Supervisory officers play a critical role in arrest governance. 
This SOP mandates: 
 
supervisory review of arrest necessity in cybercrime cases, 
 
scrutiny of documentation, 
 
correction of overreach at early stage. 
Courts have repeatedly emphasised that supervisory failure contributes to systemic misuse of 
arrest powers [56]. 
 
[[PAGE 210]]
6.53 Arrest and Post-Arrest Safeguards 
Following arrest, Investigating Officers must ensure: 
 
communication of grounds of arrest, 
 
compliance with constitutional safeguards, 
 
production before magistrate within prescribed time, 
 
medical and legal rights protection. 
Any lapse at this stage has resulted in: 
 
grant of bail, 
 
exclusion of evidence, 
 
adverse judicial remarks [57]. 
 
6.54 Judicial Trends in Cybercrime Arrest Challenges 
Judicial challenges to cybercrime arrests commonly focus on: 
 
absence of necessity reasoning, 
 
arrest before evidence consolidation, 
 
misuse for recovery, 
 
coercive extraction of digital access. 
This Part is structured to ensure that arrest decisions are defensible at the remand and trial 
stages, not merely executable. 
 
6.55 Transition to Coercive Action Workflow 
Having examined arrest doctrine, the final Part will integrate: 
 
FIR and PE sequencing, 
 
search-seizure-arrest order, 
 
supervisory approval matrices, 
 
documentation workflows. 
This integration ensures that coercive action occurs as part of a controlled process, not as 
isolated impulses. 
[[PAGE 211]]

PART V – COERCIVE ACTION WORKFLOW, SUPERVISORY CONTROL & CASE 
DIARY DISCIPLINE 
 
6.56 Purpose of an Integrated Coercive Action Workflow 
Search, seizure, and arrest are often analysed in isolation, but in practice they occur as part of a 
continuous coercive workflow. Judicial scrutiny, however, examines them as linked acts, 
testing whether each step was: 
 
lawfully triggered, 
 
procedurally sequenced, 
 
independently justified. 
[[PAGE 212]]
Courts have repeatedly held that even if individual actions are lawful in abstraction, their 
cumulative misuse can render the investigation arbitrary [58]. This Part therefore prescribes 
a sequenced, documented, and supervised workflow for coercive action in cybercrime cases. 
 
6.57 Sequencing Discipline: From FIR to Coercive Power 
6.57.1 Foundational Rule 
Coercive powers shall not precede lawful case initiation. 
The correct sequence is: 
Information → FIR / PE (where permitted) → Evidence Preservation → Search → Seizure 
→ Arrest → Prosecution 
Deviation from this sequence has been repeatedly criticised where coercive action was used to: 
 
compensate for weak complaints, 
 
create evidence, 
 
pressure parties into settlement [59]. 
 
6.57.2 FIR as the Gateway, Not a Formality 
Courts have clarified that FIR registration is not a clerical step but a jurisdictional gateway to 
coercive power. Search or arrest without a lawful FIR (except in strictly recognised 
circumstances) has been held to vitiate the action itself [60]. 
In cybercrime cases, where digital footprints may appear convincing, officers must resist the 
temptation to “secure first, register later”. 
 
6.58 Preliminary Enquiry (PE) and Its Limits 
Where BNSS permits a preliminary enquiry, courts have emphasised that PE: 
 
is not an investigation, 
 
does not authorise coercive action, 
 
exists to verify whether a cognizable offence is disclosed. 
Search, seizure, or arrest during PE, except in narrowly justified emergency situations, has been 
viewed as unlawful overreach [61]. 
[[PAGE 213]]
This SOP therefore mandates: 
 
strict PE documentation, 
 
express prohibition on routine coercive action during PE. 
 
6.59 Trigger Points for Search and Seizure 
Search and seizure may be triggered when: 
 
prima facie offence is disclosed, 
 
specific evidentiary need is identified, 
 
lawful authority is obtained, 
 
necessity and proportionality are assessed. 
Courts have criticised investigations where search was used as a discovery tool, rather than an 
evidence-preservation step [62]. 
 
6.60 Arrest as the Final Coercive Measure 
Arrest shall ordinarily be the last coercive step, not the first. 
Judicial interpretation makes it clear that: 
 
arrest is not a precondition for search or seizure, 
 
search and seizure do not automatically justify arrest, 
 
arrest must independently satisfy the necessity test [63]. 
This sequencing protects both constitutional liberty and prosecutorial sustainability. 
 
6.61 Supervisory Control: Institutionalising Restraint 
6.61.1 Rationale for Supervisory Oversight 
Courts have repeatedly observed that misuse of coercive powers is often not individual 
misconduct but institutional failure of supervision [64]. 
Cybercrime investigations, given their technical and privacy implications, require active 
supervisory engagement, not post-facto approval. 
 
[[PAGE 214]]
6.61.2 Mandatory Supervisory Touchpoints 
This SOP mandates supervisory review at the following stages: 
 
approval of warrantless search, 
 
seizure of enterprise systems or servers, 
 
arrest decisions in cybercrime cases, 
 
prolonged retention of seized devices. 
Supervisory input shall be recorded, not merely implied. 
 
6.62 Case Diary Discipline in Coercive Actions 
6.62.1 Case Diary as Judicial Record 
Courts treat the case diary as the most reliable contemporaneous record of investigative 
reasoning. Where coercive action is challenged, courts rely more on diary entries than oral 
explanations [65]. 
Accordingly, every coercive action must be reflected in the case diary with: 
 
reasons, 
 
legal basis, 
 
alternatives considered, 
 
supervisory involvement. 
 
6.62.2 What Must Be Recorded (Non-Exhaustive) 
For search: 
 
why search was necessary, 
 
why warrant / warrantless route chosen, 
 
scope and limits. 
For seizure: 
 
why seizure was required, 
 
why copying/preservation was insufficient, 
 
impact on third parties. 
[[PAGE 215]]
For arrest: 
 
necessity grounds invoked, 
 
why notice was insufficient, 
 
custody purpose. 
Absence of such entries has led courts to infer arbitrariness [66]. 
 
6.63 Documentation as a Shield Against Judicial Criticism 
Courts have repeatedly emphasised that good faith is not presumed; it is demonstrated 
through records. 
Well-documented coercive actions have been upheld even in complex cybercrime cases, whereas 
poorly documented actions have failed despite serious allegations [67]. 
This SOP therefore treats documentation not as paperwork, but as legal armour. 
 
6.64 Coordinating with Prosecution at Coercive Stages 
In complex cybercrime cases, early coordination with prosecution: 
 
improves warrant quality, 
 
prevents scope overreach, 
 
anticipates trial-stage objections. 
Courts have favourably noted investigations where prosecutorial input was sought before major 
coercive steps [68]. 
 
6.65 Common Judicially Noted Failures in Cybercrime Coercive Action 
Courts have consistently criticised: 
 
arrest before evidence consolidation, 
 
seizure without necessity analysis, 
 
use of arrest for recovery, 
 
lack of supervisory records, 
 
PE being used as investigative cover. 
[[PAGE 216]]
This Part is designed specifically to prevent these systemic failures. 
 
6.66 Institutional Accountability and Officer Protection 
A disciplined coercive workflow protects: 
 
citizens from arbitrary State power, 
 
officers from personal liability, 
 
investigations from collapse, 
 
institutions from reputational harm. 
Courts have recognised that procedural compliance protects the honest officer as much as it 
restrains the overzealous one [69]. 
 
6.67 Operational Summary of Chapter 6 
Chapter 6 establishes that in cybercrime investigations: 
 
coercive power is exceptional, not routine, 
 
sequencing is mandatory, not optional, 
 
documentation is determinative, not decorative, 
 
supervision is essential, not ceremonial. 
When these principles are applied, cybercrime investigations withstand both constitutional 
scrutiny and trial-stage testing.

 
IO quick-reference annexures, 
 
decision matrices for search, seizure, and arrest, 
 
unified endnotes consolidating all judicial and statutory authorities cited across Parts I–V.
