Chapter 10  Live and Memory Forensics 
Part I – Introduction, Fundamentals & Principles 
10.1 Conceptual Introduction 
10.1.1 Evolution of Digital Forensic Practice 
Digital forensic science has historically been grounded in the paradigm of post-mortem 
examination. Under this model, an investigator encountering a digital device would immediately 
isolate it from power, create a bit-for-bit forensic image of non-volatile storage media, and 
conduct all analysis on the static duplicate. This “pull-the-plug” approach ensured repeatability, 
minimized contamination, and aligned closely with classical forensic principles of evidence 
preservation [1]. 
However, advances in computing architecture, operating systems, encryption, distributed storage, 
and adversarial techniques have rendered this static paradigm increasingly inadequate. Modern 
systems are no longer passive repositories of data; they are dynamic, networked, encrypted, 
and memory-centric environments. Critical evidence now often exists only while a system is 
powered on and operational, disappearing irretrievably upon shutdown [2][4]. 
As a result, digital forensic practice has undergone a fundamental shift—from purely 
retrospective analysis toward real-time, situational evidence acquisition. 
10.1.2 Definition of Live Data Forensics (LDF) 
The disciplined acquisition and examination of digital evidence from a computing 
system while it remains powered on and operational, with the objective of 
preserving volatile, transient, and contextual data that would otherwise be lost 
upon system shutdown [1][3]. 
Unlike traditional static forensics, LDF focuses on the current state of the system rather than 
solely its historical artefacts. This includes data residing in Random Access Memory (RAM), 
active processes, live network connections, decrypted content, runtime configurations, and 
ephemeral execution states [4][7]. 
10.1.3 Defining Memory Forensics 
Memory forensics, also referred to as memory analysis, is the scientific process of acquiring 
and analyzing volatile data residing in a computer system’s Random Access Memory 
(RAM) with the objective of identifying, preserving, and interpreting digital evidence relevant to 
an investigation [1][7]. Unlike persistent storage media such as hard disk drives or solid-state 
drives, RAM functions as a transient execution environment. It contains data that exists only 
while the system is powered on and actively operating. 
[[PAGE 278]]
At its core, memory forensics seeks to reconstruct the runtime state of a digital system—what 
the system was doing, which processes were executing, how users and applications were 
interacting, and whether malicious activity was present at a specific moment in time. This 
runtime-centric focus distinguishes memory forensics as a unique and indispensable sub-
discipline within digital forensic science. 
10.2 The Imperative of Volatile Data 
10.2.1 Understanding Volatility in Digital Systems 
Volatile data refers to information that exists temporarily in a system’s memory and is lost when 
power is removed. Unlike data stored on hard disks or solid-state drives, volatile data has no 
persistence beyond the operational life of the system [8]. 
In digital forensics, volatility is not a binary attribute but a spectrum. RAM is the most volatile 
component, followed by cache, page files, temporary system states, and finally persistent 
storage. The more volatile the data, the higher its evidentiary fragility and investigative urgency 
[2][7]. 
 
 
[[PAGE 279]]
10.2.2 Nature of Volatile Evidence in RAM 
Random Access Memory is a rich evidentiary environment. It contains a continuously changing 
snapshot of the system’s operational reality, including: 
 Active and recently terminated processes 
 Decrypted executable code and configuration data 
 Usernames, passwords, and cryptographic material 
 Open network sockets and communication sessions 
 Command histories and in-memory artefacts of user activity 
 Injected code, rootkits, and fileless malware components 
This data often never reaches disk and therefore cannot be recovered through traditional 
forensic imaging [7][8]. 
10.2.3 Impact of Modern Technologies on Volatility 
Technological developments have significantly increased the forensic value of volatile data: 
a) Encryption 
Modern operating systems employ full-disk and volume-level encryption by default. While 
storage may be cryptographically secure at rest, encryption keys must exist in plaintext within 
memory during system operation. Shutting down the system destroys these keys and renders 
stored data effectively inaccessible [2][5]. 
b) Cloud and Network Dependency 
Cloud-based applications rely on live authentication tokens, session cookies, and volatile 
credentials. These artefacts exist transiently in RAM and are invalidated upon shutdown, 
eliminating access to remote evidence sources [1][6]. 
c) Fileless and Memory-Only Malware 
Contemporary malware increasingly avoids writing to disk, executing entirely within memory to 
evade detection. Such threats can only be identified through live memory analysis [7]. 
10.0.2.4 Consequences of the “Pull-the-Plug” Approach 
The traditional practice of immediately powering off a system results in the irreversible 
destruction of volatile evidence, including: 
 Encryption keys 
 Active network connections 
 Decrypted malicious payloads 
[[PAGE 280]]
 Live command-and-control channels 
Research has conclusively demonstrated that reliance solely on static acquisition techniques 
leads to systematic evidentiary loss in modern investigations [2][4][7]. 
Thus, volatile data acquisition is no longer optional—it is investigatively imperative. 
10.2.4 Memory as the First Priority in Live Systems 
In live systems, memory forensics assumes absolute priority. Once power is removed, the 
following evidentiary elements are permanently destroyed: 
 Full-disk encryption keys stored in memory 
 Active malware payloads executing without disk presence 
 Live command-and-control connections 
 Authenticated cloud or remote service sessions 
Research demonstrates that modern cyber threats increasingly rely on memory-only execution 
models, intentionally avoiding disk artefacts to evade detection [7][8]. 
As a result, memory forensics has become the primary evidentiary gateway in investigations 
involving advanced malware, insider threats, ransomware, and cyber espionage [4]. 
10.3 The Evidentiary Value of RAM 
10.3.1 Identification of Memory-Resident Malware 
Modern malicious software increasingly avoids writing executable files to disk. Instead, it injects 
code directly into memory, exploiting legitimate system processes to execute payloads entirely in 
RAM [7]. 
Traditional disk-based forensic tools are fundamentally incapable of detecting such threats. 
Memory forensics enables investigators to identify: 
 Suspicious memory injections 
 Process hollowing and reflective DLL loading 
 Hidden or unlinked processes 
These artefacts are visible only through memory analysis and disappear upon system shutdown 
10.3.2 Recovery of Encryption Keys and Decrypted Data 
Encryption has become ubiquitous across operating systems and applications. While encrypted 
data at rest may be unreadable, encryption keys must be loaded into RAM during use. Memory 
forensics enables the recovery of: 
[[PAGE 281]]
 Full-disk encryption keys 
 Application-level cryptographic material 
 Decrypted content in active memory buffers 
The shutdown of a system irreversibly destroys these keys, rendering encrypted storage 
effectively inaccessible [2][5]. 
10.3.3 Active Network Connections and Session States 
Memory analysis allows investigators to reconstruct: 
 Open network sockets 
 Remote IP addresses and ports 
 Active sessions and authenticated connections 
These artefacts establish temporal and contextual linkage between a suspect system and 
external actors. Once power is lost, such network state information ceases to exist [4][7]. 
10.4 Scientific & Legal Principles of Live Acquisition 
10.4.1 The Core Forensic Tension 
At the heart of Live Data Forensics lies a fundamental paradox: 
Live forensic acquisition is necessary to preserve volatile evidence, yet the act of 
live acquisition inherently alters the system under examination. 
Classical forensic doctrine emphasizes the principle that evidence should not be altered. Live 
forensics, by definition, violates this principle because every interaction with a running system 
consumes resources, allocates memory, and modifies system state [1][3]. 
This tension does not invalidate LDF; rather, it demands explicit scientific justification and 
legal articulation. 
10.0.4.2 Locard’s Exchange Principle in Digital Context 
Locard’s Exchange Principle, a foundational doctrine in forensic science, states: 
Every contact leaves a trace. 
In the digital domain, this principle manifests with exceptional clarity. Every command 
executed, tool launched, or memory dump acquired leaves a digital footprint—altered memory 
addresses, modified process tables, and changed system states [1]. 
[[PAGE 282]]
Live forensic investigators must therefore accept that zero-impact acquisition is impossible. 
The objective is not absolute non-interference, but measured, minimal, and explainable 
interaction. 
10.4.3 Footprint of Live Forensic Tools 
Empirical research demonstrates that live forensic tools themselves occupy memory, execute 
instructions, and modify RAM during acquisition. The exact footprint may vary based on tool 
design, operating system, and system load [1]. 
The forensic significance lies not in eliminating this footprint, but in: 
 Understanding its nature 
 Measuring its impact 
 Documenting its consequences 
Failure to articulate these effects undermines the credibility of the evidence and exposes the 
investigation to judicial challenge. 
10.4.4 Principle of Forensic Soundness 
Forensic soundness in live acquisition does not require an unchanged system; it requires that: 
 Evidence retains its original meaning 
 Changes introduced are necessary, proportionate, and documented 
 The process is transparent, auditable, and defensible 
Scholarly models such as structured live acquisition frameworks emphasize that comprehensive 
documentation and chain-of-custody records can reconcile system alteration with legal 
admissibility [3][6]. 
10.4.5 Legal Justification of System Interaction 
Courts increasingly recognize that certain categories of evidence cannot be obtained without live 
interaction. Analogies have been drawn between: 
 A detective touching physical evidence at a crime scene 
 A forensic examiner executing commands on a live system 
In both cases, interaction is justified when it is necessary to reveal otherwise inaccessible 
evidence, provided the investigator can clearly explain the implications of their actions [3][6]. 
[[PAGE 283]]
10.4.6 Chain of Custody and Auditability 
Live forensics places extraordinary emphasis on documentation. Because system state is 
constantly changing, repeatability in the classical sense is often impossible. Instead, credibility is 
established through: 
 Detailed action logs 
 Tool validation records 
 Time-stamped acquisition steps 
 Hash verification where applicable 
This audit trail enables courts to evaluate process integrity, even when exact reproduction of 
results is infeasible [1][4]. 
Live and Memory Forensics represent an unavoidable evolution in digital investigation. As 
systems become faster, more encrypted, and more ephemeral, volatile data becomes the 
primary evidentiary battlefield. The abandonment of static-only thinking is not a relaxation of 
forensic rigor but an adaptation of forensic science to contemporary realities [2][4][7]. 
For law enforcement agencies, including the Uttar Pradesh Police, mastery of Live Data 
Forensics is no longer an advanced specialization—it is a core investigative competency 
essential for effective cybercrime response and judicial success. 
Memory forensics represents a decisive evolution in digital forensic science. As computing 
environments become increasingly encrypted, cloud-integrated, and memory-centric, volatile 
evidence has emerged as the primary carrier of judicial truth in cyber investigations [2][7]. 
The discipline demands high technical competence, rigorous documentation, and legal 
awareness. When conducted correctly, memory forensics provides courts with direct, 
contemporaneous insight into system behavior, bridging the gap between technical reality and 
legal proof. 
For modern law enforcement and judicial systems, memory forensics is no longer optional—it is 
foundational. 
 
 
Memory forensics does not replace disk forensics; it complements it. Together, they provide a 
holistic evidentiary narrative, combining runtime behavior with historical artefacts [4]. 
Part II – Process and Procedures 
 
[[PAGE 284]]
10.5 Introduction: Operational Nature of Live and Memory Forensics 
Live and memory forensics represents a departure from traditional post-mortem digital 
investigations. Unlike static forensic examinations, which operate on powered-off systems and 
preserved storage media, live and memory forensic processes are conducted on running 
systems, where evidence is volatile, transient, and continuously changing [1][5]. 
The objective of Part II is to establish a procedurally rigorous, legally defensible framework 
for conducting live and memory forensic investigations. This framework integrates the standard 
forensic workflow, the memory evidence lifecycle, and the Liforac model for forensically 
sound live acquisition. 
Live and memory forensics are not ad-hoc technical activities but regulated investigative 
processes that must withstand adversarial scrutiny in courts of law. Unlike traditional dead 
forensics, where evidence preservation precedes analysis, live and memory forensics operate 
under temporal pressure, system volatility, and inevitable system interaction. As a result, 
procedural discipline becomes the primary guarantor of evidentiary reliability [1][2]. 
This integrated approach ensures that volatile digital evidence is not merely collected, but is 
acquired, examined, documented, and presented in a manner that withstands scientific 
scrutiny and judicial cross-examination [2][6]. 
 
10.6 Procedural Phases of Live and Memory Forensic Investigation 
Live and memory forensic investigations adhere to a five-phase workflow adapted from classical 
digital forensic process models [6]: 
1. Identification 
2. Preservation (Imaging / Acquisition) 
3. Analysis (Examination and Reduction) 
4. Documentation 
5. Presentation 
 
[[PAGE 285]]
 
Each phase is sequential, interdependent, and mandatory for evidentiary reliability. 
10.6.1 Phase I – Identification 
The Identification phase is the point at which the investigator determines the existence, 
location, and nature of volatile evidence. In live environments, this phase is time-critical, as 
evidentiary value deteriorates with every system operation [1][2]. 
Identification activities include: 
 Determining whether the system is powered on and operational 
 Identifying sources of volatile data such as RAM, caches, and live network connections 
 Assessing the presence of encryption, active sessions, or running malware 
 Evaluating the risk of evidentiary loss if the system is shut down 
Indicators that necessitate live or memory acquisition include full-disk encryption, suspected 
fileless malware, active remote connections, and logged-in user sessions [5][7]. 
Failure to correctly identify volatile evidence at this stage may result in irreversible loss of 
critical information. 
10.6.2 Phase II – Preservation (Imaging / Acquisition) 
10.6.2.1 Preservation in a Live Context 
In traditional forensics, preservation implies maintaining the evidence in an unchanged state. In 
live forensics, this principle is reinterpreted. Because volatile memory changes continuously, 
preservation focuses on preserving evidentiary meaning, not preventing change [1][4]. 
The principal method of preservation in memory forensics is the creation of a forensic memory 
image (memory dump or system snapshot). 
[[PAGE 286]]
10.6.2.2 Memory Dump Acquisition 
A memory dump is a point-in-time capture of the contents of a system’s physical memory. Once 
acquired, it becomes static evidence capable of repeatable analysis [7][9]. 
Memory dumps may contain: 
 Running and terminated process data 
 Decrypted malware and injected code 
 Encryption keys and authentication material 
 Network sockets and session metadata. 
These artefacts often never exist on disk, making memory acquisition indispensable [5][7]. 
10.6.2.3 Step-by-Step Acquisition Strategy 
Live acquisition must follow a strict step-by-step strategy to minimize system instability and 
evidentiary contamination [10]: 
1. Record visible system state (screen, time, logged-in users) 
2. Document network status and running applications 
3. Prepare sterile external storage media 
4. Deploy a validated memory acquisition tool 
5. Capture full physical memory 
6. Confirm successful completion of the dump 
7. Generate cryptographic hash values 
8. Secure and label the acquired image 
Unstructured acquisition increases the risk of system crashes, partial captures, and legal 
challenges [10]. 
10.6.2.4 Software vs. Hardware Acquisition and the Footprint Principle 
All live acquisition methods leave a footprint—measurable changes to system memory caused 
by forensic actions [1][4]. 
Software-based acquisition operates within the target operating system. 
– Rapid deployment 
– Broad compatibility 
– Consumes memory 
– Relies on OS integrity 
– Susceptible to kernel-level manipulation 
[[PAGE 287]]
Hardware-based acquisition interacts externally with memory. 
– Reduced OS reliance 
– Smaller software footprint 
– Specialized equipment 
– Limited platform support 
The investigator must select the acquisition method that produces the least intrusive footprint 
consistent with investigative objectives and must be prepared to justify this choice in court 
[1][10]. 
Forensic soundness is Live acquisition introduces predictable technical and legal risks. achieved 
not by eliminating these risks, but by anticipating, mitigating, and documenting them

10.7 Phase III – Analysis and Examination 
10.7.1 Separation of Acquisition and Analysis 
Once acquired, memory images must be write-protected and analyzed only on forensic copies. 
The original memory image remains untouched to preserve integrity [7]. 
10.7.2 Reduction: From Raw Data to Artefacts 
Memory images are not human-readable. Analysis begins with reduction, the process of 
extracting meaningful artefacts from raw binary data [7][9]. 
Reduction activities include: 
 Process reconstruction 
 Module and driver enumeration 
 Network connection analysis 
 Credential and key extraction 
 Detection of injected or anomalous code 
Reduction must be selective, methodical, and fully documented. 
10.7.3 Verification Through Multiple Analytical Passes 
Live forensic evidence lacks deterministic repeatability. To ensure judicial confidence, findings 
must be verified through: 
 Multiple analytical passes 
 Cross-tool validation 
 Correlation with disk and network evidence 
[[PAGE 289]]
Convergent results strengthen evidentiary reliability, while discrepancies must be explained 
[2][7]. 
10.7.4 Case Simulation as Validation Mechanism 
Case simulation allows investigators to test tools, procedures, and interpretations in controlled 
environments. Simulation is critical for: 
 Measuring acquisition footprint 
 Validating analytical workflows 
 Training personnel 
Simulation strengthens institutional credibility and courtroom defensibility [1][10]. 
10.8 Phase IV – Documentation and Chain of Custody 
10.8.1 Documentation as Evidentiary Substitute 
Because live system states cannot be recreated, documentation substitutes for repeatability. 
Every action must be recorded contemporaneously [1][6]. 
10.8.2 Chain of Custody 
Chain of custody records must demonstrate: 
 Who handled the evidence 
 When and where it was handled 
 What actions were performed 
 How integrity was preserved 
Any break in custody undermines admissibility [6]. 
10.8.3 Integrity Verification 
Cryptographic hash values must be generated: 
 Immediately after acquisition 
 After every transfer 
 Prior to analysis 
Matching hashes prove that evidence remains unchanged [7]. 
10.8.4 Environmental and Contextual Logs 
Investigators must log: 
[[PAGE 290]]
 Hardware configuration 
 OS version and uptime 
 Running applications 
 Network connectivity 
These details are essential during cross-examination to contextualize artefacts [1][4]. 
10.9 Phase V – Presentation 
Presentation translates technical findings into a judicial narrative. Courts evaluate not only 
what was found, but how it was found. 
Investigators must be able to: 
 Justify live acquisition 
 Explain system alteration and footprint 
 Demonstrate methodological rigor 
Credibility of process determines credibility of evidence [6]. 
Live and memory forensics is a discipline of controlled intrusion. Its legitimacy lies not in 
avoiding system change, but in minimizing, documenting, and justifying change [1][3]. 
By integrating the standard forensic workflow with the Liforac framework and disciplined 
acquisition strategies, investigators transform volatile system states into durable judicial 
evidence capable of withstanding adversarial scrutiny. 
Part III – Tools and Techniques 
 
10.10 Introduction: The Role of Tools in Live and Memory Forensics 
Live and memory forensics is not tool-driven but method-driven. Tools are merely instruments 
that operationalize forensic principles. Improper tool selection, undocumented behavior, or 
misunderstood output can compromise evidentiary reliability even when procedures are 
otherwise correct. Consequently, forensic tools used in volatile data acquisition and analysis 
must be critically evaluated, validated, and contextually justified, rather than blindly trusted 
[1][2]. 
This Part examines the tools and techniques employed in live and memory forensics from a 
technical audit perspective, focusing on acquisition technologies, analytical frameworks, 
footprint measurement, and evidence recovery methodologies. Emphasis is placed on tool 
behavior, output structure, limitations, and judicial defensibility, rather than vendor claims. 
[[PAGE 291]]
10.11 Memory Acquisition Technologies 
10.11.1 Principles Governing Memory Acquisition Tools 
Memory acquisition tools operate on a fundamental paradox: to preserve volatile data, they must 
execute within the very memory they are attempting to capture. As a result, every acquisition 
tool alters the system state, consumes memory, and introduces artefacts [1][3]. 
Therefore, evaluation of acquisition tools must consider: 
 Accuracy of memory capture 
 Transparency of tool behavior 
 Measurable memory footprint 
 Stability during acquisition 
 Suitability for field deployment 
10.11.2 Commonly Used Memory Acquisition Tools 
10.11.2.1 FTK Imager 
FTK Imager is widely used for both disk and memory acquisition and is frequently deployed in 
law-enforcement environments due to its stability and familiarity [8]. 
 Supports full physical memory capture 
 Allows acquisition of page files and hibernation files 
 Provides immediate hash generation 
FTK Imager presents acquired data in a tree-structured hierarchical view, which mirrors file-
system logic rather than memory semantics. While suitable for disk artefacts, this representation 
complicates direct memory analysis, as RAM does not follow hierarchical storage principles [8]. 
FTK Imager is appropriate for controlled acquisitions and environments where disk and 
memory acquisition must be performed together. However, it is not optimized for deep memory-
centric investigations and requires external analysis frameworks for meaningful interpretation 
[8][10]. 
10.11.2.2 Belkasoft RAM Capture 
Belkasoft provides integrated memory acquisition and analysis capabilities, often favored in 
commercial forensic laboratories [8]. 
[[PAGE 292]]
 Rapid RAM acquisition 
 Integration with Belkasoft Evidence Center 
 Support for multiple Windows architectures 
Similar to FTK Imager, Belkasoft organizes extracted artefacts using tree-based logical 
groupings. This approach enhances usability but abstracts low-level memory structures, which 
may obscure kernel-level artefacts or injected code regions [8]. 
Belkasoft is effective for triage-level memory examinations and application-centric artefact 
recovery. It is less suitable where granular memory structure analysis or independent verification 
is required [8]. 
10.11.2.3 DumpIt 
DumpIt is a lightweight, command-line memory acquisition utility specifically designed for 
minimal interaction [8][10]. 
 Single-execution binary 
 Minimal configuration 
 Outputs raw memory images 
DumpIt does not provide a graphical representation. The output is a raw memory image, 
intended for use with external analysis frameworks such as Volatility. 
DumpIt is well suited for field acquisition and incident response, where speed, minimal 
footprint, and simplicity are critical. However, it provides no analytical capabilities and relies 
entirely on downstream tools for interpretation [10].
