Chapter 13: OSINT and Social Media Investigations 
Part I – Strategic Introduction and Evolution of Cybercrime 
Cybercrime today is no longer a rare or technical offence committed by a few highly skilled 
individuals sitting behind computers. It has become a part of everyday policing, affecting 
ordinary citizens, banks, hospitals, government departments, and even national security systems. 
A large number of these crimes begin, grow, or leave traces on the open internet and social media 
platforms. This is where Open Source Intelligence, commonly known as OSINT, becomes one of 
the most powerful and lawful tools available to a modern Investigating Officer [1]. 
OSINT simply means collecting and analysing information that is already available to the public. 
This includes social media posts, websites, online forums, news reports, public databases, 
domain records, and other open digital sources. Unlike hacking or interception, OSINT does not 
involve breaking into systems or secretly monitoring private communications. When used 
correctly, OSINT respects the law while still providing valuable leads, patterns, and evidence for 
cybercrime investigations [2]. 
[[PAGE 355]]
In the early days of cybercrime, offences were mostly committed by individuals acting alone. 
These offenders were often curious or motivated by personal gain, reputation, or 
experimentation. Investigations at that time focused mainly on tracing IP addresses, analysing 
devices, and identifying technical mistakes made by offenders. Social media had a limited role, 
and digital footprints were relatively small [3]. 
Over the last decade, this situation has changed completely. Cybercrime has evolved into 
organised, profit-driven, and sometimes state-supported activity. Criminal groups now operate 
like companies. They advertise services, recruit members, outsource tasks, and share tools. This 
model is commonly known as Crime-as-a-Service. In such cases, OSINT helps investigators 
understand the structure of these groups, identify roles played by different members, and trace 
their public online presence without alerting them [4]. 
Social media platforms have become central to this new cybercrime environment. Criminals use 
them for reconnaissance, recruitment, impersonation, fraud, and psychological manipulation. 
Victims often first encounter offenders through fake profiles, fraudulent advertisements, phishing 
messages, or emotional deception. Every such interaction leaves behind small but important 
digital traces. When these traces are carefully collected and connected, they form a clear picture 
of criminal intent and activity [5]. 
From a policing perspective, OSINT is not only a technical method but also a mindset. It teaches 
the Investigating Officer to observe patterns, relationships, and behaviour rather than focusing 
only on devices and software. A Facebook profile, an Instagram photo, a username reused across 
platforms, or a public comment on a forum may appear harmless in isolation. However, when 
analysed together, these elements can reveal identity, location, networks, and even future plans of 
an offender [6]. 
In India, the importance of OSINT has increased sharply due to the widespread use of 
smartphones, affordable internet access, and digital payment systems. Citizens from all age 
groups now use social media and online platforms daily. As a result, cyber offences such as 
online cheating, identity theft, cyberstalking, deepfake abuse, and financial fraud have grown 
rapidly. Traditional investigation methods alone are no longer sufficient to deal with this scale 
and speed of crime [7]. 
At the same time, investigators must clearly understand the legal boundaries of OSINT. Not 
everything available on the internet can be freely used without thought. The Digital Personal 
Data Protection Act, 2023 recognises a difference between personal data that is privately held 
and data that an individual has voluntarily made public. This distinction is critical. OSINT 
operates lawfully only when it stays within the limits of publicly available information and 
lawful purpose [8]. 
Courts today expect cyber investigations to be transparent, proportionate, and legally justified. 
Evidence collected through OSINT must therefore be reliable, properly documented, and capable 
of being explained in simple terms before a judge. An IO must be able to show not only what 
was collected, but also how it was collected, when it was collected, and why it was legally 
permissible to do so [9]. 
[[PAGE 356]]
Another major change in cybercrime is the growing involvement of organised international 
groups and advanced persistent threat actors. These actors may target financial systems, 
government databases, or critical infrastructure. While technical forensics remains important in 
such cases, OSINT plays a key supporting role by mapping public indicators, leaked information, 
online narratives, and digital behaviour linked to such threats [10]. 
The role of OSINT is also expanding due to the rise of artificial intelligence–based crimes. 
Deepfake videos, synthetic voice fraud, and automated scam networks often rely on publicly 
available photos, videos, and personal details of victims. Understanding how criminals misuse 
open data helps investigators both detect offences and educate the public about preventive 
measures [11]. 
For young Investigating Officers and supervisory officers alike, OSINT should be seen as the 
first step in many cyber investigations. It helps in understanding the nature of the offence, 
identifying possible suspects, assessing the scale of the crime, and deciding whether further legal 
measures such as search, seizure, or interception are required. Used wisely, OSINT saves time, 
reduces unnecessary intrusion, and strengthens the overall quality of investigation [12]. 
This chapter is written with a practical purpose. It aims to explain OSINT and social media 
investigations in simple language, without technical complexity, while remaining legally 
accurate and operationally sound. The focus is not on tools alone, but on thinking like an 
investigator—observing, verifying, documenting, and presenting digital facts in a manner that 
stands scrutiny in court and serves the cause of justice [13]. 
 
Part II – Legal and Ethical Framework Governing OSINT 
Before any Investigating Officer begins collecting information from the internet or social media, 
it is essential to clearly understand what the law allows and what it restricts. OSINT is 
powerful, but if used carelessly, it can damage a case, violate individual rights, and even expose 
the officer to legal consequences. Therefore, OSINT must always be guided by law, ethics, and 
accountability [14]. 
The first legal principle an IO must understand is the difference between public information and 
private personal data. Not everything visible on the internet is legally free to use. Indian law 
recognises that individuals have a right to privacy, even in the digital world. At the same time, 
the law allows lawful use of information that a person has voluntarily placed in the public 
domain [15]. 
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 clearly explains this distinction. Section 3(c) of 
the Act states that the law does not apply to personal data that has been made publicly 
available by the individual themselves, or where such publication is required by law. This 
single provision forms the backbone of lawful OSINT in India. If a person publicly posts their 
photograph, phone number, or opinion on a social media platform, an investigator may lawfully 
view and analyse it for a legitimate investigation [16]. 
[[PAGE 357]]
However, this does not mean investigators can collect public data without responsibility. The 
purpose of collection must be lawful and connected to an investigation. OSINT should never 
become curiosity-driven surveillance. Officers must always be able to explain why a particular 
piece of information was collected and how it is relevant to the offence under investigation [17]. 
The DPDP Act also introduces the idea of lawful purpose and legitimate use. Section 4 allows 
processing of personal data only for a lawful purpose, while Section 7 permits certain legitimate 
uses, including actions taken by the State for public order, security, and prevention of crime. 
Cybercrime investigations clearly fall within this scope, provided actions remain proportionate 
and necessary [18]. 
A common mistake made during cyber investigations is treating OSINT as an informal activity 
that does not require documentation. This approach is dangerous. Courts increasingly demand 
transparency. Every screenshot, webpage capture, social media post, or online record collected 
during OSINT must be treated as potential evidence, not casual information [19]. 
This is where the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 becomes crucial. Section 63(4) lays 
down strict requirements for certification of electronic records. Any digital evidence collected 
through OSINT—such as screenshots of profiles, chats, posts, or websites—must be 
accompanied by proper certification explaining the device used, the process of capture, and 
assurance of integrity [20]. 
If this certification is missing or incomplete, even genuine OSINT findings may be rejected by 
the court. Therefore, IOs must treat OSINT evidence with the same seriousness as seized devices 
or forensic reports. Proper timestamps, hashing where possible, and documentation of source 
URLs are not optional—they are legally necessary [21]. 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 further supports lawful OSINT while placing clear limits. 
Sections 43 and 66 penalise unauthorised access to computer systems. This means that OSINT 
must never involve bypassing login barriers, privacy settings, or security controls. 
Accessing information hidden behind passwords or private groups without authorisation amounts 
to illegal access, even if the information is later found useful [22]. 
Sections 69, 69A, and 69B of the IT Act deal with interception, monitoring, and blocking of 
information. These powers require formal authorisation and cannot be confused with OSINT. 
OSINT does not include intercepting messages, monitoring private communications, or 
collecting traffic data. Any such activity without approval would be illegal and unethical [23]. 
Ethically, OSINT investigations must respect human dignity. Officers must avoid unnecessary 
exposure of personal lives, especially of victims. In cases involving women, children, or 
vulnerable individuals, even publicly available data must be handled with sensitivity. Circulating 
screenshots or storing irrelevant personal material can cause secondary harm and must be 
avoided [24]. 
Another ethical concern is confirmation bias. Investigators may unconsciously focus only on 
online information that supports their theory of the case. OSINT must therefore be verified 
[[PAGE 358]]
across multiple sources. A single social media post is not proof. Cross-checking, timeline 
analysis, and corroboration with other evidence are essential [25]. 
Senior officers and supervisory staff have a responsibility to ensure that OSINT is conducted 
within legal boundaries. Regular training, internal SOPs, and review of OSINT reports help 
prevent misuse. A well-conducted OSINT investigation strengthens prosecution, while a careless 
one weakens the entire case [26]. 
In summary, OSINT is lawful, powerful, and necessary—but only when used with legal clarity 
and ethical restraint. The investigator must always remember that the goal is justice, not 
surveillance. Lawful OSINT protects both the public and the police officer conducting the 
investigation [27]. 
 
Part III – Advanced OSINT Methodology and the Intelligence Cycle 
To use OSINT effectively, an Investigating Officer must follow a clear and disciplined method. 
OSINT is not about randomly searching the internet or scrolling through social media. It is a 
structured process that helps the officer move from confusion to clarity. This structured approach 
is commonly known as the Intelligence Cycle, and it is used worldwide by police and 
intelligence agencies [28]. 
The Intelligence Cycle has five simple stages: Direction, Collection, Processing, Analysis, and 
Dissemination. When followed properly, these steps ensure that OSINT work remains lawful, 
focused, and useful in court. Skipping steps or mixing them up often leads to wasted effort or 
unreliable conclusions [29]. 
The first stage is Direction. At this stage, the IO must clearly define what they are looking for. 
For example, is the goal to identify a suspect behind a fake profile, locate a scam operation, or 
understand how victims are being targeted? Without a clear objective, OSINT quickly becomes 
scattered and ineffective. Direction also ensures that the investigation stays within legal limits 
and does not turn into unnecessary monitoring [30]. 
During Direction, the officer should write down simple questions such as: Who may be 
involved?, Which platform is being used?, What type of crime is suspected?, and What time 
period is relevant? These questions guide all further actions and help justify the collection of 
specific data later in court [31]. 
The second stage is Collection. This is the stage most people associate with OSINT. Collection 
involves gathering information from publicly available sources such as social media profiles, 
websites, forums, online advertisements, domain records, and public documents. At this stage, 
the IO must remember that only openly accessible information may be collected, without 
bypassing privacy controls or restrictions [32]. 
[[PAGE 359]]
Collection should always be careful and quiet. Investigators should avoid actions that alert 
suspects, such as liking posts, following accounts from personal profiles, or interacting directly. 
Even simple actions can leave digital traces that warn offenders and cause them to delete 
evidence or change behaviour [33]. 
The third stage is Processing. Raw data collected from the internet is often messy and confusing. 
Processing means organising this data into a readable and usable form. Screenshots are labelled, 
links are recorded, timelines are created, and duplicate or irrelevant material is removed. This 
stage turns scattered online content into structured information [34]. 
Processing also includes preserving evidence properly. Screenshots must show date, time, URL, 
and platform details. Wherever possible, files should be stored securely, and integrity must be 
maintained. Poor processing often leads to good evidence being rejected due to lack of clarity or 
authenticity [35]. 
The fourth stage is Analysis. This is where OSINT becomes intelligence. Analysis involves 
connecting different pieces of information to identify patterns, relationships, and meaning. For 
example, a username used on multiple platforms, similar writing styles, repeated posting times, 
or shared contact details may point to the same individual or group [36]. 
Analysis requires patience and objectivity. Investigators must avoid jumping to conclusions 
based on one strong-looking clue. Instead, multiple independent indicators should support each 
conclusion. A good analyst always asks: Is there another explanation?, Can this be verified 
elsewhere?, and Does this fit the known facts of the case? [37]. 
The fifth and final stage is Dissemination. Dissemination means presenting findings clearly to 
supervisors, prosecutors, or courts. OSINT findings must be written in simple language, 
supported by evidence, and logically arranged. A good OSINT report explains what was found, 
where it was found, how it was verified, and why it is relevant [38]. 
Dissemination is not about showing technical skill. It is about communication. Judges and 
prosecutors may not be familiar with social media platforms or online culture. Therefore, 
findings must be explained clearly, without jargon, and with supporting screenshots or annexures 
where required [39]. 
An important part of advanced OSINT methodology is verification. The internet contains false 
information, fake profiles, and misleading content. Investigators must cross-check information 
across multiple sources. For example, a photograph should be checked across platforms, dates 
should be compared, and profile details should be matched with known facts [40]. 
Another key principle is timeline analysis. Cyber offences often follow patterns. Creating a 
timeline of posts, messages, transactions, or profile activity helps investigators understand 
preparation, execution, and aftermath of the crime. Timelines also help establish intent and 
continuity, which are crucial in prosecution [41]. 
[[PAGE 360]]
Advanced OSINT also includes understanding behavioural indicators. The way a person writes, 
the time they post, the language they use, and the communities they interact with often reveal 
more than technical details. Behavioural patterns are especially useful in identifying repeat 
offenders and organised groups [42]. 
For Indian investigators, it is important to remember that OSINT is most effective when 
combined with traditional policing skills. Field verification, victim statements, financial analysis, 
and technical forensics should support OSINT findings. OSINT alone rarely solves a case, but it 
often provides the missing links that make other evidence meaningful [43]. 
In conclusion, the Intelligence Cycle gives OSINT its strength and discipline. When followed 
carefully, it helps investigators collect lawful evidence, avoid mistakes, and present clear 
findings. OSINT is not guesswork—it is structured thinking applied to open information [44]. 
 
Part IV – Infrastructure OSINT, Email Analysis, and Domain Intelligence 
Many cybercrimes do not start with social media messages alone. Behind almost every phishing 
email, fake website, scam call centre, or fraudulent app, there is some form of digital 
infrastructure. Infrastructure OSINT focuses on understanding this hidden backbone of 
cybercrime. It helps investigators answer simple but crucial questions: Where is the website 
hosted?, Who controls it?, Is the same infrastructure being reused for multiple crimes? [45]. 
Infrastructure OSINT does not mean hacking into servers or networks. It involves analysing 
information that is already publicly visible on the internet, such as IP addresses, domain 
registration details, server configurations, and hosting records. When done lawfully, this form of 
OSINT often reveals links between apparently unrelated crimes [46]. 
A common example is a phishing website. To a victim, it may appear as a simple fake banking 
page. To an investigator, however, that website has a digital address, known as an IP address, 
and a registered domain name. These technical identifiers often remain visible through open 
sources and can be examined without illegal access [47]. 
Tools such as Shodan and Censys are widely used internationally for infrastructure OSINT. 
These tools scan the internet and index devices, servers, and services that openly respond to 
requests. Investigators can use them to see what type of server is running, which ports are open, 
and whether the same server has been involved in earlier criminal activity [48]. 
For example, if multiple fake websites are hosted on the same IP address or server, it may 
indicate a common operator or criminal group. This information is extremely useful in 
identifying organised cybercrime rather than treating each complaint as an isolated incident [49]. 
Another critical area of OSINT is domain name analysis. Every website has a domain name, 
which is registered through an authorised registrar. Publicly available WHOIS records often 
[[PAGE 361]]
show details such as the registration date, registrar name, country, and sometimes contact 
information. Even when details are masked, patterns can still be observed [50]. 
Investigators should pay attention to domain age. Fraudulent domains are often newly registered 
and used for short periods. A domain created just days before a crime and abandoned soon after 
is a strong indicator of malicious intent. Courts have accepted such patterns as circumstantial 
evidence when properly documented [51]. 
Email analysis is equally important in cybercrime investigations, especially in phishing, business 
email compromise, and online cheating cases. Emails carry headers, which contain routing 
information showing how the message travelled across servers. While the content of an email 
may be misleading, headers often reveal the real source or at least the path taken [52]. 
Email headers can show originating IP addresses, mail servers used, and timestamps. Analysing 
this information through OSINT helps investigators identify whether emails were sent from 
compromised systems, bulk mail services, or known malicious infrastructure. This analysis does 
not involve accessing private accounts and remains lawful when limited to provided evidence 
[53]. 
A frequent mistake by inexperienced investigators is relying only on visible sender addresses. 
Criminals often fake display names and email IDs. Infrastructure OSINT allows officers to look 
beyond appearances and understand the technical reality behind the communication [54]. 
Infrastructure OSINT is also valuable in identifying hosting providers and service platforms. 
Once a hosting provider is identified, investigators can follow lawful procedures to seek further 
information or takedown assistance. OSINT helps ensure that formal requests are targeted, 
precise, and legally justified [55]. 
Another benefit of infrastructure OSINT is link analysis. By comparing IP addresses, domains, 
SSL certificates, and hosting patterns, investigators can connect different scam websites, fake 
apps, or fraudulent campaigns. This helps in identifying larger criminal operations and 
prioritising cases with wider impact [56]. 
From an ethical and legal perspective, IOs must remember that infrastructure OSINT does not 
give a licence to intrude into systems. Attempting to access admin panels, hidden directories, or 
restricted services crosses the boundary into illegal access under the IT Act. OSINT stops at 
observation and analysis of what is openly visible [57]. 
Proper documentation is critical in infrastructure OSINT. Screenshots of search results, records 
of domain lookups, timestamps, and tool names used must be recorded carefully. Investigators 
should always assume that defence counsel will question how the information was obtained [58]. 
When explained properly, infrastructure OSINT findings are easy for courts to understand. 
Judges may not know technical details, but they understand patterns—such as repeated use of the 
same server for multiple frauds, or deliberate short-term domain registrations. Clear explanation 
turns technical data into understandable evidence [59]. 
[[PAGE 362]]
In summary, infrastructure OSINT allows investigators to see the hidden structure of cybercrime 
without crossing legal boundaries. It complements social media analysis and helps identify 
organised activity, repeat offenders, and larger criminal networks operating behind simple-
looking online scams [60]. 
 
Part V – Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT): Platform-Specific Data and 
Identity Verification 
Social media platforms have become one of the most important sources of information in 
cybercrime investigations. People now share large parts of their lives online—photos, opinions, 
locations, friendships, habits, and emotions. Criminals also use these platforms to deceive 
victims, create fake identities, and run fraud operations. Social Media Intelligence, or 
SOCMINT, helps investigators lawfully study this open information and convert it into useful 
evidence [61]. 
SOCMINT is a part of OSINT that focuses only on social media platforms such as Facebook, 
Instagram, X (Twitter), YouTube, Telegram channels, LinkedIn, and other public online 
communities. The key principle remains the same: only publicly visible information can be 
used. Private messages, closed groups, or restricted content cannot be accessed without legal 
permission [62]. 
Each social media platform leaves behind different types of digital traces, also called platform-
specific artefacts. Understanding these artefacts helps an Investigating Officer collect the right 
information and avoid irrelevant data. For example, Facebook profiles often reveal user IDs, 
public friend lists, profile creation patterns, and interaction history. Even if a name is fake, the 
underlying profile behaviour often tells a different story [63]. 
Instagram is heavily image- and video-based. Public posts may contain photographs that include 
metadata, such as date, time, and sometimes location details. Even when metadata is stripped, 
background elements in photos—signboards, landmarks, language, clothing style—can help 
determine location and identity. Criminals often forget that images speak louder than text [64]. 
Platforms like X (Twitter) are useful for understanding timelines and intent. Tweets are time-
stamped and often linked to current events. Sudden spikes in activity, coordinated posting, or 
repeated use of specific phrases may indicate organised campaigns, scams, or influence 
operations. Such behavioural patterns are important in cases involving misinformation or 
financial fraud [65]. 
Messaging platforms and open channels, such as public Telegram groups, are increasingly used 
for illegal activities. While private chats cannot be accessed through OSINT, public channels 
and groups can be lawfully observed. These spaces often reveal recruitment messages, illegal 
advertisements, or coordination signals. Investigators must document such content carefully, as it 
is often deleted quickly [66]. 
[[PAGE 363]]
One of the biggest challenges in SOCMINT is fake or anonymous profiles. Criminals 
frequently use stolen photos, random names, and newly created accounts. Investigators should 
never rely on profile names alone. Instead, they must look for deeper indicators such as posting 
time patterns, language use, reused usernames, and connections with other accounts [67]. 
Cross-platform verification is the most reliable method to confirm identity. Many offenders 
reuse the same username, profile photo, or writing style across platforms. A username found on 
Instagram may also appear on a gaming forum, a Telegram channel, or an online marketplace. 
When multiple platforms point to the same digital identity, the confidence level of attribution 
increases significantly [68]. 
Another useful method is social graph analysis. Even fake profiles interact with real people. 
Analysing comments, likes, tagged users, and public friend connections helps investigators 
understand the network around a suspect. Criminal groups often show patterns of mutual 
interaction that are not random [69]. 
SOCMINT is also valuable in understanding victim targeting and victimology. By studying 
public posts of victims, investigators can identify how offenders selected targets. For example, 
scammers often target individuals who publicly express financial stress, emotional vulnerability, 
or urgent needs. This understanding helps in both investigation and prevention [70]. 
Investigators must also be careful about context. A post taken out of context can mislead the 
investigation. Sarcasm, jokes, or cultural expressions may appear suspicious but may not indicate 
criminal intent. Therefore, SOCMINT findings should always be correlated with other evidence 
before drawing conclusions [71]. 
From a legal perspective, SOCMINT must comply with the DPDP Act, 2023. Public availability 
does not remove the responsibility to handle data carefully. Investigators should collect only 
what is relevant to the case and avoid unnecessary storage or sharing of personal content. This is 
especially important in cases involving women, children, or sensitive personal matters [72]. 
All SOCMINT findings must be properly documented. Screenshots should clearly show the 
platform name, URL, date, and time. If a profile changes or content is deleted later, the 
investigator must be able to show when and how the information was captured. Poor 
documentation often weakens otherwise strong cases [73]. 
Courts generally accept SOCMINT evidence when it is presented clearly and supported by 
proper certification under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. Judges are more interested in 
reliability and relevance than technical complexity. Simple explanations supported by clear 
visuals are always more effective [74]. 
In conclusion, SOCMINT allows investigators to understand the human side of cybercrime. It 
reveals behaviour, intent, relationships, and deception patterns that are not visible through 
technical forensics alone. When used carefully and lawfully, SOCMINT becomes one of the 
strongest tools in modern cyber policing [75]. 
[[PAGE 364]]
 
Part VI – Operational Security (OPSEC) for Investigators and Sock-Puppet 
Management 
While conducting OSINT and social media investigations, the safety of the investigation itself is 
as important as the evidence collected. Many cybercriminals today are alert, technically aware, 
and capable of detecting when they are being observed. If an investigator’s identity or activity is 
exposed, suspects may destroy evidence, mislead the investigation, or retaliate. Operational 
Security, commonly called OPSEC, exists to prevent such risks [76]. 
OPSEC in OSINT simply means ensuring that the investigator remains invisible while 
collecting publicly available information. Unlike traditional policing, where presence can 
sometimes deter crime, cyber investigations often require silence and discretion. Even a small 
mistake, such as using a personal email account or real phone number, can alert suspects that 
they are under scrutiny [77]. 
The first principle of OPSEC is digital separation. Investigators must never use personal 
devices, personal internet connections, or personal social media accounts for OSINT work. 
Dedicated official hardware, separate user accounts, and controlled internet access are essential. 
Mixing personal and official digital activity can compromise both the case and the officer’s 
privacy [78]. 
Another important OPSEC measure is digital footprint control. Every online action leaves a 
trace. Viewing profiles while logged into personal accounts, clicking links without precautions, 
or downloading files directly can expose identifying information such as IP addresses or device 
details. Investigators must always assume that suspects may be monitoring visitor activity [79]. 
Using secure and department-approved internet connections helps reduce such risks. Virtual 
private networks (VPNs), when lawfully and officially authorised, can help mask investigative 
activity. However, VPNs must never be used to bypass legal restrictions. Their role is protection, 
not deception beyond lawful limits [80]. 
A sensitive but necessary aspect of OSINT is the use of sock-puppet accounts, also known as 
investigative personas. A sock-puppet is a controlled, fictional online profile created for 
investigative purposes. These profiles allow investigators to observe criminal spaces without 
revealing their real identity. However, sock-puppets must be used carefully and lawfully [81]. 
The creation of a sock-puppet does not mean impersonating a real person. Using the identity, 
photographs, or details of an actual individual amounts to identity theft and is illegal. 
Investigative personas must be entirely fictional, neutral, and non-provocative. Their purpose is 
observation, not entrapment [82]. 
Sock-puppet accounts must also respect platform rules and Indian law. Investigators should 
avoid interactions that could be interpreted as encouragement, inducement, or participation in 
[[PAGE 365]]
illegal activity. Merely observing public content is generally safe. Actively engaging with 
criminals requires higher-level approval and legal oversight [83]. 
Another OPSEC concern is behavioural consistency. Sock-puppet profiles should behave like 
ordinary users. Sudden activity bursts, unusual questions, or copying content mechanically may 
raise suspicion. Criminal groups often test newcomers before trusting them. A poorly managed 
investigative persona can expose the entire operation [84]. 
All actions taken through sock-puppet accounts must be logged and supervised. Supervisory 
officers should know when and why such accounts are created, how they are used, and when 
they are retired. Lack of documentation can raise serious legal and ethical questions during trial 
[85]. 
Investigators must also protect themselves from psychological exposure. Continuous viewing of 
abusive content, exploitation material, or aggressive communities can affect mental well-being. 
Regular rotation of duties, peer support, and institutional awareness are necessary to protect 
officers handling such content [86]. 
OPSEC failures often do not appear immediately. A suspect may continue normal behaviour 
while quietly adapting tactics. Therefore, investigators should regularly review their digital 
practices, update security measures, and assume that mistakes can happen. Prevention is always 
easier than damage control [87]. 
From a legal standpoint, courts are increasingly attentive to how investigations are conducted 
online. Defence lawyers may argue that improper online behaviour tainted the evidence. Strong 
OPSEC practices help investigators show that evidence was collected fairly, lawfully, and 
without manipulation [88]. 
In summary, OPSEC protects not just the investigator but the integrity of the entire case. Sock-
puppet management, when done responsibly, enables lawful observation without deception that 
crosses legal boundaries. Good OPSEC ensures that the investigation stays one step ahead of the 
criminal, not the other way around [89]. 
 
Part VII – Forensic Documentation, Hashing, Timestamping, Chain of Custody, and OSINT 
Reporting 
Collecting information from the internet is only half the work. The real test of an OSINT 
investigation comes later—inside the courtroom. Courts do not decide cases based on how 
intelligent or logical an investigation looks. They decide cases based on whether the evidence is 
reliable, untampered, and legally collected. This is why forensic documentation and chain of 
custody are critical in OSINT cases [90]. 
Every piece of information collected through OSINT must be treated as digital evidence, even if 
it appears simple, such as a screenshot of a social media post or a webpage. Investigators must 
[[PAGE 366]]
assume that the defence will question authenticity, timing, and source. If documentation is weak, 
the evidence may be discarded, regardless of its importance [91]. 
The first rule of forensic OSINT is capture with clarity. When a webpage, profile, or post is 
captured, the screenshot must clearly show the platform name, full URL, date, and time. Partial 
screenshots without context create doubt. Investigators should never crop images in a way that 
removes identifying details, even if the content seems repetitive [92]. 
Whenever possible, OSINT material should be captured using tools or systems that automatically 
record metadata such as timestamps and capture logs. This helps demonstrate that the evidence 
was collected at a specific time and not altered later. Manual notes should also be maintained to 
support digital records [93]. 
The next critical step is hashing. Hashing is a method of creating a digital fingerprint of a file. 
Once a file is hashed, any change—even a single pixel in an image—will alter the hash value. 
This helps prove that the evidence has not been tampered with after collection. Courts 
increasingly expect investigators to understand and apply this concept [94]. 
Hash values should be generated immediately after capture and recorded in the case diary or 
digital evidence register. If files are copied, transferred, or stored elsewhere, the hash must be 
verified again to show continuity. Failure to do so creates gaps that defence counsel may exploit 
[95]. 
Timestamping is closely linked to hashing. Online content is often edited or deleted. A 
timestamp proves when the investigator saw and captured the content. This is particularly 
important in cases where suspects later deny posting certain material. Time consistency across 
screenshots, logs, and reports strengthens credibility [96]. 
The chain of custody refers to the documented history of evidence from the moment it is 
collected until it is produced in court. For OSINT evidence, this includes who collected it, where 
it was stored, who accessed it, and whether it was transferred. Even digital evidence needs a 
clear custody trail [97]. 
Investigators should maintain a simple but consistent chain-of-custody record. It should mention 
date, time, officer name, nature of evidence, storage location, and access history. Informal 
handling, such as sharing files through personal devices or messaging apps, must be strictly 
avoided [98]. 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 provides clear guidance on electronic evidence. 
Section 63(4) requires certification explaining the manner of production of the electronic record. 
In OSINT cases, this certification should clearly mention that the information was collected from 
publicly available sources, without unauthorised access [99]. 
A well-written OSINT report is as important as the evidence itself. The report should be simple, 
factual, and free from assumptions. It should explain what was found, where it was found, when 
it was found, and how it was verified. Opinions should be clearly separated from facts [100]. 
[[PAGE 367]]
An effective OSINT report usually follows a standard format: 
 
Objective of OSINT activity 
 
Sources consulted (public platforms, websites, etc.) 
 
Method of collection 
 
Findings (with references to annexures) 
 
Observations and linkages 
 
Limitations, if any 
This structure helps prosecutors and judges understand the investigation without confusion [101]. 
Investigators should avoid technical jargon in reports. Courts are interested in reliability, not 
complexity. Simple language, supported by annexures such as screenshots and logs, is far more 
persuasive than lengthy technical explanations [102]. 
Another important aspect is preservation. Online evidence can disappear quickly. Investigators 
must store OSINT material securely, following departmental guidelines. Backups should be 
maintained, and access should be restricted. Accidental loss of evidence can be as damaging as 
deliberate tampering [103]. 
Senior officers must ensure that IOs receive regular training in digital evidence handling. OSINT 
is no longer optional or experimental—it is a core part of cybercrime investigation. Weak 
handling at this stage can nullify months of investigative work [104]. 
In summary, forensic discipline gives OSINT its legal strength. Hashing, timestamping, 
documentation, and chain of custody are not technical formalities; they are the foundation on 
which digital cases stand. A carefully documented OSINT investigation not only survives legal 
scrutiny but also builds confidence in the justice system [105]. 
 
Part VIII – Investigative Mindset: Understanding Intent, Scale, Victimology, and Organised 
Cybercrime 
Tools, laws, and procedures alone do not make a good cyber investigation. What truly makes the 
difference is the investigative mindset of the Investigating Officer. OSINT is not about 
collecting maximum information; it is about understanding why the crime happened, who 
benefited, how many were affected, and what structure exists behind the offence. This way 
of thinking separates routine enquiries from meaningful investigations [106]. 
The first element of investigative mindset is understanding intent. In cybercrime, intent is 
rarely visible in a single act. It is usually revealed through patterns—repeated posts, messages, 
domain registrations, or financial requests. OSINT helps investigators trace these patterns over 
time. A single fake profile may look harmless, but multiple similar profiles created with the same 
behaviour indicate deliberate planning [107]. 
[[PAGE 368]]
Intent becomes clearer when online activity is placed in context. For example, a person posting 
fake job advertisements repeatedly, changing accounts after complaints, and targeting similar 
victims shows criminal intent beyond doubt. Such patterns are far more convincing in court than 
isolated screenshots [108]. 
The second element is understanding the scale of the offence. Many cybercrime complaints 
appear small when viewed individually. However, OSINT often reveals that the same message, 
website, or profile has targeted dozens or hundreds of victims. Identifying this scale changes the 
seriousness of the case and justifies higher-level investigation and coordination [109]. 
Scale also determines resource allocation. A one-time cheating case and a nationwide phishing 
operation cannot be treated the same way. OSINT helps investigators quickly assess whether a 
case involves a single offender or an organised network operating across states or countries 
The third element is victimology, which means understanding who the victims are and why they 
were targeted. Cybercriminals do not choose victims randomly. They exploit vulnerability—
financial stress, emotional distress, lack of digital awareness, or professional exposure. OSINT 
allows investigators to study public victim behaviour and identify targeting strategies [111]. 
Understanding victimology helps in two ways. First, it strengthens the case by explaining motive 
and method. Second, it supports prevention by identifying risk patterns that can be shared with 
the public. Cyber policing is not only about punishment but also about reducing future harm 
[112]. 
Another critical aspect is recognising organised cybercrime structures. Modern cybercrime 
often follows a layered model. One group may create phishing websites, another may handle 
victim communication, and a third may manage money laundering. OSINT helps map these 
layers by analysing online roles and interactions [113]. 
Crime-as-a-Service platforms openly advertise illegal services such as fake IDs, malware, 
phishing kits, and mule accounts. These advertisements are often visible on public forums or 
messaging channels. Observing such spaces lawfully helps investigators understand how 
criminals outsource tasks and scale operations [114]. 
Investigators must also recognise hierarchies within cybercriminal groups. Some individuals 
plan and direct operations, while others perform low-level tasks. OSINT analysis of 
communication tone, authority signals, and coordination patterns helps identify leadership roles, 
which are crucial for dismantling networks [115]. 
An effective investigative mindset also includes patience. Cyber investigations rarely produce 
instant results. Offenders may operate slowly, change identities, or pause activity. OSINT allows 
investigators to quietly observe over time without alerting suspects, which often yields stronger 
evidence [116]. 
[[PAGE 369]]
Another important mental discipline is avoiding assumption-driven investigation. Online 
identities are deceptive by nature. Investigators must constantly test their conclusions against 
new information. A good investigator is willing to revise their theory when evidence points 
elsewhere [117]. 
Supervisory officers play a vital role in shaping investigative mindset. They must encourage 
quality over quantity, careful documentation over speed, and ethical restraint over aggressive 
tactics. Cyber investigations are judged not only by arrests but by how well they withstand legal 
scrutiny [118]. 
In complex cases, OSINT should be used to support coordination between districts, states, and 
central agencies. Shared indicators such as domains, usernames, or payment patterns help 
connect cases that may otherwise remain fragmented. This collaborative approach is essential in 
tackling organised cybercrime [119]. 
Finally, investigators must remember that behind every digital trail is a human story—either a 
victim who suffered loss or an offender who exploited trust. OSINT, when guided by the right 
mindset, helps restore balance by uncovering truth without violating rights. This balance defines 
professional cyber policing [120]. 
 
Part IX – Ecosystem of Cyber Crime and Timeline Evolution of Cybercrime 
To understand cybercrime properly, an Investigating Officer must look beyond individual 
incidents and see the entire ecosystem in which cyber offences operate. Cybercrime is not 
random. It is a system where offenders, tools, platforms, victims, and money flows are 
connected. OSINT helps investigators visualise this ecosystem and identify pressure points 
where criminal activity can be disrupted [121]. 
A. Ecosystem of Cyber Crime (Explained Simply) 
The cybercrime ecosystem can be understood as a chain of five connected elements: 
Actors → Tools → Platforms → Victims → Monetisation. 
If any one of these elements is disrupted, the crime weakens or collapses [122]. 
The first element is Actors. These are the people involved in the crime. They may include 
planners, technical operators, social engineers, recruiters, and money handlers. OSINT helps 
identify actors through public usernames, communication styles, forum participation, and 
repeated online behaviour. Even when identities are hidden, roles often become visible [123]. 
The second element is Tools. These include phishing kits, fake websites, malware, spoofing 
software, SIM cards, mule bank accounts, and AI-based tools like deepfake generators. Many of 
these tools are openly advertised on forums or messaging channels. OSINT allows investigators 
to observe how tools are shared and reused across crimes [124]. 
[[PAGE 370]]
The third element is Platforms. Cybercriminals rely on platforms such as social media sites, 
messaging apps, email services, hosting providers, and payment gateways. These platforms are 
often legitimate services misused for illegal purposes. OSINT helps map which platforms are 
repeatedly used in specific crime types [125]. 
The fourth element is Victims. Victims include individuals, businesses, institutions, and critical 
infrastructure. OSINT helps identify victim profiles and targeting patterns. Understanding who is 
targeted helps investigators understand the offender’s strategy and motivation [1️26]. 
The final element is Monetisation. Every cybercrime aims for some form of gain—money, data, 
influence, or disruption. Monetisation may occur through bank transfers, cryptocurrencies, gift 
cards, or resale of stolen data. OSINT helps trace public indicators of these money flows and link 
them to larger networks [127]. 
 
Textual Flowchart – Ecosystem of Cyber Crime 
Cyber Criminal Actors 
        ↓ 
Crime Tools & Techniques 
        ↓ 
Online Platforms & Infrastructure 
        ↓ 
Victims (Individuals / Institutions) 
        ↓ 
Financial & Strategic Gain 
        ↓ 
Reinvestment into Crime Tools 
This cycle explains why cybercrime grows rapidly. Profits are reinvested into better tools, wider 
reach, and more deception, making the ecosystem stronger over time [128]. 
 
B. Timeline Evolution of Cybercrime 
Cybercrime did not appear suddenly in its current form. It has evolved in clear stages, each with 
increasing sophistication. Understanding this timeline helps investigators anticipate future threats 
[129]. 
Stage One – Individual Hackers (1990s–early 2000s): 
Cybercrime began with individuals experimenting with systems for curiosity, fame, or challenge. 
Crimes were small-scale, and offenders often left obvious traces. Investigations were mostly 
technical and local [130]. 
Stage Two – Financial Motivation (mid-2000s): 
With the rise of online banking and e-commerce, cybercrime shifted toward financial gain. 
[[PAGE 371]]
Phishing, card fraud, and identity theft increased. OSINT became useful in tracing fake websites 
and scam emails [131]. 
Stage Three – Organised Cybercrime (2010 onwards): 
Criminal groups began operating like businesses. Roles were divided, tools were sold, and 
operations scaled globally. Crime-as-a-Service emerged. OSINT became essential for mapping 
networks and infrastructure [132]. 
Stage Four – State-Supported and Hybrid Threats: 
Some cyber operations began showing links to state interests, espionage, or strategic disruption. 
These threats targeted governments, defence systems, and critical infrastructure. OSINT helped 
identify public indicators, narratives, and leaked data [133]. 
Stage Five – AI-Driven and Psychological Crimes (Present): 
Today’s cybercrime uses artificial intelligence, deepfakes, voice cloning, and automated scams. 
Crimes now attack trust itself. OSINT helps investigators identify misuse of public photos, 
videos, and personal data in such crimes [134]. 
 
Textual Flowchart – Timeline Evolution of Cybercrime 
Curiosity-Based Hacking 
        ↓ 
Financial Cyber Fraud 
        ↓ 
Organised Cyber Syndicates 
        ↓ 
State & Hybrid Cyber Operations 
        ↓ 
AI-Driven and Trust-Based Crimes 
This evolution shows that cybercrime is becoming less technical and more psychological. 
Investigators must therefore focus not only on devices, but also on behaviour, narratives, and 
digital identity misuse [135]. 
 
C. Why This Understanding Matters for Investigators 
Understanding the ecosystem and evolution of cybercrime helps IOs avoid tunnel vision. A 
simple fraud case today may be part of a larger network. OSINT allows investigators to see 
beyond individual FIRs and connect patterns across cases [136]. 
Senior officers must use this understanding to guide policy, training, and inter-agency 
coordination. Cybercrime cannot be tackled in isolation. It requires shared intelligence, 
standardised reporting, and continuous learning [137]. 
[[PAGE 372]]
Most importantly, this perspective helps investigators remain adaptive. Cybercrime will continue 
to evolve. Tools will change, platforms will shift, but human behaviour and criminal incentives 
remain constant. OSINT provides the lens through which these constants can be observed [138]. 
 
Part X – Emerging Threat Domains, Future Challenges, and Final Operational 
Takeaways 
Cybercrime is not a static problem. It changes faster than most laws, platforms, and institutions 
can adapt. Investigating Officers must therefore look ahead and prepare for emerging threat 
domains that are already visible today through OSINT. Many of these threats are still evolving, 
but their early indicators are clearly present in open digital spaces [139]. 
A. AI-Driven Frauds and Automated Cybercrime 
One of the most serious emerging threats is the use of artificial intelligence by cybercriminals. 
Criminals now use AI tools to generate fake emails, fake customer support chats, fake job 
interviews, and even automated scam calls. These messages often sound more natural and 
convincing than earlier scams, making detection harder for victims [140]. 
OSINT helps investigators identify such campaigns by analysing scale and repetition. When 
thousands of similar messages appear across platforms within short periods, automation is 
usually involved. Even when individual messages appear harmless, large-scale patterns expose 
organised AI-assisted fraud operations [141]. 
AI tools are also being used to scrape publicly available data from social media—photos, voice 
samples, writing style, and personal details. Criminals then use this information to personalise 
scams. This shows how misuse of open data directly fuels cybercrime, making OSINT 
awareness critical for both investigation and prevention [142]. 
B. Deepfake Crimes and Synthetic Identity Abuse 
Deepfakes represent a major shift in cybercrime. Using publicly available images and videos, 
criminals now create fake videos or audio clips that appear real. These have already been used 
for extortion, reputational harm, financial fraud, and political manipulation [143]. 
OSINT plays a key role in detecting deepfake crimes. Investigators can compare original public 
content with manipulated material, identify inconsistencies, and trace the source of reused 
images or videos. Early detection is essential, as deepfakes spread rapidly and cause irreversible 
damage if not addressed quickly [144]. 
Synthetic identity abuse is closely related. Criminals combine real and fake information to create 
believable but non-existent persons. These identities are then used to open accounts, obtain 
loans, or run scams. OSINT helps investigators identify reused photos, repeated identity patterns, 
and digital inconsistencies [145]. 
[[PAGE 373]]
C. Influence Operations and Psychological Cybercrime 
Cybercrime is no longer limited to financial loss. Psychological manipulation and influence 
operations are becoming common. These include fake narratives, targeted misinformation, 
online harassment campaigns, and coordinated social media attacks against individuals or 
institutions [146]. 
OSINT allows investigators to track narrative origins, coordination patterns, and amplification 
strategies. Studying who posts first, who amplifies content, and how narratives spread helps 
distinguish organic public opinion from organised manipulation [147]. 
Such cases require careful handling. Freedom of expression must be respected, while criminal 
coordination and harm must be addressed. OSINT provides the balance by focusing on behaviour 
and coordination rather than opinion itself [148]. 
D. OSINT in National Security and Critical Infrastructure Protection 
Cyber threats increasingly target critical infrastructure, including healthcare systems, power 
networks, transport, and government services. While technical defences are essential, OSINT 
provides early warning signals through open chatter, leaked documents, and threat actor 
communications [149]. 
Public forums and online communities often discuss vulnerabilities long before attacks occur. 
Monitoring such spaces lawfully helps agencies prepare, patch weaknesses, and coordinate 
responses. OSINT thus acts as a preventive tool, not just an investigative one [150]. 
E. Legal and Ethical Challenges Ahead 
As OSINT expands, legal and ethical challenges will grow. Investigators must continuously 
balance privacy, necessity, and proportionality. Just because data is public does not mean it 
should always be collected or stored. Relevance must guide every decision [151]. 
Training and clear SOPs are essential. Officers must understand evolving laws, platform policies, 
and judicial expectations. Lack of awareness can turn lawful investigation into legal vulnerability 
[152]. 
F. Final Operational Takeaways for Investigating Officers 
1. OSINT is a starting point, not the end. It guides investigation but must be supported by 
legal process and corroborative evidence [153]. 
2. Documentation is non-negotiable. Every action must be explainable in court [154]. 
3. Think in patterns, not incidents. Cybercrime is rarely isolated [155]. 
4. Protect yourself and the case. OPSEC failures harm investigations more than criminals 
[156]. 
5. Stay adaptive. Tools will change, but disciplined thinking remains constant [157]. 
[[PAGE 374]]
Conclusion 
OSINT and social media investigations are no longer optional skills. They are core competencies 
for modern policing. When used lawfully, ethically, and intelligently, OSINT strengthens 
investigations, protects citizens, and upholds the rule of law. When misused or misunderstood, it 
weakens cases and damages trust. 
This chapter has been written to ensure that Investigating Officers—whether new or 
experienced—understand OSINT not as a technical shortcut, but as a professional 
responsibility. Cybercrime will continue to evolve. Our response must evolve with it, guided by 
law, reason, and restraint [158]. 
 
CHAPTER 14 
DARK WEB & ANONYMOUS NETWORK INVESTIGATION 
UP Police Cyber Crime Investigation Manual 
 
1. Executive Summary  
This chapter provides Investigating Officers (IOs) of Uttar Pradesh Police with a procedural, 
court-defensible guide to investigating crimes involving the dark web and anonymous networks. 
The dark web and related anonymity technologies are increasingly exploited to commit or 
facilitate offences such as narcotics trafficking, distribution of child sexual abuse material 
(CSAM), financial fraud, identity forgery, ransomware/extortion and terrorist 
propaganda/financing. These environments deliberately obscure users, infrastructure and 
metadata, creating investigative and evidentiary challenges that, if handled improperly, can 
render evidence inadmissible or expose the investigation to legal attack. 
This chapter is not a technical hacking manual. It is a law-enforcement SOP focusing on 
identification, preservation, documentation, lawful escalation and presentation of evidence. 
IOs who may not have advanced technical training will find clear definitions, practical checklists, 
templates and cautionary notes that align with Indian legal processes — including the 
Information Technology Act, 2000, provisions of BNSS/CrPC for procedure, and the Evidence Act 
(Section 65B compliance considerations). The guidance emphasizes when to act locally, and 
when to escalate to specialist agencies such as the State Cyber Cell, Indian Cyber Crime 
Coordination Centre (I4C), CERT-In, or central investigative agencies, including when Mutual 
Legal Assistance (MLAT) is likely required. 
[[PAGE 375]]
Use this chapter as:  
(a) A first-response checklist when dark-web involvement is suspected 
(b) A preservation and documentation standard to protect admissibility  
(c) A coordination guide for lawful multi-agency and international cooperation  
(d) A court-presentation primer to address common defence challenges.  
At every critical step, IOs must note legal risks and jurisdictional limits in the case diary. When 
technical tasks exceed local capability, escalation is a procedural necessity — not a shortcoming 
— and must be recorded contemporaneously. 
 
 
2. Learning Objectives 
After reading this chapter, the IO should be able to: 
1. Identify indicators of dark web or anonymous network involvement in reported offences. 
2. Distinguish evidence types that commonly arise in dark web cases and prioritise 
preservation. 
[[PAGE 376]]
3. Apply an immediate, documented First-Response SOP that minimises evidence 
contamination. 
4. Understand the limits of technical attribution and the role of corroborative evidence 
(financial, device, behavioural). 
5. Prepare lawful preservation and coordination requests to exchanges, hosting providers, 
and foreign authorities. 
6. Coordinate with State Cyber Cell, I4C, CERT-In and central agencies following prescribed 
escalation paths. 
7. Document evidence and expert interactions to satisfy court admissibility requirements 
(Section 65B and related). 
8. Communicate realistic expectations to complainants and judiciary regarding timelines 
and jurisdictional constraints. 
 
3. Key Definitions & Glossary (IO-Friendly) 
 
Surface Web — Websites indexed by conventional search engines (e.g., google). 
 
Deep Web — Content not indexed by search engines but accessible via normal browsers 
(e.g., private databases, webmail). 
 
Dark Web — Concealed services intentionally accessible only using specific anonymity 
software (e.g., Tor). Not all deep web content is dark web. 
 
Tor (The Onion Router) — An anonymity network that routes traffic through multiple 
encrypted relays to conceal origin and destination. Investigators should treat Tor 
addresses as indicators — not proof — of identity. 
 
I2P — Another anonymity network for internal hidden services; similar investigative 
implications as Tor. 
 
Anonymous Networks — General term for systems (Tor, I2P, VPN chains) that hide user 
metadata. 
 
Onion Services — Websites accessible only via Tor; addresses usually end in “.onion”. 
 
Hidden Marketplaces — Dark web platforms that list illicit goods/services (drugs, stolen 
data, forged documents). 
[[PAGE 377]]
 
Cryptocurrency Tumblers / Mixers — Services that obfuscate traceability of 
cryptocurrency transactions. From an IO perspective, mixers increase the evidentiary 
burden for linking funds to persons. 
 
OPSEC (Investigative Perspective) — Practices IOs must follow to avoid exposing 
investigative identity, prejudicing evidence, or altering suspect behaviour. 
 
Exit Node — Final Tor relay where encrypted Tor traffic leaves to reach the public 
internet; metadata there is sensitive and often outside Indian jurisdiction. 
 
Relay / Bridge — Intermediate Tor nodes that forward encrypted traffic; do not reveal 
user identity to any single node. 
 
Attribution vs Identification — Identification may indicate an account, handle, or device 
artefact. Attribution is the legal linkage of that account/artefact to a real-world person. 
Attribution requires corroborative evidence. 
 
OSINT — Information gathered from publicly available sources. 
 
Controlled Access — Authorised, documented observation or interaction with a 
site/service only under clear legal authority and supervision. 
 
4. Dark Web Ecosystem Overview 
Types of Crimes Typically Operated via Dark Web 
 
Narcotics trafficking and cross-border supply 
 
CSAM distribution and anonymous sharing forums 
 
Financial fraud, carding, and sale of stolen credentials 
 
Fake IDs, forged documents and service providers 
 
Ransomware negotiation and extortion coordination 
 
Terrorist/Extremist propaganda, recruitment and financing 
Common Misuse Patterns in Indian Context 
 
Use of offshore hosting for illicit content with payment via cryptocurrencies or KYC-light 
exchanges. 
 
Transfer of proceeds through mixers and unregulated exchanges, then cash-out via local 
exchanges with weak AML/KYC enforcement. 
[[PAGE 378]]
 
Reuse of handles or communication channels across platforms that allow behavioural 
linkage. 
 
Distribution of CSAM/files stored in foreign jurisdictions requiring MLATs or preservation 
requests. 
Why Attribution Is Complex 
 
Anonymous networks conceal IPs and packet metadata. 
 
Actors use VPN chains, Tor bridges, and coin-mixing to create false trails. 
 
Infrastructure spans jurisdictions; server logs and data often sit with foreign providers. 
 
Alias reuse and false persona creation complicate direct identity linkage. 
LEGAL RISK: Treat any technical indicator (e.g., .onion address, Tor usage) as probative but not 
dispositive. Avoid drafting charges based solely on anonymity indicators without corroboration. 
 
 
5. Anonymous Network Technologies (High-Level, Defensive Explanation Only) 
Purpose: Provide IOs with enough conceptual understanding to make informed preservation 
and escalation decisions without instructing on compromise or exploitation. 
Tor (Conceptual) 
 
Tor routes traffic via at least three relays: entry (guard), middle (relay), and exit (for non-
onion traffic). 
[[PAGE 379]]
 
Investigative implication: A single Tor node lacks full path information; therefore, IP 
evidence from public networks is often insufficient for attribution. 
 
I2P (Brief) 
 
Peer-to-peer, internal routing for hidden services. Less common than Tor but used for 
similar purposes. 
 
Investigative implication: Similar need for cooperation with specialists and platform 
providers. 
VPN Chaining 
 
Suspect may chain multiple VPNs before connecting to Tor. 
 
Investigative implication: Identification may require cooperation from multiple VPN 
providers across jurisdictions. 
Encrypted Messaging Overlap 
 
Dark web actors commonly migrate communications to encrypted messengers (e.g., 
Signal, Telegram). 
 
Investigative implication: Evidence fragmentation — messages may be ephemeral or 
stored on foreign servers, requiring legal preservation requests. 
LEGAL RISK: IOs must not attempt unauthorised access, entrapment, or impersonation. Any 
interaction must be documented and law-compliant.

7. First-Response SOP for IOs (CRITICAL SECTION) 
All steps must be contemporaneously recorded in the case diary. Use numbered steps. 
[[PAGE 382]]
7.1 Complaint Intake 
1. Record initial complaint verbatim. Note complainant identity, contact details, and 
supporting material (URLs, screenshots, wallet addresses). 
IO ACTION: Enter initial facts in case diary with date/time and receiving IO name. 
LEGAL RISK: Unverified claims should not be repeated as facts in FIR text. 
2. Preserve original digital evidence received from complainant (email headers, files, 
screenshot originals). 
IO ACTION: Save copies using a write-once medium or secure forensic image. Label with 
unique evidence IDs. 
LEGAL RISK: Failure to preserve originals may render later testimony inadmissible. 
7.2 Initial Assessment (When Dark Web Suspected) 
3. Determine if the alleged platform is on a known anonymity network (e.g., presence of 
.onion URL, mention of Tor/I2P). 
IO ACTION: Note indicator and time of observation. Do not attempt to access hidden 
services using departmental workstations. 
LEGAL RISK: Unauthorised access to systems may violate IT Act provisions. 
4. Prioritise evidence by volatility — server logs and marketplace listings are high priority. 
IO ACTION: Prepare preservation request templates (see Section 14 Templates). 
7.3 Immediate Do’s (What IO MUST do) 
5. IO ACTION: Secure suspect devices if a lawful seizure is authorised; obtain digital 
forensic images using trained personnel or request state forensic lab assistance. 
6. IO ACTION: Preserve complainant-provided material and server URLs; capture metadata 
(email headers, EXIF if present) and note chain of custody. 
7. IO ACTION: If the platform is foreign-hosted or requires MLAT, immediately notify State 
Cyber Cell and I4C for coordination. 
8. IO ACTION: Consider preservation requests to exchanges if wallet addresses are 
involved. 
LEGAL RISK: Device seizure requires authorization under BNSS/CrPC. Ensure warrants or 
authorised seizure entries are recorded. 
7.4 Immediate Don’ts (What IO MUST NOT do) 
9. IO ACTION: DO NOT interact with suspected services using personal or departmental 
devices unless authorised and documented under Controlled Access procedures. 
[[PAGE 383]]
10. IO ACTION: DO NOT delete or alter suspect systems or files; avoid logging into suspect 
accounts or making transactions to preserve chain of evidence. 
11. IO ACTION: DO NOT attempt to de-anonymise users through intrusive or unauthorised 
technical means. Refer to specialist units. 
LEGAL RISK: Unlawful interaction or entrapment may invalidate evidence and expose the IO and 
department to legal challenge. 
7.5 When to Involve Other Agencies 
12. State Cyber Cell: For technical assistance, preservation requests to Indian providers, and 
coordination with state specialist teams. 
13. I4C: Mandatory where cross-state or international data preservation/exchange is 
needed, or for MLAT facilitation. 
14. CERT-In: Where ongoing threat mitigation, takedown, or national level notice is required. 
15. Central Agencies / Nodal Ministry: For terrorism financing, national security, or complex 
cross-border incidents. 
IO ACTION: Document time, person, and content of every escalation. 
LEGAL RISK: Failure to escalate timely may cause loss of volatile evidence and weaken 
prosecutorial position. 
 
[[PAGE 384]]
8. Controlled Access vs Evidence Preservation 
 
8.1 Observing vs Interacting — Key Differences 
 
Observing (Permissible): Viewing a page in read-only mode to record contents without 
logging in, transacting, or posting. 
 
Interacting (Restricted): Creating accounts, messaging, purchasing or otherwise 
changing state on the platform. 
IO ACTION: Prefer observing. If interaction is required, obtain prior written approval from the 
State Cyber Cell or I4C; record authorisation in the case diary. 
 
8.2 Why Unauthorised Interaction is Dangerous 
 
Can alter or contaminate evidence. 
 
May constitute unauthorised access under IT Act. 
[[PAGE 385]]
 
Risks entrapment or investigator safety. 
LEGAL RISK: Interaction without proper legal authority can result in evidence exclusion and legal 
exposure. 
8.3 Documentation Required If Access Is Permitted 
 
Written authorisation letter (signed by competent authority). 
 
A detailed plan articulating purpose, scope, and duration of access. 
 
Names and roles of personnel involved. 
 
Real-time logging of actions, timestamps, and copies of pages viewed. 
 
Independent witness presence where practical. 
IO ACTION: Use an approved Controlled Access Checklist (attach to case diary). 
 
8.4 Chain of Custody for Digital Observations 
 
Each captured item (screenshot, saved HTML, forensic image) must have: evidence ID, 
collection date/time, collector name, tools used, storage medium ID, and storage 
location. 
 
Transfer between custodians must be recorded with signatures and timestamps. 
LEGAL RISK: Weak chain of custody undermines authenticity and the weight of evidence in 
court. 
 
 
9. Attribution & Identity Challenges 
9.1 Why IP-Based Identification Fails 
 
Tor and similar networks mask IPs; exit nodes cannot be equated to origin. 
 
VPNs and proxies further obscure source. 
 
IP evidence alone is circumstantial and often insufficient for attribution. 
9.2 Role of Corroborative Evidence 
[[PAGE 386]]
 
Financial Trails: Blockchain transactions, exchange KYC, and bank transfers linking 
proceeds to a person. 
 
Device Seizure: Browser artifacts, wallet files, private keys, chat logs recovered from 
seized devices. 
 
Behavioural Correlation: Repeated behavioural patterns (posting times, language 
patterns, typo signatures). 
 
Platform Cooperation: User registration IPs, account creation metadata and payment 
method records from platforms/exchanges. 
IO ACTION: Build a multi-pronged evidentiary chain; document each linkage and its limitations. 
9.3 Managing Expectations 
 
Inform complainants and courts that attribution may require time, foreign cooperation 
(MLAT), and specialised technical analysis. 
 
Avoid definitive public statements before corroboration. 
LEGAL RISK: Overstating certainty can be used by defence to challenge integrity of investigation. 
[[PAGE 387]]
 
 
 
10. Financial Trails & Cryptocurrency Linkages 
10.1 Wallet Addresses as Evidence 
 
Public blockchain entries are persistent and can be used to show movement of funds 
between addresses. 
 
Linkage from wallet address to person requires either access to wallet private keys or 
KYC data from exchanges. 
10.2 Exchange KYC Linkage 
 
Exchanges and on-ramps may possess KYC records; preservation requests and lawful 
orders are required for production. 
 
Local exchanges may respond to Indian preservation/production notices; foreign 
exchanges often require MLAT or I4C facilitation.  
 
10.3 Preservation Requests 
 
Prepare preservation notices immediately upon identifying wallet addresses or 
suspected exchange involvement. Include timestamps, transaction IDs, and case 
reference numbers. 
 
Use standard template (see Templates section) and escalate via State Cyber Cell or I4C 
when necessary. 
[[PAGE 388]]
 
10.4 Legal Escalation Pathways 
1. Request preservation from Indian exchanges (State Cyber Cell / I4C coordination). 
2. For foreign platforms, request I4C to coordinate MLAT or international preservation via 
diplomatic/legal channels. 
3. Use asset freezing orders where applicable and available. 
IO ACTION: Log all blockchain transaction IDs, corresponding fiat on-ramps, and chain of 
custody for any downloaded transaction histories. 
LEGAL RISK: Mishandling of cryptocurrency evidence (e.g., moving funds) can destroy volatility 
and taint prosecution. 
 
 
 
 
11. Jurisdiction, MLAT & International Cooperation 
 
[[PAGE 389]]
 
11.1 When Cases Go Beyond District/State Authority 
 
If evidence or servers are hosted outside India, or suspect/user is located abroad, 
escalate. 
 
Cases involving CSAM, terrorism financing, or large-scale fraud usually require central 
coordination. 
11.2 Documentation Needed Before Escalation 
 
Detailed incident summary (facts, indicators of anonymity, IPs, .onion addresses, wallet 
addresses). 
 
Preservation requests already sent and their outcomes. 
 
Case diary extracts showing timelines and prior steps. 
11.3 Role of I4C 
 
I4C acts as the national coordination and liaison body for cybercrime, including MLAT 
facilitation and foreign preservation requests. 
[[PAGE 390]]
 
IOs must submit full technical and legal documentation to State Cyber Cell for onward 
transmission to I4C. 
11.4 Limitations IOs Must Record in Case Diaries 
 
List evidentiary gaps, jurisdictions involved, expected MLAT timelines, and potential legal 
hurdles. 
 
Record dates of all foreign preservation/MLAT requests and replies. 
LEGAL RISK: Failure to follow MLAT channels may render foreign evidence inaccessible and 
invite legal challenge. 
 
12. Legal Admissibility & Court Presentation 
12.1 What Courts Accept 
Courts accept properly authenticated electronic records with a clear chain of custody, expert 
testimony, and compliance with Section 65B (electronic records admissibility). 
 
Blockchain extracts and certified copies from exchanges/providers with proper authority 
strengthen evidentiary weight. 
 
12.2 What Courts Question 
 
Evidence collected by unauthorised access or without proper preservation. 
 
Screenshots without metadata or expert verification. 
 
Attribution claims not supported by corroborative evidence. 
12.3 Importance of: 
 
Documentation: Every step, authorisation, access, and transfer must be 
contemporaneously recorded. 
 
Expert Testimony: Use forensic experts (state lab or accredited private labs) to explain 
technical evidence. 
 
Section 65B Compliance: Maintain proper certificates/attestations for electronic records 
— where applicable — and retain originals/forensic images. 
12.4 Common Defence Challenges & Mitigation 
[[PAGE 391]]
 
Challenge: Evidence is fabricated or tampered. 
Mitigation: Maintain robust chain of custody, cryptographic hashes of forensic images, 
and independent witness signatures. 
 
Challenge: IO exceeded jurisdiction or accessed systems unlawfully. 
Mitigation: Keep written authorisations; escalate questionable technical steps to 
authorised agencies. 
 
Challenge: Attribution is speculative. 
Mitigation: Present multi-source linkage (financial, device, behavioural) and specialist 
IO ACTION: Before court presentation, prepare an evidence index and expert summaries to 
simplify technical matters for the court. 
 
13. Case Vignettes (2–3 Court-Friendly Examples) 
All vignettes are fictional and intended to illustrate procedural points. 
Vignette A — Dark Web Marketplace Fraud 
Facts: Complainant reports purchase of high-value electronics from a dark web marketplace; 
payment made via cryptocurrency; item never delivered. Complainant provides .onion listing 
screenshot and transaction ID. 
 
 
1. IO ACTION: Record initial complaint and preserve original screenshot (with metadata). 
2. IO ACTION: Log blockchain transaction ID and request immediate preservation from 
Indian exchanges for corresponding KYC. 
3. IO ACTION: Secure any suspect devices if there is an identified local seller; involve State 
Cyber Cell for technical assistance. 
4. IO ACTION: Escalate to I4C if marketplace hosting is offshore. 
Mistakes Avoided: IO did not attempt to purchase from marketplace (no interaction); did not 
rely solely on screenshot as proof. 
[[PAGE 392]]
Investigator Takeaways: Blockchain persistence helped track flows; exchange KYC provided 
identity linkage; robust documentation supported court admissibility. 
Vignette B — CSAM Distribution over Anonymous Forum 
Facts: Anonymous tip leads to discovery of CSAM shared over a hidden forum. Files appear 
hosted abroad. 
1. IO ACTION: Immediately notify I4C and State Cyber Cell; request emergency 
preservation and takedown coordination. 
2. IO ACTION: Obtain court orders for mirror image of any suspect’s device if local suspects 
identified. 
3. IO ACTION: Coordinate with specialized unit for victim identification and support. 
Mistakes Avoided: IOs did not download or redistribute material; all observations were logged 
and forwarded to authorized agencies. 
Investigator Takeaways: CSAM cases require urgent multi-agency action; local action alone is 
insufficient for foreign hosting. 
Vignette C — Crypto-Based Extortion (Ransomware) 
Facts: Company receives ransom demand with cryptocurrency address. Logs indicate extortion 
coordinator used dark web communication channels. 
1. IO ACTION: Record ransom note and transaction details; advise company not to pay 
before consulting State Cyber Cell. 
2. IO ACTION: Request blockchain tracing and preservation of funds; prepare preservation 
notice to exchanges. 
3. IO ACTION: Escalate to I4C and central agencies due to cross-border implications. 
Mistakes Avoided: IO did not instruct company to transfer funds; did not interact with the 
extortionist. 
Investigator Takeaways: Preservation notices combined with blockchain tracing and exchange 
KYC produced actionable leads. 
 
[[PAGE 393]]
14. Templates (Word-Ready, Plain Text) 
Paste these into FIRs, preservation letters, or case diaries as required. Modify case-specific 
details in the bracketed sections. 
14.1 FIR Introductory Paragraph (Dark Web Case) 
FIR — [Date] 
 
On [Date and Time], [Complainant Name], resident of [Address], reported to [Police Station] 
that they were defrauded / extorted / victimised through an online service believed to be 
accessible via the dark web (.onion). The complainant has provided [screenshots / transaction 
ID / wallet address / URL] as supporting material. Preliminary indicators suggest use of 
anonymous networks and possible offshore hosting of the alleged offending service. 
Investigation is required to preserve electronic evidence, identify the responsible parties, and 
determine jurisdictional issues. 
 
Enter FIR under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code, Information Technology Act, 2000, 
and other applicable laws. Immediate steps for preservation, device seizure (if any), and 
coordination with State Cyber Cell / I4C are requested and authorised. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
14.2 Preservation Notice to Exchanges / Platforms 
To: [Designated Officer, Exchange/Platform Name] 
From: [Officer Name], [Designation], [Police Station / Unit] 
Date: [Date] 
 
Subject: Preservation Request — URGENT (Case No. [Case No.]) 
[[PAGE 394]]
 
This is to request immediate preservation of all records, logs, and subscriber information related 
to the following identifier(s): 
 
1. Wallet / Address / Transaction ID: [value] 
2. Account / Email / Username: [value] 
3. URL / .onion address: [value] 
4. Time Range: [from UTC dd/mm/yyyy hh:mm to UTC dd/mm/yyyy hh:mm] 
 
Please preserve the requested data without alteration pending lawful process. Provide an 
acknowledgement of receipt and preservation action to [contact details]. This preservation 
request is made in support of an ongoing criminal investigation under [relevant sections] and 
may be followed by a formal production order or MLAT request. 
 
Signed, 
[Officer Name], [Designation], [Contact]
