16. Formatting & Procedural Requirements (Checklist) 
 
Use numbered SOP steps for all operational instructions. 
 
Use IO ACTION: callouts to specify required IO activities. 
 
Use LEGAL RISK: warnings where improper action may jeopardise prosecution. 
 
Use tables (e.g., evidence prioritisation) to clarify volatile items. 
 
Maintain case diary entries as contemporaneous, legible, and signed. 
 
When producing documents for court, include a plain evidence index and expert 
summaries. 
 
 
17. Final Section — Verification Notes (Items to Update Periodically) 
[[PAGE 397]]
The following items change frequently and must be reviewed and updated in the manual at least 
annually (or sooner where notified by State/National authorities): 
1. Platform Policies & Contact Points — Exchanges, major hosting providers, and their 
preservation contact details and legal process requirements. 
2. Cryptocurrency Regulations & AML Guidance — RBI / Government notifications, 
changes in regulation for crypto exchanges, and freezing authorities. 
3. Central Agency SOP Changes — I4C, CERT-In, and central investigative agency 
escalation procedures. 
4. MLAT Timelines & Processes — Changes to diplomatic/legal channels and contact 
points for foreign preservation/production requests. 
5. Statutory Amendments — Amendments to the Information Technology Act, Evidence 
Act (Section 65B or corresponding provisions), BNSS/CrPC procedures. 
6. Forensic Standards — Updates to admissible forensic formats, lab accreditation 
requirements, and hash algorithms. 
7. Court Precedents — Recent judicial decisions impacting admissibility of dark web 
8. Training & Resource Listings — Accredited forensic labs, expert panels, and contact 
lists for technical support. 
IO ACTION: The Investigating Officer must note in the case diary the version of this chapter 
used and any deviations required by updated instructions at the time of investigation. 
 
Closing Notes (Procedural Emphasis) 
 
Preserve first, investigate next. Volatile third-party server logs and exchange records 
are often lost quickly; preservation requests should be initiated immediately and recorded 
in the diary. 
 
Document everything. Contemporaneous notes, signed transfer records, and clear 
indexing of digital exhibits are essential for court admissibility. 
 
Respect jurisdictional boundaries. Forensic or investigative steps requiring foreign 
cooperation must go through State Cyber Cell → I4C → MLAT/diplomatic channels. Do 
not attempt unilateral foreign takedowns or interactions. 
 
When in doubt, escalate. Technical complexity or potential international elements 
demand specialist involvement. Escalation is a procedural strength and should be 
transparently recorded. 
 
 
 
[[PAGE 398]]
CHAPTER 15 - FINANCIAL CYBER CRIMES AND BANKING 
ANALYSIS 
PART I: The Financial Cyber Crime Landscape 
1.1 Introduction: Nature of Financial Cyber Crime in Contemporary Policing 
Financial cybercrime today represents the most organised, scalable and rapidly evolving form of 
criminal activity confronting law enforcement agencies in India. Unlike conventional property 
crimes, cyber-enabled financial offences are executed remotely, often across jurisdictions, and 
rely on speed, anonymity, psychological manipulation and abuse of legitimate digital payment 
infrastructures rather than physical force or presence [1]. 
From the perspective of cyber policing, financial cybercrime must not be viewed merely as 
“online cheating” or “digital fraud”. It is, in effect, a money movement crime, where deception 
is only the entry point and the primary objective is rapid extraction, dispersal and laundering of 
funds before institutional controls can respond [2]. The crime scene is not a physical location but 
a transaction trail, dispersed across banks, payment gateways, wallets and, increasingly, virtual 
digital asset platforms. 
Indian law enforcement experience over the last five years demonstrates that successful 
investigation and recovery do not depend solely on identifying the accused, but on how quickly 
the money trail is intercepted, frozen, analysed and lawfully restored [3]. This chapter 
therefore begins with a structured understanding of the financial cybercrime landscape, focusing 
on typologies of fund movement rather than only modes of deception. 
 
1.2 Typologies of Financial Cyber Crimes Based on Fund Movement 
For operational clarity, financial cybercrimes are best categorised on the basis of how the money 
leaves the victim’s control, rather than the social engineering technique employed. This 
classification assists the Investigating Officer (IO) in deciding urgency, freezing strategy and 
institutional coordination [4]. 
Broadly, financial cybercrimes fall into three functional categories: 
 
1.2.1 Push Payment Frauds (Victim-Authorised Transfers) 
Push payment frauds are those where the victim is deceived into voluntarily authorising the 
transfer of funds from their own bank account or payment instrument. Legally and 
operationally, these cases require careful handling because the transaction is technically 
“authorised” by the account holder, even though consent is obtained through deception [5]. 
[[PAGE 399]]
Common push payment frauds encountered in India include: 
 
UPI investment scams (stock tips, crypto returns, IPO allocations) 
 
Task-based earning scams 
 
Fake customer care and refund scams 
 
Online marketplace advance payment frauds 
In these cases, funds typically move through UPI, IMPS or NEFT, often in multiple small-value 
transactions to avoid automated bank alerts [6]. The fraudster’s operational advantage lies in 
persuading the victim to complete the transaction themselves, thereby bypassing several bank-
side fraud controls. 
From a policing standpoint, push payment frauds demand immediate financial intervention, as 
delay drastically reduces recovery probability. Experience shows that if funds are not intercepted 
within the first few hours, they are quickly layered through mule accounts or converted into cash 
or crypto assets [7]. 
 
1.2.2 Pull Payment Frauds (Attacker-Initiated Transfers) 
Pull payment frauds occur where the attacker initiates the transaction without the victim’s 
knowledge, typically after compromising credentials or authentication mechanisms. These cases 
are more traditional in legal terms, as they involve unauthorised access and theft [8]. 
Common pull-based financial cybercrimes include: 
 
Phishing-based internet banking frauds 
 
OTP theft through malware or screen-sharing apps 
 
SIM swap–enabled account takeovers 
 
Card-not-present (CNP) frauds 
Here, the attacker controls the transaction flow, often executing rapid bulk transfers within 
minutes of access [9]. Such cases show a higher incidence of high-velocity transfers, midnight 
or early-morning activity, and immediate ATM withdrawals or wallet loading. 
For the IO, pull payment frauds require parallel investigation on two fronts: 
(a) Money trail analysis, and 
(b) Digital access compromise (IP logs, device fingerprinting, telecom data). 
However, recovery efforts remain fundamentally dependent on timely freezing of beneficiary 
accounts [10]. 
 
[[PAGE 400]]
1.2.3 Mule Layering and Fund Laundering Chains 
Irrespective of whether the initial transaction is push or pull based, the defining characteristic of 
organised financial cybercrime is mule layering. This refers to the deliberate movement of funds 
through multiple intermediary accounts to obscure origin and frustrate recovery [11]. 
A typical layering sequence observed in Indian cases is: 
Victim → Mule Account 1 → Mule Account 2 → ATM Withdrawal / Wallet / Crypto 
Exchange 
Each layer serves a specific purpose: 
 
First mule: receives victim funds and provides temporary parking 
 
Second mule: facilitates withdrawal or conversion 
 
Final layer: extraction into cash or virtual assets 
Mule accounts may belong to: 
 
Unwitting victims (duped account holders) 
 
Semi-aware participants (commission-based accounts) 
 
Professional mule operators selling verified bank accounts 
The detection of mule networks is now a central challenge in cyber policing. Data from national 
systems indicates that mule accounts often exhibit patterns such as recent account opening, 
disproportionate turnover, immediate withdrawals and frequent inter-bank transfers [12]. 
 
1.3 The “Golden Hour” Concept in Financial Cyber Crime Response 
In financial cybercrime investigations, the first one to two hours after reporting constitute what 
is operationally known as the Golden Hour. This is the period during which law enforcement 
intervention has the highest probability of preventing dissipation of funds [13]. 
Unlike physical crimes, where evidence persists, digital financial evidence is volatile. Funds can 
move across multiple banks within minutes, and beyond domestic jurisdiction equally fast [14]. 
Recognising this, the Government of India operationalised: 
 
The 1930 Cybercrime Helpline 
 
The Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System 
(CFCFRMS) 
[[PAGE 401]]
These systems are designed specifically to facilitate real-time financial blocking, even before 
FIR registration [15]. 
 
1.3.1 Role of Helpline 1930 
Helpline 1930 functions as a first-response financial interception tool, allowing victims to 
report fraud immediately. Upon intake, key transaction identifiers (bank, amount, UPI ID, 
account number) are captured and relayed to the banking ecosystem through CFCFRMS 
integration [16]. 
For police officers, it is essential to understand that 1930 reporting is not a mere grievance 
mechanism; it is a preventive enforcement tool intended to arrest the money trail at inception. 
Delay in encouraging victims to use 1930 directly correlates with reduced recovery outcomes 
[17]. 
 
1.3.2 CFCFRMS: Institutionalising Real-Time Freezing 
CFCFRMS represents a paradigm shift in cybercrime policing by enabling: 
 
Immediate marking of suspicious transactions 
 
Automated alerts to beneficiary banks 
 
Provisional holds on suspected accounts 
This system allows law enforcement to act before judicial orders, within the bounds of 
statutory authority, and subject to later legal ratification [18]. It is therefore imperative that 
Investigating Officers are trained to treat CFCFRMS alerts with urgency and precision. 
Field experience indicates that partial holds and proportional freezes, when executed early, 
significantly improve restitution rates while reducing downstream litigation [19]. 
 
1.4 Strategic Shift: From Accused-Centric to Proceeds-Centric Investigation 
Traditional criminal investigation frameworks prioritised identification and arrest of accused 
persons. In financial cybercrime, this approach is often insufficient and sometimes 
counterproductive if it delays financial intervention [20]. 
Modern cybercrime policing demands a proceeds-of-crime–centric approach, where: 
 
Fund interception precedes suspect identification 
 
Financial analysis guides investigative direction 
[[PAGE 402]]
 
Arrest follows evidentiary consolidation, not vice versa 
This shift aligns with global best practices and domestic legal evolution under the Bharatiya 
Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which emphasises seizure, custody and lawful disposal of 
property linked to crime [21]. 
Investigating Officers must therefore internalise that money is the primary evidence in 
financial cybercrime, and delay in securing it is equivalent to loss of the crime scene. 
 
1.5 Operational Takeaways for Investigating Officers 
From an SOP perspective, the following principles must guide all financial cybercrime responses 
at the field level: 
1. Time is the most critical variable in recovery [22]. 
2. Fund movement typology determines response strategy, not merely the fraud narrative 
[23]. 
3. Mule accounts are structural enablers, not incidental participants [24]. 
4. 1930 and CFCFRMS are enforcement tools, not administrative formalities [25]. 
5. Financial freezing must be proportionate, documented and legally sustainable from 
inception [26]. 
These principles form the foundation upon which the subsequent parts of this chapter will 
elaborate legal powers, banking SOPs, payment ecosystem analysis and recovery mechanisms. 
 
PART II: Legal Powers, Proportionality and Banking Interface 
2.1 Why Legal Precision Matters in Financial Cyber Crime Cases 
In financial cybercrime investigations, the strongest cases often fail not because the fraud did not 
occur, but because police action on bank accounts was legally excessive, poorly documented, 
or disproportionate. Over the last few years, courts across India have repeatedly scrutinised 
freezing orders, lien markings and prolonged account restrictions imposed by police during cyber 
fraud investigations [27]. 
Investigating Officers must therefore understand that bank accounts are not merely evidence 
containers; they are livelihood instruments for citizens and businesses. Any police action 
affecting bank operations attracts immediate judicial attention, including writ jurisdiction, 
consumer forums and banking ombudsman proceedings [28]. 
[[PAGE 403]]
This part of the chapter explains, in simple operational language, what legal powers exist, how 
far they extend, and where restraint is mandatory, so that investigations remain effective 
without inviting adverse court orders. 
 
2.2 Statutory Power to Seize or Freeze Bank Accounts 
2.2.1 Section 106 BNSS – Power to Seize “Suspicious Property” 
Under Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) (corresponding 
to Section 102 of the old CrPC), a police officer has the power to seize or prohibit the 
operation of property suspected to be connected with the commission of an offence [29]. 
For financial cybercrime cases, courts have consistently recognised that: 
 
Money lying in a bank account qualifies as “property” 
 
Temporary freezing of such money is permissible if there is a clear nexus with the 
offence 
However, the power under Section 106 BNSS is preventive and protective, not punitive. Its 
purpose is: 
 
To preserve suspected proceeds of crime 
 
To prevent further dissipation or laundering 
 
To secure funds for possible restitution to victims 
It is not meant to paralyse entire banking operations indefinitely [30]. 
 
2.2.2 Section 91 BNSS – Power to Call for Documents 
Section 91 BNSS (earlier Section 91 CrPC) empowers the Investigating Officer to issue written 
notices to banks, payment intermediaries and financial institutions for production of documents 
[31]. 
In cyber financial fraud cases, this section is routinely used to obtain: 
 
KYC documents (CAF, Aadhaar, PAN, video KYC metadata) 
 
Detailed account statements in Excel or CSV format 
 
IP logs and access timestamps 
 
Linked account or wallet details 
[[PAGE 404]]
IOs must remember that Section 91 BNSS is a cooperation tool, not an enforcement tool. Banks 
are legally bound to comply, but the request must be: 
 
Case-specific 
 
Time-bound 
 
Properly referenced to FIR/NCRP complaint 
Vague or bulk fishing requests are increasingly objected to by banks and questioned in courts 
[32]. 
 
2.3 Debit Freeze vs Lien: The Most Critical Operational Distinction 
2.3.1 What is a Debit Freeze 
A Debit Freeze means: 
 
Complete stoppage of withdrawals and transfers 
 
Account holder cannot access any funds 
 
Salary credits, business receipts continue but cannot be used 
Police often default to debit freezes because they are easy to request and quickly implemented. 
However, courts have repeatedly observed that blanket debit freezes cause disproportionate 
hardship, especially where the fraud amount is small compared to the total balance [33]. 
 
2.3.2 What is a Lien Marking 
A Lien is a limited restriction, where: 
 
Only the exact disputed amount is blocked 
 
Remaining balance remains accessible 
 
Business and livelihood disruption is avoided 
From a legal perspective, lien marking is the preferred method once the fraudulent amount is 
clearly identified [34]. 
Every Investigating Officer must internalise this rule: 
If the suspected fraud amount is identifiable, a lien must be used instead of a debit freeze. 
Failure to do so is one of the main reasons police actions are quashed in writ proceedings. 
 
[[PAGE 405]]
2.4 Doctrine of Proportionality: Why Courts Intervene 
The Doctrine of Proportionality, now firmly applied by Indian courts, requires that: 
 
State action must be necessary 
 
Action must be least restrictive 
 
Harm caused must not exceed the objective sought 
In cybercrime cases, freezing an account containing ₹10 lakh for an alleged fraud of ₹15,
5,000 is 
viewed as grossly disproportionate, unless strong reasons are recorded [35]. 
Judicial scrutiny often focuses on: 
 
Whether police recorded reasons for choosing debit freeze 
 
Whether alternatives like lien were considered 
 
Duration of the freeze without court reporting 
 
Absence of victim restitution steps 
The RBI has also cautioned banks and law enforcement against mechanical freezing, especially 
after the Supreme Court’s emphasis on natural justice principles [36]. 
 
2.5 Reporting to Court: Mandatory and Non-Negotiable 
Once a bank account is frozen or liened under Section 106 BNSS, the Investigating Officer must 
inform the jurisdictional Magistrate without delay. This requirement is not optional [37]. 
Best practice (now widely accepted by courts) is: 
 
Mention freezing action in the Case Diary 
 
Place a brief report before the Magistrate 
 
Attach bank communication and transaction trail summary 
Failure to report timely has resulted in courts ordering immediate defreezing, even when fraud 
was otherwise proved [38]. 
 
2.6 Interaction with Banks: Understanding Their Legal Constraints 
IOs must appreciate that banks operate under: 
 
RBI Master Directions 
[[PAGE 406]]
 
NPCI operational rules 
 
Consumer protection mandates 
Banks are accountable for customer rights, and therefore often resist: 
 
Indefinite freezes without court follow-up 
 
Requests lacking FIR/NCRP reference 
 
Verbal or WhatsApp-based instructions 
The RBI Revised Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management (July 2024) mandate banks 
to: 
 
Follow principles of natural justice 
 
Avoid arbitrary restrictions 
 
Maintain audit trails for enforcement actions [39] 
Accordingly, Investigating Officers must issue: 
 
Written, reasoned requests 
 
Clearly specify freeze or lien 
 
Mention amount involved and offence details 
This cooperation-based approach significantly reduces resistance and litigation. 
 
2.7 NCRP–CFCFRMS and Police Powers: Clearing the Confusion 
A common misconception among field officers is that only FIR-based actions are enforceable. 
This is incorrect in the context of financial cybercrime. 
The CFCFRMS mechanism, operating through NCRP and the 1930 helpline, enables: 
 
Provisional holds 
 
Real-time alerts 
 
Inter-bank coordination 
These actions are preventive in nature and legally sustainable, provided they are: 
 
Followed by FIR or enquiry 
 
Converted into formal investigation promptly 
 
Reported to court where required [40] 
[[PAGE 407]]
CFCFRMS should be treated as: 
An emergency brake, not a substitute for investigation. 
 
2.8 Practical Checklist for IOs (Legal Compliance) 
Before freezing or liening any bank account, the IO should ask: 
1. Is the fraud amount clearly identifiable? 
2. Can a lien suffice instead of debit freeze? 
3. Have reasons been recorded in the case diary? 
4. Has the bank received a written, formal request? 
5. Has the Magistrate been informed promptly? 
If the answer to any of these is “No”, corrective action must be taken immediately [41]. 
 
2.9 Training Note for Court Proceedings 
When questioned in court, IOs should be prepared to explain: 
 
Why the specific action was necessary 
 
Why lesser restrictive alternatives were inadequate 
 
How victim interest was protected 
 
Steps taken for early restitution 
Courts respond positively when police demonstrate measured, reasoned enforcement rather 
than blanket restrictions [42]. 
 
PART III: Banking Investigation SOP – Account Analysis, KYC and Mule Identification 
3.1 Why Bank-Centric Investigation is the Core of Financial Cyber Crime Cases 
In financial cybercrime cases, the bank account is not just a medium of loss; it is the primary 
crime scene. Unlike conventional offences, where money may be incidental, in cyber-enabled 
financial crimes the entire offence revolves around movement, parking, layering and 
withdrawal of funds [43]. 
Field experience across States has shown that cases with weak bank analysis almost always 
result in: 
[[PAGE 408]]
 
Failure to trace accused persons 
 
Collapse of money trail 
 
Adverse judicial remarks on investigation quality 
Accordingly, Investigating Officers must approach bank investigation as a structured, 
document-driven exercise, not as an ad-hoc request for statements [44]. 
 
3.2 The “Trinity” of Banking Documents: What Every IO Must Collect 
For every beneficiary or suspected account in a financial cybercrime case, three categories of 
documents are non-negotiable. These are referred to operationally as the Banking Trinity [45]. 
 
3.2.1 KYC Packet – Establishing Account Identity 
The KYC packet forms the foundation of account-holder identification. It must include: 
 
Customer Application Form (CAF) 
 
Aadhaar / PAN / passport copies 
 
Address proof 
 
Photograph 
 
Video KYC records and metadata, where applicable 
IOs must not be satisfied with photocopies alone. Video KYC metadata, including: 
 
Date and time 
 
Device used 
 
IP address 
 
Geo-coordinates (if available) 
often provide the first technical linkage between an account and a suspect location [46]. 
It is equally important to examine whether: 
 
Documents appear forged or recycled 
 
Same photograph appears in multiple accounts 
 
Address corresponds to shared accommodation, hostels or vacant premises 
Such indicators frequently point towards organised mule operations [47]. 
[[PAGE 409]]
 
3.2.2 Account Statement – Understanding Transaction Behaviour 
The bank statement must always be sought in Excel or CSV format, not PDF. This allows 
sorting, filtering and behavioural analysis [48]. 
While examining statements, IOs should look for: 
 
Sudden spikes in credits 
 
Multiple credits within short intervals 
 
Immediate outward transfers after credit 
 
Near-zero end-of-day balances 
A genuine personal account usually shows patterned, predictable behaviour. Mule or fraud 
accounts display high-velocity, non-purposeful transactions, often without narration 
consistency [49]. 
 
3.2.3 Access Logs – Digital Footprints of Control 
Modern banking platforms record access logs, especially for: 
 
Internet banking 
 
Mobile banking 
 
UPI-linked apps 
IOs should specifically request: 
 
IP addresses used for login 
 
Date and time of access 
 
Device or browser identifiers, if logged 
 
Failed login attempts 
Access logs often establish whether: 
 
Account holder himself operated the account 
 
Third-party devices controlled transactions 
 
Multiple geographically distant logins occurred within short durations 
[[PAGE 410]]
These logs become extremely valuable during court examination to distinguish victim-mules 
from professional mules [50]. 
 
3.3 Investigating the Beneficiary: Not All Account Holders Are Criminals 
A common investigative mistake is treating every beneficiary account holder as an accused. 
Courts have repeatedly cautioned against this approach, especially in cyber fraud cases [51]. 
From an SOP perspective, beneficiaries fall into two broad categories: 
 
3.3.1 Victim-Mules (Unknowing Participants) 
Victim-mules are individuals who: 
 
Are themselves deceived into sharing account access 
 
Are promised commissions or temporary use 
 
Often do not understand the illegality involved 
Indicators include: 
 
Immediate reporting after bank blocking 
 
Cooperation with police 
 
Limited financial benefit retained 
Such persons may still be legally liable, but investigation must carefully document mens rea, 
otherwise charges often fail in court [52]. 
 
3.3.2 Professional Mules (Account Sellers / Renters) 
Professional mules knowingly participate by: 
 
Opening accounts for commission 
 
Handing over ATM cards, UPI access, or credentials 
 
Maintaining multiple accounts across banks 
Indicators include: 
 
Multiple accounts linked to same device or IP 
 
Consistent commission credits 
[[PAGE 411]]
 
Prior involvement in similar cases 
Proper differentiation between these two categories protects investigations from wrongful 
implication and strengthens prosecution against real offenders [53]. 
 
3.4 Mule Account Identification: Field Checklist 
Based on national data and RBI-led fraud analytics, mule accounts commonly show the 
following characteristics [54]: 
1. Account opened within last 3–12 months 
2. Minimal or no prior banking activity 
3. Sudden high-value turnover unrelated to profile 
4. Immediate cash withdrawals or crypto transfers 
5. Transactions occurring late night or early morning 
6. Rapid movement through IMPS/UPI channels 
IOs must not rely on a single indicator. A combination of red flags, when documented properly, 
is judicially sustainable [55]. 
 
3.5 Layered Transaction Analysis: Following the Money Beyond One Account 
Stopping investigation at the first beneficiary account is one of the biggest reasons cybercrime 
cases stagnate. Money almost always moves further [56]. 
Operationally, transactions are mapped as: 
 
Layer 1 – Direct beneficiary account 
 
Layer 2 – Subsequent transfer account 
 
Layer 3 – Cash, wallet or crypto exit 
Each layer requires fresh Section 91 BNSS requests and proportional freezing or lien action. IOs 
must maintain layer-wise documentation, which later becomes critical during charge-sheet 
drafting [57]. 
 
3.6 Linking Banking Evidence with Technical Evidence 
[[PAGE 412]]
Bank records alone establish money flow, not always identity. Therefore, IOs must correlate 
banking evidence with: 
 
Mobile numbers linked to accounts 
 
UPI device IDs 
 
IP addresses mapped to ISP/TSP 
 
Location data from telecom providers 
This convergence of evidence forms the backbone of cybercrime prosecution and significantly 
improves conviction prospects [58]. 
 
3.7 Coordination with Bank Nodal Officers 
Banks function through designated Law Enforcement Nodal Officers. Effective coordination 
requires: 
 
Clear subject line mentioning FIR/NCRP number 
 
Specific document requests 
 
Reasonable timelines 
Informal communication may speed up processes initially but weakens evidentiary value later. 
All critical requests must be on record [59]. 
 
3.8 Documentation Discipline: Case Diary and Court Readiness 
Every banking action must reflect in: 
 
Case diary entries 
 
Annexed bank replies 
 
Freeze or lien instructions 
Courts increasingly ask IOs: 
“Where is the record of why this account was frozen?” 
A well-maintained diary with banking reasoning often decides whether police action survives 
judicial scrutiny [60]. 
 
3.9 Operational Takeaways for Field Officers 
[[PAGE 413]]
1. Always collect the Banking Trinity documents 
2. Demand statements in analyzable formats 
3. Distinguish victim-mules from professional mules 
4. Follow money beyond first account 
5. Correlate banking data with digital footprints 
These principles must be treated as non-negotiable SOP standards for all financial cybercrime 
investigations [61]. 
 
PART IV: Payment Ecosystem SOP – UPI, Payment Gateways and Wallets 
4.1 Understanding the Digital Payment Ecosystem: Why IOs Must Go Beyond Banks 
Modern financial cybercrimes do not move money only through traditional bank-to-bank 
transfers. A significant volume of fraud proceeds now passes through UPI apps, payment 
gateways, wallets and pooled settlement accounts, often within minutes of the initial 
transaction [62]. 
Investigating Officers must therefore understand that the visible bank statement is often only 
the surface layer. The real beneficiary is frequently concealed behind: 
 
UPI Virtual Payment Addresses (VPAs) 
 
Payment gateway settlement cycles 
 
Wallet pool accounts 
 
Merchant aggregators 
Failure to understand this ecosystem results in investigations stopping prematurely at the wrong 
node, leading to poor recovery and weak prosecution [63]. 
 
4.2 UPI Investigation SOP: Practical Understanding for Field Officers 
4.2.1 Anatomy of a UPI Transaction 
A UPI transaction typically involves: 
 
Remitter Bank (victim’s bank) 
 
Paying App / PSP (PhonePe, GPay, Paytm, etc.) 
 
Beneficiary Bank 
[[PAGE 414]]
 
Receiving App 
 
NPCI as the switching authority 
Every UPI transaction generates two critical identifiers: 
1. Transaction ID 
2. RRN (Retrieval Reference Number) 
The RRN is the single most important identifier for tracing UPI transactions across banks and 
apps. IOs must always ensure RRNs are captured in complaints and notices [64]. 
 
4.2.2 Decoding UPI VPA Handles 
UPI VPAs follow a structured format, such as: 
 
user@okicici 
 
merchant@paytm 
 
name@upi 
The suffix often indicates: 
 
The PSP or bank 
 
Whether the account is merchant-linked 
 
Whether it is wallet-routed 
Understanding the VPA helps IOs quickly determine which entity to contact first and whether 
the transaction was routed through a bank or intermediary [65]. 
 
4.2.3 PSPs vs TPAPs: Why This Distinction Matters 
 
PSPs (Payment Service Providers) are banks authorised by NPCI. 
 
TPAPs (Third Party App Providers) include PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm, etc. 
TPAPs do not hold money, but they: 
 
Maintain session logs 
 
Store device identifiers 
 
Record authentication attempts 
Therefore, in UPI fraud cases, IOs must issue parallel requests: 
[[PAGE 415]]
 
To banks for account and statement details 
 
To TPAPs for session logs and device data 
Relying only on bank statements leaves a major evidentiary gap [66]. 
 
4.3 NPCI Dispute Redressal vs Criminal Investigation: Drawing the Legal Line 
A recurring issue in cybercrime policing is confusion between: 
 
Payment disputes, and 
 
Criminal fraud investigations 
NPCI’s Dispute Redressal Mechanism is designed primarily for: 
 
Failed transactions 
 
Duplicate debits 
 
Technical reversals 
It is not a substitute for criminal investigation when deception, impersonation or organised 
fraud is involved [67]. 
However, IOs must understand that banks and courts expect police to justify criminal 
intervention when a transaction is technically successful but disputed by the customer. 
Best practice is: 
 
Encourage victim to initiate NPCI dispute in parallel 
 
Police action focuses on freezing proceeds of crime 
 
Both processes proceed independently but in coordination [68] 
This dual-track approach strengthens legal defensibility and victim confidence. 
 
4.4 Payment Gateway (PG) Investigation: Tracing the Real Merchant 
4.4.1 Identifying a Payment Gateway in Bank Statements 
Payment gateway transactions usually appear in statements with narrations such as: 
 
“Razorpay” 
 
“CCavenue” 
 
“PayU” 
[[PAGE 416]]
 
“BillDesk” 
IOs must recognise that the bank account receiving money is often the gateway’s pool 
account, not the fraudster [69]. 
Freezing a gateway pool account without proper analysis can disrupt thousands of legitimate 
merchants and invites immediate legal action. 
 
4.4.2 Merchant Settlement Details: The Key Document 
The correct SOP is: 
 
Identify the payment gateway 
 
Issue Section 91 BNSS notice to the gateway 
 
Seek Merchant Settlement Report, including: 
o Merchant ID 
o Linked bank account 
o Settlement dates 
o Refund history 
This report reveals where the money actually went, allowing targeted freezing of the end 
beneficiary instead of indiscriminate action [70]. 
 
4.5 Wallets and Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs) 
4.5.1 Open vs Closed Wallets 
 
Closed wallets (e.g., Amazon Pay balance used within platform) have restricted usage. 
 
Open wallets allow transfer, withdrawal or merchant payments. 
Fraud proceeds are often routed into wallets because: 
 
KYC thresholds may be lower 
 
Withdrawals are faster 
 
Audit trails are fragmented 
IOs must specifically ask wallet providers for user ledger statements, not just summary 
balances [71]. 
[[PAGE 417]]
 
4.5.2 Pool Accounts and Ledger Bypass 
Most wallet companies use pool accounts, where: 
 
Funds of multiple users are held together 
 
Individual balances exist only in internal ledgers 
Freezing pool accounts is rarely appropriate. Instead, IOs must: 
 
Identify individual user ledger 
 
Mark lien equivalent internally 
 
Seek withdrawal blocks for that user only [72] 
Courts have repeatedly frowned upon blanket freezing of wallet pool accounts. 
 
4.6 Layering Through Payment Systems: Why Speed Matters 
Fraudsters deliberately move funds through: 
 
UPI → Wallet → Bank → Cash 
 
UPI → PG → Merchant → ATM 
Each hop reduces recovery probability. The first 2–4 hours remain critical, even within the 
payment ecosystem [73]. 
IOs must therefore: 
 
Act immediately on CFCFRMS alerts 
 
Issue simultaneous notices to banks, TPAPs, PGs and wallets 
 
Avoid sequential delays 
 
4.7 Documentation for Court: What Judges Look For 
In payment ecosystem cases, courts usually ask: 
 
Did police identify the correct beneficiary? 
 
Was the action proportionate? 
 
Were third parties (gateways, wallets) unnecessarily affected? 
[[PAGE 418]]
Well-documented merchant settlement analysis and VPA decoding often make the difference 
between confirmation and quashing of police action [74]. 
 
4.8 Operational Dos and Don’ts for IOs 
Do: 
 
Always capture RRN 
 
Identify PSP/TPAP early 
 
Request merchant settlement details 
 
Use lien instead of blanket freezes 
Don’t: 
 
Freeze payment gateway pool accounts casually 
 
Treat NPCI dispute as a criminal substitute 
 
Ignore wallet internal ledgers 
These practical rules ensure investigation remains focused, legal and effective [75]. 
 
PART V: Money Trail Visualisation and Analytical Presentation 
5.1 Why Visualising the Money Trail is Non-Negotiable 
In financial cybercrime cases, the quality of investigation is often judged not by how much data 
was collected, but by how clearly the movement of money is explained. Courts, prosecutors 
and senior officers repeatedly observe that bulky bank statements without structured analysis do 
not establish criminal linkage [76]. 
Money trail visualisation serves three purposes simultaneously: 
 
It clarifies the sequence of transactions 
 
It establishes conscious movement and layering 
 
It supports judicial reasoning for freezing, seizure and restitution 
Investigating Officers must therefore treat money-trail visualisation as an integral evidentiary 
step, not as an optional annexure [77]. 
 
5.2 Fund Flow Diagrams: Translating Transactions into Logic 
[[PAGE 419]]
5.2.1 Concept of a Fund Flow Diagram 
A fund flow diagram is a simple, chronological representation of how money moved from the 
victim to final exit points. It converts complex spreadsheets into an understandable narrative, 
usable even by non-technical judges [78]. 
A basic representation follows the format: 
Victim (A) → ₹50,000 → Beneficiary (B) 
Beneficiary (B) → ₹20,000 → ATM Withdrawal 
Beneficiary (B) → ₹30,0,000 → Mule Account (C) 
This clarity allows courts to immediately grasp: 
 
Who received the money 
 
How much was retained 
 
Where it exited the system [79] 
 
5.2.2 Standard Symbols Used in Fund Flow Representation 
While no statute mandates a specific format, field-tested best practice uses: 
 
Rectangles for persons/accounts 
 
Arrows for transfers 
 
Labels indicating amount and date 
 
Circles to mark cash or wallet exits 
Consistency in symbols across case diaries improves readability and avoids confusion during 
examination [80]. 
 
5.3 Layer-Wise Mapping: Establishing Criminal Continuity 
Money trail analysis must always be structured layer-wise: 
 
Layer 1: Direct beneficiary 
 
Layer 2: Immediate onward transfers 
 
Layer 3: Cash, wallet or crypto exits 
Each layer strengthens inference of intentional laundering, especially where transactions occur 
rapidly and without economic purpose [81]. 
[[PAGE 420]]
Courts are more receptive when the IO demonstrates progressive movement rather than isolated 
transactions. 
 
5.4 Bulk Statement Analysis: Handling Multiple Banks and Accounts 
5.4.1 Why Bulk Analysis is Required 
In organised cyber fraud, funds often pass through multiple banks in parallel, making single-
account analysis inadequate. IOs must therefore consolidate statements from: 
 
Different banks 
 
Different accounts 
 
Different dates 
This allows identification of common destination accounts, which often represent control 
points of fraud networks [82]. 
 
5.4.2 Analytical Approach (Conceptual, Not Technical) 
Without resorting to complex tools, IOs can: 
 
Sort transactions by credit and debit 
 
Align timestamps across banks 
 
Identify repeated account numbers 
 
Note transaction proximity in time 
This structured approach reveals patterns invisible in isolated statements, such as 
synchronized transfers or repeated use of the same mule account [83]. 
 
5.5 Identifying the Final Exit Point 
The most critical evidentiary finding in any financial cybercrime case is the exit point, where 
funds leave traceable banking channels. Exit points typically include: 
 
ATM withdrawals 
 
Wallet cash-outs 
 
Crypto exchange deposits 
 
Merchant settlements followed by cash use 
[[PAGE 421]]
Once the exit is identified, further tracing often requires telecom, CCTV or crypto exchange 
coordination, which must be documented clearly to justify investigative direction [84]. 
 
5.6 Correlating Money Flow with Human Behaviour 
Courts increasingly expect IOs to correlate money movement with conduct, such as: 
 
Immediate withdrawals after credit 
 
Night-time transactions 
 
Rapid dispersal without retention 
These behavioural patterns, when supported by bank records, allow the court to infer knowledge 
and intent, especially in mule and organised fraud cases [85]. 
 
5.7 Presentation in Case Diary and Charge Sheet 
Fund flow analysis must appear in: 
 
Case diary entries (narrative form) 
 
Annexed diagrams 
 
Charge sheet summaries 
IOs should avoid dumping raw statements. Instead, they should include: 
 
Brief explanation of each layer 
 
Reference to annexed diagrams 
 
Clear mention of seized or liened amounts 
This approach significantly improves prosecutorial effectiveness and reduces court queries [86]. 
 
5.8 Common Errors to Avoid 
Field experience highlights recurring mistakes: 
 
Mixing narrative and analysis 
 
Failing to label amounts and dates 
 
Ignoring small-value repeated transfers 
 
Stopping analysis at first beneficiary 
[[PAGE 422]]
Avoiding these errors ensures the investigation withstands judicial examination [87]. 
 
5.9 Operational Takeaways 
1. Money trail must be visual, chronological and logical 
2. Layer-wise mapping is essential 
3. Bulk analysis identifies network control points 
4. Exit points decide recovery potential 
5. Presentation quality affects court outcomes 
These principles convert financial data into legally usable evidence [88]. 
 
PART VI: Recovery, Release and Restoration of Funds (The End Game) 
6.1 Why Recovery is the True Measure of Investigation Success 
In financial cybercrime cases, investigation does not end with identification of accused or filing 
of charge-sheet. From the victim’s perspective, justice is meaningful only when lost money is 
restored in a lawful and timely manner. Courts also increasingly evaluate police performance 
by recovery outcomes, not merely by registration statistics [89]. 
Experience shows that poor understanding of recovery procedures results in: 
 
Long-term freezing of funds without restitution 
 
Victim frustration and litigation against police 
 
Banks refusing to act citing legal uncertainty 
Therefore, Investigating Officers must clearly understand the legal pathways for returning 
money, while ensuring compliance with BNSS, banking norms and judicial directions [90]. 
 
6.2 Legal Framework for Disposal and Restoration of Property 
6.2.1 Section 503 BNSS – Disposal of Property 
Section 503 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 empowers the competent court to 
pass orders regarding custody, disposal or restoration of property seized during investigation 
[91]. 
In financial cybercrime cases, “property” typically includes: 
[[PAGE 423]]
 
Amounts frozen in bank accounts 
 
Amounts held under lien 
 
Wallet balances blocked under law enforcement instruction 
Courts may order: 
 
Interim release to victim 
 
Final release after adjudication 
 
Transfer between accounts under court supervision 
Investigating Officers must proactively move the court for such orders, instead of waiting for 
trial conclusion [92]. 
 
6.3 Interim Custody of Funds: Practical SOP for IOs 
Interim custody refers to temporary release of funds to the victim, even while investigation is 
ongoing. NCRP–CFCFRMS SOP provides structured guidance for such cases [93]. 
Common scenarios permitting interim custody: 
 
Single victim, clearly identifiable amount 
 
Beneficiary account traced and secured 
 
No competing claims over funds 
In such cases, IO should: 
1. Prepare a concise report explaining money trail 
2. Attach bank confirmation of available balance 
3. Move an application before jurisdictional Magistrate 
Courts increasingly favour interim custody where police action is prompt and transparent [94]. 
 
6.4 Multiple Victims and Proportionate Distribution 
In cases involving multiple victims whose funds are pooled into one account, recovery becomes 
more complex. Blanket release to a single complainant is legally impermissible [95]. 
Best practice involves: 
 
Identifying victim-wise contribution 
[[PAGE 424]]
 
Preparing a proportionate distribution statement 
 
Seeking court guidance on apportionment 
CFCFRMS SOP explicitly discourages arbitrary releases and emphasises equitable restitution 
under judicial supervision [96]. 
 
6.5 Indemnity Bonds: Facilitating Faster Victim Relief 
6.5.1 Purpose of Indemnity Bonds 
Indemnity bonds allow banks to release funds to victims without waiting for full trial 
completion, while safeguarding against future claims [97]. 
Typically, indemnity bonds: 
 
Are executed by the victim 
 
Undertake to refund money if court later directs otherwise 
 
Reduce hesitation on part of banks 
Investigating Officers should encourage use of indemnity bonds, especially where: 
 
Fraud is clear 
 
Funds are uncontested 
 
Delay would cause undue hardship [98]. 
 
6.6 Role of Banks in Recovery and Release 
Banks are operational partners in recovery but they act strictly within: 
 
RBI directions 
 
Court orders 
 
Internal audit accountability 
Therefore, IOs must avoid: 
 
Verbal release instructions 
 
Informal assurances 
 
Pressure tactics 
Every release must be backed by: 
[[PAGE 425]]
 
Written court order, or 
 
Clear indemnity bond process approved by the court [99]. 
 
6.7 Wallets, PGs and Recovery Challenges 
Recovery from wallets and payment gateways requires additional care: 
 
Wallets operate on pooled accounts 
 
PG settlements follow merchant cycles 
Courts usually direct: 
 
Internal ledger adjustments 
 
User-specific releases 
 
No disturbance to unrelated third-party balances 
Proper documentation of ledger-based recovery prevents legal challenges from intermediaries 
[100]. 
 
6.8 Timeline Discipline: Avoiding Prolonged Freezes 
One of the strongest judicial criticisms in cyber fraud cases is indefinite freezing. IOs must 
periodically: 
 
Review frozen balances 
 
Update courts 
 
Seek modification or release orders 
Unreviewed freezes beyond reasonable periods often result in courts ordering immediate 
defreezing, sometimes with adverse remarks [101]. 
 
6.9 Communicating with Victims: A Policing Obligation 
Victims frequently approach courts because: 
 
They are not informed of recovery steps 
 
They do not understand delays 
IOs should: 
[[PAGE 426]]
 
Explain recovery stages 
 
Clarify court-dependency 
 
Avoid unrealistic assurances 
Transparent communication reduces grievance escalation and improves institutional trust [102]. 
 
6.10 Operational Checklist for IOs (Recovery Stage) 
Before concluding investigation, ensure: 
1. All frozen or liened amounts are reviewed 
2. Court orders for custody/disposal are sought 
3. Indemnity bond option is examined 
4. Banks and intermediaries are formally instructed 
5. Victim is informed of outcome 
This checklist ensures lawful closure of the financial dimension of the case [103]. 
 
6.11 Strategic Perspective: Recovery as Deterrence 
Effective recovery does not merely compensate victims. It: 
 
Disrupts cybercrime business models 
 
Deters mule participation 
 
Strengthens public confidence 
From a policy perspective, money recovered is crime prevented, and this principle must guide 
all financial cybercrime investigations [104]. 
PART VII: Graphical and Flow-Based Representation of Financial Cybercrime 
7.1 Standard Financial Cybercrime Investigation Flow (Macro Level) 
The end-to-end investigation flow may be understood in the following sequential stages: 
Stage 1: Reporting 
 
Victim reports fraud via 1930 / NCRP 
 
Basic transaction details captured 
[[PAGE 427]]
 
Golden Hour intervention triggered 
Stage 2: Financial Interception 
 
CFCFRMS alerts generated 
 
Provisional hold / freeze initiated 
 
Beneficiary bank(s) alerted 
Stage 3: Legal Formalisation 
 
FIR or formal enquiry registered 
 
Section 91 BNSS notices issued 
 
Section 106 BNSS freezing/lien confirmed 
Stage 4: Money Trail Expansion 
 
Layer 1, Layer 2, Layer 3 accounts traced 
 
Wallets, PGs, crypto (if any) identified 
Stage 5: Analysis & Attribution 
 
Beneficiary classification (victim-mule / professional mule) 
 
Behavioural and temporal analysis 
 
Linking digital and banking evidence 
Stage 6: Recovery & Restoration 
 
Interim custody applications 
 
Indemnity bonds (where applicable) 
 
Court-directed release 
Stage 7: Prosecution & Closure 
 
Charge sheet / final report 
 
Court-monitored disposal 
 
Victim informed 
This macro flow ensures that no investigative stage is skipped, which is critical for judicial 
sustainability [107]. 
 
[[PAGE 428]]
7.3 Standard Fund Flow Diagram (Micro Level – Case Specific) 
A case-specific fund flow should always be drafted in simple linear form. A recommended 
illustration is as follows: 
Victim Account (A) 
↓ ₹50,000 (UPI, Date & Time) 
Beneficiary Account (B – Layer 1) 
↓ ₹30,000 (IMPS within 5 minutes) 
Mule Account (C – Layer 2) 
↓ ₹30,000 
• ₹20,000 ATM Withdrawal 
• ₹10,000 Wallet Transfer 
This representation must clearly mention: 
 
Amount 
 
Mode of transfer 
 
Time gap 
 
Exit method 
Courts repeatedly note that clarity is more important than complexity [108]. 
 
7.4 UPI-Centric Flow Representation (Field Use) 
For UPI cases, IOs should visualise flow as: 
Victim Bank → UPI App (TPAP) → NPCI Switch → Beneficiary Bank 
Below this, IOs should annotate: 
 
Transaction ID 
 
RRN 
 
VPA 
 
PSP/TPAP involved 
This helps the court immediately understand which entity controlled which segment of the 
transaction, avoiding misdirected blame or procedural confusion [109]. 
 
7.5 Payment Gateway Flow Representation 
[[PAGE 429]]
For payment gateway cases, the flow must explicitly show pool account separation: 
Victim → Payment Gateway Pool Account 
(No criminal inference at this stage) 
↓ 
Merchant Settlement Account (End Beneficiary) 
↓ 
ATM / Wallet / Cash Exit 
This representation is essential to justify why: 
 
Gateway pool was not frozen 
 
Only merchant settlement account was targeted 
Incorrect representation at this stage is one of the most common causes of adverse judicial orders 
 
7.6 Recovery and Court Flow Representation 
During recovery, IOs should represent the following flow to court: 
Frozen / Liened Amount 
↓ 
Court Application (Interim Custody / Disposal) 
↓ 
Bank Compliance 
↓ 
Victim Restoration / Final Disposal 
This demonstrates that police action remained under judicial supervision, insulating officers 
from allegations of excess or arbitrariness [111]. 
 
7.7 Common Visual Errors Observed in Case Diaries 
Supervisory reviews and court observations reveal frequent errors such as: 
 
Missing dates and time gaps 
 
No indication of transaction mode 
 
Mixing suspects and victims without distinction 
 
Absence of exit-point marking 
[[PAGE 430]]
IOs must understand that poor visual explanation is treated as poor investigation, even if data 
exists [112]. 
 
7.8 Training Note: How IOs Should Explain the Flow in Court 
When asked in court, IOs should explain the flow verbally as follows: 
 
“The victim’s amount was first credited into the beneficiary account…” 
 
“Within minutes, the amount was transferred further…” 
 
“The final exit occurred through cash withdrawal / wallet…” 
Courts prefer step-by-step narration aligned with the diagram, not technical jargon [113]. 
 
7.9 Strategic Value of Flow-Based Investigation 
Flow-based investigation: 
 
Accelerates supervisory review 
 
Strengthens prosecution clarity 
 
Improves recovery outcomes 
 
Reduces legal challenges 
From an institutional perspective, flow clarity equals investigative credibility [114]. 
 
7.10 Concluding Operational Guidance 
Every Investigating Officer handling financial cybercrime must ensure: 
1. One macro investigation flow 
2. One case-specific fund flow 
3. Clear marking of exit points 
4. Alignment between diagram, diary and charge sheet 
This approach standardises investigation quality across units and courts [115]. 
 
 
[[PAGE 431]]
CHAPTER 17: ADVANCED & EMERGING 
DIGITAL FORENSICS 
17.1 Introduction 
Crime is no longer just physical; it is digital and invisible. 
The days when an investigation relied solely on a dropped weapon, a fingerprint on a glass, or an 
eyewitness account are disappearing. Today, the most critical witness to a crime may not be a 
person at all. It might be a silent sensor on a wall, a computer inside a car, or a cloud server 
thousands of miles away. 
The criminal is using tools that did not exist five years ago. They are using Artificial Intelligence 
(AI) to clone voices for extortion. They are using smart vehicles to transport contraband while 
leaving digital tracks they believe you cannot see. They are using drones to survey sensitive 
areas or drop packages. To catch them, you must look beyond the physical scene. You must learn 
to see the "Invisible Evidence". 
17.1.1 The Rise of Silent Witnesses 
We now work in an environment filled with "silent witnesses." These are the devices and 
services that watch, listen, and record our daily lives. 
1. Smart Homes: A suspect may deny being at home, but their Alexa or Google Nest speaker 
may have recorded their voice command at the exact time of the murder. 
2. Connected Vehicles: A hit-and-run driver may repair the bumper, but the car’s internal 
computer (ECU) has frozen the exact speed and braking data from the moment of impact. 
3. Wearables: A victim’s smartwatch monitors their heart rate, potentially telling us the exact 
minute a struggle occurred or when life ceased. 
4. AI Traces: A video of a politician or official inciting violence may look real, but it is a 
"Deepfake"—a manipulation created by software, not reality. 
This chapter exists because traditional evidence handling is no longer enough. You cannot pick 
up a digital signal with tweezers. You cannot put a cloud server in an evidence bag. These 
items—telemetry, logs, AI media—are fragile. If you handle them like a physical object, or if 
you power them down incorrectly, the evidence vanishes instantly. 
17.1.2 Why You Must Master This Now: The Legal Mandate 
This shift is not just technical; it is legal. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 
2023, has modernised our procedural powers for search and seizure, explicitly recognising 
[[PAGE 432]]
electronic records. Furthermore, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, defines new 
offences involving digital and AI-enabled conduct, such as impersonation using synthetic media. 
However, the most critical legal anchor for you is Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act. This 
section governs the admissibility of electronic records. Courts in India are strict: if digital 
evidence is not collected, preserved, and certified correctly, it is rejected. It does not matter if the 
evidence proves the crime; if the process is wrong, the evidence is worthless in court. 
Emerging evidence faces three specific enemies that traditional evidence does not: 
1. Volatility: Data in a smart device or running car exists in temporary memory (RAM). If you 
switch the device off, the evidence is deleted automatically. 
2. Third-Party Control: Evidence often sits with a company (like Google, Amazon, or a car 
manufacturer), not with the suspect. You need to know how to demand this data legally. 
3. Invisibility: You cannot see a Wi-Fi log or a GPS track with your naked eye. You must know 
where to look and how to "freeze" the scene digitally. 
 
 
 
17.1.3 Your Role as the First Responder 
[[PAGE 433]]
You do not need to be a computer scientist to handle this evidence. You are the IO. Your job is to 
secure, preserve, and escalate. This chapter effectively redesigns your approach to the crime 
scene. It moves you away from "Standard" forensics (like seizing mobile phones or checking call 
records, which you already know) and focuses entirely on the new threats: AI, Internet of Things 
(IoT), and Mobility systems. 
By following the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) in this chapter, you ensure that the 
advanced digital evidence you find is court-ready. You will learn to spot the blinking light of a 
router that holds the suspect's internet history. You will learn to freeze a smart car's data without 
erasing it. You will learn to question a video that looks "too perfect." 
Do not fear the technology. The criminal uses it to hide; you will use it to seek the truth. 
17.2 Learning Objectives 
By the end of this chapter, an Investigating Officer (IO) will be able to: 
1. Spot "Invisible" Evidence: Identify emerging digital sources at a crime scene, including 
Smart TVs, IoT sensors, drones, and vehicle telematics, which are often overlooked. 
2. Detect AI-Generated Media: Perform the "Naked Eye Test" to recognise signs of Deepfakes 
(synthetic audio/video) and take immediate steps to prevent the spread of fake content. 
3. Secure Volatile IoT & Vehicle Data: Apply the correct "Do Not Power Off" rules for smart 
devices and vehicles to prevent the loss of temporary memory and location logs. 
4. Execute Lawful Preservation: Issue immediate Preservation Notices to service providers 
(Cloud, App, or Drone companies) to freeze data before it is auto-deleted, ensuring compliance 
with the BNSS. 
5. Escalate Correctly: Distinguish between evidence an IO can seize and complex evidence 
(Encrypted ECUs, Deepfakes) that must be strictly escalated to the State Forensic Science 
Laboratory (FSL).

17.4 AI & Synthetic Media Forensics 
17.4.1 Introduction: When the Camera Lies 
In the past, a video or audio recording was considered the "ultimate truth" in an investigation. If 
you saw a suspect on video, they were there. If you heard a voice, it was them. That era is over. 
Criminals are now using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create Deepfakes—synthetic media that 
looks and sounds exactly like a real person but is entirely fake. This is not science fiction; it is a 
tool currently used for fraud, extortion, and defamation. 
As an Investigating Officer (IO), you will encounter two primary forms of AI crime: 
[[PAGE 436]]
1. Voice Cloning (Vishing): Criminals take a 3-second sample of a person's voice (from social 
media) and use AI to make that voice say anything. Example: "Fake Kidnapping" calls where 
parents hear their child screaming for help, or a "Senior Officer" ordering a junior to transfer 
funds immediately. 
2. Face Swapping/Deepfake Video: AI software superimposes a suspect's face onto another 
body or animates a photo to speak. Example: Video KYC fraud where a fraudster uses a fake 
live video to open a bank account, or "Sextortion" where a victim’s face is pasted onto a 
pornographic video to blackmail them. 
This section is the most critical part of this manual. If you handle AI evidence like a normal 
video file, you will destroy the hidden data (provenance) needed to prove it is a fake. 
 
 
 
17.4.2 The "Naked Eye" Test  
Before you seize the device, you must make a preliminary assessment. AI is powerful, but it is 
not perfect. It often leaves "glitches" that the human eye can spot if you know where to look. 
Use this checklist at the scene to identify suspected Deepfakes: 
[[PAGE 437]]
A. Visual Signs (Video) 
1. The Blinking Test: Does the person blink normally? Early Deepfakes often do not blink 
at all, or they blink in a strange, "fluttery" way. 
2. The Ear & Edge Check: Look at the edges of the face, the jawline, and the ears. Is the 
skin blurry? Does the hair look like it is "floating" or detached from the head? 
3. Lip-Sync Errors: Watch the mouth closely. Does the movement of the lips actually 
match the words being spoken? Sometimes the mouth moves like a robotic puppet. 
4. Lighting Mismatch: Does the lighting on the face match the lighting in the background? 
If the room is dark but the face is brightly lit, it may be a pasted overlay. 
B. Audio Signs (Voice) 
1. The Robot Breath: Humans take breaths when they speak. AI often forgets to add 
breathing sounds, resulting in long, unbroken sentences. 
2. Metallic Tone: Does the voice sound slightly "tinny" or metallic at the end of words? 
3. Emotion Mismatch: Does the tone of voice match the situation? (e.g., A "kidnapped 
child" speaking calmly, or an angry politician whose voice sounds flat). 
17.4.3 SOP for Seizure: The "Do Not Forward" Rule 
If you suspect a video or audio file is a Deepfake, your goal is to capture the Provenance (the 
digital history of the file). This history is hidden inside the file's metadata. 
Step 1: Secure the Device & Stop Deletion 
1. Take physical control of the device (phone/laptop) immediately. 
2. Stop the user from deleting the message or chat history. 
3. Isolate the device from the network (Airplane Mode) to prevent the sender from using 
"Delete for Everyone". 
Step 2: The Golden Rule — DO NOT FORWARD 
1. WARNING: The biggest mistake IOs make is asking the complainant to "WhatsApp the 
video to me." 
2. Why this destroys evidence: Social media apps (WhatsApp, Telegram, Facebook) use 
compression. They shrink the video size to send it quickly. This compression process 
strips away the metadata and the digital fingerprints needed by the Forensic Lab to 
prove the video is AI-generated. 
3. Correct Action: You must seize the Original File in its original container. 
Step 3: Hash and Seal the Original 
[[PAGE 438]]
1. Method A (If seizing the phone): Seize the mobile device itself. Seal it in a Faraday bag. 
Record the "Last Modified" time of the file in your seizure memo. 
2. Method B (If seizing the file only): Use a forensic imager or a write-blocker to copy the 
specific file to a clean USB drive. 
3. Hashing: Immediately generate a Hash Value (SHA-256) of the seized file. This is the 
"digital seal" that proves to the court that the file has not been altered since you seized it. 
Step 4: Issue Preservation Notices 
1. The video on the phone is just a copy. The original upload sits on the server (Facebook, 
Instagram, YouTube). 
2. Immediate Action: Send a Preservation Notice under the BNSS/IT Act to the platform. 
Request the Upload Logs, IP Address of the Uploader, and the Original 
Uncompressed File. 
17.4.4 Legal Section: BNS & IT Act Integration 
To prosecute AI crimes, you must link the technical evidence to specific offences. 
A. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023: 
1. ◦ Impersonation & Cheating: If AI is used to mimic a person to steal money or data 
(e.g., Voice Cloning fraud), apply sections relevant to cheating by personation. 
2. ◦ Forgery: If a Deepfake is created to be used as genuine evidence (e.g., a fake video of a 
crime), it falls under forgery of electronic records. 
3. ◦ Extortion: If the Deepfake is used to blackmail a victim (Sextortion), apply BNS 
extortion sections. 
B. Information Technology Act, 2000: 
1. ◦ Section 66D: Cheating by personation using computer resources. 
2. ◦ Section 66E: Violation of privacy (for deepfake pornography). 
C. Evidence Act (Section 65B): 
      1. A Deepfake is an electronic record. You must maintain a Chain of Custody log from the 
moment of seizure. If you cannot prove the file is the original, the defence will claim the police 
altered the video. The Hash Value is your protection. 
17.4.5 Case Vignette: "The Deepfake Extortion" 
The Scenario: Mr. Sharma, a prominent businessman inLucknow, rushes to the police station. 
He is panicking. He shows the IO, Sub-Inspector (SI) Verma, a video on WhatsApp. The video 
[[PAGE 439]]
appears to show Mr. Sharma accepting a bribe from a known criminal. The sender is demanding 
₹50 Lakhs or they will release the video to the news. Mr. Sharma swears, "Sir, I have never met 
this man. That is my face, but that is not my body." 
The Mistake Avoided: Mr. Sharma tries to forward the video to SI Verma’s personal number. SI 
Verma shouts, "Stop! Do not forward it." He explains that forwarding it via WhatsApp will 
compress the file and erase the AI traces. 
17.4.6 The IO Action: 
1. Naked Eye Test: SI Verma watches the video closely. He notices Mr. Sharma’s "face" in the 
video does not blink for 15 seconds. He also sees that the collar of the shirt looks blurry where it 
touches the neck. 
2. Seizure: SI Verma takes Mr. Sharma’s phone into custody. He photographs the chat screen 
showing the sender's number and the time received. 
3. Hashing: Using the station's cyber kit, he extracts the video file directly to a secure USB and 
generates a Hash Value (SHA-256). 
4. Escalation: He writes a memo: "Suspected Synthetic Media/Deepfake. Original file secured. 
Requesting Provenance Analysis." He sends the evidence to the State FSL AI Unit. 
The Outcome: The State FSL analyses the file. They find "artifacts" (digital leftovers) showing 
the face was swapped using a specific AI software. The Preservation Notice sent to the telecom 
provider links the sender's IP address to a known cyber-gang in a neighbouring district. The 
video is proven fake in court. 
17.5 Internet of Things (IoT) & Smart Devices 
17.5.1 The "Smart" Crime Scene: A Scenario 
Imagine a burglary occurs in a locked house in Noida. There are no broken windows, no 
fingerprints, and no human eyewitnesses. In the past, this might have been a dead-end case. But 
today, the house itself is the witness. The Smart Lightbulb in the hallway has a log showing 
exactly when it sensed motion and turned on. The Alexa in the living room may have recorded 
the sound of a voice command or a struggle. The Smart TV knows that someone opened 
YouTube at 2:00 AM. 
These devices are the "Silent Witnesses." They are watching, listening, and recording constantly. 
As an IO, you must learn to interview them. 
 
[[PAGE 440]]
 
17.5.2 Device Breakdown: Where Evidence Hides 
1. Smart Speakers (Alexa, Google Nest, Siri): These devices are not just speakers; they are 
cloud-connected microphones. They record voice commands and send them to servers owned by 
Amazon or Google. 
What they record:  
Voice recordings of commands (e.g., "Alexa, turn on lights"), timestamps of activity, and 
sometimes background audio if the "wake word" was triggered accidentally. 
How to Seize: 
    ◦ Stop! Do NOT Speak: The biggest mistake an IO can make is speaking near the device. If 
you say the wake word (e.g., "Alexa"), the device will start recording you and may overwrite the 
previous temporary logs. 
    ◦ Photograph: Take a picture of the device location and the serial number on the bottom. 
    ◦ Preservation Notice is Key: The evidence is not inside the plastic speaker; it is on the Cloud 
Server. You must immediately send a Preservation Notice to the service provider 
(Amazon/Google) under the BNSS/IT Act to freeze the account data. 
 
[[PAGE 441]]
2. Smart TVs & Set-Top Boxes: Criminals often claim, "I was not at the scene." A Smart TV 
can prove them wrong. 
The "Presence" Test:  
Smart TVs log user activity. If the suspect's personal Netflix or YouTube account was used on the 
TV at the time of the crime, it proves presence. 
SOP:  
Photograph the screen if it is on. Document any visible account names or email addresses logged 
in. Do not browse through the history yourself, as this alters the "Last Viewed" metadata. 
3. CCTV & Network Video Recorders (NVR): CCTV is common, but IOs often corrupt the 
evidence by seizing it incorrectly. 
The Timestamp Trap:  
Most CCTV systems have the wrong date and time settings. If the CCTV shows 2:00 PM but the 
real time is 2:15 PM, you must document this Time Offset in your seizure memo. If you don't, the 
defence will claim the video does not match the crime time. 
Extraction:  
Do NOT just rip out the Hard Disk Drive (HDD). This can corrupt the proprietary file system. 
Use the system’s "Export" function to save the video to a clean USB drive. If the system is 
password-protected, escalate to the State FSL immediately. 
4. Routers: The "Digital Entry Register": Think of the Wi-Fi Router as the guard at the gate. It 
keeps a list of every device that enters the house. 
What it records:  
The MAC Address (unique hardware ID) of every phone or laptop that connected to the Wi-Fi. It 
also logs DHCP requests (assigning IP addresses). 
Forensic Value:  
If a suspect claims they never visited the victim's house, but the router logs show their mobile 
phone’s MAC address connected to the Wi-Fi at 10:00 PM, their lie is caught. 
SOP:  
Photograph the back of the router (showing SSID/Model/MAC). Do NOT press the small 
"Reset" button; this wipes the logs instantly. 
17.5.3 The "Do Not Unplug" Rule 
[[PAGE 442]]
When you find a digital device, your instinct may be to pull the plug to stop it from working. 
Stop. You must decide based on the device type. 
A. WHEN TO LEAVE POWER ON (The "Volatile" Rule) 
1. Devices: Laptops, Mobile Phones, Running Servers. 
2. Reason: These devices hold evidence in RAM (Random Access Memory). RAM is 
volatile—it only exists while electricity is flowing. If you pull the plug, the RAM is deleted 
instantly. You lose open chats, encryption keys, and active network connections. 
3. Action: If the device is running, keep it running. Isolate it from the network (Faraday bag or 
Airplane mode) and call the Cyber Unit/FSL for "Live Acquisition". 
B. WHEN TO UNPLUG 
• Devices: Simple IoT sensors (Smart bulbs), or if instructed by FSL for a specific Desktop PC 
situation to prevent remote wiping. 
• Warning: Even then, simply pulling the plug is risky. Always consult the "Escalation Matrix" 
(Section 17.15) before killing power. 
WARNING: DATA DESTRUCTION RISK Never press the "Factory Reset" button on any 
device. Never allow a suspect to touch the device "to help you unlock it."  
17.6 Vehicles  
17.6.1 Vehicle Telematics (The Computer on Wheels) 
Concept: The Digital Crime Scene You must stop thinking of a vehicle merely as a means of 
transport. In modern investigations, a car is a "Computer on Wheels." Criminals use vehicles to 
transport contraband, escape crime scenes, or stalk victims. While they drive, the car is 
constantly recording. Modern vehicles contain dozens of computers that talk to each other, 
recording where the suspect went, how fast they drove, and even when they opened the door. 
This data is often more accurate than a witness statement. 
17.6.2 Evidence Sources: Where the Data Hides 
A. Infotainment System (The Dashboard Screen): Think of this as a mobile phone built into 
the dashboard. Just like a smartphone, it stores massive amounts of personal data. 
1. What it holds: Call logs, contact lists, and SMS messages synced from the driver's phone. 
Most importantly, it holds GPS history and "Recent Destinations," even if the suspect claims 
they were never at the crime scene. 
[[PAGE 443]]
2. The Trap: If a suspect connects their phone via Bluetooth or USB to play music, the car often 
downloads their contact list automatically. Even if you seize the phone, the car still holds the 
B. ECU & EDR (The "Black Box"): The Electronic Control Unit (ECU) is the brain of the car. 
The Event Data Recorder (EDR) is its memory during a crash. 
1. What it holds: If a vehicle is involved in a hit-and-run or accident, the EDR freezes the data 
for the 5 seconds before the impact. It records the exact speed, throttle position (was the driver 
accelerating?), and braking status (did they try to stop?),. 
2. Legal Value: This is hard, technical evidence. Courts accept EDR data to prove speeding or 
intent (e.g., no braking) in grievous hurt cases. 
 
 
 
17.6.3 WARNING: THE GOLDEN RULE OF VEHICLE FORENSICS 
1. DO NOT Start the Engine.  
Why: Turning the ignition ON creates new data logs. This can overwrite the old GPS location 
data you are trying to find. 
2. DO NOT Disconnect the Battery.  
[[PAGE 444]]
Why: Much like a computer, the car’s system uses volatile memory (RAM). If you cut the 
power, this memory is wiped instantly. You may lose the navigation history and recent sensor 
logs. 
ACTION: Tow the vehicle to a secure facility. Call the State FSL Automotive Unit immediately 
for controlled extraction. 
17.7 Drone Forensics (UAVs) 
17.7.1 The Scenario:  
 A drone is found crashed inside the perimeter of a high-security prison, carrying a package of 
narcotics or a drone is spotted hovering over a sensitive border area before landing in a field. The 
pilot is gone, but the digital evidence remains. To catch the pilot, you must look at the "Triangle 
of Evidence." 
17.7.2 The Triangle of Evidence:  
Digital evidence in drone cases is rarely found in just one place. It is split across three 
components: 
 
 
 
[[PAGE 445]]
1. The Drone (Bird): The aircraft itself holds the Flight Logs. These logs prove exactly where 
the drone flew (GPS path) and where it took off (Launch Point). It usually contains an SD card 
with photos or video of the flight path. 
2. The Controller (Remote): The handheld remote is often overlooked, but it is critical. It holds 
the Pairing Data. If you find a suspect with a controller in their backpack, forensic analysis can 
prove that specific controller is paired to the crashed drone. 
3. The Mobile Device (Phone/Tablet): Most pilots use a mobile app (like DJI Fly) to see the 
camera feed. This phone holds the most detailed user data, including the pilot’s account login, 
cloud sync history, and cached images from the flight. 
 
17.7.3 Detailed SOP for Officers 
Step 1:  
Safety First — The Battery Threat: Drones use Lithium-Polymer (LiPo) batteries. These are 
chemically unstable. If the drone has crashed and the battery is swollen, punctured, or smoking, 
it is a fire hazard. 
Action: Do not remove a damaged battery yourself. Isolate the drone in a fire-safe area or sand 
bucket. Call FSL or Bomb Disposal if the payload is suspicious,. 
Step 2:  
Isolation — Stop the Remote Wipe: A suspect can remotely command a drone to "Return to 
Home" or wipe its data if it is still connected to the network. 
Action: Immediately place the drone and the mobile device into Faraday Bags (signal-blocking 
bags). If a Faraday bag is not available, move the device to an area with no signal (like a 
basement) until FSL arrives. 
Step 3:  
The "Do Not Pair" Rule: Your instinct might be to turn on the controller to see if it connects to 
the captured drone. Do not do this. 
Why: Turning on the equipment creates new "handshake" logs between the controller and the 
drone. This changes the digital timestamps and ruins the timeline evidence. 
Action: Seize the drone and controller separately. Label them clearly. Let the FSL perform the 
pairing test in a controlled lab environment. 
Step 4:  
[[PAGE 446]]
Seize the Storage (SD Cards): Most drones have a Micro-SD card slot (often hidden near the 
battery or camera gimbal). 
Action: If safe to do so, remove the SD card, photograph it, and seal it in an anti-static bag. This 
card often contains video footage of the pilot launching the drone, which is direct evidence of 
identity. 
Step 5:  
Cloud Preservation: Pilots often sync their flight logs to the cloud (e.g., DJI Cloud). 
Action: If you identify the pilot’s account or email from the mobile device app, issue an 
immediate Preservation Notice to the drone manufacturer or cloud provider under the BNSS/IT 
Act.

to identify the evidence type and route it to the correct expert immediately. Use this table to 
decide your next move.
