17.9 Master Field Checklist 
17.9.1 Dos and Don'ts  
THE GREEN LIST: ALWAYS DO THIS 
• [ ] Secure the Scene: Stop anyone from touching digital devices. Record the names of all 
persons present in the Mahazar. 
• [ ] Photograph Everything: Use the "Wide → Mid → Close" rule. Photograph screens, cables, 
and serial numbers before moving anything. 
• [ ] Isolate Signals: Place mobile devices, drones, and smart keys in Faraday Bags. If 
unavailable, switch to "Airplane Mode" immediately. 
• [ ] Issue Preservation Notices: Send an official email/letter to the service provider (Google, 
Jio, Facebook) within the first hour to stop data deletion. 
• [ ] Hash the Evidence: If you copy a file (e.g., a video), generate its Hash Value (SHA-256) 
immediately to seal its integrity. 
• [ ] Maintain Chain of Custody: Every transfer of evidence must be written down. Who took 
it? When? Why? Gaps here will destroy your case in court. 
THE RED LIST: NEVER DO THIS 
• [X] NEVER Forward Evidence on WhatsApp: This compresses the file and destroys the 
AI/metadata proofs. 
• [X] NEVER Unlock a Suspect’s Device: Do not use FaceID or ask the suspect to unlock it. 
This alters the timestamps and system logs. 
• [X] NEVER Start a Seized Vehicle: Turning the ignition ON overwrites the GPS location 
history you need. 
• [X] NEVER Pair a Drone Controller: Do not check "if it works." This changes the digital 
pairing logs. 
[[PAGE 448]]
• [X] NEVER Use "Factory Reset": This wipes the evidence forever. 
• [X] NEVER Unplug a Router/Server Instantly: Check if it has volatile memory (RAM). If in 
doubt, call the FSL before pulling the plug. 
17.10 Conclusion 
Process is More Important Than Technology. 
The landscape of crime in Uttar Pradesh has changed. As we have seen in this chapter, the threats 
are now digital, automated, and often invisible. The Deepfake video, the silent Drone, and the 
spying Smart Home are not future problems—they are today's cases. 
However, you do not need to be a computer scientist to be a successful Investigating Officer. You 
simply need to be a disciplined one. 
The court does not expect you to decode the algorithm of a Deepfake. The court expects you to 
seize the original file, preserve the chain of custody, and escalate it to the expert without 
corrupting it. Most digital evidence fails in court not because the technology was too hard, but 
because the IO made a procedural error—like forwarding a video on WhatsApp or starting a 
seized car. 
Your role is to be the guardian of the evidence. By following the "Preserve and Escalate" 
protocols in this chapter, you ensure that the truth—no matter how high-tech—survives the 
journey from the crime scene to the courtroom. 
Adapt to these tools. Master the process. Let the experts handle the code, while you deliver the 
justice. 
17.11 Relevant Acts & Legal Provisions 
1. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023: For search, seizure, and chain of 
custody procedures. 
2. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023: For offences regarding impersonation, forgery, and 
digital fraud. 
3. Information Technology Act, 2000 (and Amendments): For definitions of electronic records 
and intermediaries. 
4. Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023: For handling personal data privacy 
during investigations. 
5. Indian Evidence Act (Section 65B): For the admissibility of electronic records. 
[[PAGE 449]]
CHAPTER 18 – ANTI-FORENSIC TECHNIQUES & 
DETECTION 
PART A: Foundations & Conceptual Framework of Anti-Forensics 
 
18.1 Introduction: The Changing Nature of Digital Evidence 
Digital evidence today rarely exists in a pristine or untouched state. In contemporary cybercrime 
investigations, investigators increasingly encounter environments where traces have been 
deliberately altered, concealed, or destroyed prior to seizure. Unlike traditional crimes where 
evidence destruction is often physical and observable, digital evidence destruction can be silent, 
automated, and technically sophisticated, leaving behind little that appears suspicious at first 
glance. This reality has forced modern cybercrime investigations to move beyond mere data 
recovery and into the domain of detecting intentional manipulation of the forensic process itself, 
commonly referred to as anti-forensics [1]. 
Anti-forensic techniques represent a strategic shift by offenders from committing crimes to 
actively obstructing investigations. The objective is not merely to delete incriminating files, but 
to undermine the reliability, completeness, and interpretive value of digital evidence so that 
investigators cannot confidently reconstruct events. For law enforcement agencies such as the UP 
Police Cyber Crime Unit, understanding anti-forensics is therefore not optional, it is foundational 
to effective digital investigations in the present era [2]. 
 
18.2 Defining Anti-Forensics: Concept, Scope, and Intent 
Anti-forensics may be defined as any deliberate action or technique designed to compromise the 
availability, integrity, authenticity, or interpretability of digital evidence during a forensic 
investigation. These techniques aim to either prevent evidence from being created in the first 
place, alter it after creation, or overwhelm investigators with misleading artifacts. Importantly, 
anti-forensics operates at multiple layers—file systems, operating systems, applications, logs, 
memory, and even forensic tools themselves [3]. 
The defining feature of anti-forensic activity is intent. Accidental data loss, system crashes, or 
routine system maintenance do not constitute anti-forensics. Anti-forensic conduct involves 
conscious actions taken with the knowledge that an investigation may occur, and with the 
objective of frustrating that investigation. This intent-driven nature makes anti-forensics 
particularly relevant in criminal adjudication, as it may indicate mens rea relating not only to the 
primary offence but also to obstruction of justice [4]. 
 
[[PAGE 450]]
18.3 Anti-Forensics vs Legitimate Privacy Practices 
A critical conceptual distinction must be drawn between anti-forensics and legitimate privacy-
protective practices. Encryption, secure deletion, and anonymization tools are widely used by 
individuals and organizations for lawful purposes such as data protection, regulatory compliance, 
and personal privacy. The mere presence of such tools does not automatically imply criminal 
intent or anti-forensic behavior [5]. 
However, when these techniques are deployed selectively, temporally close to an incident, or in a 
manner inconsistent with normal user behavior, they may cross the boundary from privacy 
protection into forensic evasion. For example, routine disk encryption applied at the time of 
system installation differs significantly from sudden encryption of specific directories 
immediately after suspicious activity. Investigators must therefore assess context, timing, and 
scope before categorizing an action as anti-forensic [6]. 
 
18.4 Evolution of Anti-Forensic Techniques 
Historically, early anti-forensic techniques were rudimentary, involving simple file deletion or 
basic overwriting utilities. As forensic tools evolved to recover deleted data and reconstruct 
timelines, anti-forensic methods also matured, incorporating secure wiping algorithms, 
timestamp manipulation, log tampering, and memory-resident operations that leave minimal 
traces on disk. This evolution mirrors the broader arms race between forensic science and 
cybercriminal methodology [7]. 
In recent years, anti-forensics has further expanded into areas such as encryption abuse, 
steganography, and exploitation of limitations or assumptions within forensic tools themselves. 
Sophisticated actors now design their operational workflows with forensic resistance in mind 
from the outset, ensuring that evidence generation is minimized rather than cleaned up after the 
fact. This pre-emptive approach represents a significant challenge for post-incident investigations 
 
18.5 Objectives and Goals of Anti-Forensic Activity 
Anti-forensic techniques are typically deployed to achieve one or more identifiable objectives. 
The primary goal is to prevent detection of malicious activity by removing or hiding 
incriminating artifacts. Secondary goals may include increasing the time and cost of 
investigation, creating ambiguity in forensic conclusions, or introducing doubt regarding the 
reliability of recovered evidence [9]. 
Another critical objective is evidentiary pollution—deliberately generating false or misleading 
data so that investigators are forced to sift through irrelevant artifacts. This tactic exploits the 
[[PAGE 451]]
finite time and resources available to law enforcement agencies. In extreme cases, anti-forensic 
techniques may be used to falsely implicate innocent users or systems, thereby diverting 
investigative focus and weakening prosecutorial narratives [10]. 
 
18.6 Classification of Anti-Forensic Techniques 
For analytical clarity, anti-forensic techniques can be broadly classified into several overlapping 
categories. These include data destruction techniques (such as secure wiping), data hiding 
techniques (such as steganography and hidden partitions), artifact manipulation (including log 
and timestamp tampering), encryption-based obstruction, and forensic tool interference. Each 
category targets a different phase of the forensic process, from acquisition to analysis and 
reporting [11]. 
This classification is not rigid, as many techniques operate across multiple layers simultaneously. 
For instance, encryption abuse may also involve data hiding, while timestamp manipulation often 
coincides with log tampering. Investigators must therefore approach anti-forensics as a systemic 
strategy rather than a collection of isolated tactics [12]. 
 
18.7 Anti-Forensics as Deliberate Evidence Destruction 
From a legal and investigative standpoint, anti-forensics should be understood as a form of 
deliberate evidence destruction or suppression. Unlike physical evidence destruction, digital anti-
forensics often leaves behind secondary indicators rather than direct proof of deletion. These 
indicators include inconsistencies in timelines, gaps in logs, anomalous metadata patterns, and 
unexplained absence of expected artifacts [13]. 
Recognizing anti-forensics as evidence destruction has significant implications for criminal 
investigations. It allows investigators to frame the absence or manipulation of evidence itself as 
probative, provided it can be demonstrated through expert analysis. This approach aligns with 
judicial recognition that digital evidence tampering can be inferred from circumstantial technical 
indicators rather than direct observation [14]. 
 
18.8 Relevance to Cybercrime Investigations in India 
In the Indian cybercrime landscape, anti-forensic techniques are increasingly observed in cases 
involving financial fraud, data theft, cyber espionage, and organized cybercrime. The widespread 
availability of wiping tools, encryption software, and system-level utilities has lowered the 
technical barrier for offenders to engage in evidence destruction. Consequently, investigators can 
no longer assume that absence of data implies absence of activity [15]. 
[[PAGE 452]]
For UP Police Cyber Crime units, this reality necessitates a shift in investigative mindset—from 
searching solely for incriminating files to analyzing why expected evidence is missing. Anti-
forensic awareness enables investigators to identify deliberate suppression attempts and to 
document them systematically for judicial scrutiny [16]. 
 
18.9 Investigative Red Flags Indicating Anti-Forensic Activity 
Certain indicators may suggest the presence of anti-forensic techniques during an investigation. 
These include sudden use of secure deletion tools, unexplained clearing of system or application 
logs, inconsistent timestamp values across metadata structures, selective encryption of specific 
files, and abnormal disk or memory states inconsistent with normal user behavior [17]. 
While no single indicator conclusively proves anti-forensic intent, the convergence of multiple 
red flags strengthens investigative inference. Proper documentation of these indicators is 
essential, as they form the basis for expert testimony and forensic explanation before courts. 
Failure to recognize these signs at an early stage may result in loss of investigative opportunities 
or misinterpretation of evidence [18]. 
 
18.10 Purpose of This Chapter within the SOP Framework 
This chapter is designed to equip investigators with a conceptual and practical understanding of 
anti-forensic techniques and their detection. It does not aim to turn investigators into tool 
developers, but rather to enhance their ability to recognize deliberate evidence manipulation, 
apply appropriate counter-techniques, and articulate their findings clearly within legal 
proceedings [19]. 
By grounding anti-forensics within both technical and legal frameworks, this chapter supports 
the broader objective of ensuring that cybercrime investigations remain resilient, credible, and 
defensible in court, even when faced with sophisticated attempts to undermine the forensic 
process [20]. 
 
PART B: Evidence Destruction Techniques – Secure Wiping, Log Manipulation & 
Timestamping 
 
18.11 Evidence Destruction as an Anti-Forensic Strategy 
Evidence destruction is the most direct and commonly observed form of anti-forensic activity. 
Unlike passive evasion methods, evidence destruction reflects an active attempt to remove, 
corrupt, or render unusable digital artifacts that could otherwise support investigative 
[[PAGE 453]]
reconstruction. In cybercrime cases, such destruction is rarely random; it is selective, timed, and 
often targeted at high-value artifacts such as logs, metadata, communication records, and 
temporary files [21]. 
For investigators, evidence destruction does not merely signify absence of proof; it often 
becomes proof of intent. Modern forensic methodology therefore treats evidence destruction as a 
behavioral indicator, requiring analysis of what was destroyed, when it was destroyed, and how 
systematically it was executed. These questions form the backbone of anti-forensic detection in 
professional cyber investigations [22]. 
 
18.12 Secure Wiping Tools: Concept and Operational Logic 
Secure wiping tools are designed to permanently erase data by overwriting storage locations with 
predefined or randomized patterns, thereby preventing recovery through conventional forensic 
methods. Unlike standard deletion, which merely removes file system references, secure wiping 
targets both file content and, in many cases, associated metadata. These tools may operate at the 
file level, directory level, or entire disk level depending on configuration and intent [23]. 
From an investigative perspective, the presence of secure wiping is significant because such tools 
are rarely used by ordinary users during routine operations. Their execution often coincides with 
incident timelines, system compromise indicators, or suspicious user behavior. The deliberate 
invocation of secure wiping utilities shortly before device seizure or immediately after illicit 
activity is a strong indicator of anti-forensic intent [24]. 
 
[[PAGE 454]]
 
[[PAGE 455]]
 
[[PAGE 456]]
4 
 
18.13 Types of Secure Wiping Techniques 
Secure wiping techniques vary in sophistication and forensic impact. File-level wiping targets 
specific files or directories, overwriting their allocated clusters while leaving surrounding disk 
structures intact. Disk-level wiping, by contrast, overwrites entire partitions or storage devices, 
often eliminating both user data and system artifacts. Some wiping tools additionally target slack 
space, unallocated space, and file system journals to remove residual traces [25]. 
Advanced wiping techniques may also interfere with solid-state drive (SSD) behavior by 
triggering internal garbage collection or TRIM commands, which complicate post-seizure 
recovery. The forensic challenge here lies not in detecting that data is gone, but in determining 
whether its absence is consistent with normal system operation or deliberate destruction [26]. 
 
18.14 Detection Indicators of Secure Wiping 
Despite their destructive intent, secure wiping tools often leave behind indirect indicators. These 
may include anomalous patterns of zeroed or randomized sectors, sudden loss of historical 
artifacts without corresponding system activity, remnants of wiping tool binaries, execution 
traces in prefetch files, registry entries, or memory artifacts. Investigators must therefore 
examine the system holistically rather than focusing solely on missing data [27]. 
Another key indicator is asymmetry—where certain categories of data are entirely absent while 
others remain intact. For example, the selective removal of browser history, messaging 
databases, or financial records while leaving unrelated files untouched may indicate targeted 
wiping rather than routine cleanup. Such asymmetry is rarely accidental and should raise 
immediate investigative concern [28]. 
 
18.15 Log Manipulation: Purpose and Forensic Impact 
System and application logs serve as chronological records of system behavior and user activity. 
Anti-forensic manipulation of logs aims to erase, alter, or fabricate these records to disrupt 
timeline reconstruction. Log manipulation may involve deletion of entire log files, truncation of 
specific entries, or modification of timestamps and event identifiers. In some cases, attackers 
disable logging altogether to prevent future evidence generation [29]. 
The forensic significance of log manipulation lies in its potential to undermine investigative 
confidence. When logs are missing or inconsistent, investigators may struggle to correlate events 
across systems, weakening attribution and causality. As such, log manipulation is frequently 
[[PAGE 457]]
employed in conjunction with other anti-forensic techniques to maximize investigative disruption 
[30]. 
 
 
[[PAGE 458]]
 
4 
 
18.16 Common Log Manipulation Techniques 
Log manipulation can be broadly categorized into deletion, alteration, and suppression. Deletion 
involves removing entire log files or clearing event logs using built-in system utilities or third-
party tools. Alteration involves modifying specific log entries to falsify activity records, often by 
changing timestamps, usernames, or event descriptions. Suppression refers to disabling logging 
services or reducing log verbosity to prevent future records [31]. 
In sophisticated cases, attackers may selectively delete logs relating only to specific time 
windows or activities, preserving earlier and later records to avoid suspicion. This selective 
manipulation requires knowledge of system logging mechanisms and reflects a higher degree of 
forensic awareness on the part of the offender [32]. 
 
18.17 Detection of Log Manipulation 
Detecting log manipulation requires cross-validation across multiple data sources. Investigators 
should compare system logs with application logs, network records, backup logs, and external 
monitoring data. Inconsistencies between these sources often reveal manipulation attempts. For 
example, evidence of network connections without corresponding log entries may indicate 
deliberate log deletion [33]. 
Additionally, metadata analysis of log files themselves may reveal anomalies such as unexpected 
file sizes, modification times, or access patterns. The absence of routine log rotation artifacts or 
[[PAGE 459]]
sudden resets of log sequences can further support inferences of anti-forensic activity. Such 
findings must be carefully documented to support later legal explanation [34]. 
 
18.18 Timestamp Manipulation (Timestomping): Conceptual Overview 
Timestamp manipulation, commonly referred to as timestomping, involves altering file or system 
timestamps to obscure the true chronology of events. Digital forensic investigations rely heavily 
on temporal analysis, making timestamps a prime target for anti-forensic interference. By 
modifying timestamps, offenders attempt to shift incriminating activity outside investigative 
timeframes or blend malicious files into benign historical contexts [35]. 
Timestomping typically targets file creation, modification, access, and metadata change times. In 
modern file systems, multiple timestamp structures exist, and manipulating one without affecting 
others may create detectable inconsistencies. Nevertheless, basic timestomping remains effective 
against superficial forensic review [36]. 
 
[[PAGE 460]]
 
 
4 
 
18.19 Techniques Used in Timestamp Manipulation 
Timestamp manipulation may be performed using specialized tools, system utilities, or direct 
API calls. Some tools allow bulk modification of timestamps to arbitrary historical values, while 
others synchronize malicious files with legitimate system files to camouflage them. In certain 
cases, attackers exploit backup restoration or file copying behaviors to inherit misleading 
timestamps [37]. 
[[PAGE 461]]
More advanced techniques involve manipulating specific timestamp attributes while leaving 
others untouched. This selective manipulation may evade cursory checks but often introduces 
subtle discrepancies detectable through deeper metadata analysis. Understanding these 
techniques is critical for accurate forensic interpretation [38]. 
 
18.20 Detection of Timestomping and Temporal Inconsistencies 
Effective detection of timestomping requires comparison across independent timestamp sources. 
Investigators should correlate file system timestamps with log entries, registry records, backup 
metadata, and external event data. Discrepancies such as impossible temporal sequences, 
identical timestamps across unrelated files, or timestamps inconsistent with system installation 
dates may indicate manipulation [39]. 
Particularly valuable is the comparison of multiple timestamp attributes within file system 
metadata structures. Where one timestamp reflects recent activity while another suggests 
historical origin, the inconsistency itself becomes evidence of tampering. Such findings must be 
explained clearly in investigative reports to avoid misinterpretation [40]. 
 
18.21 SOP-Oriented Flow: Detecting Evidence Destruction 
Conceptual Detection Flow (Textual SOP Representation): 
Initial Seizure & Imaging 
        ↓ 
Baseline Artifact Assessment 
        ↓ 
Identify Missing / Inconsistent Evidence 
        ↓ 
Check for Wiping / Log / Timestamp Indicators 
        ↓ 
Cross-Source Correlation 
        ↓ 
Inference of Deliberate Evidence Destruction 
        ↓ 
[[PAGE 462]]
Documentation for Legal Proceedings 
This structured approach ensures that evidence destruction is identified systematically rather than 
assumed prematurely. It also supports defensible conclusions during judicial review by 
demonstrating methodological rigor [41]. 
 
18.22 Legal and Investigative Implications 
From a legal standpoint, secure wiping, log manipulation, and timestomping collectively point 
toward intentional obstruction of investigation. While the absence of data alone may not 
establish guilt, forensic demonstration of deliberate destruction can significantly strengthen 
prosecutorial narratives. Courts increasingly recognize expert testimony on such techniques 
when supported by technical reasoning and documented inconsistencies [42]. 
For investigators, the challenge lies in articulating how destruction occurred and why it cannot be 
attributed to routine system behavior. Clear explanation, supported by reproducible forensic 
observations, is therefore essential to ensure that anti-forensic findings withstand legal scrutiny 
[43]. 
 
PART C: Encryption Abuse & Data Hiding Techniques 
 
18.23 Encryption as an Anti-Forensic Tool: Beyond Legitimate Security 
Encryption is one of the most powerful and controversial tools encountered in modern digital 
investigations. While encryption is widely accepted as a legitimate means of protecting 
confidentiality and privacy, its misuse for obstructing forensic analysis constitutes a significant 
anti-forensic challenge. Encryption abuse occurs when cryptographic mechanisms are 
deliberately deployed to deny investigators access to evidence, particularly when applied 
selectively or post-incident [44]. 
From an investigative standpoint, encryption becomes anti-forensic not because it exists, but 
because of how, when, and where it is applied. Full-disk encryption enabled during system setup 
differs fundamentally from selective encryption of folders immediately after suspicious activity. 
This contextual distinction is critical when evaluating whether encryption represents lawful data 
protection or deliberate evidence concealment [45]. 
 
18.24 Forms of Encryption Abuse in Cybercrime Investigations 
[[PAGE 463]]
Encryption abuse manifests in multiple operational forms. Full-disk encryption may be activated 
to block access to an entire device, particularly when suspects anticipate seizure. Container-
based encryption allows offenders to hide incriminating data within encrypted volumes disguised 
as ordinary files. In some cases, cloud-synced encrypted repositories are used so that local 
devices contain no readable evidence at all [46]. 
A particularly problematic form is the use of plausible deniability features, where encrypted 
containers are designed to appear empty or benign unless accessed with a secondary secret. This 
technique directly challenges the evidentiary principle of completeness, as investigators may be 
unable to prove the existence of concealed data even when encryption use is evident [47]. 
 
[[PAGE 464]]
 
 
4 
 
[[PAGE 465]]
18.25 Investigative Indicators of Encryption Abuse 
Despite its strength, encryption misuse often leaves indirect indicators. These may include the 
sudden appearance of encrypted volumes, unexplained loss of previously accessible files, 
encrypted containers with recent timestamps, or discrepancies between reported disk usage and 
visible data. Investigators may also encounter encrypted archives with misleading filenames 
intended to blend into benign file structures [48]. 
Another indicator is behavioral inconsistency—systems showing evidence of intensive usage but 
lacking corresponding artifacts such as documents, logs, or caches. Such asymmetry may suggest 
that data exists but is intentionally rendered inaccessible through encryption. These indicators, 
while circumstantial, gain probative value when corroborated with other anti-forensic findings 
[49]. 
 
18.26 Legal Treatment of Encryption in Investigations 
Encryption poses unique legal challenges, particularly when suspects refuse to disclose keys or 
credentials. In such situations, investigators must rely on circumstantial forensic evidence to 
demonstrate intentional obstruction. Courts may assess whether encryption was used routinely or 
deployed in response to investigative risk, and whether its use aligns with legitimate security 
practices [50]. 
From a reporting perspective, it is essential that investigators document not merely the presence 
of encryption, but its forensic context—timing, scope, selectivity, and interaction with other anti-
forensic techniques. This contextual analysis enables courts to draw informed inferences 
regarding intent without relying on speculative assumptions [51]. 
 
18.27 Data Hiding Techniques: Conceptual Overview 
Data hiding refers to techniques that conceal information within other data or storage structures 
so that it remains undiscovered during routine forensic analysis. Unlike encryption, which 
renders data unreadable, data hiding aims to render data invisible. These techniques exploit 
assumptions in forensic tools and investigator workflows, often allowing hidden data to persist 
undetected for extended periods [52]. 
Data hiding is particularly effective because it does not necessarily alter visible file system 
structures. As a result, investigators may falsely conclude that no evidence exists, when in reality 
it is merely concealed. This makes data hiding a favored technique among sophisticated 
offenders seeking long-term forensic evasion [53]. 
 
[[PAGE 466]]
18.28 Steganography and Embedded Data Concealment 
Steganography involves embedding data within seemingly innocuous files such as images, audio, 
or video. Unlike encryption, steganography does not draw immediate attention because the 
carrier file appears normal and functional. The hidden data may be accessed only through 
specialized tools or keys, further complicating detection [54]. 
Forensic detection of steganography is challenging, as it often requires statistical or behavioral 
analysis rather than direct observation. Unusually large file sizes, anomalous entropy values, or 
repeated access to benign-looking media files may provide indirect clues. However, absence of 
detection does not imply absence of concealed data, necessitating cautious investigative 
conclusions [55]. 
 
 
[[PAGE 467]]
 
4 
 
18.29 File System–Level Data Hiding Techniques 
Beyond steganography, data may be hidden directly within file system structures. Common 
methods include Alternate Data Streams (ADS) in NTFS, hidden partitions, unallocated space 
storage, and slack space usage. These techniques exploit areas of storage not typically examined 
during superficial forensic review [56]. 
Such methods often leave minimal visible traces, as standard directory listings do not reveal their 
presence. Investigators must therefore deliberately examine file system metadata and storage 
anomalies. Failure to do so may result in incomplete evidence acquisition and erroneous 
investigative conclusions [57]. 
 
18.30 Detection Indicators of Data Hiding 
[[PAGE 468]]
Detection of data hiding relies heavily on anomaly analysis. Indicators may include unexplained 
disk usage, mismatches between logical and physical storage reports, abnormal file entropy, or 
inconsistencies between file system metadata and observed content. These indicators are rarely 
conclusive on their own but become compelling when viewed collectively [58]. 
Investigators should also consider user behavior patterns. Repeated access to non-obvious 
storage areas, unexplained system slowdowns, or evidence of specialized tool usage may signal 
hidden data. Thorough documentation of such observations is essential for later forensic 
explanation [59]. 
 
18.31 Memory-Based and Live-System Anti-Forensics 
Memory-based anti-forensics represents an advanced class of techniques where malicious 
activity is conducted primarily in volatile memory, leaving little or no disk-based evidence. Such 
techniques may involve memory-resident encryption, transient data storage, or execution of tools 
that self-delete upon termination. This approach exploits the fact that volatile memory is lost 
upon system shutdown [60]. 
Live-system anti-forensics complicates post-mortem analysis, as traditional disk imaging may 
reveal minimal artifacts. Investigators must therefore emphasize timely live acquisition and 
memory analysis to counteract such techniques. Failure to capture volatile data may result in 
irreversible evidence loss [61]. 
 
[[PAGE 469]]
 
 
4 
 
18.32 SOP Flow: Detecting Encryption Abuse and Data Hiding 
Conceptual Detection Flow (SOP-Oriented): 
Device Seizure & Imaging 
        ↓ 
Assess Encryption Presence 
        ↓ 
Evaluate Timing & Selectivity 
[[PAGE 470]]
        ↓ 
Analyze Disk Usage Anomalies 
        ↓ 
Inspect File System & Memory 
        ↓ 
Correlate with Logs & Timelines 
        ↓ 
Inference of Concealment Intent 
This flow emphasizes structured analysis rather than assumption. Each step generates observable 
indicators that collectively support or refute anti-forensic inference, ensuring methodological 
defensibility [62]. 
 
18.33 Investigative and Evidentiary Implications 
Encryption abuse and data hiding significantly increase investigative complexity, but they also 
introduce behavioral evidence of intent. When properly documented, such techniques can 
demonstrate conscious efforts to obstruct investigation, even in the absence of readable content. 
Courts increasingly rely on expert explanations of these methods to contextualize missing or 
inaccessible evidence [63]. 
For investigators, the key challenge lies in balancing technical analysis with clear 
communication. Anti-forensic findings must be explained in plain yet precise language, linking 
technical anomalies to investigative reasoning. This ensures that encryption and data hiding are 
understood not as neutral technical features, but as deliberate actions within a broader criminal 
context [64]. 
 
PART D: Recovery Techniques, Courtroom Explanation & SOP Conclusions 
 
18.34 Recovery in the Presence of Anti-Forensic Activity 
Recovery in anti-forensic scenarios does not always mean restoring deleted or encrypted data. In 
many investigations, recovery refers to reconstructing events, intent, and behavior through 
indirect technical indicators. When primary evidence has been destroyed or concealed, 
investigators must rely on secondary and tertiary artifacts to establish continuity and causation. 
[[PAGE 471]]
This shift from content recovery to behavioral reconstruction represents a fundamental evolution 
in digital forensic methodology [65]. 
Anti-forensic techniques are designed to remove evidence, but they rarely eliminate all traces. 
System behavior, storage inconsistencies, memory remnants, and external correlations often 
survive and become the focus of recovery efforts. Investigators must therefore approach recovery 
holistically, recognizing that absence of data may itself be evidentiary when contextualized 
properly [66]. 
 
18.35 Recovery after Secure Wiping and Data Destruction 
In cases involving secure wiping, traditional file recovery is usually ineffective. However, 
recovery may still be possible at the metadata, structural, or statistical level. Investigators can 
analyze disk layout patterns, overwritten sector distributions, and anomalies in unallocated space 
to infer wiping activity. These observations may reveal the method and timing of destruction 
even when content is irretrievable [67]. 
Additionally, recovery may involve correlating system-level evidence such as tool execution 
traces, registry artifacts, prefetch remnants, or memory residues that indicate the use of wiping 
utilities. Such artifacts help establish deliberate intent and refute claims of accidental data loss. 
Proper interpretation of these indicators is essential for credible forensic reporting [68]. 
[[PAGE 472]]
 
[[PAGE 473]]
 
 
4 
 
18.36 Recovery in Log Manipulation Scenarios 
When logs have been deleted or altered, recovery focuses on reconstructing timelines using 
alternative sources. These may include application caches, shadow copies, backup logs, network 
records, or external monitoring systems. Cross-correlation across independent sources often 
reveals discrepancies that expose log tampering [69]. 
Investigators should also analyze log file metadata for anomalies such as unexpected truncation, 
abnormal modification times, or irregular rotation patterns. Even when logs are cleared, the act 
of clearing itself may generate secondary records. These subtle indicators are critical in 
demonstrating deliberate interference with logging mechanisms [70]. 
 
18.37 Recovery in Timestamp Manipulation Cases 
Timestamp manipulation does not destroy data but distorts chronology. Recovery in such cases 
involves re-establishing accurate timelines by comparing multiple timestamp sources. File 
system metadata, registry entries, log records, backup timestamps, and external event data must 
be analyzed collectively to identify inconsistencies [71]. 
[[PAGE 474]]
In many cases, only some timestamp attributes are altered, leaving others intact. These partial 
manipulations create detectable contradictions that allow investigators to infer original activity 
windows. Recovery here is analytical rather than restorative, emphasizing reasoning over 
reconstruction [72]. 
 
18.38 Recovery in Encryption and Data Hiding Contexts 
When encryption prevents access to content, recovery shifts to contextual inference. 
Investigators may assess encryption timing, scope, selectivity, and interaction with other anti-
forensic techniques. For example, sudden encryption of specific directories following suspicious 
activity may support an inference of concealment intent [73]. 
In data hiding cases, recovery often depends on anomaly detection rather than direct extraction. 
Unexplained storage usage, abnormal entropy values, or hidden file system structures may 
demonstrate the presence of concealed data even if it cannot be accessed. These findings must be 
articulated carefully to avoid speculative conclusions [74]. 
 
[[PAGE 475]]
 
 
4 
 
18.39 Explaining Anti-Forensic Findings Before Court 
[[PAGE 476]]
One of the most challenging aspects of anti-forensic investigations is courtroom explanation. 
Courts do not expect investigators to recover every piece of destroyed data, but they do require 
clear, logical, and reproducible explanations of how and why evidence is missing. Expert 
testimony must therefore focus on methodology, indicators, and inference rather than technical 
jargon [75]. 
Investigators should explain anti-forensics as deliberate actions designed to obstruct 
investigation, supported by observable technical facts. Visual aids, timelines, and simplified 
analogies are often effective in conveying complex concepts. The goal is to demonstrate that 
conclusions are based on systematic analysis rather than assumption [76]. 
 
18.40 Evidentiary Value of Destroyed or Concealed Evidence 
The destruction or concealment of evidence does not render an investigation void. On the 
contrary, when properly documented, anti-forensic behavior can strengthen evidentiary 
narratives by demonstrating consciousness of guilt or intent to obstruct justice. Courts have 
increasingly accepted expert explanations of such behavior when grounded in technical 
reasoning [77]. 
However, investigators must avoid overstatement. It is essential to distinguish between inference 
and proof, clearly articulating limitations while explaining why alternative innocent explanations 
are unlikely. This balanced approach enhances credibility and withstands cross-examination [78]. 
 
18.41 SOP Flowchart: Anti-Forensic Detection to Court Presentation 
Comprehensive SOP Flow (Textual Representation): 
Incident Detection / Complaint 
        ↓ 
Device Seizure & Forensic Imaging 
        ↓

        ↓ 
Identification of Missing / Anomalous Evidence 
        ↓ 
Anti-Forensic Technique Indicators Assessment 
[[PAGE 477]]
        ↓ 
Cross-Source Correlation & Behavioral Inference 
        ↓ 
Recovery Attempts (Direct / Indirect) 
        ↓ 
Expert Interpretation & Documentation 
        ↓ 
Courtroom Explanation & Testimony 
This flow ensures that anti-forensic analysis is integrated throughout the investigation lifecycle, 
from seizure to testimony. It emphasizes documentation, reasoning, and reproducibility—key 
requirements for legal defensibility [79]. 
[[PAGE 478]]
 
[[PAGE 479]]
 
 
4 
 
18.42 Limitations and Investigative Caution 
[[PAGE 480]]
Despite advanced techniques, anti-forensic investigations have inherent limitations. Complete 
data destruction, strong encryption, or volatile-memory-only activity may permanently eliminate 
content. Investigators must therefore avoid definitive claims where uncertainty exists and should 
clearly document investigative constraints [80]. 
Transparency regarding limitations does not weaken a case; rather, it strengthens expert 
credibility. Courts are more likely to accept balanced testimony that acknowledges uncertainty 
while explaining why conclusions remain reasonable and grounded in evidence [81]. 
 
18.43 Operational Guidance for UP Police Cyber Crime Units 
For UP Police Cyber Crime investigators, the practical takeaway from this chapter is clear: anti-
forensics must be treated as a routine investigative consideration, not an exceptional occurrence. 
Investigators should expect evidence manipulation in serious cybercrime cases and plan 
acquisition, analysis, and reporting accordingly [82]. 
Standard operating procedures should emphasize early volatile data capture, comprehensive 
artifact correlation, and meticulous documentation of anomalies. Continuous training and 
awareness are essential, as anti-forensic techniques evolve alongside forensic capabilities [83]. 
 
18.44 Concluding Observations 
Anti-forensic techniques represent a deliberate attempt to undermine the integrity of digital 
investigations. While they pose significant challenges, they also reveal behavioral evidence that 
can be powerful when properly understood and explained. This chapter has demonstrated that 
effective anti-forensic detection relies not on any single tool, but on structured reasoning, cross-
correlation, and clear communication [84]. 
Ultimately, the goal of anti-forensic analysis is not merely to recover lost data, but to preserve 
the credibility of the investigative process itself. By integrating technical expertise with legal 
awareness, investigators can ensure that justice is not defeated by the absence of evidence, but 
informed by the understanding of why that evidence is missing [85]. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
[[PAGE 481]]
CHAPTER 19 – Legal & Judicial Admissibility of Digital Evidence 
Part I: Conceptual Foundations, Court Philosophy & Statutory 
Evolution 
19.1 Introduction: Why Admissibility is the Most Critical Stage of Cyber 
Crime Investigation 
In cybercrime investigation, the success or failure of a case is rarely determined by the 
sophistication of forensic tools or the gravity of the offence alone. It is ultimately determined 
inside the courtroom, where the judge does not test technological brilliance but legal 
admissibility. Digital evidence, no matter how incriminating, becomes legally irrelevant if it fails 
to satisfy statutory requirements, judicial precedents, and procedural discipline established by 
law [1]. 
Unlike conventional physical evidence, digital evidence is fragile, replicable, volatile, and 
susceptible to allegations of manipulation. Courts in India have repeatedly emphasized that 
electronic evidence is not inherently trustworthy and must therefore pass through stricter scrutiny 
before it can be relied upon for conviction [2]. This judicial skepticism is not anti-technology; it 
is a constitutional safeguard to protect fair trial rights under Articles 20 and 21 of the 
Constitution of India. 
This chapter is therefore drafted not as an academic discussion but as a court-facing operational 
guide for Investigating Officers (IOs), Supervisory Officers, Cyber Forensic Analysts, and 
Prosecutors. Its core objective is to ensure that evidence collected during cyber crime 
investigation does not collapse at the stage of admissibility due to avoidable technical, 
procedural, or certification lapses [3]. 
19.2 Meaning of Admissibility: Legal Perspective vs Investigative Perspective 
Admissibility of evidence refers to the legal acceptability of material placed before a court for 
proving or disproving a fact in issue. Under Indian law, admissibility is governed not by 
relevance alone but by compliance with statutory conditions prescribed for that category of 
evidence [4]. 
From an investigative perspective, digital evidence is anything that links a suspect to an act 
through data, logs, devices, networks, or electronic trails. From a judicial perspective, however, 
digital evidence is merely a claim unless it satisfies: 
 
Statutory definition of electronic record 
 
Prescribed mode of proof 
 
Certification requirements 
[[PAGE 482]]
 
Integrity and authenticity safeguards 
 
Lawful collection and seizure 
 
Chain of custody continuity 
Courts have consistently held that relevance without admissibility has no evidentiary value. A 
WhatsApp chat, CCTV footage, CDR, IP log, or cloud data may appear decisive to an 
investigator but can be rejected outright if statutory compliance is missing [5]. 
This divergence between investigative confidence and judicial acceptance is the single biggest 
cause of acquittals in cyber crime trials. 
19.3 Evolution of Digital Evidence Law in India: From Skepticism to 
Structured Acceptance 
19.3.1 Pre-Information Technology Act Era 
Before the enactment of the Information Technology Act, 2000, Indian courts relied upon the 
Indian Evidence Act, 1872 to assess all documentary material. Electronic material was treated as 
secondary evidence, proved through printouts or oral testimony of a person who produced the 
record [6]. 
This approach was inadequate for modern electronic systems, as it failed to address issues of 
integrity, system reliability, and ease of manipulation. Courts often struggled to assess 
authenticity because the law did not distinguish between mechanically reproduced documents 
and dynamically generated electronic data [7]. 
19.3.2 Post-IT Act, 2000: Statutory Recognition of Electronic Records 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 marked a paradigm shift by legally recognizing 
electronic records and electronic signatures. Consequential amendments were made to the Indian 
Evidence Act, introducing: 
 
Recognition of electronic records as documentary evidence 
 
Special provisions for proof of electronic records 
 
Distinct treatment of computer outputs 
Sections 65A and 65B of the Indian Evidence Act were introduced as a self-contained code 
governing admissibility of electronic evidence [8]. This statutory framework acknowledged that 
electronic evidence required a different standard of proof compared to traditional documents. 
19.3.3 Judicial Confusion and Clarification 
[[PAGE 483]]
Despite statutory amendments, inconsistent judicial interpretation led to uncertainty. Conflicting 
Supreme Court decisions created ambiguity regarding whether certification under Section 65B 
was mandatory in all cases or could be relaxed under judicial discretion [9]. 
This confusion severely affected cyber crime prosecutions, with trial courts often admitting 
evidence that later failed appellate scrutiny. The law was finally clarified through authoritative 
judicial pronouncements reaffirming that statutory conditions cannot be bypassed merely for 
convenience or investigative difficulty [10]. 
19.4 Digital Evidence under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) replaces the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and 
represents a modernized evidentiary framework aligned with digital realities. While preserving 
the foundational principles of evidence law, BSA introduces clarity, continuity, and codified 
recognition of electronic evidence [11]. 
Under BSA: 
 
Electronic records are expressly included within documentary evidence 
 
Proof of electronic records continues to require statutory compliance 
 
Certification requirements have been retained in substance 
Section 63(4) of BSA corresponds to former Section 65B and continues to govern admissibility 
of computer outputs. The legislative intent clearly reflects that Parliament did not dilute 
safeguards but reaffirmed the necessity of certification, integrity, and lawful handling of 
electronic evidence [12]. 
For IOs, this continuity is critical. Old habits of assuming that screenshots, printouts, or 
downloaded files are self-proving must be abandoned permanently. 
19.5 Distinct Nature of Digital Evidence: Why Courts Demand Higher 
Standards 
Digital evidence differs fundamentally from physical evidence in several respects: 
1. Perfect Replicability – Copies are indistinguishable from originals 
2. Volatility – Data can be altered or destroyed without visible traces 
3. Dependency on Systems – Evidence depends on hardware, software, and configurations 
4. Ease of Fabrication – Metadata and content can be manipulated 
5. Remote Creation and Storage – Data may exist across jurisdictions 
Because of these characteristics, courts presume vulnerability unless integrity is affirmatively 
demonstrated by the prosecution [13]. 
[[PAGE 484]]
This is why courts insist on: 
 
System reliability certification 
 
Explanation of data generation process 
 
Proof of lawful access and extraction 
 
Hash values and forensic discipline 
 
Continuous chain of custody 
Failure to address these aspects invites defence objections that often succeed even in otherwise 
strong cases [14]. 
19.6 Court-Centric Philosophy: Investigation Must Begin with the Judge in 
Mind 
One of the most damaging misconceptions among investigating officers is the belief that 
admissibility issues can be “managed later” during trial. Courts have categorically rejected this 
approach. Admissibility is not cured by oral explanations or post-facto justification [15]. 
Every cyber crime investigation must therefore begin with a court-centric mindset, asking: 
 
Will this method of seizure withstand cross-examination? 
 
Can I certify this evidence under statutory provisions? 
 
Is the source lawful and traceable? 
 
Can I explain the technical process in simple judicial language? 
This philosophy requires IOs to treat documentation, certification, and procedural compliance as 
integral to investigation, not as administrative formalities. 
19.7 Role of the Investigating Officer as a Legal Custodian of Evidence 
In cyber crime cases, the IO is not merely a fact collector. He is the legal custodian of digital 
truth. Courts expect IOs to demonstrate: 
 
Understanding of statutory requirements 
 
Awareness of judicial precedents 
 
Procedural discipline in handling electronic material 
 
Neutrality and transparency in evidence management 
An IO who cannot explain how evidence was collected, preserved, certified, and produced 
invites judicial doubt, even if forensic experts support the findings [16]. 
[[PAGE 485]]
This chapter therefore treats the IO as the first judicial gatekeeper, whose actions determine 
whether digital evidence survives scrutiny or collapses under cross-examination. 
 
Part II: Statutory Framework Governing Admissibility of Digital 
19.9 Statutory Architecture of Digital Evidence Admissibility in India 
The admissibility of digital evidence in India is not governed by a single enactment but by an 
interlinked statutory architecture. Courts do not examine electronic evidence in isolation; they 
assess it through a cumulative reading of substantive law, procedural law, evidentiary law, and 
sector-specific regulatory statutes. Any investigation that relies on digital evidence but ignores 
this composite legal structure risks fatal admissibility failure at trial [17]. 
For cyber crime investigations in Uttar Pradesh and across India, the principal statutes impacting 
admissibility include: 
 
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) 
 
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) 
 
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) 
 
 
Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 
2021 
 
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and DPDP Rules, 2025 
 
Telecommunications Act, 2023 
 
Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891 
Each of these statutes plays a distinct but complementary role in determining whether digital 
evidence will be legally received, relied upon, or rejected by courts [18]. 
19.10 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023: Core Evidentiary Statute 
19.10.1 Recognition of Electronic Records as Evidence 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 replaces the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and expressly 
recognizes electronic records as documentary evidence. Section 2 of BSA expands the definition 
of evidence to include electronic records produced for inspection of the court, thereby 
eliminating any residual ambiguity regarding their evidentiary status [19]. 
[[PAGE 486]]
However, recognition does not equate to automatic admissibility. Courts have emphasized that 
electronic records are admissible only when proved in the manner prescribed by law. This 
principle remains unchanged under the new enactment, reaffirming that the mode of proof is as 
important as the content itself [20]. 
19.10.2 Section 63(4) BSA: The Heart of Digital Evidence Proof 
Section 63(4) of BSA corresponds substantively to former Section 65B of the Indian Evidence 
Act. It governs the admissibility of computer outputs such as printouts, screenshots, copied files, 
logs, and extracted data [21]. 
Under this provision, any information contained in an electronic record which is sought to be 
produced as evidence must be accompanied by a statutory certificate identifying: 
 
The electronic record 
 
The manner of its production 
 
The device involved 
 
Compliance with conditions of system reliability 
Courts have consistently held that this requirement is mandatory and non-negotiable. Absence of 
certification renders the evidence legally inadmissible, regardless of its probative value [22]. 
19.10.3 Judicial Continuity Despite Legislative Change 
A critical operational point for IOs is that the transition from the Evidence Act to BSA has not 
diluted judicial safeguards. Supreme Court jurisprudence under Section 65B continues to apply 
with full force to Section 63(4) of BSA, as the legislative intent clearly preserves the same 
evidentiary discipline [23]. 
Investigating officers must therefore avoid assuming that the new law is more relaxed. Any such 
assumption is legally dangerous and unsupported by statutory language or judicial interpretation. 
19.11 Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023: Procedural Legitimacy of 
19.11.1 Search, Seizure, and Collection of Digital Evidence 
BNSS governs the procedural legality of how digital evidence is collected. Courts scrutinize not 
only the content of electronic evidence but also the legality of its acquisition. Evidence collected 
in violation of procedural safeguards may be excluded or its credibility severely weakened [24]. 
Digital searches under BNSS must comply with: 
 
Jurisdictional competence 
 
Recording of reasons 
[[PAGE 487]]
 
Proportionality 
 
Presence of independent witnesses (where applicable) 
 
Proper seizure documentation 
Failure to follow these requirements often becomes the foundation of defence challenges alleging 
illegal search, privacy violation, or fabricated recovery [25]. 
19.11.2 Seizure of Electronic Devices and Data 
BNSS empowers police to seize electronic devices such as mobile phones, computers, storage 
media, and servers. However, courts have clarified that indiscriminate seizure without recording 
necessity or relevance is impermissible [26]. 
Where data extraction is possible without physical seizure, IOs must justify why seizure was 
unavoidable. This justification becomes particularly important in cases involving professionals, 
journalists, or businesses where devices contain third-party data [27]. 
19.12 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Substantive Offences and Evidentiary 
Nexus 
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita defines substantive criminal offences that may be proved using 
digital evidence. While BNS does not directly govern admissibility, it determines relevance by 
linking digital artefacts to elements of offences such as cheating, forgery, criminal breach of 
trust, stalking, intimidation, and organized cyber fraud [28]. 
Courts assess whether the electronic evidence directly establishes mens rea, actus reus, or 
conspiracy elements. Evidence that does not connect clearly with offence ingredients risks being 
dismissed as collateral or speculative [29]. 
IOs must therefore map each digital artefact to specific offence elements during investigation 
itself, rather than attempting to establish relevance later during trial. 
19.13 Information Technology Act, 2000: Legal Backbone of Electronic 
Records 
19.13.1 Definition and Recognition of Electronic Records 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 provides the foundational definition of electronic records 
under Section 2(1)(t). This definition is critical because courts often examine whether the 
material relied upon actually qualifies as an electronic record under law [30]. 
Emails, logs, databases, cloud files, call data records, transaction records, and metadata all fall 
within this definition, provided they are generated, stored, received, or transmitted electronically. 
 
[[PAGE 488]]
19.13.2 Section 79A: Examiner of Electronic Evidence 
Section 79A authorizes the Central Government to notify Examiners of Electronic Evidence. 
Reports from notified forensic laboratories carry enhanced evidentiary credibility and are often 
relied upon by courts to assess authenticity and integrity [31]. 
However, courts have clarified that forensic examiner reports do not substitute statutory 
certification requirements under evidence law. They supplement, but do not replace, Section 
63(4) compliance [32]. 
19.14 IT Rules, 2021: Intermediary Compliance and Evidentiary Reliability 
The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 
2021 play a crucial role in digital evidence admissibility, particularly in cases involving social 
media platforms, messaging services, ISPs, and hosting providers [33]. 
These rules impose obligations on intermediaries regarding: 
 
Preservation of data 
 
Timely cooperation with law enforcement 
 
Lawful disclosure mechanisms 
 
Grievance redressal and traceability 
Evidence obtained from intermediaries in violation of prescribed procedures is vulnerable to 
challenge on grounds of illegality or unreliability [34]. 
19.15 Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and DPDP Rules, 2025 
19.15.1 Privacy-Admissibility Balance 
The DPDP Act, 2023 introduces a rights-based framework for personal data processing. Courts 
now examine whether digital evidence involving personal data was collected in compliance with 
lawful purpose, necessity, and proportionality [35]. 
While law enforcement enjoys statutory exemptions, these are not absolute. IOs must 
demonstrate that data collection was necessary for investigation and not excessive or arbitrary 
[36]. 
19.15.2 Impact on Evidence Collection 
Unlawful or overbroad data extraction can lead to judicial criticism and exclusion. Courts 
increasingly insist that IOs justify why specific datasets were accessed and how unrelated 
personal data was safeguarded [37]. 
This has direct implications for mobile phone dumps, cloud backups, email accounts, and 
financial records. 
[[PAGE 489]]
19.16 Telecommunications Act, 2023: Call Data Records and Interception 
The Telecommunications Act, 2023 governs lawful interception, monitoring, and access to 
telecom data. Call Data Records (CDRs), IPDRs, and location data are admissible only when 
obtained through authorized channels and proper legal sanction [38]. 
Courts routinely reject telecom evidence if: 
 
Authorization orders are absent 
 
Jurisdiction is unclear 
 
Retention limits are violated 
 
Chain of custody is broken 
IOs must therefore treat telecom evidence as highly sensitive and procedurally strict material 
[39]. 
19.17 Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891: Financial Digital Evidence 
Digital banking records are admissible under the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act when certified in 
accordance with statutory requirements. Courts accept certified electronic copies of bank records 
as prima facie evidence, subject to integrity and authenticity [40]. 
Failure to obtain proper certification from banks has resulted in acquittals even in large-scale 
cyber fraud cases [41]. 
19.18 Inter-Statutory Harmony: Why Partial Compliance Is Not Enough 
Courts do not examine compliance statute-wise in isolation. They assess whether the entire 
evidentiary chain—from collection to production—meets cumulative statutory standards [42]. 
An electronic record may comply with IT Act definitions but fail BSA certification. A lawful 
seizure under BNSS may still violate DPDP principles. Such partial compliance is insufficient 
for admissibility. 
The investigating officer must therefore internalize that digital evidence survives only when all 
applicable statutes are satisfied simultaneously. 
19.19 Transition to Procedural Safeguards and Certification 
The statutory framework discussed above forms the legal skeleton. The next part of this chapter 
will translate these laws into operational SOPs, focusing on: 
 
Section 63(4) / former 65B certification practices 
 
Who can issue certificates and when 
[[PAGE 490]]
 
Drafting errors that courts reject 
 
Judicial reasoning from leading cases 
This transition from law to practice is where most investigations fail—and where this SOP aims 
to intervene decisively. 
 
Part III: Section 63(4) BSA / Former Section 65B – Certification 
Doctrine, Judicial Interpretation & Operational SOP 
19.20 Why Certification Is the Single Most Litigated Issue in Digital Evidence 
Among all admissibility requirements governing digital evidence, certification under Section 
63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (formerly Section 65B of the Indian 
Evidence Act) has generated the highest volume of litigation, acquittals, and appellate reversals 
in India [43]. 
Courts have repeatedly observed that investigating agencies often succeed in tracing digital trails 
but fail in legally proving them. The failure is not technological; it is procedural and legal. 
Certification lapses account for a significant proportion of cyber crime acquittals, even in cases 
involving serious financial fraud, terrorism, and organized cyber offences [44]. 
This part of the chapter therefore treats certification not as a formality but as a foundational 
evidentiary act, without which digital evidence has no legal existence in court. 
19.21 Statutory Text and Purpose of Section 63(4) BSA 
Section 63(4) of BSA provides that where a party seeks to rely upon a computer output, such 
output shall be accompanied by a certificate that: 
 
Identifies the electronic record 
 
Describes the manner of its production 
 
Specifies particulars of the device involved 
 
Certifies compliance with system reliability conditions 
The purpose of this provision is twofold: 
1. To replace the impractical requirement of producing original electronic devices in court 
2. To ensure trustworthiness of electronic records through responsible human certification 
Courts have clarified that the certificate substitutes the oath of the machine with the 
responsibility of a human custodian [45]. 
[[PAGE 491]]
19.22 Section 63(4) as a Mandatory Condition, Not a Discretionary Rule 
The Supreme Court has unequivocally held that certification under Section 65B (now Section 
63(4) BSA) is mandatory, not directory. The provision begins with a non-obstante clause, 
making it a complete code for admissibility of electronic evidence [46]. 
Any attempt to bypass certification by invoking general evidence principles, oral testimony, or 
forensic reports has been rejected consistently. Courts have ruled that judicial discretion cannot 
override statutory command [47]. 
This position has profound operational consequences. IOs cannot assume that: 
 
Screenshots speak for themselves 
 
Forensic expert testimony cures certification defects 
 
Admission by accused waives certification 
 
Public documents are exempt 
None of these assumptions survive judicial scrutiny. 
19.23 Judicial Evolution of the Certification Doctrine 
19.23.1 Early Confusion and Divergence 
Initially, courts adopted inconsistent positions. Some judgments suggested flexibility where 
certification was difficult to obtain, particularly when devices were not in possession of the party 
relying on evidence [48]. 
This created investigative complacency, with IOs often postponing certification or ignoring it 
altogether. 
19.23.2 Definitive Clarification by the Supreme Court 
The confusion was decisively resolved when the Supreme Court authoritatively held that: 
 
Certification is mandatory in all cases involving computer outputs 
 
The timing of certification may be flexible, but its existence is not 
 
Courts cannot admit electronic evidence without certification 
The Court emphasized that relaxing certification would open floodgates for fabricated and 
manipulated digital material [49]. 
This judgment remains binding and continues to govern Section 63(4) under BSA. 
19.24 What Constitutes a “Computer Output” 
[[PAGE 492]]
Understanding what requires certification is crucial. Courts have clarified that any electronic 
record produced in a human-readable form qualifies as a computer output, including: 
 
Printouts of emails, chats, or messages 
 
Screenshots of mobile applications 
 
Extracted call detail records 
 
Downloaded cloud files 
 
Copied CCTV footage 
 
Logs, metadata, transaction histories 
If data has passed through a computer system and is produced as a copy, certification is 
mandatory [50]. 
IOs must therefore presume certification is required unless expressly exempted by statute, which 
is rare. 
19.25 Who Is Competent to Issue the Certificate 
19.25.1 The “Responsible Official Position” Requirement 
The certificate must be signed by a person occupying a responsible official position in relation 
to: 
 
Operation of the device, or 
 
Management of the relevant activity 
Courts have interpreted this phrase pragmatically, not formally. The signatory need not be the 
owner of the device but must be someone who can legitimately vouch for system operation and 
data integrity [51]. 
19.25.2 Practical Examples of Competent Signatories 
 
Service provider official for CDRs and IP logs 
 
Bank official for transaction records 
 
System administrator for server logs 
 
Investigating Officer for data extracted under his control 
 
Authorized intermediary compliance officer 
Courts reject certificates signed by persons who lack demonstrable control or knowledge of 
system functioning [52]. 
19.26 Can the Investigating Officer Issue the Certificate 
[[PAGE 493]]
Courts have clarified that an Investigating Officer can issue a certificate for electronic evidence 
extracted by him, provided: 
 
He lawfully accessed the device or data 
 
He supervised the extraction process 
 
He can certify system operation to the best of his knowledge and belief 
However, courts scrutinize such certificates strictly. Any indication of mechanical signing or lack 
of technical understanding weakens credibility [53]. 
As a best practice, IO-issued certificates should be supported by contemporaneous 
documentation such as seizure memos, hash reports, and forensic notes. 
19.27 Timing of Certification: At What Stage Must It Be Produced 
The Supreme Court has clarified that certification need not accompany the charge-sheet but must 
be produced before the evidence is admitted at trial [54]. 
However, operationally, delaying certification is dangerous. Witnesses change, officials transfer, 
and systems evolve. Courts view delayed certificates with suspicion, particularly if created after 
defence objections are raised. 
Best practice demands certification at the time of extraction or immediately thereafter. 
19.28 Common Drafting Errors That Lead to Rejection of Certificates 
Trial courts frequently reject certificates due to drafting defects rather than substantive non-
compliance. Common errors include: 
 
Failure to identify the electronic record precisely 
 
Absence of device particulars 
 
Generic language copied from templates 
 
No mention of system reliability conditions 
 
Certificate signed without date or designation 
 
Certificate referring to multiple unrelated records 
Courts have held that vague or omnibus certificates defeat the purpose of statutory safeguards 
[55]. 
19.29 Certification Is Evidence, Not a Covering Letter 
[[PAGE 494]]
A critical misunderstanding among IOs is treating certification as a procedural annexure. Courts 
have clarified that a Section 63(4) certificate is substantive evidence and must stand 
independently [56]. 
It should be: 
 
Clear 
 
Specific 
 
Self-explanatory 
 
Capable of withstanding cross-examination 
Certificates drafted casually invite defence attacks and judicial distrust. 
19.30 Relationship Between Forensic Reports and Certification 
Forensic examination under Section 79A IT Act enhances credibility but does not substitute 
certification. Courts have repeatedly held that: 
 
Forensic reports prove analysis 
 
Certification proves admissibility 
Both operate in distinct legal domains. Absence of certification cannot be cured by expert 
opinion [57]. 
IOs must therefore ensure that forensic workflows incorporate certification planning from 
inception. 
19.31 Defence Strategies Targeting Certification 
Experienced defence counsel routinely challenge digital evidence by questioning: 
 
Competence of certifying authority 
 
Timing of certificate 
 
Knowledge of system functioning 
 
Possibility of tampering 
 
Chain of custody gaps 
Courts have acquitted accused solely on certification defects even where substantive guilt 
appeared evident [58]. 
Understanding these defence strategies is essential for drafting legally resilient certificates. 
19.32 Operational SOP for Investigating Officers 
[[PAGE 495]]
Mandatory SOP Checklist: 
1. Identify all electronic records likely to be relied upon 
2. Determine the system and device generating the record 
3. Identify competent certifying authority 
4. Prepare certificate contemporaneously 
5. Ensure specificity and clarity 
6. Preserve supporting documentation 
7. Produce certificate at trial stage 
Failure at any step creates admissibility vulnerability. 
19.33 Transition to Chain of Custody and Procedural Integrity 
Certification proves admissibility, but admissibility alone is insufficient. Courts further require 
assurance that evidence remained untampered from seizure to production. 
The next part of this chapter therefore examines chain of custody, documentation standards, and 
judicial expectations regarding evidence integrity—areas where many otherwise valid 
certificates still fail. 
Part IV: Chain of Custody, Search & Seizure Legality, and 
Procedural Integrity 
19.34 Why Chain of Custody Is the Second Pillar of Admissibility 
If certification under Section 63(4) is the first legal gate for digital evidence, chain of custody is 
the second. Courts have repeatedly held that even a perfectly certified electronic record loses 
evidentiary value if the prosecution fails to establish an unbroken, transparent, and credible chain 
of custody from the moment of seizure till production before court [59]. 
Chain of custody answers a fundamental judicial concern: “How can the court be sure that this 
data is the same data that was originally seized?” In digital evidence, where alteration leaves 
little or no visible trace, this concern is amplified [60]. 
For Investigating Officers, chain of custody is not a technical formality but a constitutional 
safeguard ensuring fairness of trial. 
19.35 Concept and Legal Meaning of Chain of Custody 
Chain of custody refers to the chronological documentation showing: 
 
Who collected the evidence 
[[PAGE 496]]
 
From where and when it was collected 
 
How it was preserved 
 
Who accessed it and for what purpose 
 
Where it was stored 
 
How it reached the courtroom 
Courts examine chain of custody to rule out possibilities of manipulation, substitution, 
contamination, or selective extraction [61]. 
In cyber crime cases, courts are less concerned with the quantity of documentation and more 
concerned with its continuity and coherence. 
19.36 Chain of Custody under Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam and BNSS 
While BSA does not explicitly define “chain of custody,” courts derive its necessity from: 
 
Principles of proof and authenticity 
 
Burden on prosecution to establish reliability 
 
Right to fair trial under Article 21 
BNSS provides procedural legitimacy to seizure and handling of evidence. Any break in 
procedural compliance under BNSS directly impacts chain of custody credibility [62]. 
19.37 Search and Seizure of Digital Evidence: Legal Thresholds 
19.37.1 Search Must Be Lawful, Necessary, and Proportionate 
Courts have made it clear that digital search is more intrusive than physical search. Electronic 
devices often contain years of personal, professional, and third-party data. Therefore, search and 
seizure must satisfy heightened standards of legality, necessity, and proportionality [63]. 
Blanket seizure of devices without recorded reasons invites judicial criticism and constitutional 
challenge. 
19.37.2 Authorization and Jurisdiction 
Search of digital devices must be supported by: 
 
Proper authorization under BNSS 
 
Jurisdictional competence 
 
Recorded reasons linking device to offence 
Evidence collected through jurisdictionally defective or unauthorized searches has been excluded 
by courts or treated with suspicion [64]. 
[[PAGE 497]]
19.38 Seizure vs Extraction: Judicial Preference 
Courts increasingly prefer data extraction over device seizure, especially where: 
 
Device contains third-party or privileged data 
 
Accused cooperates with investigation 
 
Relevant data can be isolated 
Where devices are seized, IOs must justify why extraction was not feasible. Failure to justify 
seizure has been held to violate privacy principles laid down by constitutional courts [65]. 
19.39 Seizure Memo: The First Link in the Chain 
The seizure memo is the foundation of chain of custody. Courts expect seizure memos to record: 
 
Exact description of device 
 
Make, model, serial number, IMEI 
 
Physical condition of device 
 
State of power (on/off) 
 
Presence of storage media 
 
Date, time, and place of seizure 
 
Signatures of witnesses 
Generic seizure memos are a common ground for defence challenge [66]. 
19.40 Hash Values and Forensic Imaging 
19.40.1 Importance of Hashing 
Hash values act as digital fingerprints. Courts increasingly rely on hash verification to ensure 
that data examined later is identical to data seized earlier [67]. 
Failure to record hash values at the time of imaging weakens prosecution claims of data integrity. 
19.40.2 Master Copy and Working Copy Doctrine 
Best forensic practice requires: 
 
Creation of a master copy (sealed and preserved) 
 
Creation of a working copy for analysis 
Courts view deviation from this practice with suspicion, especially when original devices are 
repeatedly accessed [68]. 
[[PAGE 498]]
19.41 Documentation of Every Access and Transfer 
Every movement or access of digital evidence must be documented. This includes: 
 
Transfer to forensic lab 
 
Opening of sealed packages 
 
Extraction activities 
 
Analysis sessions 
 
Storage changes 
Undocumented access creates gaps that defence counsel exploit effectively [69]. 
19.42 Storage and Preservation of Digital Evidence 
Courts expect digital evidence to be stored in: 
 
Secure, access-controlled environments 
 
Tamper-evident packaging 
 
Logged storage systems 
Improper storage, shared access, or casual handling has led courts to question authenticity and 
reliability [70]. 
19.43 Chain of Custody in Cloud and Intermediary Data 
Digital evidence sourced from intermediaries or cloud platforms introduces additional custody 
layers. Courts expect IOs to establish: 
 
Lawful request under applicable rules 
 
Identity of intermediary official supplying data 
 
Mode of data transmission 
 
Preservation steps taken by intermediary 
Failure to establish these links weakens admissibility [71]. 
19.44 Defence Challenges Based on Chain of Custody 
Common defence arguments include: 
 
Unexplained delay between seizure and analysis 
 
Missing custody logs 
 
Multiple unexplained handlers 
[[PAGE 499]]
 
Access without authorization 
 
Absence of hash verification 
Courts have accepted these objections even when substantive evidence existed [72]. 
19.45 Judicial Approach: Chain of Custody Is About Credibility, Not 
Perfection 
Courts do not demand impossible perfection. Minor discrepancies may be overlooked if overall 
custody integrity is established. However, unexplained gaps, casual handling, or contradictory 
records are fatal [73]. 
The standard applied is whether the prosecution has created reasonable confidence that 
evidence remained untampered. 
19.46 Operational SOP: Chain of Custody for IOs 
Mandatory IO Checklist: 
1. Record lawful authority before search 
2. Prepare detailed seizure memo 
3. Secure device immediately 
4. Record hash values at imaging 
5. Create master and working copies 
6. Document every access and transfer 
7. Store evidence securely 
8. Produce custody log in court 
Skipping any step invites admissibility risk. 
19.47 Transition to Judicial Objections and Defence Strategies 
Certification and chain of custody together form the backbone of admissibility. Yet, even when 
both are complied with, cases fail due to predictable judicial objections and defence strategies 
that IOs often underestimate. 
The next part addresses these objections directly, equipping IOs to anticipate, prevent, and 
neutralize them effectively. 
Part V: Judicial Objections, Defence Tactics, and IO Counter-
Strategies 
[[PAGE 500]]
19.48 Why Most Cyber Crime Cases Fail Inside the Courtroom 
Empirical experience from trial courts across India shows that cyber crime cases rarely fail 
because the offence did not occur. They fail because the prosecution fails to anticipate and 
neutralize predictable judicial objections and defence strategies targeting admissibility of 
digital evidence [74]. 
Judges, especially at the trial stage, are not cyber-forensics experts. Their primary concern is 
legality, credibility, and procedural fairness. Defence counsel exploit this by shifting the court’s 
focus away from the crime and towards how the evidence was collected, preserved, and proved 
[75]. 
This part of the chapter is therefore written from the perspective of cross-examination and 
judicial scepticism, not investigation optimism. 
19.49 Classification of Judicial Objections in Digital Evidence Cases 
Judicial objections typically fall into five recurring categories: 
1. Admissibility objections (statutory non-compliance) 
2. Authenticity objections (possibility of tampering) 
3. Legality objections (illegal search or privacy breach) 
4. Reliability objections (system or process doubts) 
5. Linkage objections (failure to connect accused with data) 
Each category demands a different investigative response. Treating all objections as 
technicalities is a fatal mistake [76].
