19.51 Cumulative Defence Strategy: Death by a Thousand Cuts 
Often, defence counsel do not rely on a single objection. They raise multiple small 
inconsistencies to cumulatively erode judicial confidence [87]. 
Courts may note: 
“Individually these lapses may appear minor, but cumulatively they render the prosecution case 
unsafe.” 
This cumulative assessment is deadly for poorly documented cyber investigations. 
19.52 Judicial Mindset: Why Judges Are Naturally Skeptical of Digital 
Judges are trained in law, not technology. They are conscious that: 
 
Digital evidence is invisible 
 
Manipulation is difficult to detect 
 
Over-reliance on technology may cause injustice 
Therefore, courts demand higher discipline from prosecution, not lower standards [88]. 
Understanding this mindset helps IOs frame their investigation defensively rather than 
optimistically. 
19.53 Role of the Prosecutor and IO Coordination 
Many admissibility failures occur due to lack of coordination between IOs and prosecutors. 
Prosecutors encounter defects for the first time during trial, when correction is impossible [89]. 
Best practice requires: 
 
Pre-trial scrutiny of certificates 
 
Review of custody logs 
 
Anticipation of defence objections 
Cyber crime prosecution is a team effort, not a handover ritual. 
19.54 Transition to Court-Ready Formats and Operational Tools 
[[PAGE 503]]
After understanding judicial objections and defence strategies, the final part of this chapter 
translates law into ready-to-use operational tools, including: 
 
Court-ready checklists 
 
Documentation formats 
 
Flowcharts for admissibility decision-making 
 
IO dos and don’ts 
These tools are designed to make admissibility compliance routine rather than accidental. 
Part VI: Court-Ready Checklists, Formats, Flowcharts, and IO Dos 
& Don’ts 
19.55 Why SOP Tools Decide Conviction or Acquittal 
Judicial experience demonstrates that cyber crime cases do not collapse because officers lack 
knowledge of law, but because that knowledge is not translated into routine operational 
behaviour. Courts do not reward intention; they reward documentation, discipline, and 
demonstrable compliance [90]. 
This final part converts the legal principles discussed earlier into usable, repeatable, court-
defensible SOP tools. These tools are designed so that even under pressure, transfer, or 
workload stress, admissibility compliance remains intact. 
 
19.56 Master Admissibility Checklist for Investigating Officers 
This checklist must be mentally applied before filing the charge-sheet and physically reviewed 
before evidence is tendered in court. 
A. Statutory Compliance Check 
 
Does the material qualify as an electronic record under law? [91] 
 
Is it relevant to ingredients of the offence charged? 
 
Are all applicable statutes identified (BSA, IT Act, BNSS, DPDP, Telecom Act, etc.)? 
B. Certification Check (Section 63(4) BSA) 
 
Is there a certificate for each distinct electronic record? 
 
Is the signatory competent and identifiable? 
 
Does the certificate describe the device, manner of production, and system reliability? 
[[PAGE 504]]
 
Is the certificate dated, signed, and designation mentioned? [92] 
C. Chain of Custody Check 
 
Is the seizure memo detailed and specific? 
 
Are hash values recorded at imaging stage? 
 
Is there documentation of every access and transfer? 
 
Is storage secure and logged? [93] 
D. Search Legality Check 
 
Was search authorized and jurisdictionally valid? 
 
Are reasons for seizure documented? 
 
Was scope proportionate to offence? [94] 
E. Attribution Check 
 
Is linkage between accused and device/account clearly established? 
 
Is corroborative evidence available? 
 
Are alternative access possibilities addressed? [95] 
Failure at any one stage places the entire case at admissibility risk. 
19.57 Standard Documentation Formats (Conceptual Structure) 
19.57.1 Seizure Memo – Digital Evidence 
A seizure memo must avoid generic language. Courts expect specificity. It should record: 
 
Device description (make, model, serial/IMEI) 
 
Physical condition and state of power 
 
Location and context of seizure 
 
Witness details 
 
Time-stamp and officer identity 
Vague descriptions have repeatedly weakened prosecution credibility [96]. 
19.57.2 Chain of Custody Log 
A custody log must chronologically record: 
 
Date and time of transfer 
 
From whom to whom 
[[PAGE 505]]
 
Purpose of access 
 
Condition of seal 
 
Signature of handler 
Courts view undocumented access as potential tampering [97]. 
19.57.3 Section 63(4) Certificate – Conceptual Elements 
While formats may vary, courts insist that certificates contain: 
 
Identification of electronic record 
 
Description of production process 
 
Device/system particulars 
 
Statement of system reliability 
 
Responsible signatory 
Certificates lacking clarity are treated as legally non-existent [98].

19.60 Supervisory Officer Responsibilities 
Senior officers must ensure that: 
 
Certification compliance is reviewed before charge-sheet 
 
Custody logs are complete 
 
Search legality is documented 
 
Prosecutors are briefed 
Supervisory failure often becomes institutional failure during trial [101]. 
19.61 Preventing Acquittals Due to Technical Failures 
Most acquittals attributed to “lack of evidence” are actually failures of admissibility discipline. 
Courts have repeatedly observed that technology does not weaken justice; poor procedure does 
[102]. 
A cyber crime investigation that survives judicial scrutiny is one where: 
 
Law guides technology 
 
Procedure guides enthusiasm 
 
Documentation guides memory 
19.62 Concluding Note: Admissibility as Professional Integrity 
[[PAGE 507]]
Admissibility is not a hurdle imposed by courts; it is the ethical boundary between truth and 
coercion, efficiency and fairness. When IOs respect admissibility principles, courts trust digital 
evidence. When they do not, even truth appears doubtful [103]. 
This chapter is therefore not merely instructional. It is a reminder that every byte presented in 
court carries constitutional responsibility. 
PART VII – Judicial Precedents Referenced in Chapter 19: Purpose, Context, 
and Defensive Use 
19.63 Why a Case-Law Mapping Section Is Necessary for IOs 
Investigating Officers often cite Supreme Court or High Court judgments mechanically, without 
understanding why those cases matter or how they protect the investigation when challenged in 
court. This creates a credibility gap during judicial interaction and cross-examination. 
This section is therefore included not for citation reproduction, but for defensive application 
enabling IOs to explain to the court “why their procedure aligns with settled law and why defence 
objections must fail.”

19.66 Defensive Mindset Reminder for IOs 
When a judge asks “Why did you do it this way?”, the safest answer is not: 
“Because it is SOP” 
But: 
“Because the Supreme Court has consistently held that this is necessary to ensure 
admissibility and fairness.” 
That is the real purpose of this case-law mapping. 
EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW 
[[PAGE 510]]
Chapter 20: Intermediary & Platform-Based Investigations 
1. Contextual Premise: The Platform-Centric Crime Reality 
In the contemporary digital ecosystem, almost every serious offence—whether cyber fraud, 
sexual exploitation, communal provocation, misinformation, impersonation, or organized 
crime—contains a social media or digital platform component. Crimes are no longer merely 
reported on platforms; they are planned, executed, amplified, monetized, and concealed through 
intermediaries operating at scale1. For law enforcement, this has fundamentally altered the locus 
of evidence, shifting it away from traditional physical spaces to platform-controlled digital 
repositories—servers, logs, metadata, and algorithmic systems.2 
Historically, police responses to platform-based crimes have remained reactive and informal, 
often limited to sending emails, issuing requests through law enforcement portals, or waiting for 
voluntary cooperation from multinational corporations. This approach has repeatedly resulted in 
loss of volatile evidence, delayed takedowns, destruction of logs, and strategic non-
responsiveness, particularly in time-sensitive cases involving violence, sexual offences, or 
public disorder.3 
This chapter is designed to end that dependency model. 
2. Core Objective: Transition from Cooperation to Compliance 
The primary purpose of Chapter 20 is to bridge the structural gap between technical 
investigation and legal enforcement by repositioning intermediaries from external 
collaborators to statutorily accountable entities under Indian law4. The chapter operationalizes 
the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines 
and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 
(BNSS), and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), into a single enforcement-centric 
SOP framework.5 
The focus is no longer on asking platforms for data, but on compelling compliance through 
lawful orders, enforceable timelines, personal accountability of resident officers, and statutory 
consequences for failure.6 
In short, this chapter transitions UP Police from a request-driven posture to a compliance-
driven operational model.

3. Reframing “Safe Harbour”: From Shield to Conditional Privilege 
A critical conceptual foundation of this chapter is the correct understanding of the “Safe 
Harbour” doctrine under Section 79 of the IT Act. Contrary to popular misinterpretation, safe 
harbour is not an absolute immunity; it is a conditional statutory privilege contingent upon 
continuous due diligence and obedience to lawful directions.7 
The moment an intermediary: 
 
fails to preserve evidence, 
 
ignores a lawful order, 
 
delays takedown beyond statutory timelines, 
 
refuses assistance citing internal policy, or 
 
obstructs traceability mandates, 
it steps outside the protective boundary of Section 79 and becomes legally exposed to 
prosecution under applicable penal provisions.8 
This chapter equips Investigating Officers (IOs) with a clear certification pathway to record 
and trigger the loss of safe harbour, transforming non-cooperation into criminal liability rather 
than a mere compliance issue.9 
4. Strategic Enforcement Goals of Chapter 20 
Chapter 20 is structured around five non-negotiable enforcement outcomes, each mapped to 
statutory authority and operational action: 
(a) Zero-Hour Evidence Preservation 
Ensuring that volatile digital evidence—logs, IP data, device identifiers, account metadata—is 
preserved immediately using BNSS Section 94 and IT Rules obligations, preventing deliberate 
or automated deletion.10 
(b) Strategic Removal of Unlawful Content 
Not merely deleting content, but doing so within enforceable statutory timelines (36 hours / 24 
hours), while preserving forensic copies and preventing re-upload through hash-based controls.11 
(c) Execution of Traceability Mandate 
Operationalizing Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 to identify first originators of viral unlawful 
                                                     
7 Information Technology Act, 2000, § 79 (India). 
8 Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (India).

10 BNSS, 2023, § 94. 
11 IT Rules, 2021, Rule 3(1)(d), provisos. 
[[PAGE 512]]
content, particularly on encrypted platforms, without being derailed by generic encryption 
objections.12 
(d) Direct Accountability of Resident Officers 
Activating the legal responsibility of India-resident Chief Compliance Officers, Nodal Officers, 
and Grievance Officers through physical summons, personal service, and criminal joinder 
where required.13 
(e) Stripping of Safe Harbour Protection 
Formally documenting and triggering the intermediary’s loss of immunity, enabling prosecution 
under substantive penal laws and procedural coercion under BNSS.14 
5. Jurisdictional Assertion: No Server-Location Excuse 
This chapter establishes unequivocally that any intermediary offering services to users located 
within Uttar Pradesh falls within the territorial and subject-matter jurisdiction of UP 
Police, irrespective of: 
 
server location, 
 
place of incorporation, 
 
data hosting geography, or 
 
internal corporate structuring.15 
Indian courts have consistently recognized that effects-based jurisdiction applies to online 
offences, and that digital platforms cannot evade lawful authority merely by situating 
infrastructure outside India.16 Accordingly, IOs are instructed to proceed without hesitation in 
issuing notices, summons, and enforcement actions against intermediaries operating within the 
state’s digital footprint. 
6. Ending the “Email Culture”: Institutionalizing Enforcement Timelines 
One of the most damaging practices in platform-based investigations has been the informal 
“email culture”, where investigators wait indefinitely for platform responses with no escalation 
framework.17 Chapter 20 replaces this with a hard-timeline enforcement model, where: 
 
statutory notices trigger countdown clocks, 
 
failure to respond escalates automatically to physical summons, and 
                                                     
12 IT Rules, 2021, Rule 4(2). 
13 IT Rules, 2021, Rule 4(1). 
14 Information Technology Act, 2000, § 79(3).

17 Parliamentary Standing Committee on IT, Report on Digital Platforms (India). 
[[PAGE 513]]
 
continued non-compliance attracts criminal and procedural consequences.18 
The operational mantra embedded in this chapter is clear: 
“Delay equals defiance, and defiance equals liability.” 
7. Evidentiary Integrity: From Platform Response to Courtroom Proof 
Beyond investigation, this chapter ensures that data received from intermediaries survives 
judicial scrutiny. Detailed protocols are laid down for: 
 
certification under BSA Sections 63 and 65B, 
 
documentation of chain of custody, 
 
forensic integrity of platform-provided data, and 
 
rebuttal of defence challenges based on authenticity or tampering.19 
This ensures that intermediary responses are not merely investigative leads, but court-
admissible evidence capable of sustaining conviction. 
8. Institutional Impact 
By implementing this chapter, the UP Police institutionalizes: 
 
uniform district-level practice, 
 
reduction of platform-induced investigative delays, 
 
deterrence against corporate non-compliance, 
 
enhanced victim protection in time-critical cases, and 
 
restoration of sovereign law enforcement authority in the digital domain.20 
Chapter 20 is therefore not just a procedural addition—it is a structural correction to how 
digital power asymmetry between the State and global platforms is addressed. 
Section 20.1: Legal Foundations & Jurisdiction 
 
20.1.1 Re-Conceptualising Intermediary Liability: From Passive Conduit to Regulated 
Actor 
                                                     
18 Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §§ 94, 179, 210. 
19 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §§ 63, 65B. 
20 Press Information Bureau, Government of India, Platform Accountability and Law Enforcement Coordination 
(2025). 
[[PAGE 514]]
Indian cyber law does not treat intermediaries as neutral bystanders. From its inception, the 
Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”) conceived intermediaries as entities occupying a 
position of controlled facilitation, not immunity by default. Section 2(1)(w) of the IT Act 
defines an intermediary expansively to include any person who receives, stores, transmits, or 
provides services with respect to electronic records on behalf of another, thereby covering social 
media platforms, messaging services, cloud providers, search engines, and hosting entities [1]. 
For Investigating Officers (IOs), this definition is not merely classificatory; it is jurisdiction-
triggering. The moment an intermediary stores or processes user data connected to an offence 
affecting persons, property, or public order within Uttar Pradesh, it becomes a legally regulated 
participant in the investigative ecosystem. The intermediary’s role is therefore not external to 
the offence but procedurally linked to it [2]. 
This chapter rejects the outdated notion that intermediaries are only “technical carriers” of 
information. In the 2020s, platforms curate content, algorithmically amplify reach, retain 
metadata, control access, and decide response timelines. Such control brings statutory 
responsibility, not discretion [3]. 
 
20.1.2 The “Safe Harbour” Doctrine Under Section 79 IT Act: Conditional, Not Absolute 
Section 79 of the IT Act is frequently misrepresented—often even by platforms themselves—as a 
blanket immunity against legal consequences. This interpretation is legally incorrect. Section 79 
provides conditional exemption from liability, subject to strict compliance with statutory duties 
and due diligence requirements [4]. 
The protection under Section 79 is available only when the intermediary establishes cumulatively 
1. Its role is limited to providing access or transmission, 
2. It does not initiate, modify, or select the transmission, and 
3. It observes due diligence and complies with lawful directions [5]. 
Failure on any one of these conditions collapses the safe harbour shield. This position was 
authoritatively clarified by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, where the 
Court upheld Section 79 precisely because it is conditional and enforceable, not absolute [6]. 
For SOP purposes, IOs must internalize a crucial operational rule: 
Safe harbour is a privilege earned continuously, not a right possessed permanently. 
The moment an intermediary refuses, delays, or selectively complies with a lawful order, it 
forfeits this privilege in respect of the concerned offence [7]. 
[[PAGE 515]]
 
20.1.3 Statutory Triggers That Disable Safe Harbour Protection 
Under Section 79(3) of the IT Act, an intermediary loses safe harbour protection if it: 
 
Has actual knowledge of unlawful content and fails to act expeditiously, or 
 
Fails to comply with a lawful order issued by a competent authority [8]. 
The IT Rules, 2021 significantly expand and operationalise these triggers by defining specific 
timelines, officer responsibilities, and response duties, thereby removing ambiguity about what 
constitutes “expeditious” action [9]. 
For Investigating Officers, the following actions automatically create a safe harbour risk zone 
for intermediaries: 
 
Non-preservation of data after receipt of notice, 
 
Failure to remove unlawful content within statutory timelines, 
 
Refusal to provide basic subscriber or metadata information, 
 
Non-appearance of resident officers despite summons, 
 
Blanket reliance on “encryption” without legal substantiation [10]. 
Once any of the above occurs, the intermediary’s conduct must be documented as wilful non-
compliance, paving the way for enforcement escalation under BNSS and substantive penal 
provisions [11]. 
 
20.1.4 Integration of BNSS, 2023: Procedural Supremacy Over Platforms 
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (“B (“BNSS”) fundamentally alters the procedural 
landscape of platform-based investigations. Unlike earlier practice, BNSS does not recognize 
“corporate inconvenience” or “foreign incorporation” as grounds for resisting lawful process 
Key BNSS provisions relevant to intermediaries include: 
 
Section 94: Power to order production and preservation of documents and electronic 
records, 
 
Section 179: Service of summons on companies and responsible officers, 
 
Section 210: Penal consequences for non-compliance with lawful authority [13]. 
[[PAGE 516]]
For SOP purposes, this means that digital evidence is procedurally equivalent to physical 
evidence, and intermediaries are procedurally equivalent to custodians of case property. Any 
refusal to comply attracts the same consequences as obstruction by a physical custodian [14]. 
BNSS thus removes the artificial distinction between “tech companies” and “persons bound by 
criminal procedure”. 
 
20.1.5 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023: Legal Recognition of Platform-Held Evidence 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (“B (“BSA”) reinforces the evidentiary centrality of 
intermediary-held data by explicitly recognizing electronic records as primary and secondary 
evidence, subject to certification and integrity safeguards [15]. 
Sections 63 and 65B of the BSA require that electronic evidence be accompanied by certification 
regarding: 
 
Source, 
 
Method of generation, 
 
Integrity of storage, and 
 
Chain of custody [16]. 
This statutory framework places intermediaries in a dual role: 
1. As custodians of potential evidence, and 
2. As certifying authorities for authenticity of records under their control. 
An intermediary that withholds, alters, or delays such records not only obstructs investigation but 
also undermines evidentiary administration, exposing itself to adverse judicial inference and 
criminal liability [17]. 
 
20.1.6 Jurisdiction in Platform-Based Offences: Effects Doctrine Applies 
A recurring defensive argument by intermediaries is lack of territorial jurisdiction based on 
server location or foreign incorporation. This argument has no legal standing under Indian law. 
Indian courts have consistently applied the effects doctrine, whereby jurisdiction is determined 
by the location where the harmful effect occurs, not where the infrastructure is situated [18]. 
In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, the Supreme Court affirmed that digital actions affecting 
fundamental rights and public order within India fall squarely within domestic jurisdiction, 
irrespective of backend architecture [19]. Similarly, in Faheema Shirin R.K. v. State of Kerala, 
[[PAGE 517]]
access to the internet and its regulation was recognised as having territorial impact where users 
reside [20]. 
For UP Police, the jurisdictional rule is clear: 
If the victim, offender, data subject, or public impact is within Uttar Pradesh, jurisdiction 
exists. 
Server location, data routing paths, or corporate domicile are legally irrelevant for investigative 
initiation and compliance enforcement [21]. 
 
20.1.7 Subject-Matter Jurisdiction: Platforms as Sites of Crime, Not Just Tools 
Platform-based offences are not merely crimes committed using platforms; in many cases, the 
platform itself becomes the site of offence, where acts of publication, transmission, 
monetisation, or concealment occur [22]. 
This distinction is critical for: 
 
Hate speech, 
 
NCII circulation, 
 
Fraudulent impersonation, 
 
Organized misinformation, 
 
Child sexual abuse material (CSAM). 
In such cases, intermediary action or inaction directly shapes the continuation and impact of the 
offence. Jurisdiction therefore attaches not only to the offender but also to the intermediary as a 
regulated entity facilitating the offence environment [23]. 
 
20.1.8 SOP Directive for IOs (Legal Foundation Stage) 
At the jurisdiction-establishment stage, Investigating Officers shall: 
1. Record the intermediary’s status under Section 2(1)(w) IT Act. 
2. Assert jurisdiction based on victim/user impact within UP. 
3. Cite Section 79 as conditional immunity, not absolute protection. 
4. Invoke BNSS procedural powers without deferring to platform policy. 
5. Treat intermediary-held data as potential case property. 
6. Document all non-compliance as potential loss of safe harbour [24]. 
[[PAGE 518]]
Failure to assert jurisdiction early results in evidence loss and procedural dilution. This SOP 
therefore mandates early legal framing, not post-facto justification. 
 
Section 20.2: Classification of Intermediaries & the Resident Officer Mandate 
20.2.1 Why Classification Matters: One Size Does Not Fit All 
Not all intermediaries perform the same technical or legal function. Treating a global social 
media platform, an encrypted messaging service, a cloud storage provider, and an OTT platform 
under a single investigative approach leads to procedural errors, avoidable delays, and 
evidentiary gaps. Indian cyber law therefore adopts a functional classification model, where the 
nature of intermediary services determines the scope of obligations, timelines, and accountability 
For Investigating Officers (IOs), correct classification at the outset is not academic. It decides: 
 
what data can be demanded, 
 
from whom it can be demanded, 
 
within what time frame, and 
 
under which statutory consequence. 
This section standardizes that classification for operational use. 
 
20.2.2 Statutory Classification Under the IT Act and IT Rules, 2021 
Section 2(1)(w) of the IT Act provides a broad definition of intermediaries. However, the 
Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 
2021 (“IT Rules, 2021”)”) introduce functional sub-categories with distinct compliance burdens 
At an SOP level, intermediaries relevant to cybercrime investigations fall into four principal 
categories: 
1. Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) 
2. Messaging-Based Intermediaries (Including E2EE Platforms) 
3. OTT Platforms and Cloud Service Providers 
4. Ancillary and Infrastructure Intermediaries 
Each category is examined separately below. 
 
[[PAGE 519]]
20.2.3 Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) 
(a) Definition and Threshold 
A Significant Social Media Intermediary (SSMI) is a social media intermediary having more 
than fifty lakh (five million) registered users in India, as notified by the Central Government 
under Rule 2(1)(v) of the IT Rules, 2021 [3]. 
Platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, X (formerly Twitter), YouTube, and similar large-scale 
services typically fall within this category. 
The classification is user-base driven, not incorporation-driven. Whether the company is Indian 
or foreign is irrelevant. 
 
(b) Enhanced Due Diligence Obligations 
SSMIs are subject to enhanced due diligence obligations under Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021, 
reflecting the disproportionate societal impact of their platforms [4]. 
These obligations include: 
 
Appointment of specific resident officers, 
 
Deployment of automated tools for proactive identification of unlawful content, 
 
Publication of compliance reports, 
 
Enabling traceability in prescribed cases. 
For IOs, this means higher compliance expectations and lower tolerance for delay when 
dealing with SSMIs. 
 
(c) Operational SOP Implication for IOs 
When dealing with an SSMI, IOs shall: 
1. Record the platform’s SSMI status in the case diary, 
2. Invoke Rule 4 obligations explicitly in notices, 
3. Demand officer-level compliance, not generic helpdesk responses, 
4. Escalate non-response as wilful defiance, not logistical delay [5]. 
 
20.2.4 Messaging Platforms and End-to-End Encrypted Services 
[[PAGE 520]]
(a) Nature of Messaging Intermediaries 
Messaging intermediaries provide private or semi-private communication services, often 
employing end-to-end encryption (E2EE). Examples include WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, and 
similar platforms. 
Encryption does not place these platforms outside the regulatory framework. Indian law 
recognizes encryption as a technical feature, not a legal immunity [6]. 
 
(b) Legal Position on Encryption 
Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 mandates that messaging-based SSMIs enable identification of 
the “first originator” of information upon a lawful order relating to specified serious offences 
This obligation is narrowly tailored and does not require disclosure of message content. It 
focuses on: 
 
originator identity, 
 
metadata, 
 
cryptographic identifiers (hashes). 
The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal recognized that intermediary obligations may coexist with 
free speech protections when backed by procedural safeguards [8]. 
 
(c) SOP Guidance for IOs 
When dealing with encrypted platforms, IOs shall: 
1. Avoid vague or overbroad requests, 
2. Specify offence category triggering Rule 4(2), 
3. Provide message identifiers, URLs, or hashes where available, 
4. Reject blanket “encryption” refusals unsupported by legal reasoning [9]. 
Encryption is not a defence to non-cooperation; it is a technical constraint to be navigated 
within law. 
 
20.2.5 OTT Platforms and Cloud Service Providers 
(a) Scope and Relevance 
[[PAGE 521]]
OTT platforms (streaming services) and cloud service providers store, transmit, and monetize 
digital content at scale. Examples include video streaming services, cloud storage platforms, and 
content hosting providers. 
These entities often possess: 
 
upload logs, 
 
IP records, 
 
device fingerprints, 
 
payment and subscription data. 
Such data is frequently critical in cases involving obscenity, copyright fraud, impersonation, 
CSAM, and organized cybercrime [10]. 
 
(b) Legal Obligations 
OTT and cloud intermediaries are bound by: 
 
IT Act obligations, 
 
IT Rules, 2021 due diligence requirements, 
 
BNSS procedural mandates relating to production of records [11]. 
They cannot claim editorial neutrality when they actively host, recommend, or monetize content. 
 
(c) SOP Directive 
IOs shall treat OTT and cloud platforms as custodians of digital premises, similar to physical 
premises under criminal law. Preservation notices and production orders must be issued early, 
before automated data deletion cycles operate [12]. 
 
20.2.6 Ancillary and Infrastructure Intermediaries 
This category includes: 
 
Domain registrars, 
 
Hosting providers, 
 
Payment gateways, 
 
E-wallets, 
[[PAGE 522]]
 
App stores. 
Though often overlooked, these intermediaries provide infrastructure continuity to unlawful 
activity. Shutting down financial or hosting access frequently disrupts criminal networks faster 
than content takedowns alone [13]. 
IOs are instructed to integrate these entities into platform-based investigations where relevant. 
 
20.2.7 The Resident Officer Mandate: Core Enforcement Lever 
(a) Mandatory Officers Under IT Rules, 2021 
Rule 4(1) of the IT Rules, 2021 mandates that SSMIs appoint the following officers, all of whom 
must be residents of India [14]: 
1. Chief Compliance Officer (CCO) 
2. Nodal Contact Person 
3. Resident Grievance Officer 
These appointments are not symbolic. They exist to ensure direct legal accountability within 
Indian jurisdiction. 
 
(b) Statutory Role of Each Officer 
 
Chief Compliance Officer (CCO) 
Responsible for ensuring compliance with the IT Act and IT Rules. The CCO is expressly 
made liable for proceedings relating to non-compliance [15]. 
 
Nodal Contact Person 
Serves as the 24×7 coordination point for law enforcement agencies. Failure to respond 
constitutes breach of statutory duty [16]. 
 
Resident Grievance Officer 
Handles user complaints and takedown obligations, particularly in cases involving 
privacy, impersonation, and NCII [17]. 
 
(c) SOP Shift: From Email to Physical Accountability 
This chapter mandates a paradigm shift: 
 
From emailing global legal teams, 
 
To serving physical summons on resident officers under BNSS Section 179. 
[[PAGE 523]]
1. Identify the resident officer details published by the platform, 
2. Serve summons physically or through lawful electronic means, 
3. Record acknowledgment and start statutory countdowns, 
4. Escalate non-appearance under BNSS Section 210 [18]. 
The presence of resident officers removes all jurisdictional ambiguity. 
 
20.2.8 Criminal Liability of Resident Officers 
Rule 4(1)(a) explicitly states that the Chief Compliance Officer shall be liable for any 
proceedings relating to any relevant third-party information for failure to ensure compliance 
[19]. 
This provision pierces the corporate veil and enables: 
 
joinder of CCOs as accused, 
 
initiation of prosecution for abetment or obstruction, 
 
denial of safe harbour to the platform itself. 
IOs must treat this as an enforcement tool, not a last resort. 
 
20.2.9 SOP Checklist: Classification & Officer Mapping 
At the initial stage of platform-based investigation, IOs shall document: 
1. Category of intermediary, 
2. Whether it qualifies as an SSMI, 
3. Applicable IT Rules provisions, 
4. Names and addresses of resident officers, 
5. Applicable compliance timelines, 
6. Consequences of non-compliance [20]. 
Failure to classify correctly at inception weakens later enforcement. 
 
Section 20.3: Data Preservation & Retrieval Protocol 
[[PAGE 524]]
20.3.1 The Central Problem: Evidence Dies Faster Than Crime 
Digital evidence is uniquely fragile. Unlike physical evidence, which deteriorates slowly, 
platform-held electronic evidence is routinely overwritten, anonymised, auto-deleted, or 
rendered inaccessible within hours or days, often through automated retention policies rather 
than human intervention [1]. In platform-based crimes, the decisive factor is therefore not 
detection but speed of preservation. 
Historically, investigating agencies have lost critical cases because: 
 
preservation notices were delayed, 
 
requests were informal or misdirected, 
 
platforms claimed data had already expired, 
 
or evidence was altered during internal moderation cycles [2]. 
This section establishes a Zero-Hour Evidence Preservation Doctrine, making early 
preservation not optional, but mandatory. 
 
20.3.2 Legal Authority for Preservation: Section 94 BNSS as the Primary Weapon 
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (“B (“BNSS”) fundamentally empowers IOs through 
Section 94, which authorizes any police officer conducting an investigation to require the 
production, preservation, or retention of any document or electronic record necessary for 
the investigation [3]. 
For SOP purposes, Section 94 must be treated as: 
 
self-executing, 
 
not contingent on court approval at the preservation stage, and 
 
enforceable against any person or entity in possession or control of the data. 
Intermediaries fall squarely within the ambit of “persons in possession or control” of electronic 
records. Failure to comply attracts penal consequences under BNSS [4]. 
 
20.3.3 Standard Preservation Notice (SPN): Mandatory First-Step Action 
(a) Timing 
The Standard Preservation Notice (SPN) shall be issued immediately upon registration of 
FIR or receipt of credible information, whichever is earlier. Delay beyond this stage is 
procedurally unjustifiable [5]. 
[[PAGE 525]]
(b) Duration 
In alignment with IT Rules, 2021, intermediaries are mandated to preserve: 
 
removed or disabled content, and 
 
user registration and transactional data 
for a minimum of 180 days, or longer if directed by law enforcement [6]. 
(c) Content of SPN 
An SPN shall clearly specify: 
1. FIR number or inquiry reference, 
2. User identifiers (URLs, usernames, phone numbers, email IDs), 
3. Nature of data to be preserved, 
4. Explicit prohibition on deletion, anonymisation, or alteration, 
5. Legal basis: Section 94 BNSS + IT Rules, 2021, 
6. Warning of consequences for non-compliance [7]. 
Vague or generic notices weaken enforceability and shall be avoided. 
 
20.3.4 Preservation Is Not Disclosure: Clarifying the Legal Distinction 
A frequent intermediary tactic is to resist preservation by conflating it with disclosure. This is 
legally incorrect. Preservation only freezes data in its existing state; it does not require 
immediate handover [8]. 
This distinction is critical because: 
 
preservation does not implicate privacy or encryption concerns, 
 
it prevents spoliation of evidence, 
 
it creates a legal duty of care on the intermediary. 
IOs shall explicitly state in notices that preservation is neutral, temporary, and investigatively 
necessary, and that objections to disclosure can be raised later, but not to preservation itself [9]. 
 
20.3.5 Emergency Disclosure Requests (EDR): The 24×7 Exception Protocol 
(a) Situations Warranting EDR 
[[PAGE 526]]
Emergency Disclosure Requests may be invoked where delay poses an imminent risk to: 
 
life or bodily safety, 
 
sexual exploitation of a child, 
 
communal violence, 
 
suicide or self-harm, 
 
active financial fraud or extortion [10]. 
Such situations justify bypassing routine judicial timelines, though not statutory authority. 
 
(b) Legal Basis 
EDRs are justified under: 
 
Section 94 BNSS (urgent production), 
 
IT Rules, 2021 (law enforcement assistance), 
 
and constitutional duty of the State to protect life under Article 21 [11]. 
Platforms are legally obligated to maintain 24×7 response mechanisms through their Nodal 
Contact Persons. 
 
(c) SOP for IOs 
In EDR situations, IOs shall: 
1. Record emergency justification in the case diary, 
2. Contact the platform’s nodal officer immediately, 
3. Follow up with written confirmation within 24 hours, 
4. Seek only minimum necessary data (IP logs, location, subscriber info), 
5. Transition to formal orders post-emergency [12]. 
Abuse of EDR mechanisms dilutes credibility and shall be avoided. 
 
20.3.6 Metadata vs Content: Tactical Retrieval Strategy 
(a) Understanding the Difference 
Metadata includes: 
[[PAGE 527]]
 
IP addresses, 
 
timestamps, 
 
 
registration details, 
 
login history. 
Content refers to: 
 
messages, 
 
images, 
 
videos, 
 
audio files. 
In many investigations, metadata alone is sufficient to establish identity, location, and 
continuity of offence, even where content is encrypted or unavailable [13]. 
 
(b) Strategic Advantage of Metadata 
Metadata: 
 
is rarely encrypted end-to-end, 
 
is retained longer, 
 
attracts fewer legal objections, 
 
is often decisive in court when corroborated [14]. 
IOs are instructed to prioritize metadata requests early, especially where content access is 
contested. 
 
20.3.7 Handling “Encryption” Objections at the Preservation Stage 
Encryption objections are irrelevant at the preservation stage. Encryption affects readability, 
not existence of data. Platforms cannot lawfully destroy or allow loss of encrypted data merely 
because it is encrypted [15]. 
 
reject encryption-based refusal to preserve, 
 
document such refusal as wilful non-compliance, 
[[PAGE 528]]
 
escalate under BNSS Section 210 where necessary [16]. 
 
20.3.8 The Law Enforcement Request System (LERS) Ecosystem 
(a) Nature of LERS 
Most major platforms operate Law Enforcement Request Systems (LERS)—secure portals for 
submission of legal requests. While useful, these systems are procedural tools, not legal 
authorities [17]. 
LERS usage does not replace statutory notices under BNSS or IT Act. 
 
(b) SOP Position on LERS 
IOs may use LERS for: 
 
speed, 
 
audit trails, 
 
technical efficiency. 
However: 
 
all LERS requests must be backed by formal legal authority, 
 
failure of LERS response does not excuse non-compliance, 
 
offline or physical service of notices remains valid and enforceable [18]. 
LERS is a convenience, not a shield. 
 
20.3.9 Cross-Border Data and MLAT Excuse 
Intermediaries often claim that data is stored overseas and requires Mutual Legal Assistance 
Treaty (MLAT) processes. This argument does not apply to preservation and often does not 
apply to basic subscriber information [19]. 
Indian law binds intermediaries operating in India, not merely hosting data in India. IOs shall: 
 
proceed with domestic preservation orders, 
 
initiate MLAT only where content disclosure genuinely requires it, 
 
not allow MLAT to become a delay tactic [20]. 
 
[[PAGE 529]]
20.3.10 Consequences of Non-Preservation: Evidentiary and Penal 
Failure to preserve data after lawful notice results in: 
 
loss of safe harbour under Section 79 IT Act, 
 
adverse inference under evidentiary law, 
 
potential prosecution for obstruction or abetment [21]. 
IOs must formally record non-preservation as a material fact in the case diary and charge 
sheet. 
 
20.3.11 SOP Checklist: Data Preservation & Retrieval 
At this stage, IOs shall ensure: 
1. Immediate issuance of SPN, 
2. Correct statutory invocation (BNSS + IT Rules), 
3. Clear distinction between preservation and disclosure, 
4. Early metadata prioritisation, 
5. Emergency protocol documentation (if invoked), 
6. Escalation for non-compliance [22]. 
This checklist is mandatory, not advisory. 
 
Section 20.4: Content Management & Takedown Protocol 
20.4.1 From Evidence Preservation to Harm Containment 
While data preservation secures evidentiary integrity, content takedown addresses continuing 
harm. In platform-based offences, unlawful content often remains accessible even after FIR 
registration, compounding victim injury, escalating public disorder, or enabling repeat 
victimisation. Indian cyber law therefore treats removal of unlawful content as an independent 
statutory obligation, not as a discretionary act contingent upon internal platform review [1]. 
This section establishes a time-bound, coercive takedown framework, ensuring that 
Investigating Officers (IOs) act decisively to neutralise harm without compromising evidence. 
 
20.4.2 Legal Architecture Governing Content Removal 
[[PAGE 530]]
Content takedown obligations arise from a layered statutory framework comprising: 
 
Section 79(3), IT Act, 2000 – loss of safe harbour upon failure to act on lawful orders, 
 
Rule 3(1)(d), IT Rules, 2021 – mandatory removal within 36 hours, 
 
Rule 3(2)(b), IT Rules, 2021 – expedited takedown of certain categories of content, 
 
Section 69A, IT Act, 2000 – blocking of information in the interest of sovereignty, public 
order, or security of State, 
 
BNSS, 2023 – procedural enforcement and penal consequences [2]. 
IOs must treat these provisions as complementary, not alternative. 
 
20.4.3 The 36-Hour Removal Rule: Rule 3(1)(d) IT Rules, 2021 
(a) Scope of the Obligation 
Rule 3(1)(d) mandates that intermediaries shall remove or disable access to unlawful content 
within 36 hours of receiving: 
 
a court order, or 
 
a lawful order from a government agency [3]. 
Unlawful content includes, inter alia: 
 
sexually explicit material, 
 
defamatory or impersonation content, 
 
content inciting violence or hatred, 
 
content facilitating fraud or cheating, 
 
content prohibited under any law in force. 
The rule leaves no discretion to intermediaries regarding timelines. 
 
(b) SOP Directive for IOs 
When invoking the 36-hour rule, IOs shall: 
1. Issue a written takedown direction citing Rule 3(1)(d), 
2. Specify exact URLs, account handles, or content identifiers, 
3. Direct disablement of access, not merely “review”, 
[[PAGE 531]]
4. Preserve content prior to removal under Section 94 BNSS, 
5. Record start and expiry of the 36-hour countdown in the case diary [4]. 
Failure to remove content within this window automatically exposes the intermediary to loss of 
safe harbour. 
 
20.4.4 The 24-Hour NCII Rule: Immediate Protection of Dignity 
(a) Nature of NCII Obligations 
Rule 3(2)(b) of the IT Rules, 2021 mandates that intermediaries remove or disable access to: 
 
content exposing private areas, 
 
nudity or sexual acts, 
 
impersonation in intimate imagery, 
within 24 hours of receiving a complaint, even without a court order [5]. 
This provision is designed to address Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery (NCII) and similar 
sexual exploitation offences. 
 
(b) No Judicial Precondition 
Unlike general takedowns, NCII removal: 
 
does not require FIR registration, 
 
does not require court direction, 
 
overrides platform moderation policies. 
The obligation arises immediately upon receipt of complaint or law enforcement notice. 
 
(c) SOP Mandate 
In NCII cases, IOs shall: 
1. Direct immediate takedown under Rule 3(2)(b), 
2. Ensure parallel preservation of content for evidence, 
3. Avoid delay under the pretext of victim verification, 
4. Escalate non-compliance directly to resident officers [6]. 
[[PAGE 532]]
Any delay in NCII takedown constitutes statutory violation, not procedural lapse. 
 
20.4.5 Preservation Before Takedown: Non-Negotiable Sequence 
A recurring investigative failure has been ordering takedown before preservation, resulting in 
loss of primary evidence. This SOP mandates a strict sequence: 
Preserve → Certify → Remove 
IOs shall explicitly direct intermediaries to: 
 
retain forensic copies, 
 
preserve metadata and access logs, 
 
ensure content is not permanently destroyed until lawful disposal [7]. 
Takedown does not mean erasure from existence; it means disabling public access. 
 
20.4.6 Section 69A IT Act: Centralised Blocking Mechanism 
(a) Nature of Section 69A Powers 
Section 69A empowers the Central Government to block public access to information in the 
interest of: 
 
sovereignty and integrity of India, 
 
defence or security of the State, 
 
public order, 
 
prevention of incitement to offences [8]. 
This mechanism is typically invoked for: 
 
large-scale communal content, 
 
coordinated misinformation campaigns, 
 
national security threats. 
 
(b) Role of State Police 
While Section 69A orders are issued centrally, State Police play a critical initiating role by: 
 
identifying emergent threats, 
[[PAGE 533]]
 
preparing factual blocking proposals, 
 
routing requests through designated nodal officers (e.g., ADG Cyber) [9]. 
IOs must not hesitate to recommend Section 69A action where platform-level takedowns are 
insufficient. 
 
20.4.7 Proactive Monitoring and Hash-Based Controls 
(a) Preventing Re-Upload of Banned Content 
Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, 2021 requires SSMIs to deploy technology-based measures to identify 
and prevent re-upload of content that has already been removed [10]. 
This includes: 
 
hash-matching, 
 
content fingerprinting, 
 
automated detection systems. 
 
(b) SOP Application 
In serious cases, IOs shall: 
1. Direct platforms to apply hash-based blocking, 
2. Provide known hashes or reference files where available, 
3. Demand confirmation of deployment, 
4. Monitor recurrence of content post-takedown [11]. 
Repeated re-appearance of the same content is evidence of platform negligence, not user 
ingenuity. 
 
20.4.8 Dealing with “Community Guidelines” Excuse 
Platforms often attempt to replace statutory obligations with references to “community 
standards” or internal review boards. Such references are legally irrelevant once a lawful order 
is issued [12]. 
 
reject policy-based delays, 
[[PAGE 534]]
 
insist on statutory compliance, 
 
record policy defiance as wilful non-compliance. 
Corporate policies cannot override Indian law. 
 
20.4.9 Consequences of Takedown Failure 
Failure to remove unlawful content within statutory timelines results in: 
 
loss of Section 79 safe harbour, 
 
exposure to prosecution for abetment or facilitation, 
 
personal liability of resident officers, 
 
adverse judicial inference [13]. 
This SOP treats non-takedown not as passive omission but as active continuation of harm. 
 
20.4.10 SOP Checklist: Content Management & Takedown 
IOs shall ensure: 
1. Correct identification of unlawful content, 
2. Preservation before removal, 
3. Proper invocation of 36-hour or 24-hour rule, 
4. Escalation to resident officers on delay, 
5. Consideration of Section 69A where required, 
6. Documentation of compliance or defiance [14]. 
 
Section 20.5: Traceability & Identification of Originators 
20.5.1 Why Traceability Is the Decisive Investigative Lever 
In platform-based offences, content virality is rarely accidental. Misinformation, communal 
provocation, financial scams, and sexual exploitation material usually originate from a 
deliberate source, are amplified through coordinated networks, and are shielded by anonymity 
claims. Without identifying the first originator, investigations collapse into chasing downstream 
forwards while the architect remains insulated [1]. 
[[PAGE 535]]
Indian cyber law therefore treats traceability not as mass surveillance, but as a targeted 
investigative necessity—activated only for serious offences and backed by procedural 
safeguards. This section converts the traceability mandate into a precise operational protocol, 
preventing Investigating Officers (IOs) from being stalled by generic encryption objections. 
 
20.5.2 Rule 4(2) IT Rules, 2021: Statutory Basis for Traceability 
Rule 4(2) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics 
Code) Rules, 2021 mandates that Significant Social Media Intermediaries providing 
messaging services shall enable identification of the first originator of information upon a 
lawful order relating to specified offences [2]. 
The rule is: 
 
conditional, not blanket, 
 
case-specific, not continuous, 
 
identity-focused, not content-focused. 
It does not require decryption of messages or mass monitoring of user communications. 
 
20.5.3 Offence Categories Triggering Traceability 
Traceability may be lawfully demanded only for offences relating to: 
 
sovereignty and integrity of India, 
 
security of the State, 
 
public order, 
 
rape, sexual abuse, or sexually explicit material involving children, 
 
offences punishable with imprisonment of five years or more [3]. 
IOs must explicitly record the applicable offence category in the case diary to justify invocation 
of Rule 4(2). 
 
20.5.4 Understanding “First Originator”: Legal Meaning 
The “first originator” is not the most influential sharer, group admin, or viral amplifier. It refers 
to the earliest identifiable account or device that introduced the unlawful content into the 
platform ecosystem in India [4]. 
[[PAGE 536]]
Where the originator is located outside India, the intermediary is required to identify: 
 
the first Indian originator, or 
 
the account that first made the content available in India. 
This distinction is critical for jurisdictional validity. 
 
20.5.5 Technical Thresholds: What IOs Must Provide 
Traceability is not a fishing expedition. Platforms are legally entitled to receive specific 
technical identifiers to execute origin tracing. IOs shall, wherever possible, provide: 
 
exact message text or media file, 
 
timestamps, 
 
message IDs, 
 
URLs or group identifiers, 
 
cryptographic hashes (where available) [5]. 
Vague requests (“trace fake news”) invite resistance and delay. 
 
20.5.6 Metadata-Centric Traceability: Avoiding Encryption Deadlocks 
End-to-end encryption (E2EE) protects message content in transit but does not eliminate 
metadata. Platforms retain: 
 
account creation details, 
 
IP logs, 
 
 
message routing records [6]. 
Traceability under Rule 4(2) can be executed through metadata correlation, without accessing 
content. IOs must insist on this distinction and reject claims that encryption makes traceability 
legally or technically impossible. 
 
20.5.7 Handling Platform Refusal Based on Encryption Claims 
[[PAGE 537]]
Platforms frequently argue that traceability violates privacy or breaks encryption. Such 
objections are policy arguments, not legal defences. Indian law has already balanced privacy 
concerns by limiting traceability to serious offences and lawful orders [7]. 
SOP response to refusal: 
1. Demand written legal justification citing specific statutory conflict, 
2. Record refusal as potential non-compliance under Rule 7, 
3. Escalate to resident Chief Compliance Officer, 
4. Initiate loss-of-safe-harbour assessment [8]. 
Encryption is not a veto power. 
 
20.5.8 Judicial Backing and Constitutional Balance 
The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed that privacy is not absolute and may be restricted by 
procedure established by law. Traceability under Rule 4(2), when invoked narrowly, satisfies: 
 
legality, 
 
necessity, 
 
proportionality [9]. 
IOs must frame traceability orders precisely to withstand judicial scrutiny. 
 
20.5.9 SOP Checklist: Traceability Execution 
Before invoking traceability, IOs shall ensure: 
1. FIR reflects qualifying offence, 
2. Written lawful order is prepared, 
3. Technical identifiers are attached, 
4. Resident officers are served, 
5. Timeline for compliance is recorded, 
6. Refusal or delay is documented [10]. 
Traceability is an enforcement tool, not a negotiation. 
 
Section 20.6: Enforcement & Accountability (The “Power Section”) 
[[PAGE 538]]
20.6.1 Purpose of This Section: Converting Law Into Leverage 
All prior sections of this chapter—classification, preservation, takedown, and traceability—
culminate here. Section 20.6 is the enforcement spine of the SOP. Its objective is explicit: to 
ensure that non-cooperative intermediaries face real, personal, and immediate legal 
consequences, not prolonged correspondence or symbolic warnings [1]. 
Historically, enforcement against digital platforms failed not because the law was absent, but 
because the law was under-used. This section institutionalises a shift from persuasion to 
compulsion, from delay tolerance to deadline discipline, and from corporate opacity to personal 
accountability [2]. 
 
20.6.2 The Safe Harbour Trap: How Intermediaries Lose Section 79 Protection 
(a) Legal Nature of Safe Harbour 
Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 does not grant immunity; it grants conditional exemption. Once 
conditions fail, the intermediary stands in the same position as any other accused facilitator or 
abettor [3]. 
Section 79(3) explicitly removes protection where an intermediary: 
 
has actual knowledge of unlawful activity and fails to act, or 
 
fails to comply with a lawful government or court order [4]. 
This SOP treats non-compliance as the trigger, not judicial declaration. 
 
(b) Certification of Safe Harbour Loss (Operational Step) 
Investigating Officers shall formally record a “Safe Harbour Loss Note” in the case diary when 
any of the following occur: 
 
failure to preserve data after notice, 
 
failure to remove content within 24/36 hours, 
 
refusal to provide traceability data, 
 
non-appearance of resident officers despite summons, 
 
reliance on internal policy over statutory command [5]. 
This note becomes the legal foundation for escalation, joinder, and prosecution. 
 
[[PAGE 539]]
20.6.3 Rule 7 IT Rules, 2021: Automatic Consequence Clause 
Rule 7 of the IT Rules, 2021 states that non-observance of due diligence results in loss of 
Section 79 protection and exposure to punishment under any law in force [6]. 
This provision is critical because: 
 
it requires no further notification, 
 
it operates automatically upon breach, 
 
it pierces the intermediary’s claim to neutrality. 
IOs must cite Rule 7 expressly in escalation notices. 
 
20.6.4 Personal Criminal Liability of Resident Officers 
(a) Chief Compliance Officer (CCO): Statutory Liability 
Rule 4(1)(a) of the IT Rules, 2021 states that the Chief Compliance Officer shall be liable in 
proceedings relating to failure of compliance [7]. 
This is not symbolic responsibility. It is a personal legal hook. 
Where deliberate non-compliance is evident, IOs may: 
 
array the CCO as a co-accused, 
 
proceed under relevant BNS provisions, 
 
seek custodial or non-custodial measures as per law [8]. 
 
(b) Nodal Officer & Grievance Officer 
Failure of the Nodal Officer to respond to lawful requests, or of the Grievance Officer to act 
within mandated timelines, constitutes wilful neglect of statutory duty. 
Such conduct supports: 
 
prosecution for obstruction, 
 
adverse inference against the platform, 
 
escalation under BNSS Section 210 [9]. 
 
20.6.5 BNSS, 2023: Procedural Coercion Framework 
[[PAGE 540]]
(a) Section 179 BNSS: Summons on Companies & Officers 
Section 179 BNSS authorises service of summons on companies through principal officers. 
This removes ambiguity regarding service on foreign platforms operating in India [10]. 
 
serve summons physically where required, 
 
document refusal or evasion, 
 
escalate non-appearance without delay. 
 
(b) Section 210 BNSS: Penal Consequences 
Section 210 penalises failure to comply with lawful directions of public servants. This provision 
applies squarely to resident officers who ignore notices, delay compliance, or obstruct 
investigation [11]. 
This SOP directs IOs to actively invoke Section 210, rather than treating it as a theoretical 
power. 
 
20.6.6 Using BNS, 2023: Substantive Criminal Exposure 
Once safe harbour is lost, intermediaries and officers may attract liability under: 
 
abetment provisions, 
 
organized cybercrime sections, 
 
obstruction of justice clauses [12]. 
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 enables prosecution where platform conduct materially aids 
continuation of the offence. 
IOs must coordinate with prosecutors early to frame correct charges. 
 
20.6.7 Judiciary, Delay, and Tactical Escalation 
(a) Avoiding Procedural Paralysis 
Platforms often seek time through: 
 
repeated “legal review” claims, 
 
writ petitions, 
[[PAGE 541]]
 
jurisdiction objections. 
This SOP mandates parallel progression: 
 
continue investigation, 
 
document non-compliance, 
 
move for coercive orders where required [13]. 
 
(b) John Doe / Ashok Kumar Orders 
In cases involving mass dissemination, IOs may seek John Doe orders to: 
 
block entire classes of URLs, 
 
restrain unknown offenders, 
 
compel platforms to act proactively [14]. 
Such orders are particularly effective in piracy, NCII, and misinformation cases. 
 
20.6.8 Actionable “Power Moves” for Investigating Officers 
This SOP authorises the following lawful enforcement actions: 
1. Serving physical summons instead of email follow-ups, 
2. Naming resident officers personally in notices, 
3. Triggering safe harbour loss documentation, 
4. Initiating Section 210 BNSS proceedings, 
5. Recommending Section 69A blocking, 
6. Seeking judicial monitoring where obstruction persists [15]. 
These are not extraordinary measures; they are intended statutory tools. 
 
20.6.9 SOP Checklist: Enforcement & Accountability 
IOs shall ensure: 
1. Documentation of non-compliance, 
2. Invocation of Rule 7 IT Rules, 
3. Service of summons on resident officers, 
[[PAGE 542]]
4. Consideration of BNS charges, 
5. Coordination with prosecution, 
6. Judicial escalation where needed [16]. 
Failure to enforce weakens deterrence across the ecosystem. 
 
Section 20.7: Admissibility of Evidence & Chain of Custody 
20.7.1 Why Admissibility Is the Final Battlefield 
In platform-based investigations, the hardest work often collapses inside the courtroom, not 
during investigation. Perfectly preserved data, lawfully obtained disclosures, and timely 
takedowns lose all value if defence counsel successfully challenges authenticity, continuity, or 
certification of digital evidence. This section ensures that every intermediary response is 
converted from “useful information” into legally admissible proof under the Bharatiya Sakshya 
Adhiniyam, 2023 (“BSA”) [1].
]. 
The core principle is simple: 
If evidence cannot survive judicial scrutiny, the investigation has failed—no matter how 
strong the facts are. 
 
20.7.2 Legal Framework Governing Digital Evidence 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 modernises Indian evidence law by explicitly 
recognising electronic records as admissible evidence, subject to statutory safeguards. Sections 
63 and 65B of the BSA provide the foundation for admissibility of digital material received from 
intermediaries [2]. 
Under this framework: 
 
electronic records may constitute primary or secondary evidence, 
 
admissibility depends on certification, not format, 
 
the burden of proving integrity lies on the prosecution. 
This section converts these legal principles into step-by-step SOP actions. 
 
20.7.3 Nature of Platform-Provided Evidence 
Evidence received from intermediaries generally falls into the following categories: 
[[PAGE 543]]
 
subscriber information, 
 
IP and login logs, 
 
 
account creation and usage history, 
 
preserved content (images, videos, messages), 
 
compliance certificates or affidavits [3]. 
Each category carries different evidentiary risks and must be handled accordingly. 
 
20.7.4 Section 63 & 65B BSA: Certification Requirements 
(a) Mandatory Certification 
Sections 63 and 65B of the BSA require that electronic records be accompanied by a certificate 
specifying: 
1. the manner of production, 
2. the device or system involved, 
3. integrity of the data, 
4. affirmation that the record is a true and accurate reproduction [4]. 
For platform-based evidence, this certificate is usually generated by the intermediary itself. 
 
(b) SOP Directive for IOs 
 
explicitly demand BSA-compliant certificates while requesting data, 
 
reject uncertified data for evidentiary purposes (though it may guide investigation), 
 
ensure the certificate is signed by an authorised platform officer [5]. 
Absence of certification is a fatal defect unless cured before trial. 
 
20.7.5 Who Can Issue the Certificate 
The certificate must be issued by: 
 
a person occupying a responsible official position, 
[[PAGE 544]]
 
having lawful control over the computer system or data, 
 
typically the platform’s compliance or legal officer [6]. 
Generic disclaimers, automated emails, or unsigned portal downloads do not satisfy statutory 
requirements. 
 
20.7.6 Chain of Custody: Digital Continuity, Not Physical Possession 
Unlike physical evidence, digital evidence does not pass through visible custody. Courts 
therefore scrutinise documented continuity, not physical sealing. Chain of custody must 
establish: 
 
where the data originated, 
 
how it was transmitted, 
 
where it was stored, 
 
who accessed it, and 
 
whether it was altered [7]. 
 
(a) SOP Documentation Requirements 
IOs shall maintain: 
1. date and time of receipt from intermediary, 
2. mode of transfer (LERS, secure email, physical media), 
3. hash values (where applicable), 
4. storage location (digital evidence locker), 
5. access logs, 
6. forwarding details to FSL or court [8]. 
Each transfer point must be recorded contemporaneously. 
 
20.7.7 Preservation of Original Digital Form 
Platform data must be preserved in its native digital format. Conversion to printouts, 
screenshots, or transcriptions without preserving the original file weakens evidentiary value [9]. 
Printouts may be used for reference, but originals must be retained for: 
[[PAGE 545]]
 
forensic verification, 
 
hash comparison, 
 
defence inspection if ordered. 
 
20.7.8 Handling Defence Challenges 
Common defence objections include: 
 
“data could have been manipulated”, 
 
“certificate is defective”, 
 
“platform is an interested party”, 
 
“chain of custody is broken” [10]. 
IOs must anticipate these challenges by: 
 
ensuring strict compliance with certification rules, 
 
preserving audit trails, 
 
documenting every interaction with intermediaries. 
Courts have repeatedly held that minor procedural lapses may be cured, but systemic gaps are 
fatal. 
 
20.7.9 Adverse Inference Against Non-Cooperative Platforms 
Where an intermediary: 
 
delays certification, 
 
provides incomplete logs, 
 
refuses clarification, 
IOs shall place such conduct on record. Courts are empowered to draw adverse inference 
against parties who control evidence but fail to produce it fully [11]. 
This reinforces the enforcement posture established in Section 20.6. 
 
20.7.10 Integration with Forensic Examination 
Where platform data is subjected to forensic analysis: 
[[PAGE 546]]
 
original hashes must be recorded prior to analysis, 
 
forensic copies must be generated, 
 
examiner reports must reference the source certificates [12]. 
Coordination with FSLs must begin early, not at charge-sheet stage. 
 
20.7.11 SOP Checklist: Evidence Admissibility 
Before filing charge-sheet, IOs shall verify: 
1. all platform data is certified under BSA, 
2. chain of custody is fully documented, 
3. originals are preserved, 
4. forensic reports are linked, 
5. non-cooperation is recorded, 
6. prosecution brief is complete [13]. 
This checklist is mandatory, not advisory.
