[[PAGE 553]]
CHAPTER 21 – International Cooperation & Cross-Border Cases 
Part I: Jurisdictional Complexity & the Imperative of International Cooperation 
21.1 Introduction: The Borderless Nature of Cybercrime and the Limits of Territorial 
Policing 
Cybercrime investigations in the contemporary digital ecosystem rarely remain confined within 
the territorial boundaries of a single State. Unlike conventional crimes, where the locus delicti is 
often geographically identifiable, cyber offences operate across distributed networks, cloud 
infrastructures, and anonymised routing paths that routinely traverse multiple jurisdictions within 
seconds. For Investigating Officers (IOs) of the Uttar Pradesh Police, this reality presents a 
structural challenge: the crime may be committed in Uttar Pradesh, the victim may be located in 
another Indian State, the service provider may be incorporated in the United States, and the 
relevant logs or content data may be stored in data centres located in Ireland, Singapore, or the 
Netherlands [1]. 
This jurisdictional diffusion fundamentally disrupts traditional assumptions of criminal 
investigation under territorial criminal law. Digital evidence is no longer physically seizable 
within the investigator’s jurisdiction; instead, it is controlled by foreign intermediaries subject to 
foreign domestic laws, privacy regimes, and disclosure thresholds. As a result, effective 
cybercrime investigation now depends as much on international legal cooperation as on local 
forensic capability. This chapter is designed to equip IOs with a structured, lawful, and time-
sensitive framework to navigate these transnational realities without compromising evidentiary 
admissibility or sovereign comity [2]. 
 
21.2 Extraterritoriality in Indian Cyber Law: From Substantive Reach to Investigative 
Reality 
Indian law recognises the extraterritorial application of criminal statutes in cybercrime matters. 
Section 1(2) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with Section 75, explicitly extends 
the Act’s applicability to offences committed outside India where the computer system or 
network affected is located in India [3]. This position is reinforced under the Bharatiya Nyaya 
Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), which continues the principle that offences having consequences within 
India may be prosecuted irrespective of the offender’s physical location [4]. 
However, while substantive jurisdiction is statutorily asserted, investigative jurisdiction remains 
constrained by international law principles. Indian courts may try an offence with extraterritorial 
elements, but Indian police officers cannot unilaterally exercise coercive investigative powers—
such as search, seizure, or compelled disclosure—within the territory of a foreign State. This 
distinction between jurisdiction to prescribe and jurisdiction to enforce is critical for IOs to 
[[PAGE 554]]
understand, as overreach at the investigative stage can render otherwise valid prosecutions 
vulnerable to judicial challenge [5]. 
Judicial discourse has repeatedly emphasised that due process and legality of evidence collection 
are integral to fair trial guarantees. Evidence obtained in violation of international law principles 
or foreign domestic law may face admissibility objections under the Bharatiya Sakshya 
Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), particularly where chain of custody, authenticity, or lawful acquisition 
is questioned [6]. 
 
21.3 Digital Evidence as a Volatile and Time-Sensitive Asset 
One of the defining characteristics of cybercrime investigations is the volatility of digital 
evidence. Unlike physical evidence, server logs, IP allocation records, session metadata, and 
cloud-stored communications are routinely overwritten or deleted in accordance with service 
provider retention policies. Major global platforms often retain certain categories of data for 
limited periods—sometimes as short as 90 days—unless a lawful preservation request is received 
This creates a critical operational dilemma for IOs. Formal mechanisms such as Mutual Legal 
Assistance Treaties (MLATs) and Letters Rogatory (LRs), while legally robust, are procedurally 
slow and may take several months to yield results. In contrast, digital evidence may cease to 
exist long before such requests are executed. Recognising this mismatch between evidentiary 
lifespan and diplomatic timelines is essential for effective investigation strategy [8]. 
International research and comparative studies consistently highlight that delays in preservation 
requests are among the primary causes of investigative failure in cross-border cybercrime cases. 
The inability to act swiftly often results not in acquittal, but in cases collapsing at the threshold 
due to lack of corroborative digital evidence [9]. 
 
21.4 Sovereignty, Comity, and the Prohibition of Unilateral Cross-Border Searches 
International law is anchored in the principle of State sovereignty, which prohibits one State’s 
law enforcement agencies from exercising enforcement jurisdiction within the territory of 
another State without consent. The classical position, articulated in international jurisprudence 
and scholarly analysis, holds that unilateral cross-border searches—particularly remote digital 
searches—may amount to a violation of sovereignty if conducted without authorisation [10]. 
In the cyber context, this issue becomes particularly complex. Remote access techniques, cross-
border data extraction, and direct platform engagement without appropriate legal channels may 
appear operationally efficient, but they risk diplomatic fallout and evidentiary invalidation. 
[[PAGE 555]]
Scholarly analysis of remote cross-border searches underscores that while technological 
capability exists, legal legitimacy remains contested and context-dependent [11]. 
For Indian IOs, this means that investigative urgency must be balanced against procedural 
legality. The correct response is not unilateral action, but the intelligent sequencing of informal 
preservation mechanisms followed by formal legal requests routed through designated central 
authorities. This approach preserves evidence while maintaining compliance with international 
norms [12]. 
 
21.5 The Centralised Architecture of International Cooperation in India 
India has adopted a centralised model for international legal cooperation in criminal matters. 
Unlike domestic investigations, where police stations and cyber cells exercise direct authority, 
cross-border requests must be routed through designated nodal agencies. The Ministry of Home 
Affairs (MHA) functions as the central authority for MLAT and LR requests, while the Central 
Bureau of Investigation (CBI), acting as the National Central Bureau (NCB), interfaces with 
international police cooperation mechanisms [13]. 
This architecture serves multiple purposes. It ensures uniformity in outgoing requests, 
compliance with treaty obligations, and diplomatic vetting of sensitive investigations. However, 
it also introduces procedural layers that may appear cumbersome at the field level. This chapter 
does not seek to bypass these structures, but to help IOs work within them more effectively by 
understanding timelines, documentation standards, and escalation pathways [14]. 
Coordination with these central agencies is not optional; it is a legal necessity. Courts have 
consistently recognised that evidence obtained through internationally recognised channels 
carries greater evidentiary weight and is less susceptible to defence challenges regarding legality 
or authenticity [15]. 
 
21.6 Strategic Rationale for International Cooperation: Beyond Evidence Collection 
International cooperation in cybercrime investigations serves purposes beyond mere evidence 
acquisition. It enables intelligence sharing, identification of transnational criminal syndicates, 
financial tracing across jurisdictions, and coordinated disruption of criminal infrastructure. In 
cases involving Business Email Compromise (BEC), international investment fraud, or child 
sexual abuse material (CSAM), isolated domestic action is rarely sufficient to dismantle the 
broader criminal network [16]. 
Global reports on transnational cybercrime consistently emphasise that effective enforcement 
now depends on collaborative frameworks that integrate law enforcement, judicial authorities, 
and private service providers. The failure to engage internationally not only weakens individual 
[[PAGE 556]]
cases but also allows organised cybercriminal groups to exploit jurisdictional fragmentation as a 
defensive strategy [17]. 
For the UP Police, developing institutional familiarity with international cooperation 
mechanisms is therefore not a matter of exceptional cases, but a routine investigative 
competency in an increasingly digitised crime environment. 
 
21.7 Indicative Flow of a Cross-Border Cybercrime Investigation (Conceptual Overview) 
Textual Flow Representation (for SOP understanding): 
1. Offence Detected in UP 
↓ 
2. Preliminary Attribution Indicates Foreign Server / Platform 
↓ 
3. Immediate Preservation Request Issued (Domestic Legal Basis) 
↓ 
4. Simultaneous Coordination with Nodal Cyber Cell & Central Agency 
↓ 
5. Formal MLAT / LR Prepared and Routed via MHA / CBI-NCB 
↓ 
6. Foreign Authority Executes Request & Shares Evidence 
↓ 
7. Evidence Analysed, Corroborated, and Presented Before Court 
This flow underscores the central theme of this chapter: speed without illegality, and legality 
without paralysis [18]. 
 
21.8 Conclusion: Setting the Foundation for Procedural Precision 
This Part has sought to establish the conceptual and legal foundations for international 
cooperation in cybercrime investigations. For IOs, understanding jurisdictional limits is not an 
abstract legal exercise but a practical necessity that determines whether an investigation succeeds 
or fails. The subsequent Parts of this chapter will translate these principles into actionable SOPs, 
detailing the exact procedures for MLATs, Letters Rogatory, INTERPOL engagement, 
emergency preservation, and court-facing justification of foreign evidence [19]. 
[[PAGE 557]]
By internalising these foundations, the UP Police can ensure that its cybercrime investigations 
remain legally robust, internationally compliant, and operationally effective in a borderless 
digital world. 
 
Part II: Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs) & Letters Rogatory (LRs) 
21.9 Introduction: Formal Legal Pathways for Cross-Border Evidence 
Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs) and Letters Rogatory (LRs) constitute the backbone 
of formal international cooperation in criminal investigations involving extraterritorial elements. 
For cybercrime investigations undertaken by the Uttar Pradesh Police, these mechanisms 
represent the only legally unimpeachable routes for securing foreign-based digital evidence that 
is intended to be relied upon during trial. While operationally slower than informal channels, 
MLATs and LRs provide evidentiary sanctity, judicial confidence, and diplomatic legitimacy—
attributes that are indispensable in complex cyber prosecutions [1]. 
In practice, many cybercrime cases fail not because the offender cannot be identified, but 
because the evidence necessary to prove attribution, intent, or financial trail is located outside 
India and has not been lawfully obtained. This Part therefore focuses on demystifying MLATs 
and LRs for IOs, clarifying when each mechanism is to be invoked, how requests must be 
structured, and how investigative strategy must be aligned with procedural timelines under 
Indian law and international practice [2]. 
 
21.10 Conceptual Distinction Between MLATs and Letters Rogatory 
Although often used interchangeably in colloquial policing language, MLATs and Letters 
Rogatory are distinct legal instruments with different procedural foundations. 
An MLAT is a bilateral or multilateral treaty-based mechanism through which States agree in 
advance to assist each other in criminal investigations and prosecutions. India has entered into 
MLATs with numerous countries, including the United States, United Kingdom, Singapore, and 
several European jurisdictions. Requests made under MLATs are executed pursuant to treaty 
obligations, which generally results in higher compliance rates and clearer timelines [3]. 
A Letter Rogatory, on the other hand, is a formal judicial request issued by a court in one 
country to a court in another country seeking assistance in the collection of evidence. LRs are 
typically used where no MLAT exists between the requesting and requested States. Because LRs 
operate through diplomatic and judicial channels rather than treaty frameworks, they are 
inherently slower and subject to greater procedural variability [4]. 
[[PAGE 558]]
For IOs, understanding this distinction is crucial. The choice between MLAT and LR is not 
discretionary but dictated by the existence (or absence) of a treaty relationship with the foreign 
State where the evidence is located. 
 
21.11 Legal Basis for MLATs and LRs Under Indian Law 
Under Indian law, the authority to seek international assistance in criminal matters flows from 
procedural statutes rather than substantive criminal law alone. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha 
Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which has replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, continues to 
recognise reciprocal arrangements and international cooperation for investigation and evidence 
collection [5]. 
Judicial involvement becomes mandatory at the stage of issuing Letters Rogatory, as courts must 
apply their mind to the relevance, necessity, and proportionality of the evidence sought. This 
judicial imprimatur is a safeguard against fishing expeditions and reinforces the admissibility of 
evidence once received [6]. 
Additionally, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) functions as the Central Authority for 
outgoing and incoming MLAT and LR requests. IOs do not directly correspond with foreign 
governments; instead, all formal requests must be routed through prescribed central channels to 
ensure consistency with India’s treaty obligations and diplomatic posture [7]. 
 
21.12 Procedural Workflow for MLAT Requests: Step-by-Step 
From an SOP perspective, the MLAT process must be visualised as a multi-stage pipeline rather 
than a single application. The following stages are critical: 
1. Identification of Foreign Nexus 
During preliminary investigation, the IO identifies that key evidence—such as subscriber 
information, IP logs, transactional records, or content data—is held by a foreign service 
provider or authority [8]. 
2. Assessment of Treaty Availability 
The IO, in coordination with the District Cyber Cell or State Cyber Crime Unit, confirms 
whether India has an MLAT with the concerned country. This determination directly 
influences the format and routing of the request [9]. 
3. Preparation of MLAT Proposal 
The IO prepares a detailed proposal outlining: 
o Facts of the case 
o Legal provisions invoked (BNS, IT Act, PMLA where applicable) 
[[PAGE 559]]
o Nature of evidence sought 
o Relevance of evidence to investigation or prosecution 
o Assurance of reciprocity and lawful use of evidence 
This proposal must be precise, legally grounded, and proportionate, as vague or 
overly broad requests are a common cause of rejection [10]. 
4. Routing Through State & Central Authorities 
The proposal is forwarded through the State Home Department to the MHA, which 
scrutinises the request for treaty compliance, clarity, and diplomatic sensitivity before 
transmitting it to the requested State [11]. 
5. Execution by Foreign Authority 
Upon receipt, the foreign Central Authority executes the request in accordance with its 
domestic law. The pace and scope of execution are governed by the requested State’s 
legal standards, not Indian law [12]. 
6. Transmission of Evidence to India 
Evidence is transmitted back through official channels, typically accompanied by 
certification or attestation to support admissibility in Indian courts [13]. 
This workflow underscores why MLATs, though reliable, are time-intensive and must be 
complemented by interim preservation strategies discussed in later Parts of this chapter. 
 
21.13 Letters Rogatory: Judicial Instruments of Last Resort 
Letters Rogatory occupy a unique position in international criminal procedure. They are invoked 
primarily in two situations: (a) where no MLAT exists, or (b) where the nature of evidence 
sought requires direct judicial intervention, such as examination of witnesses or court-supervised 
production of records [14]. 
The LR process begins with an application by the investigating agency before the competent 
Indian court. The court must be satisfied that the evidence sought is necessary for a fair and 
effective investigation. Once approved, the LR is transmitted through the MHA and Ministry of 
External Affairs (MEA) to the foreign court via diplomatic channels [15]. 
From an investigative standpoint, LRs present two major challenges. First, they are procedurally 
slow, often taking several months or even years. Second, the executing foreign court applies its 
own evidentiary standards, which may differ significantly from Indian expectations. As a result, 
IOs must carefully calibrate LR requests to avoid seeking evidence that is unlikely to be 
compelled under foreign law [16]. 
 
[[PAGE 560]]
21.14 Common Deficiencies in MLAT and LR Requests 
Empirical studies and international reports repeatedly identify recurring deficiencies in outgoing 
MLAT and LR requests from developing jurisdictions. Among the most frequent issues are: 
 
Overbroad Requests: Seeking “all data” without temporal or factual limitation, leading 
to rejection on proportionality grounds [17]. 
 
Inadequate Legal Mapping: Failure to clearly link the evidence sought with specific 
offences under Indian law. 
 
Lack of Urgency Justification: Absence of explanation regarding data volatility or risk 
of deletion. 
 
Improper Formatting: Non-compliance with treaty-specific templates or language 
requirements [18]. 
For UP Police IOs, avoiding these pitfalls is essential. A well-drafted request not only accelerates 
execution but also enhances the credibility of Indian investigations in the eyes of foreign 
counterparts. 
 
21.15 Evidentiary Value of MLAT-Obtained Material in Indian Courts 
Evidence obtained through MLATs and LRs generally enjoys high probative value in Indian 
courts, provided that chain of custody and authenticity are established. The Bharatiya Sakshya 
Adhiniyam, 2023 recognises electronic records and foreign certifications, subject to judicial 
scrutiny regarding reliability and lawful acquisition [19]. 
Indian courts have historically placed greater trust in evidence obtained through recognised 
international cooperation mechanisms, as opposed to informal or unilateral methods. This 
judicial attitude reinforces the strategic importance of MLATs and LRs, even when operational 
delays are frustrating at the investigative stage [20]. 
 
21.16 Strategic Integration of MLATs into Cybercrime Investigations 
MLATs and LRs should not be viewed as isolated procedural steps, but as integral components of 
a broader investigative strategy. Effective IOs plan their investigations around expected MLAT 
timelines, ensuring that domestic evidence collection, suspect examination, and financial 
analysis progress in parallel rather than awaiting foreign responses [21]. 
This integrated approach prevents investigative stagnation and ensures that when foreign 
evidence arrives, it fits seamlessly into an already developed prosecutorial narrative. 
 
[[PAGE 561]]
21.17 Conceptual Flowchart: MLAT vs LR Decision Path 
Textual SOP Flow: 
1. Evidence Located Abroad Identified 
↓ 
2. Check Existence of MLAT with Requested State 
→ Yes → Initiate MLAT Process 
→ No → Seek Court Approval for Letter Rogatory 
↓ 
3. Simultaneous Preservation Request (if applicable) 
↓ 
4. Formal Transmission via MHA / MEA 
↓ 
5. Execution by Foreign Authority / Court 
↓ 
6. Receipt and Legal Vetting of Evidence 
This decision flow highlights that MLATs and LRs are complementary tools, not interchangeable 
shortcuts [22]. 
 
21.18 Conclusion: Formal Cooperation as the Backbone of Cross-Border Legality 
MLATs and Letters Rogatory remain indispensable instruments for cross-border cybercrime 
investigations. While they may appear procedurally burdensome, their value lies in the legal 
certainty they confer upon evidence and prosecutions. For the UP Police, mastering these 
mechanisms is not merely a bureaucratic requirement but a strategic necessity in an era where 
cybercrime routinely transcends national borders [23]. 
The next Part will examine informal and emergency cooperation mechanisms, including 
INTERPOL channels, the G7 24/7 Network, and preservation requests—tools that complement 
formal processes by addressing the problem of evidentiary urgency. 
 
Part III: INTERPOL Channels, G7 24/7 Network & Emergency Evidence Preservation 
21.19 Introduction: Bridging the Time Gap Between Crime and Diplomacy 
Formal cooperation mechanisms such as MLATs and Letters Rogatory are legally sound but 
inherently slow. In cybercrime investigations, this delay often collides with the volatile nature of 
[[PAGE 562]]
digital evidence. Server logs are overwritten, IP allocation records expire, cloud-hosted content is 
deleted, and accounts are disabled pursuant to platform policies. To address this temporal 
mismatch, international law enforcement has developed informal yet structured cooperation 
channels designed to operate in parallel with formal requests [1]. 
For Investigating Officers (IOs) of the Uttar Pradesh Police, familiarity with INTERPOL 
communication systems, the G7 24/7 Cybercrime Network, and emergency preservation 
mechanisms is essential. These channels do not replace MLATs or Letters Rogatory; rather, they 
function as force multipliers, enabling investigators to secure time-sensitive evidence while 
formal legal processes are underway [2]. 
 
21.20 INTERPOL as an Operational Bridge in Cybercrime Investigations 
INTERPOL is the world’s largest international police organisation, facilitating cooperation 
among member countries through secure communication platforms and operational support. 
India participates in INTERPOL through the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), which 
functions as the National Central Bureau (NCB-India). All INTERPOL-related communications 
from Indian law enforcement agencies must be routed through NCB-India, ensuring centralised 
oversight and compliance with international protocols [3]. 
In cybercrime matters, INTERPOL does not exercise investigative powers itself. Instead, it acts 
as a conduit for information exchange, intelligence dissemination, and coordination between 
national law enforcement agencies. This role is particularly valuable in cases involving unknown 
suspects, transnational syndicates, or infrastructure spanning multiple jurisdictions [4]. 
 
21.21 The I-24/7 Secure Communication System 
INTERPOL’s I-24/7 system is a secure global police communications network connecting law 
enforcement agencies across member countries. It enables real-time exchange of messages, 
notices, and alerts, significantly reducing response times compared to diplomatic correspondence 
For cybercrime investigations, I-24/7 is commonly used to: 
 
Share preliminary intelligence regarding IP addresses, email accounts, or cryptocurrency 
wallets 
 
Request confirmation of subscriber details or account existence 
 
Alert foreign counterparts about ongoing cyber fraud patterns or active threat actors [6] 
However, IOs must understand that information shared via I-24/7 is intelligence, not evidence. 
Any data obtained through this channel must be subsequently formalised through MLATs or LRs 
[[PAGE 563]]
if it is to be relied upon in court. Courts may permit the use of such intelligence for investigation 
leads, but not as substantive proof of guilt [7]. 
 
21.22 INTERPOL Notices and Diffusions in Cybercrime Context 
INTERPOL issues several types of notices, of which the Red Notice is the most well-known. In 
cybercrime cases, Red Notices are typically sought when an accused person is located abroad 
and is wanted for prosecution or to serve a sentence. However, Red Notices are not arrest 
warrants; their execution depends on domestic law of the requested State [8]. 
In addition to Notices, INTERPOL facilitates Diffusions, which are less formal alerts circulated 
directly by NCBs to selected countries. Diffusions are particularly useful for rapidly sharing 
information about emerging cybercrime threats, suspected offenders, or modus operandi patterns 
[9]. 
For UP Police IOs, the practical takeaway is that INTERPOL Notices and Diffusions are 
strategic tools for person-centric cooperation, complementing evidence-centric mechanisms like 
MLATs. 
 
21.23 The G7 24/7 Cybercrime Network: Speed Over Formality 
The G7 24/7 Cybercrime Network was established to provide a rapid-response framework for 
international cooperation in cybercrime investigations. Participating countries designate points of 
contact available on a 24/7 basis to handle urgent requests related to cybercrime, including 
preservation of electronic evidence [10]. 
India participates in this network through designated central agencies, and requests from State 
police units must be routed through appropriate national channels. The defining feature of the G7 
24/7 Network is speed. Requests can be transmitted within hours, making it particularly effective 
for preserving data that is at imminent risk of deletion [11]. 
Unlike MLATs, the G7 24/7 Network does not require extensive documentation or judicial 
approval at the initial stage. However, its scope is limited to urgent assistance and does not 
extend to compelled disclosure of content data without subsequent formal requests [12]. 
 
21.24 Emergency Evidence Preservation: Legal Basis and Operational Necessity 
Preservation of digital evidence is the cornerstone of effective cross-border cybercrime 
investigation. Under Indian law, preservation requests are typically issued under procedural 
powers corresponding to the erstwhile Section 91 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, now 
reflected in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 [13]. 
[[PAGE 564]]
Emergency preservation requests are directed at service providers—both domestic and foreign—
to prevent deletion or alteration of specified data for a limited period. Major global platforms 
such as Google, Meta, and X (formerly Twitter) maintain law enforcement portals that accept 
preservation requests pending receipt of formal legal process [14]. 
From an SOP perspective, IOs must ensure that preservation requests: 
 
Clearly identify the account, identifier, or data sought 
 
Specify the legal basis for the request 
 
Indicate the urgency and risk of data loss 
 
Are followed up by formal MLAT or LR within prescribed timelines [15] 
Failure to convert a preservation request into a formal legal demand within the stipulated period 
may result in automatic release of preserved data. 
 
21.25 Interplay Between Preservation Requests and Formal Cooperation 
Emergency preservation is not an end in itself; it is a procedural bridge. Its purpose is to “freeze” 
the evidentiary status quo until formal cooperation mechanisms can be activated. International 
best practices emphasise that preservation requests must be sent immediately upon identification 
of foreign data, even before attribution is fully established [16]. 
For UP Police IOs, this means that hesitation or delay at the early stages of investigation can 
irreversibly compromise the case. Preservation should be treated as a default response in any 
cybercrime investigation with cross-border indicators. 
 
21.26 Risks and Legal Sensitivities in Informal Cooperation 
While informal channels offer speed, they also carry legal sensitivities. Overreliance on informal 
cooperation without transitioning to formal processes may invite defence challenges regarding 
legality and admissibility of evidence. Courts may scrutinise whether data was preserved or 
accessed in a manner consistent with due process and international norms [17]. 
Additionally, IOs must avoid direct contact with foreign service providers or law enforcement 
agencies outside approved channels. Such actions may violate diplomatic protocols and expose 
the investigation to procedural objections. 
 
21.27 Integrated SOP Flow: Informal to Formal Transition 
Textual SOP Flowchart: 
[[PAGE 565]]
1. Cross-Border Data Identified 
↓ 
2. Immediate Preservation Request Issued 
↓ 
3. Parallel Use of INTERPOL / G7 24/7 for Intelligence & Alerts 
↓ 
4. Formal MLAT / LR Prepared and Submitted 
↓ 
5. Preserved Data Disclosed Through Formal Legal Process 
↓ 
6. Evidence Analysed and Presented in Court 
This integrated flow ensures that speed and legality reinforce, rather than undermine, each other 
 
21.28 Strategic Value of Informal Cooperation in Transnational Crimes 
In complex cybercrime cases—such as Business Email Compromise, international investment 
fraud, and CSAM—informal cooperation channels often provide the first actionable leads. 
Intelligence shared through INTERPOL or preserved via emergency requests enables 
investigators to identify suspects, trace financial flows, and disrupt criminal operations before 
they escalate [19]. 
Global studies consistently show that jurisdictions which effectively combine informal and 
formal cooperation mechanisms achieve higher case resolution rates and stronger prosecutorial 
outcomes [20]. 
 
21.29 Conclusion: Speed with Accountability 
INTERPOL channels, the G7 24/7 Network, and emergency preservation mechanisms form the 
operational backbone of time-sensitive international cybercrime investigations. For the UP 
Police, mastering these tools is not optional; it is essential to prevent evidence loss and maintain 
investigative momentum. However, speed must always be accompanied by accountability, with 
informal actions promptly anchored in formal legal processes to ensure admissibility and judicial 
confidence [21]. 
[[PAGE 566]]
The next Part will address foreign evidence admissibility, extradition linkage, and judicial 
strategy, focusing on how cross-border evidence is ultimately evaluated by Indian courts and 
how investigative decisions shape prosecutorial success. 
 
Part IV: Foreign Evidence Admissibility, Extradition Linkage & Judicial Strategy 
21.30 Introduction: When Investigation Meets the Courtroom 
The ultimate success of a cross-border cybercrime investigation is determined not at the stage of 
data collection, but at the moment when foreign-sourced evidence is tested before an Indian 
court. For Investigating Officers (IOs) of the Uttar Pradesh Police, this transition—from 
investigative diligence to judicial scrutiny—requires a clear understanding of evidentiary law, 
procedural safeguards, and the strategic linkage between evidence collection and extradition 
proceedings. Foreign evidence, if not collected, preserved, and presented in a legally coherent 
manner, risks exclusion or dilution during trial, regardless of the seriousness of the offence or the 
strength of suspicion [1]. 
This Part focuses on how Indian courts assess foreign digital evidence, how admissibility 
standards under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) apply to cross-border material, 
and how extradition considerations influence investigative choices from an early stage. 
 
21.31 Concept of “Foreign Evidence” in Cybercrime Investigations 
Foreign evidence in cybercrime cases typically includes subscriber information, IP logs, 
transactional data, content records, cloud-stored files, and financial intelligence obtained from 
entities or authorities located outside India. Such evidence may be produced by foreign service 
providers, foreign law enforcement agencies, or foreign courts acting on Indian requests [2]. 
Indian law does not treat foreign evidence as inherently inadmissible. Instead, admissibility 
depends on the manner of acquisition, authenticity, and relevance of the material. Courts are 
primarily concerned with whether the evidence was obtained through lawful means recognised 
by both Indian law and international cooperation norms [3]. 
In cybercrime matters, where digital evidence forms the backbone of attribution and mens rea, 
foreign evidence often carries decisive probative value. This makes procedural compliance at the 
collection stage critically important. 
 
21.32 Admissibility Framework Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 modernises the evidentiary framework governing 
electronic records and continues to recognise digital evidence as admissible, subject to 
[[PAGE 567]]
satisfaction of authenticity and reliability standards. Electronic records obtained from foreign 
jurisdictions are evaluated on the same foundational principles as domestic electronic evidence, 
though courts apply heightened scrutiny given the cross-border context [4]. 
Key considerations for admissibility include: 
 
Whether the evidence is an “electronic record” within the meaning of the Act 
 
Whether the source and integrity of the data are established 
 
Whether certification or attestation accompanies the record, where applicable 
 
Whether the chain of custody is demonstrable and unbroken [5] 
Courts have consistently held that procedural irregularities in obtaining electronic evidence may 
not automatically render it inadmissible, but serious violations of law or due process can 
undermine evidentiary weight or lead to exclusion [6]. 
 
21.33 Role of Certification and Attestation in Foreign Electronic Evidence 
Certification plays a central role in establishing the authenticity of foreign electronic evidence. 
Where evidence is obtained through MLATs or Letters Rogatory, it is commonly accompanied 
by official certification from the executing authority or service provider. Such certification serves 
as prima facie proof of authenticity and reduces the burden on the prosecution to independently 
establish technical integrity [7]. 
In practice, Indian courts have shown greater willingness to rely on foreign electronic records 
when they are accompanied by: 
 
Official covering letters from foreign authorities 
 
Seals or attestations of executing courts or agencies 
 
Statements describing the method of data extraction and preservation [8] 
For IOs, ensuring that requests explicitly seek certified copies or authenticated extracts is a 
strategic necessity rather than a clerical detail. 
 
21.34 Chain of Custody in Cross-Border Contexts 
Chain of custody refers to the documented history of evidence from the point of collection to its 
production in court. In cross-border cybercrime cases, the chain of custody often spans multiple 
jurisdictions, agencies, and systems, increasing the risk of gaps or ambiguities [9]. 
Courts examine whether: 
[[PAGE 568]]
 
The evidence remained secure and unaltered 
 
Each transfer of custody is documented 
 
There is no unexplained delay or discrepancy in handling [10] 
While absolute perfection is not required, unexplained breaks in the chain may be exploited by 
the defence to cast doubt on reliability. IOs must therefore maintain meticulous records of when 
preservation was sought, when data was received, and how it was stored and analysed thereafter. 
 
21.35 Judicial Attitude Towards Evidence Obtained Through International Cooperation 
Indian courts have historically demonstrated a pragmatic approach towards foreign evidence 
obtained through recognised international cooperation mechanisms. Evidence sourced via 
MLATs, LRs, or official INTERPOL channels is generally viewed as more credible than material 
obtained through informal or unilateral means [11]. 
The judiciary recognises the practical realities of cybercrime investigations and has emphasised 
that insistence on hyper-technical compliance should not defeat substantive justice, particularly 
where serious offences affecting public interest are involved. However, this judicial latitude is 
contingent upon good faith compliance with established procedures [12]. 
 
21.36 Extradition as a Strategic Consideration in Cybercrime Investigations 
Extradition is not merely a post-investigation process; it is a strategic consideration that should 
inform investigative planning from an early stage. In cybercrime cases involving accused 
persons located abroad, the viability of extradition depends on factors such as dual criminality, 
treaty obligations, and the strength of evidence presented by the requesting State [13]. 
Weak or procedurally flawed evidence can undermine extradition requests, even where the 
offence is otherwise extraditable. Foreign courts assessing extradition requests often examine 
whether the requesting State has prima facie evidence sufficient to justify trial [14]. 
This makes the quality of foreign evidence, and the manner in which it is integrated with 
domestic material, a decisive factor in securing custody of accused persons. 
 
21.37 Linkage Between Evidence Collection and Extradition Proceedings 
There is a direct linkage between how evidence is collected and the success of extradition 
proceedings. Evidence obtained unlawfully or without clear legal basis may be challenged before 
foreign courts on human rights or due process grounds, resulting in refusal of extradition [15]. 
[[PAGE 569]]
International practice demonstrates that extradition requests supported by evidence collected 
through formal cooperation channels are more likely to succeed. Conversely, reliance on 
intelligence-only material or informally obtained data may be insufficient to meet foreign 
judicial thresholds [16]. 
For UP Police IOs, this underscores the importance of aligning investigative urgency with 
extradition strategy, rather than treating them as separate phases. 
 
21.38 Judicial Strategy: Presenting Cross-Border Evidence Effectively 
From a prosecutorial perspective, the presentation of foreign evidence requires careful judicial 
strategy. Courts must be guided through: 
 
The necessity of international cooperation 
 
The steps taken to preserve legality and authenticity 
 
The relevance of foreign evidence to specific charges [17] 
IOs play a crucial role in this process by preparing clear case diaries, annexing correspondence 
with central authorities, and assisting prosecutors in explaining the investigative chronology. A 
coherent narrative that demonstrates diligence, proportionality, and respect for international 
norms strengthens judicial confidence in the prosecution case [18]. 
 
21.39 Indicative Judicial Evaluation Flow for Foreign Evidence 
Textual Judicial Flow (Conceptual): 
1. Source of Evidence Identified (Foreign Jurisdiction) 
↓ 
2. Method of Acquisition Scrutinised (MLAT / LR / Formal Channel) 
↓ 
3. Authenticity & Certification Examined 
↓ 
4. Chain of Custody Verified 
↓ 
5. Relevance to Charged Offences Assessed 
↓ 
6. Admissibility Determined; Weight Assigned 
[[PAGE 570]]
Understanding this evaluative sequence allows IOs to anticipate judicial concerns and 
proactively address them during investigation [19]. 
 
21.40 Conclusion: Evidence, Extradition, and the Court as the Final Arbiter 
Foreign evidence is the linchpin of cross-border cybercrime prosecutions, but its value depends 
entirely on procedural integrity and strategic foresight. For the UP Police, success lies in 
recognising that international cooperation is not only about obtaining data, but about obtaining it 
in a manner that survives judicial scrutiny and supports extradition where necessary. By aligning 
investigative practices with evidentiary and extradition standards, IOs can ensure that cybercrime 
offenders are not only identified, but effectively prosecuted [20]. 
The final Part of this chapter will address specialised transnational cybercrime categories, 
consolidated SOPs, and integrated flowcharts, bringing together all elements discussed thus 
far into a unified operational framework. 
 
Part V: Transnational Cybercrime SOPs, Consolidated Flowcharts & Chapter Conclusion 
21.41 Introduction: From Legal Theory to Operational SOPs 
The preceding Parts of this Chapter have examined the legal architecture, cooperation 
mechanisms, evidentiary standards, and judicial strategy relevant to cross-border cybercrime 
investigations. This final Part translates those principles into crime-specific Standard 
Operating Procedures (SOPs) and consolidated operational flows for day-to-day use by 
Investigating Officers (IOs) of the Uttar Pradesh Police. 
The objective here is practical clarity. Transnational cybercrime investigations demand rapid, 
legally compliant, and well-documented responses. IOs are often required to act under time 
pressure, with incomplete information, while navigating international legal constraints. A 
structured SOP framework reduces uncertainty, minimises procedural errors, and enhances 
prosecutorial success [1]. 
 
SECTION A: CRIME-SPECIFIC TRANSNATIONAL SOPs 
 
21.42 SOP for Business Email Compromise (BEC) & International Payment Fraud 
Business Email Compromise (BEC) represents one of the most financially damaging categories 
of transnational cybercrime. These offences typically involve compromised email accounts, 
[[PAGE 571]]
spoofed domains, and cross-border fund transfers routed through mule accounts in multiple 
jurisdictions [2]. 
1. Immediate Incident Containment 
o Secure victim’s email systems and identify compromised credentials. 
o Preserve headers, login logs, and email content without alteration [3]. 
2. Urgent Financial Action 
o Coordinate with banks for immediate freezing of accounts under domestic 
banking and PMLA mechanisms. 
o Notify FIUs where cross-border money laundering indicators exist [4]. 
3. Emergency Preservation 
o Issue preservation requests to foreign email service providers (e.g., Google, 
Microsoft) and cloud platforms. 
o Preserve IP logs, session data, and account recovery details [5]. 
4. International Cooperation 
o Use INTERPOL / G7 24/7 Network to alert foreign counterparts where funds 
have landed. 
o Initiate MLAT requests for subscriber data, payment records, and account 
ownership details [6]. 
5. Prosecution Alignment 
o Map foreign evidence with offences under BNS, IT Act, and PMLA. 
o Maintain documentation for extradition feasibility if accused is located abroad 
 
21.43 SOP for International Investment & Crypto-Based Scams 
International investment scams increasingly exploit cryptocurrencies, foreign exchanges, and 
shell entities incorporated overseas. These cases often involve layered transactions designed to 
frustrate jurisdictional tracing [8]. 
1. Victim Statement & Transaction Mapping 
[[PAGE 572]]
o Obtain detailed investment trail, wallet addresses, and communication records. 
o Preserve screenshots and platform transaction IDs [9]. 
2. Blockchain & Financial Intelligence 
o Coordinate with specialised cyber forensic units for blockchain analysis. 
o Identify exchanges or custodial wallets located outside India [10]. 
3. Preservation & Platform Engagement 
o Send preservation requests to foreign exchanges and wallet service providers. 
o Document all responses and platform timelines [11]. 
4. Formal Legal Requests 
o MLATs for KYC records, transaction logs, and withdrawal destinations. 
o Letters Rogatory where treaty mechanisms are unavailable [12]. 
5. Judicial Strategy 
o Clearly explain technical financial flows to prosecutors and courts. 
o Align evidence with cheating, criminal breach of trust, and laundering offences 
 
21.44 SOP for Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) with Foreign Nexus 
CSAM cases demand heightened urgency due to the continuing harm to victims and stringent 
international obligations. Digital platforms hosting or transmitting CSAM are often 
headquartered abroad [14]. 
1. Immediate Content Securing 
o Do not download or redistribute content unnecessarily. 
o Secure hashes, URLs, and platform identifiers [15]. 
2. Emergency Preservation 
o Immediate preservation requests to platforms hosting or transmitting CSAM. 
o Notify national nodal agencies as per standing instructions [16]. 
3. INTERPOL Coordination 
[[PAGE 573]]
o Use NCB-India to trigger international victim identification mechanisms. 
o Share intelligence for offender tracking across jurisdictions [17]. 
4. Formal Requests & Prosecution 
o MLATs for uploader identification, IP logs, and account history. 
o Ensure strict chain of custody and confidentiality [18]. 
5. Victim-Centric Approach 
o Coordinate with child protection units. 
o Avoid investigative delays that perpetuate victimisation [19].





 
Preservation steps demonstrated 
 
Formal cooperation route documented 


 
Relevance to charges clearly articulated 
Such structured explanation significantly improves judicial confidence in complex cybercrime

SECTION C: INSTITUTIONAL & STRATEGIC TAKEAWAYS 
21.47 Institutional Coordination within the Indian Cybercrime Ecosystem 
Effective handling of transnational cybercrime requires coordination beyond the investigating 
police station. IOs must actively engage with: 
 
State Cyber Crime Units 
 
I4C platforms and reporting portals 
 
Central agencies such as MHA, CBI-NCB, and MEA 
Fragmented or siloed action weakens international credibility and delays evidence acquisition 
[22]. 
21.48 Capacity Building and Procedural Discipline 
Global experience demonstrates that jurisdictions with trained investigators and standardised 
templates achieve faster international cooperation outcomes. Procedural discipline—timely 
preservation, accurate documentation, and legally precise requests—is often more decisive than 
technological sophistication alone [23]. 
21.49 Chapter Conclusion: Enforcing Law Beyond Borders, Lawfully 
Cybercrime has redefined the meaning of jurisdiction, evidence, and enforcement. For the Uttar 
Pradesh Police, the challenge is no longer whether crimes cross borders, but how effectively law 
enforcement can respond within the constraints of international law. This Chapter has provided a 
[[PAGE 575]]
comprehensive SOP framework to ensure that Investigating Officers can act swiftly without 
sacrificing legality, and pursue offenders globally while remaining anchored to domestic due 
process [24]. 
International cooperation is not a procedural burden; it is an operational necessity. When used 
intelligently—combining emergency preservation, informal coordination, and formal legal 
requests—it transforms jurisdictional complexity into investigative strength. Ultimately, the 
legitimacy of cybercrime enforcement lies not in unilateral reach, but in coordinated, lawful, and 
accountable action across borders [25]. 
 
CHAPTER 22 
REPORTING, CHARGESHEET & PROSECUTION SUPPORT 
PART I 
PHILOSOPHY OF REPORTING & THE DIGITAL-TO-LEGAL TRANSLATION 
FRAMEWORK 
 
22.1 Prefatory Note from Headquarters 
Cyber crime investigation does not fail in court because technology is weak; it fails because 
technology is not translated into law with the discipline and narrative clarity that a criminal 
court requires. Over the last decade, including the transition phase from the Indian Evidence Act 
to the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, repeated acquittals in cyber-enabled offences have 
shown a consistent pattern: evidence exists, forensic reports are technically sound, but the 
reporting and presentation do not speak the language of adjudication [1]. 
This chapter, therefore, begins with a doctrinal shift. Reporting is not clerical. A chargesheet is 
not a compilation of documents. Prosecution support is not an afterthought. Together, they form 
a continuum of translation, where a volatile digital trace must be converted into a stable legal 
fact capable of surviving judicial scrutiny under cross-examination and appellate review [2]. 
 
22.2 Reporting as a Judicial Interface, Not an Administrative Closure 
In conventional policing, the Final Report or Chargesheet has often been treated as the terminal 
point of investigation. In cyber crime, this approach is structurally flawed. Digital evidence has 
no self-evident meaning. An IP address, a hash value, a server log, or a blockchain transaction 
does not “speak” unless the Investigating Officer explains what it means, how it was 
generated, and why it is reliable [3]. 
[[PAGE 576]]
The report submitted under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 is, in effect, the first 
judicial exposure to the case. For many Magistrates and even Sessions Courts, the police report 
becomes the primary lens through which the complexity of cyber operations is understood. Any 
ambiguity, excessive jargon, or unexplained forensic assertion at this stage permanently weakens 
the prosecution [4]. 
Therefore, reporting in cyber cases must be treated as a judicial communication document, 
drafted with the conscious assumption that the reader is legally trained but technologically non-
specialist. 
 
22.3 The Digital-to-Legal Translation Problem 
Cyber investigations generate three categories of material: 
1. Machine-generated data (logs, metadata, hash outputs) 
2. Forensic interpretations (expert conclusions, timelines, correlations) 
3. Human conduct in digital space (intent, deception, concealment) 
Courts do not convict on data. Courts convict on proved facts and legally inferred intent. The 
gap between these two is the digital-to-legal translation problem [5]. 
For example, a forensic report may state that a log file was deleted at 14:03 hours. This, by itself, 
is a neutral technical fact. The reporting officer must translate this into a legally relevant 
inference: that the deletion occurred after receipt of the lawful notice, or immediately 
following the fraudulent transaction, indicating conscious suppression of evidence [6]. 
Without this translation, even accurate forensic findings remain evidentiary fragments, not 
prosecutable facts. 
 
22.4 Understanding the Judge’s Cognitive Framework 
A criminal court operates on structured presumptions defined by the Bharatiya Sakshya 
Adhiniyam, 2023. Sections 57 and 63, read together, demand clarity on three issues: 
 
What is the original electronic record 
 
How was the copy produced 
 
Why should the Court rely on it [7] 
Judges are trained to distrust evidence that appears opaque or excessively technical without 
explanation. In cyber cases, this distrust is often subconscious. The Investigating Officer must 
[[PAGE 577]]
therefore pre-empt judicial discomfort by explaining digital processes through legal analogies, 
not engineering manuals [8]. 
This chapter repeatedly emphasises that the IO’s role extends beyond collection into interpretive 
authorship. 
 
22.5 The Concept of the “Digital-to-Legal Translation Matrix” 
The Digital-to-Legal Translation Matrix is an internal conceptual tool that every cyber 
investigator must apply before final reporting. It answers four mandatory questions for every 
digital artefact: 
1. What exactly is this artefact? 
2. How was it generated or seized? 
3. What does it prove in human terms? 
4. Which legal ingredient does it satisfy? 
If any artefact cannot be mapped across all four axes, it is evidentially incomplete and must 
either be supplemented or excluded [9]. 
This matrix ensures that the chargesheet is not a dump of forensic outputs but a coherent legal 
narrative supported by technology. 
 
22.6 Explaining Hash Values: From Mathematics to Judicial Trust 
One of the most misunderstood elements in cyber trials is the hash value. Investigators often 
mention hash values mechanically, without explaining their legal relevance. This has resulted in 
courts treating hashes as ornamental rather than foundational [10]. 
A hash value must be explained as a digital fingerprint — a unique mathematical summary of a 
file at a particular point in time. Just as a human fingerprint confirms identity and non-tampering, 
a hash confirms that the electronic record presented in court is the same record that was seized 
or generated during investigation [11]. 
The report must explicitly state: 
 
When the hash was generated 
 
On which device or system 
 
Whether the hash remained consistent throughout custody 
Failure to narrate this chain breaks evidentiary continuity under Section 63(4) of the BSA [12]. 
[[PAGE 578]]
 
22.7 Artefact Narratives: From Technical Finding to Criminal Conduct 
Courts do not assess artefacts in isolation. They assess conduct. Therefore, every digital artefact 
must be embedded within a behavioural narrative. 
A registry key indicating disabled logging is meaningless unless the IO explains: 
 
That logging was active prior to the incident 
 
That it was disabled shortly before or after the offence 
 
That such disabling is not system-default behaviour 
This narrative establishes conscious intervention, a critical element in proving mens rea in 
cyber offences involving cheating, impersonation, or forgery [13]. 
The chargesheet must therefore convert “what was found” into “what was done” and finally into 
“why it was done”. 
 
22.8 Reporting as the Foundation of Double-Barrelled Prosecution 
Cyber offences in India rarely survive on the Information Technology Act alone. Experience has 
shown that convictions improve significantly when IT Act offences are paired with substantive 
offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [14]. 
This pairing, however, must begin at the reporting stage. If the report does not narrate deception, 
inducement, wrongful gain, or concealment in human terms, the BNS sections appear artificially 
added later, weakening prosecutorial coherence [15]. 
Thus, Part I establishes that reporting is the architectural base upon which charges, annexures, 
and prosecution strategy are constructed. 
 
22.9 Institutional Consequences of Poor Reporting 
Poor cyber reporting has systemic costs: 
 
Acquittals that embolden organised cyber syndicates 
 
Judicial scepticism toward future police evidence 
 
Repeated remands for “clarification”, delaying justice 
[[PAGE 579]]
Conversely, well-structured reporting has resulted in courts relying heavily on police narratives 
even in technically complex cases, provided the explanation is legally disciplined and factually 
restrained [16]. 
This chapter does not seek verbosity; it seeks clarity with accountability. 
 
22.10 Transition to Chargesheet Architecture 
Having established the philosophical and doctrinal foundations of reporting, the next part of this 
chapter will move from why reporting matters to how a cyber chargesheet must be 
constructed. Part II will deal with narrative sequencing, section mapping, annexure engineering, 
and the creation of a Digital Evidence Folder designed specifically for judicial consumption. 
 
PART II 
CYBER-SPECIFIC CHARGESHEET CONSTRUCTION & NARRATIVE ARCHITECTURE 
 
22.11 The Chargesheet as a Digital Case Narrative, Not a Form-Filling Exercise 
In cyber crime investigations, the chargesheet is the primary narrative artefact through which 
the State presents a technologically complex crime in legally comprehensible form. It is not a 
clerical summary of investigation steps, nor merely a statutory compliance document under the 
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. It is, instead, a curated story of digital conduct, 
sequenced in a manner that allows a judicial mind to travel from allegation to attribution, from 
attribution to intent, and from intent to offence [1]. 
Experience at Cyber Crime Police Headquarters has repeatedly shown that technically strong 
cases collapse when the chargesheet reads like a laboratory inventory. Conversely, even 
moderately complex cyber cases have resulted in conviction where the chargesheet narrates a 
clear, linear digital trail supported by legally mapped evidence [2]. 
 
22.12 Principle of Narrative Primacy in Cyber Chargesheets 
The first structural principle in cyber-specific chargesheet drafting is narrative primacy. The 
court must be able to understand the case without opening annexures on first reading. 
Annexures support the story; they do not replace it [3]. 
Accordingly, the narrative section of the chargesheet must answer, in plain but legally precise 
language: 
[[PAGE 580]]
 
Who initiated the digital interaction 
 
Through which platform or medium 
 
What deception or unauthorised act occurred 
 
How the digital trail establishes authorship 
 
Why the conduct satisfies statutory ingredients 
This narrative discipline is essential because cyber offences are process crimes, not event 
crimes. The offence unfolds over time, across devices, platforms, and jurisdictions [4]. 
 
22.13 The “Digital Trail” Doctrine 
Unlike physical crimes, cyber crimes leave no single crime scene. The crime scene is 
distributed across servers, devices, telecom networks, financial platforms, and cloud 
infrastructure. The chargesheet must therefore follow what is termed the Digital Trail Doctrine 
This doctrine mandates that the chargesheet narrative be organised chronologically along the 
digital trail, typically in the following sequence: 
1. Genesis Point – account creation, SIM activation, domain registration, or wallet creation 
2. Operational Phase – execution of fraudulent acts, communications, transactions 
3. Monetisation Phase – transfer, layering, withdrawal, or conversion of proceeds 
4. Concealment Phase – deletion of logs, VPN usage, identity masking 
5. Attribution Phase – forensic linkage to accused persons 
Any deviation from this order confuses causality and weakens evidentiary appreciation [6]. 
 
22.14 Structuring the Chargesheet: Recommended Architecture 
A cyber-specific chargesheet should adopt the following internal architecture, even if the 
external format follows state or district templates: 
1. Introductory Synopsis 
2. Chronological Digital Narrative 
3. Role Attribution of Each Accused 
4. Legal Section Mapping 
[[PAGE 581]]
5. Evidence Index with Purpose Statement 
6. Annexure Overview & Certification Reference 
This structure ensures that the court encounters the case as a coherent digital story, not a 
disjointed set of facts [7]. 
 
22.15 Introductory Synopsis: Setting the Judicial Context 
The introductory synopsis should be concise but conceptually rich. It must inform the court: 
 
Nature of cyber offence 
 
Platform(s) involved 
 
Victim profile 
 
Financial or data impact 
 
Cross-border or organised elements, if any 
This section functions as the judicial orientation paragraph. It should avoid technical jargon 
while clearly indicating that the offence involves specialised digital evidence [8]. 
Failure to properly frame this synopsis often leads courts to underestimate the complexity and 
seriousness of the offence. 
 
22.16 Chronological Digital Narrative: Time as the Spine 
Time sequencing is the backbone of cyber chargesheets. Every digital event must be placed on a 
timeline. Vague expressions such as “during investigation it was found” must be avoided. 
Instead, the chargesheet should specify: 
 
Date and time of digital events 
 
Time zone reference, if logs are server-generated 
 
Correlation between different timelines 
Courts have repeatedly emphasised that absence of temporal clarity undermines the reliability of 
digital evidence [9]. 
 
22.17 IP Address Allocation to Device Attribution 
[[PAGE 582]]
One of the most critical narrative transitions in cyber chargesheets is the movement from IP 
address identification to human attribution. An IP address is not a person. The chargesheet 
must explicitly bridge this gap [10]. 
This bridge requires narration of: 
 
ISP allocation records 
 
Subscriber details 
 
Correlation with device seizure 
 
Matching of device artefacts with network logs 
Without this narrative bridge, defence arguments of open Wi-Fi, shared networks, or spoofing 
gain disproportionate traction [11]. 
 
22.18 Device Seizure as a Narrative Turning Point 
The seizure of digital devices is not merely a procedural step; it is a narrative turning point. 
The chargesheet must explain: 
 
Why the device was relevant 
 
How it was identified 
 
Under what authority it was seized 
 
How its integrity was preserved 
This explanation is crucial to establish continuity between online activity and offline possession 
Courts scrutinise device seizures intensely, particularly in cyber cases involving multiple users or 
shared premises. 
 
22.19 Forensic Match as the Moment of Attribution 
The forensic match — between seized device artefacts and online activity — represents the 
moment of attribution. This must be narrated carefully, without overstatement. 
The chargesheet should explain: 
 
What artefact was found 
 
How it corresponds to the online activity 
[[PAGE 583]]
 
Why coincidence is improbable 
Forensic certainty must be presented as reasoned confidence, not absolute infallibility. Over-
assertion has repeatedly backfired under cross-examination [13]. 
 
22.20 Legal Section Mapping: The Double-Barrelled Model 
Cyber offences rarely fit neatly into a single statute. Effective prosecution requires double-
barrelled section mapping, combining the Information Technology Act, 2000 with the 
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [14]. 
For example: 
 
Identity theft under §66C IT Act must be mapped with cheating or impersonation 
provisions under the BNS. 
 
Online fraud under §66D IT Act must be supported by sections relating to dishonest 
inducement and wrongful gain. 
This mapping must be explained in the chargesheet narrative, not left for the prosecutor to 
reconstruct later [15]. 
22.21 Avoiding Mechanical Section Listing 
A common error is the mechanical listing of multiple sections without explaining how each 
ingredient is satisfied. Courts have consistently disapproved of this approach [16]. 
For each section invoked, the chargesheet should briefly state: 
 
The legal ingredient 
 
The factual assertion satisfying it 
 
The supporting evidence category 
This practice significantly strengthens the prosecution’s position at the stage of framing of 
charge. 
22.22 The Role Attribution Matrix 
In cases involving multiple accused, particularly organised cyber frauds, the chargesheet must 
clearly differentiate roles. Collective narration creates ambiguity and benefits the defence [17]. 
Role attribution should specify: 
 
Who created accounts 
 
Who operated communication channels 
[[PAGE 584]]
 
Who handled proceeds 
 
Who provided technical facilitation 
Even where conspiracy is alleged, individual acts must be narrated with specificity. 
22.23 Evidence Indexing with Purpose Statements 
Merely annexing documents is insufficient. Each annexure should be referenced in the 
chargesheet with a purpose statement, explaining what it proves [18]. 
For example: 
 
“Annexure-12 2 establishes that the accused’s device accessed the fraudulent account at the 
relevant time.” 
This practice aligns with judicial expectations under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 and 
reduces the burden on the trial court [19]. 
22.24 The Digital Evidence Folder Concept 
Cyber chargesheets should include a distinct Digital Evidence Folder within the physical or 
electronic file. This folder must contain: 
 
Certified electronic records 
 
Hash value documentation 
 
Chain of custody records 
 
Section 63(4) certificates 
Segregating digital evidence prevents confusion and reinforces evidentiary discipline [20]. 
22.25 Section 63(4) Certification Integration 
Certificates under Section 63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 must not be treated 
as detachable appendices. The chargesheet narrative should explicitly reference: 
 
Who issued the certificate 
 
For which record 
 
At what stage 
Failure to integrate certification into the narrative has resulted in exclusion of otherwise reliable 
evidence [21]. 
22.26 Common Narrative Pitfalls in Cyber Chargesheets 
Field review of failed prosecutions has revealed recurring narrative defects: 
[[PAGE 585]]
 
Excessive reproduction of forensic reports 
 
Absence of human conduct explanation 
 
Poor time correlation 
 
Over-technical language without legal framing 
These defects are not technical failures; they are narrative failures [22]. 
22.27 Chargesheet as Prosecution-Ready Document 
The ultimate test of a cyber chargesheet is simple: Can a prosecutor argue the case without re-
investigating it? If the answer is no, the chargesheet has failed in its core purpose [23]. 
A well-constructed cyber chargesheet should allow the prosecutor to focus on persuasion, not 
reconstruction. 
22.28 Transition to Annexure Strategy and Evidence Engineering 
Having established the architecture and narrative discipline of cyber chargesheets, the next part 
of this chapter will address Annexure Strategy, Digital Evidence Indexing, and Certification 
Protocols in detail. Part III will focus on transforming evidence from admissible to unassailable. 
PART III  
 ANNEXURE STRATEGY, DIGITAL EVIDENCE INDEXING & ADMISSIBILITY 
ENGINEERING 
22.29 Why Annexures Decide Cyber Trials 
In cyber crime prosecutions, courts do not reject cases because offences are not proved; they 
reject them because evidence is not legally consumable. The annexure section of a chargesheet 
is where most cyber cases silently fail. Either documents are voluminous but directionless, or 
technically accurate but legally uncertified. Both defects are fatal [1]. 
Annexures are not supplementary paperwork. They are the legal scaffolding that supports the 
narrative constructed in the chargesheet. If the narrative is the story, annexures are the proof 
architecture. In cyber cases, where the “original” exists only in electronic form, annexure 
discipline determines admissibility itself [2]. 
22.30 The Shift from Collection to Engineering 
Traditional policing treats annexures as a by-product of investigation. Cyber policing must treat 
annexures as engineered outputs, deliberately curated to meet statutory thresholds under the 
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. This is not a matter of form, but of constitutional fair trial 
standards [3]. 
Every annexure must be evaluated on three axes before filing: 
[[PAGE 586]]
1. Source legitimacy – where did it originate? 
2. Integrity assurance – how is tampering excluded? 
3. Judicial intelligibility – can a court understand its relevance? 
If any annexure fails even one axis, it must be corrected or excluded, irrespective of investigative 
effort invested in it [4]. 
22.31 Understanding “Original” in Digital Evidence 
One of the most persistent misconceptions among investigators is the notion of an “original” 
electronic record. Unlike paper documents, digital records do not have a single physical original. 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 resolves this by legally recognising certain electronic 
outputs as admissible provided statutory conditions are met [5]. 
The annexure strategy must therefore clearly identify: 
 
What constitutes the original source system 
 
How the data was extracted from that system 
 
In what form it is being produced before court 
Ambiguity on this issue has led courts to treat evidence as secondary without proper 
certification, resulting in exclusion [6]. 
22.32 The Digital Evidence Folder: Structural Separation 
Every cyber chargesheet must contain a clearly demarcated Digital Evidence Folder within the 
case file. This folder is not symbolic; it is functional. It segregates electronic evidence from 
conventional documents and signals to the court that special evidentiary rules apply [7]. 
The Digital Evidence Folder should be indexed separately and include: 
 
Certified electronic records 
 
Forensic reports with hash values 
 
Chain of custody documentation 
 
Section 63(4) certificates 
 
Extraction logs and screenshots 
This segregation reduces judicial confusion and enhances evidentiary clarity during trial [8]. 
22.33 Evidence Indexing as a Judicial Navigation Tool 
[[PAGE 587]]
Courts do not read annexures linearly. They navigate them selectively. A poorly indexed 
annexure bundle burdens the court and irritates the adjudicator, subconsciously affecting 
evidentiary appreciation [9]. 
Each annexure must therefore be indexed with: 
 
Annexure number 
 
Description of content 
 
Source of record 
 
Purpose statement (what it proves) 
This index is not a formality. It is a judicial navigation tool, enabling quick correlation between 
narrative assertions and evidentiary support [10]. 
22.34 Purpose Statements: The Missing Link 
A common defect observed in cyber cases is annexures without purpose statements. Documents 
are annexed, but the court is left to guess their relevance. This is unacceptable [11]. 
For every digital annexure, the chargesheet must briefly state: 
“This annexure establishes…” 
This single sentence transforms a document from passive data into active evidence. It also aligns 
with judicial expectations under Sections 57 and 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 
22.35 Certification under Section 63(4): Not a Ritual 
Certification under Section 63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 is often treated 
mechanically. This has been a major cause of cyber acquittals. Certification is not a ritualistic 
attachment; it is a jurisdictional requirement for admissibility [13]. 
The annexure strategy must ensure that: 
 
Every electronic record relied upon has a corresponding certificate 
 
The certificate identifies the device or system 
 
The process of production is described 
 
The signatory is legally competent 
A missing or defective certificate cannot be cured at the stage of argument without risking 
exclusion [14]. 
22.36 Integrating Certificates into the Narrative 
[[PAGE 588]]
Another common error is treating certificates as detachable appendices. Courts have repeatedly 
held that certificates must be linked to the evidence they authenticate [15]. 
The chargesheet narrative should explicitly refer to: 
 
Annexure number 
 
Corresponding certificate number 
 
Issuing authority 
This integration prevents defence arguments that certificates were filed belatedly or without 
nexus [16]. 
22.37 Hash Values as Integrity Anchors 
Hash values are the backbone of digital integrity assurance. However, annexures often mention 
hashes without context, rendering them meaningless [17]. 
The annexure strategy must ensure that: 
 
Hash values are mentioned at the point of extraction 
 
Re-hashing at subsequent stages is documented 
 
Consistency is explicitly stated 
Hash documentation must be chronological. A hash without temporal context invites doubt rather 
than trust [18]. 
22.38 Chain of Custody: From Device to Courtroom 
Chain of custody is not merely a seizure memo. In cyber cases, it is a continuous integrity 
narrative from device seizure to courtroom production [19]. 
The Digital Evidence Folder must include: 
 
Seizure memo with device identifiers 
 
Storage conditions 
 
Access logs 
 
Transfer records 
Any unexplained gap in custody creates a presumption of vulnerability, even without proof of 
tampering [20]. 
22.39 Screenshots, Printouts, and Judicial Skepticism 
[[PAGE 589]]
Screenshots and printouts are frequently used but poorly explained. Courts are sceptical of such 
evidence unless extraction methodology is clearly documented [21]. 
Annexures containing screenshots must specify: 
 
Source URL or application 
 
Date and time of capture 
 
Device used 
 
Certification reference 
Uncertified screenshots are among the most commonly rejected forms of cyber evidence [22]. 
22.40 Forensic Reports: Annexing Without Abdicating 
Forensic reports must be annexed, but not blindly reproduced. The chargesheet must explain why 
the report matters, not merely what it states [23]. 
Annexure strategy requires that: 
 
Reports are summarised in narrative 
 
Key findings are highlighted 
 
Technical jargon is translated into legal relevance 
The court relies on the IO’s explanation to contextualise expert opinion [24]. 
22.41 Examiner of Electronic Evidence and Institutional Credibility 
Reports from notified Examiners of Electronic Evidence under the Information Technology Act, 
2000 carry enhanced credibility. Annexure indexing should clearly identify such reports and their 
statutory status [25]. 
Failure to highlight examiner status often results in courts treating expert reports as ordinary 
opinion evidence [26]. 
22.42 Avoiding the “Data Dump” Syndrome 
Volume does not equal strength. One of the gravest mistakes in cyber chargesheets is annexing 
excessive data without filtration. This overwhelms courts and obscures critical evidence [27]. 
Annexure strategy must prioritise relevance over quantity. Redundant data should be excluded, 
even if lawfully collected. 
22.43 Admissibility Engineering as Conviction Strategy 
Admissibility engineering is the conscious design of evidence presentation to withstand 
exclusionary objections. It requires anticipating defence challenges before they are raised [28]. 
[[PAGE 590]]
Every annexure must be tested against probable objections: 
 
Source authenticity 
 
Integrity 
 
 
Relevance 
If an annexure cannot survive this mental cross-examination, it should not reach court in its 
present form [29]. 
22.44 Institutional Learning from Failed Annexures 
Internal audits of acquittals reveal that most failures arise not from absence of evidence, but from 
inadmissible evidence. This is an institutional problem, not an individual lapse [30]. 
This SOP mandates that annexure scrutiny be treated as a supervisory function, not left solely to 
the IO. 
22.45 Transition to Prosecution Support and Trial Readiness 
Having addressed annexure strategy and admissibility engineering, the next part of this chapter 
will focus on Prosecution Support & Trial Readiness, including prosecutor tech-briefs, 
courtroom translation of complex cyber concepts, and failure-aware pre-trial checklists. 
 
PART V - FAILURE-AWARE CHECKLIST: 50 COMMON REASONS FOR CYBER 
ACQUITTALS & PREVENTIVE CONTROLS 
22.62 Why Cyber Acquittals Are Predictable, Not Accidental 
Cyber acquittals rarely occur due to absence of criminal conduct. They occur because failure 
patterns repeat across jurisdictions, investigators, and trial courts. These failures are not 
random; they are systemic and therefore predictable. A failure-aware investigation treats acquittal 
reasons as risk indicators, not post-mortem statistics [1]. 
This Part converts years of judicial feedback, trial observations, and appellate reasoning into a 
preventive control framework, enabling investigators and prosecutors to intercept weaknesses 
before filing or before evidence is led [2]. 
 
22.63 Philosophy of the Failure-Aware Checklist 
[[PAGE 591]]
The checklist is not punitive. It is institutional. Its objective is not to blame the Investigating 
Officer, but to ensure that no avoidable defect travels into court. Each failure reason is paired 
with a corrective control, making this section operational rather than theoretical [3]. 
This checklist must be applied: 
 
Before filing the chargesheet 
 
Before cognizance 
 
Before commencement of prosecution evidence
