CHAPTER 24 
 
PART I – THE CONSTITUTIONAL COMPASS FOR CYBER INVESTIGATORS  
 
1.1 Opening Note from Headquarters 
Cyber crime investigation in the present era is no longer a contest of technical superiority alone; 
it is equally a test of constitutional discipline. Every digital footprint accessed by a police officer 
carries with it an invisible but enforceable envelope of fundamental rights, most notably the right 
to privacy under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. This chapter is therefore not an advisory 
note but a binding operational doctrine for all Cyber Crime Police Stations, District Cyber Units, 
and Special Task Forces functioning under the Uttar Pradesh Police. Its object is to ensure that 
investigations remain legally sustainable, ethically defensible, and institutionally honourable, 
even under intense public or political pressure [1]. 
Field experience from cyber fraud, social media abuse, and organised online financial crime 
cases has repeatedly demonstrated that technically correct investigations still fail in court due to 
constitutional lapses at the data collection stage. Courts do not assess intent; they assess 
compliance. A single unjustified intrusion into private digital space can contaminate the entire 
evidentiary chain, regardless of how strong the remaining evidence may appear [2]. 
 
1.2 Privacy as a Fundamental Right: Operational Meaning for Police 
The Supreme Court of India, in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, conclusively 
held that the right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under 
Article 21. Importantly for police officers, the Court clarified that privacy includes 
informational privacy, which directly governs personal data stored on mobile phones, laptops, 
cloud accounts, financial apps, email servers, and social media platforms [3]. 
In practical terms, this means that a seized smartphone is not merely an object; it is a repository 
of an individual’s medical history, intimate relationships, financial behaviour, beliefs, and 
communications. Treating such a device as a routine exhibit without constitutional sensitivity 
exposes the investigation to judicial invalidation. The Supreme Court has made it clear that 
digital lives deserve the same, if not higher, protection than physical spaces [4]. 
 
1.3 The Three-Fold Test: From Judgment to Field Practice 
[[PAGE 662]]
The Puttaswamy judgment laid down a three-fold test to assess privacy infringements: legality, 
legitimate state aim, and proportionality. These principles must now be read into every cyber 
investigation file, seizure memo, and forensic requisition prepared by an Investigating Officer 
Legality (Field Illustration): 
In multiple cyber fraud cases, devices have been seized merely because they were “available at 
the spot”. Such seizures, without linkage to a statutory power under the Bharatiya Nagarik 
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 or a judicial warrant, have been questioned by courts. In Pooran Mal v. 
Director of Inspection, the Supreme Court cautioned that unlawful searches may not 
automatically invalidate evidence, but modern privacy jurisprudence has significantly narrowed 
this tolerance, especially for digital data [6]. 
Legitimate State Aim (Field Illustration): 
In online defamation or social media comment cases, entire account histories have been 
requisitioned despite the alleged offence relating to a single post. Courts have increasingly 
viewed such actions as investigative overreach lacking a legitimate state aim. The Delhi High 
Court, in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, emphasised that state action affecting fundamental 
rights must be demonstrably linked to a public interest objective, not administrative convenience 
Proportionality (Field Illustration): 
A recurring mistake observed is full mobile phone cloning when only WhatsApp chat logs or 
UPI transaction records are relevant. In Canara Bank v. Union of India, the Supreme Court 
reiterated that privacy invasion must be proportionate to necessity. Wholesale data extraction, 
particularly of photos, personal videos, or unrelated communications, has been judicially 
frowned upon and can render forensic reports vulnerable to exclusion [8]. 
 
1.4 Constitutional Consequences of Over-Collection 
Over-collection of digital data is not a harmless investigative excess; it is a constitutional breach 
with cascading consequences. Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, courts are 
required to examine the lawfulness of acquisition, integrity of handling, and authenticity of 
electronic records. Evidence tainted by unconstitutional collection methods risks being 
disbelieved or struck off entirely [9]. 
In State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh, although decided in a different context, the Supreme Court 
underscored that procedural safeguards are not empty formalities. This principle now applies 
with even greater force to cyber investigations, where the scope for abuse is significantly higher 
due to the volume and sensitivity of data involved [10]. 
 
[[PAGE 663]]
1.5 Balancing Investigation and Liberty: The Police Ethos 
Effective cyber policing does not demand maximum intrusion; it demands measured intrusion. 
Investigations that respect constitutional limits tend to withstand cross-examination, appellate 
scrutiny, and defence challenges far better than aggressive but legally fragile operations. This is 
not theory; it is the lived experience of cyber prosecutors across districts [11]. 
The Supreme Court in Selvi v. State of Karnataka categorically held that investigative shortcuts 
violating personal liberty, even if scientifically advanced, cannot override constitutional 
guarantees. This judgment serves as a constant reminder that technology cannot be used to 
bypass rights that the Constitution has placed beyond executive convenience [12]. 
 
1.6 Hindi Operational Note (Field Guidance) 
मैदानी स्तर पर क्रनदेश: 
यकद ककसी केस में केवल बैंक ट्ाींज़ैक्शन या ककसी कवशेष चैट की आवश्यकता है, तो पूरे मोबाइल फोन या 
ईमेल अकाउींट का डेटा कनकालना उकचत नहीीं है। 
जाूँच अकधकारी को यह कलक्तखत रूप में स्पष्ट करना होगा कक कौन-सा डेटा ककस अपराध से जुड़ा है। 
अनावश्यक कनजी फोटो, वीकडयो या बातचीत देखने से केस कोटभ में कमजोर पड़ सकता है और अकधकारी 
की जवाबदेही तय हो सकती है [13]. 
 
1.7 Scope of This Chapter 
The subsequent parts of this chapter will convert constitutional principles into clear operational 
SOPs, covering search and seizure documentation, intermediary data requests, cloud evidence 
handling, victim privacy protocols, ethical undercover cyber operations, and institutional 
accountability frameworks. Officers must treat this chapter as a living compliance manual, not 
merely a policy statement [14]. 
 
PART II – PRIVACY JURISPRUDENCE & THE K.S. PUTTASWAMY STANDARD 
(OPERATIONALISATION FOR CYBER INVESTIGATIONS) 
 
2.1 From Constitutional Declaration to Police Duty 
The recognition of privacy as a fundamental right by the Supreme Court in Justice K.S. 
Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India did not merely expand individual liberty; it simultaneously 
imposed a heightened constitutional duty upon law enforcement agencies. For cyber 
investigators, this duty is particularly acute, as digital investigations inherently involve access to 
[[PAGE 664]]
personal, behavioural, financial, and relational data on a scale never previously encountered in 
conventional policing [1]. 
Unlike physical searches, where intrusion is visible and limited by space, digital searches are 
silent, expansive, and capable of reconstructing an individual’s entire life over several years. The 
Supreme Court explicitly warned that unchecked technological power in the hands of the State 
poses a serious threat to liberty. Therefore, cyber investigations must be conducted not only 
within the letter of the law, but within the spirit of constitutional restraint [2]. 
 
2.2 The Puttaswamy Test as a Mandatory Investigative Filter 
The three-fold test laid down in Puttaswamy—legality, legitimate aim, and proportionality—
must be treated as a mandatory investigative filter, to be mentally and procedurally applied 
before any digital intrusion. This test is not optional, nor is it satisfied by post-facto reasoning. 
Courts have repeatedly emphasised that constitutional compliance must exist at the time of 
action, not as an afterthought [3]. 
Every cyber investigation file must therefore internally answer three questions: 
1. Under which law is this action being taken? 
2. What specific public interest does it serve? 
3. Is the scope of intrusion the least intrusive method available? 
Failure to answer even one of these questions weakens the investigation at its foundation [4]. 
 
2.3 Legality: Clear Statutory Anchoring of Every Action 
Legality demands that every search, seizure, interception, monitoring, or data requisition must be 
traceable to an explicit statutory power. In cyber investigations, legality most commonly flows 
from provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, the Information Technology 
Act, 2000, or a judicial warrant issued by a competent court [5]. 
The Supreme Court has consistently held that executive convenience cannot substitute statutory 
authority. In District Registrar and Collector v. Canara Bank, the Court invalidated broad, 
unguided access to private records, holding that absence of procedural safeguards renders state 
action unconstitutional. For cyber police, this translates into a strict prohibition on informal 
access, voluntary disclosures without documentation, or data acquisition based on verbal 
permissions [6]. 
[[PAGE 665]]
Importantly, “industry practice” or “platform cooperation” does not constitute legality. Even 
when intermediaries are willing to share data, police officers must ensure that such sharing is 
backed by lawful requisition and documented necessity [7]. 
 
2.4 Legitimate State Aim: Narrowing the Purpose of Intrusion 
The second limb—legitimate state aim—requires that the investigative action must pursue a 
constitutionally permissible objective. Cyber investigations typically satisfy this requirement 
when dealing with cyber terrorism, online financial fraud, ransomware, child sexual abuse 
material, identity theft, organised cybercrime, or threats to public order [8]. 
However, courts have shown increasing intolerance towards vague or overbroad justifications. In 
Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that restrictions on fundamental 
rights must be justified by specific facts and objectives, not by general assertions of necessity. 
Applying this reasoning, cyber investigators must precisely define the offence under 
investigation and align the data sought strictly with that offence [9]. 
For example, in a cyber stalking case, requisitioning full historical location data or unrelated 
email content without justification may be held to exceed the legitimate aim. The objective of 
investigation cannot be expanded merely because technology permits it [10]. 
 
2.5 Proportionality: The Most Critical and Most Violated Principle 
Proportionality is the most operationally challenging limb and the most frequent point of failure 
in cyber investigations. It requires that the scope, duration, and intensity of privacy intrusion 
must be proportionate to the seriousness of the offence and the evidentiary need [11]. 
In Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh, the Supreme Court clarified that 
proportionality requires a rational nexus between means and ends, and mandates choosing the 
least restrictive alternative. In cyber policing, this means preferring targeted extraction over full-
device cloning, metadata over content where feasible, and time-bound data access instead of 
indefinite retention [12]. 
Courts have begun scrutinising forensic reports that contain vast quantities of irrelevant personal 
data. Such reports not only raise privacy concerns but also weaken evidentiary focus, giving 
defence counsel unnecessary material to challenge credibility and intent [13]. 
 
2.6 Privacy, Accused Persons, and the Myth of “Nothing to Hide” 
A dangerous misconception occasionally observed in cyber investigations is the belief that 
accused persons forfeit their privacy rights. This assumption has been repeatedly rejected by 
[[PAGE 666]]
constitutional courts. In Selvi v. State of Karnataka, the Supreme Court held that even accused 
persons retain personal liberty and mental privacy, subject only to lawful restrictions [14]. 
Digital searches that expose intimate photos, unrelated conversations, medical records, or family 
communications of accused persons without evidentiary relevance risk being classified as 
punitive rather than investigative. Such actions not only violate Article 21 but may also attract 
departmental scrutiny and judicial displeasure [15]. 
 
2.7 Interplay with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 reinforces constitutional privacy principles by 
imposing statutory discipline on the processing of digital personal data. While the Act provides 
exemptions for lawful state functions, these exemptions are not absolute and are conditioned 
upon necessity, proportionality, and safeguards against misuse [16]. 
Cyber investigators must therefore treat personal data accessed during investigation as entrusted 
material, not exploitable information. Unauthorised sharing, casual viewing, or non-case-related 
use of such data may expose officers to liability under both departmental rules and statutory 
provisions, including Section 72 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [17]. 
 
2.8 Supervisory Responsibility and Institutional Memory 
The responsibility for constitutional compliance does not rest solely with the Investigating 
Officer. Supervisory officers—SHOs, ACPs, DCPs—carry an affirmative duty to examine 
whether proposed or executed cyber actions satisfy the Puttaswamy standard. Judicial scrutiny 
often extends beyond the field officer to supervisory oversight failures [18]. 
Institutional memory must be built by documenting judicial objections, adverse remarks, and 
acquittal reasons linked to privacy violations. These lessons must inform future SOP refinements, 
training modules, and internal audits. Cyber policing is an evolving discipline; constitutional 
discipline must evolve with it [19]. 
 
2.9 Hindi Compliance Note for Supervisory Officers 
पयटवेक्षण अक्रिकाररयदीं हेतु क्रनदेश: 
यकद ककसी केस में डेटा की मात्रा आवश्यकता से अकधक प्रतीत होती है, तो उसकी अनुमकत न दी जाए। 
यह मानकर न चला जाए कक “कोटभ में देख लेंगे”। अदालतें अब जाूँच के प्रारींकर्क चरण की सींवैधाकनक 
वैधता को गींर्ीरता से परख रही हैं। गलत अनुमकत पूरे केस को कमजोर कर सकती है [20]. 
 
[[PAGE 667]]
2.10 Transition to Operational SOPs 
Having established the constitutional and jurisprudential framework governing privacy, the next 
part of this chapter will translate these principles into concrete procedural boundaries, 
particularly focusing on data minimisation, scope-limited seizure, and forensic extraction 
discipline. These operational controls are essential to prevent constitutional violations at the 
execution stage [21]. 
 
PART III  
 DATA MINIMISATION & PROCEDURAL BOUNDARIES (OPERATIONAL SOP FOR 
CYBER INVESTIGATORS) 
 
3.1 The Doctrine of Data Minimisation in Criminal Investigation 
Data minimisation is no longer a concept confined to data protection law or corporate 
compliance. In cyber crime investigations, it has emerged as a constitutional necessity and a 
procedural safeguard. The principle requires that investigators collect, process, and retain only 
that quantum of digital data which is strictly necessary to establish the elements of the 
alleged offence [1]. 
The Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India expressly recognised 
data minimisation as an inherent component of informational privacy. For cyber police officers, 
this translates into a binding obligation to resist the temptation of “collect everything now, filter 
later”. Courts have repeatedly indicated that indiscriminate data hoarding is incompatible with 
the right to privacy [2]. 
 
3.2 Why Over-Collection Weakens Cyber Prosecutions 
Contrary to popular belief, collecting more data does not strengthen a case; it often weakens it. 
Excessive extraction dilutes evidentiary focus, complicates forensic reports, and provides 
defence counsel with opportunities to allege fishing enquiries, mala fide intent, or privacy abuse. 
Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, courts examine not only the relevance of 
evidence but also the manner in which it was obtained [3]. 
In several cyber fraud and social media cases, courts have expressed concern where irrelevant 
personal chats, photographs, or unrelated documents formed part of the forensic record. Such 
inclusions create doubt regarding investigative discipline and can trigger adverse judicial 
remarks. An investigation that appears invasive risks being perceived as punitive rather than 
probative [4]. 
[[PAGE 668]]
 
3.3 Scope-Specific Seizure: Devices Are Not Automatically Evidence 
A critical procedural boundary often ignored at the field level is the assumption that possession 
equals relevance. Merely because a device is found with an accused does not mean it must be 
seized. Seizure must be justified by a clear nexus between the device and the offence [5]. 
For example, in a UPI fraud case involving a single transaction, seizing multiple family 
members’ phones or unrelated office laptops without recorded justification exposes the 
investigation to constitutional challenge. Courts have emphasised that search and seizure powers 
are intrusive by nature and must therefore be exercised with restraint. This principle finds 
resonance in District Registrar and Collector v. Canara Bank, where the Supreme Court warned 
against unguided access to private records [6]. 
 
3.4 Documenting “Necessity” in Seizure Memos 
Every seizure memo involving digital devices must explicitly record why the specific device is 
necessary for investigation. Generic phrases such as “for further investigation” or “for forensic 
examination” are no longer sufficient. Courts now expect a reasoned articulation of necessity, 
especially when privacy-sensitive devices are involved [7]. 
Investigating Officers must specify: 
 
The suspected role of the device in the offence 
 
The type of data sought (e.g., transaction logs, chat records) 
 
The relevance of that data to the offence under investigation 
Failure to do so weakens the legality limb of the Puttaswamy test and invites judicial scrutiny at 
the charge or trial stage [8]. 
 
3.5 Filtered Extraction: Precision Over Volume 
Modern forensic tools allow selective extraction of data categories such as messages, call logs, 
application-specific data, or time-bound records. Investigators are expected to use these 
capabilities responsibly. Full physical or logical extraction of a device should be treated as an 
exception, not the rule [9]. 
In Canara Bank v. Union of India, the Supreme Court observed that privacy infringement must 
be narrowly tailored. Applying this reasoning, if WhatsApp chats for a specific period are 
relevant, extracting entire gallery contents, browser histories, or unrelated application data is 
[[PAGE 669]]
disproportionate. Precision extraction not only protects privacy but also improves evidentiary 
clarity [10]. 
 
3.6 Anti-Forensic Indicators and the Limits of Recovery 
While investigators must remain alert to anti-forensic behaviour such as data deletion, encryption 
misuse, or log tampering, the response to such indicators must remain proportionate. The mere 
suspicion of data destruction does not justify unrestricted intrusion into all personal data domains 
[11]. 
For instance, recovery of deleted financial transaction data may be justified in a fraud case, but 
extending the recovery process into private photographs, health records, or unrelated 
communications without evidentiary linkage is constitutionally unsafe. Courts have recognised 
that anti-forensic vigilance cannot become a license for privacy erosion [12]. 
 
3.7 Cloud Data and the Risk of Unlimited Reach 
Cloud-based data presents a unique challenge to data minimisation because of its scale and 
persistence. Email archives, cloud backups, and social media accounts may span several years. 
Investigators must therefore define temporal, subject-matter, and account-specific limits 
before initiating cloud data requests [13]. 
In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, the Supreme Court underscored that even where state 
action is justified, it must be proportionate and narrowly tailored. Applying this principle, cloud 
data requisitions must avoid blanket requests such as “entire account history” unless the gravity 
of the offence demonstrably warrants such intrusion [14]. 
 
3.8 Retention, Access Control, and Internal Boundaries 
Data minimisation does not end with collection; it extends to retention and access. Extracted 
digital data must be stored securely, accessed only by authorised personnel, and retained only for 
the duration necessary for investigation and trial. Casual sharing within units, informal viewing, 
or retention beyond necessity undermines institutional integrity [15]. 
Section 72 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 criminalises unauthorised disclosure of 
information obtained under lawful authority. Investigators must remember that misuse of 
lawfully accessed data is as damaging as unlawful access itself [16]. 
 
3.9 Supervisory Gatekeeping and Accountability 
[[PAGE 670]]
Supervisory officers play a crucial role in enforcing data minimisation. SHOs and ACPs must 
actively question: 
 
Whether seizure was unavoidable 
 
Whether extraction scope was justified 
 
Whether irrelevant data has been excluded 
Judicial scrutiny increasingly focuses on supervisory oversight failures. Approval without 
application of mind may attract adverse remarks and institutional embarrassment [17]. 
 
3.10 Hindi Field-Level Instruction 
मैदानी क्रनदेश: 
हर कडकजटल कडवाइस को ज़ब्त करना आवश्यक नहीीं है। 
यकद केवल एक ऐप या सीकमत अवकध का डेटा चाकहए, तो उतना ही कनकाला जाए। 
अनावश्यक डेटा कनकालने से केस कमज़ोर होता है और अदालत में पुकलस की मींशा पर सवाल उठते हैं 
 
3.11 Transition to Victim and Sensitive Data Protection 
Having established procedural boundaries for data minimisation, the next part of this chapter will 
address victim privacy and sensitivity SOPs, with special focus on crimes against women and 
children, CSAM cases, and sextortion investigations. These areas demand the highest ethical 
discipline and zero tolerance for procedural lapses [19]. 
 
PART III – ADDENDUM 
SPECIMEN TEMPLATES FOR DIGITAL SEIZURE & DATA EXTRACTION MEMOS 
 
3.A Core Drafting Principle (Read Before Using Templates) 
Every seizure memo involving digital devices must answer three judicial questions on its face: 
1. Why this device? 
2. What data is required? 
3. Why lesser intrusion is insufficient? 
[[PAGE 671]]
Failure to reflect these elements has repeatedly resulted in courts terming the seizure as roving, 
disproportionate, or privacy-violative [1]. 
 
3.B Specimen Language – Digital Device Seizure Memo (Minimal & Proportionate) 
(i) Justification Clause – Mandatory 
“Whereas during the course of investigation in FIR No. ___ / 20__ under Sections ___ of the 
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IT Act, credible material has emerged indicating that the mobile 
device bearing make ___, model ___, IMEI ___, allegedly used by the accused, was utilised for 
execution of the offence, specifically for [e.g., conducting UPI transactions / communicating 
with victim / accessing fraudulent account]. 
The seizure of the said device is therefore necessary and proportionate for the purpose of 
extracting limited digital evidence directly connected with the alleged offence.” [2] 
 
(ii) Scope Limitation Clause (Highly Recommended) 
“It is recorded that the seizure and proposed forensic examination of the said device shall be 
restricted to data categories relevant to the offence, namely [e.g., transaction logs, specified 
application chats, call detail records for the period ___ to ___], and no unrelated personal data 
shall be accessed or extracted unless subsequently authorised in accordance with law.” [3] 
 
(iii) Privacy Safeguard Clause 
“It is further recorded that personal photographs, videos, documents, or communications 
unrelated to the alleged offence shall not be accessed, copied, or relied upon, in view of the 
constitutional right to privacy under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.” [4] 
 
3.C Specimen Language – When Full Device Extraction Is Unavoidable (Exceptional 
Cases) 
(To be used only in serious offences like cyber terrorism, large-scale financial fraud, CSAM) 
*“Considering the nature and gravity of the offence, and credible indications of data deletion / 
encryption / anti-forensic activity, limited targeted extraction is assessed as insufficient. 
Accordingly, full logical / physical extraction of the device is being undertaken as a 
proportionate investigative necessity, subject to strict internal access controls and judicial 
oversight.”* [5] 
[[PAGE 672]]
⚠️ Note: Absence of this reasoning has resulted in courts rejecting forensic reports in serious 
cases. 
 
3.D Specimen Language – Cloud / Email / Social Media Data Requisition 
(i) Narrow Purpose Statement 
“The requisition for data from the service provider is confined to the account ___ for the period 
___ to ___, solely for the purpose of investigating the alleged offence under FIR No. ___. No 
blanket or historical data beyond the stated scope is being sought.” [6] 
 
(ii) Proportionality Declaration 
“This requisition satisfies the test of legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality as laid 
down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India.” [7] 
 
3.E Specimen Language – Case Diary Entry (Highly Advisable) 
“Today, before proceeding with digital seizure/extraction, the necessity, scope, and 
proportionality of the proposed action were assessed. It was consciously decided to limit data 
collection to offence-linked digital artefacts only, to avoid unwarranted intrusion into personal 
privacy.” [8] 
Courts increasingly rely on case diary reasoning to judge investigative intent. 
 
3.F Supervisory Endorsement Template (SHO / ACP / DCP) 
“I have perused the seizure proposal and am satisfied that the scope of digital seizure/extraction 
is necessary, proportionate, and limited to offence-related data. The Investigating Officer is 
directed to ensure strict compliance with privacy safeguards.” [9] 
This single endorsement line has saved multiple prosecutions from being struck down. 
 
3.G Hindi Ready-Use Draft (Field Friendly) 
क्रर्क्रिटल ज़ब्ती हेतु आवश्यक भाषा (उदाहरण): 
*“यह मोबाइल फोन केवल उि अपराध से सींबींकधत डेटा (लेन-देन / चैट / कॉल कववरण) प्राप्त करने हेतु 
ज़ब्त ककया गया है। 
[[PAGE 673]]
इससे असींबींकधत कनजी फोटो, वीकडयो या दस्तावेज़ोीं की जाूँच नहीीं की जाएगी, कजससे सींकवधान के अनुच्छेद 
21 के अींतगभत कनजता के अकधकार का उल्लींघन न हो।”* [10] 
 
3.H Common Drafting Mistakes (Strictly Avoid) 
❌ “For further investigation” 
❌ “All data required” 
❌ “As per practice” 
❌ No mention of why this device 
Courts have repeatedly held such language to be constitutionally hollow [11]. 
 
3.I Institutional Direction 
All cyber units under UP Police shall standardise seizure memo language in line with the 
above templates. Deviations must be specifically justified in the case diary. This is not a drafting 
preference; it is a constitutional compliance requirement [12]. 
 
With data minimisation and seizure discipline established, the next part will address Victim 
Privacy & Sensitivity SOPs, where procedural lapses can cause irreversible harm and legal 
collapse. 
 
PART IV – VICTIM PRIVACY & SENSITIVITY SOPs (NON-NEGOTIABLE 
OPERATIONAL STANDARDS) 
 
4.1 Victim Privacy as a Constitutional and Ethical Absolute 
In cyber crime investigations, the privacy of victims occupies a higher constitutional pedestal 
than that of accused persons. Victims approach law enforcement not merely for redress, but with 
an expectation of dignity, confidentiality, and protection from further harm. Any failure to 
safeguard victim data constitutes not only an investigative lapse but a violation of Article 21 of 
the Constitution of India, which guarantees life with dignity [1]. 
The Supreme Court has consistently held that the criminal justice system must not become a 
secondary site of victimisation. In State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh, the Court emphasised that 
[[PAGE 674]]
procedural safeguards exist to protect victims from exposure, humiliation, and re-traumatisation. 
This principle applies with even greater force in cyber crimes, where data can be copied, leaked, 
or permanently circulated within seconds [2]. 
 
4.2 Categories of High-Sensitivity Cyber Victim Data 
Investigating Officers must treat certain categories of victim data as ultra-sensitive, requiring 
heightened protection and restricted access. These include: 
 
Sexual content or intimate images 
 
Child sexual abuse material (CSAM) 
 
Medical, psychological, or counselling records 
 
Personal identifiers linked to online abuse or stalking 
 
Financial data of fraud victims 
 
Communication logs revealing personal relationships 
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 reinforces this duty by recognising the State as a 
lawful processor only when processing is strictly necessary and safeguarded. Casual handling, 
copying, or sharing of such data is legally indefensible [3]. 
 
4.3 Crimes Against Women: Privacy as a Core Investigation Principle 
In cases involving online harassment, revenge pornography, sextortion, morphing, or cyber 
stalking of women, the investigation itself must not aggravate harm. Courts have repeatedly 
expressed concern where victim images or chats appear unnecessarily in case records, forensic 
annexures, or internal circulation [4]. 
The Supreme Court in Nipun Saxena v. Union of India categorically held that disclosure of 
identity or details leading to identification of victims of sexual offences is impermissible. This 
principle applies equally to digital records. Inclusion of victim names, photographs, usernames, 
or handles in unsecured formats exposes the investigation to legal challenge and reputational 
damage [5]. 
 
4.4 Child Victims & CSAM: Zero-Tolerance Protocol 
Cases involving children demand the highest degree of sensitivity and procedural discipline. 
Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) is not ordinary digital evidence; it is illegal to possess, 
[[PAGE 675]]
view, copy, or circulate except strictly for lawful investigative purposes. Any deviation exposes 
officers to criminal liability under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and allied laws [6]. 
In Alakh Alok Srivastava v. Union of India, the Supreme Court underscored the obligation of 
authorities to prevent re-circulation of CSAM even during investigation. Accordingly, CSAM 
shall never be: 
 
Copied unnecessarily 
 
Stored on personal devices 
 
Shared through unsecured platforms 
 
Displayed in open court without safeguards 
Only hashed references, redacted stills (where unavoidable), or judicially permitted methods 
shall be used [7]. 
 
4.5 Handling Sextortion & Intimate Image Abuse Cases 
Sextortion cases require a delicate balance between evidence preservation and victim dignity. 
Victims often hesitate to cooperate due to fear of exposure. Investigators must therefore adopt a 
victim-first evidence strategy, assuring confidentiality at every stage [8]. 
Extraction of intimate material must be: 
 
Strictly limited to evidentiary necessity 
 
Stored in encrypted, access-controlled systems 
 
Viewed only by designated officers 
 
Never included verbatim in general case diaries 
Courts have criticised investigations where intimate victim content appears casually in records or 
annexures, treating such conduct as secondary victimisation [9]. 
 
4.6 Anonymisation & Redaction in Reports and Training 
Victim anonymity does not end with trial; it extends to internal reports, training material, 
presentations, and inter-departmental communications. Investigating Officers must ensure that 
victim identities are anonymised using pseudonyms or codes in all non-judicial documents [10]. 
Failure to redact identifying details in training presentations or review meetings has previously 
resulted in information leaks and public embarrassment. Such lapses reflect institutional 
indiscipline and must be treated seriously [11]. 
[[PAGE 676]]
 
4.7 Victim Consent Is Not a Blanket Waiver 
A common misconception is that victim consent permits unrestricted access or use of personal 
data. This is incorrect. Consent is context-specific and purpose-limited. Even where a victim 
voluntarily shares devices or accounts, investigators must still apply data minimisation and 
relevance principles [12]. 
The Supreme Court has clarified that fundamental rights cannot be waived casually, especially in 
situations of vulnerability. Victim cooperation does not authorise unnecessary intrusion into 
unrelated aspects of personal life [13]. 
 
4.8 Access Control & Internal Confidentiality 
Victim data must be accessible only to officers directly involved in investigation. Curiosity-based 
access, informal viewing, or discussion of sensitive material within units constitutes misconduct. 
Supervisory officers are duty-bound to enforce strict access controls [14]. 
Section 72 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 criminalises unauthorised disclosure of 
information obtained under lawful authority. Officers must internalise that lawful access does not 
grant unlimited discretion [15]. 
 
4.9 Court Presentation: Protecting Victims During Trial 
When presenting digital evidence involving victims, Investigating Officers must proactively 
request in-camera proceedings, sealed covers, or redaction orders where appropriate. Allowing 
sensitive material to be displayed openly without safeguards may invite judicial criticism and 
harm the victim irreversibly [16]. 
The Supreme Court has consistently encouraged courts and prosecutors to adopt victim-centric 
procedures. Police officers must assist the prosecution in enforcing these safeguards, not remain 
passive [17]. 
 
4.10 Hindi Field Instructions (Non-Negotiable) 
महत्वपूणट क्रनदेश: 
पीकड़त का डेटा जाूँच के कलए है, प्रदशभन के कलए नहीीं। 
यकद ककसी केस में मकहला या बच्चे से सींबींकधत कनजी फोटो, वीकडयो या चैट हैं, तो उनका उपयोग अत्यींत 
सीकमत और सुरकित तरीके से ककया जाए। 
[[PAGE 677]]
लापरवाही से न केवल केस कमजोर होता है, बक्ति पीकड़त को दोबारा मानकसक आघात र्ी पहुूँचता है 
 
4.11 Supervisory Accountability in Victim-Centric Cases 
SHOs, ACPs, and DCPs must personally review investigations involving women and children to 
ensure privacy safeguards are implemented. Judicial scrutiny increasingly extends to supervisory 
failure, not just IO misconduct [19]. 
Institutional credibility depends on how the police treat victims, not how aggressively they 
pursue accused persons. This principle must guide every cyber investigation [20]. 
 
4.12 Transition to Ethical Undercover Operations 
Having established victim-centric privacy safeguards, the next part will examine Ethical 
Undercover Operations, including the use of sock-puppet accounts, online infiltration, and dark 
web investigations. This area poses significant risks of entrapment, overreach, and constitutional 
violation if not carefully regulated [21]. 
 
PART IV – ADDENDUM 
SPECIMEN REDACTION, ANONYMISATION & CSAM HANDLING PROTOCOLS 
 
A. SPECIMEN REDACTION & VICTIM ANONYMISATION FORMATS 
4.A.1 Foundational Rule (Non-Negotiable) 
No document generated during investigation—FIR, case diary, seizure memo, forensic report, 
charge-sheet, training material, or internal briefing—shall contain identifiable victim data 
unless strictly required for judicial proceedings and protected by law [1]. 
Failure to anonymise is treated as procedural illegality, not clerical error [2].

(i) Identity Masking Template 
Replace victim identifiers as follows:

Violations have resulted in disciplinary action in multiple jurisdictions. 
 
B. SEPARATE CSAM HANDLING CHECKLIST (ZERO-TOLERANCE SOP) 
This checklist applies to all cases involving minors, including CSAM, grooming, online 
exploitation, or suspected child abuse. 
 
4.B.1 Legal Position (Absolute) 
CSAM is contraband, not conventional evidence. 
Possession, viewing, copying, or circulation is illegal even for police, except to the minimum 
extent strictly necessary for investigation [8]. 
 
4.B.2 CSAM HANDLING – STEP-BY-STEP CHECKLIST 
✅ DOs (Mandatory) 
✔ Record reasoned necessity before accessing CSAM 
✔ Limit viewing to designated IO / forensic expert only 
✔ Use hash values wherever possible instead of images 
✔ Store material in encrypted, access-controlled storage 
✔ Maintain viewing log (who, when, why) 
[[PAGE 680]]
✔ Seek judicial directions for court production 
✔ Use sealed covers / in-camera proceedings [9] 
 
❌ DON’Ts (Zero Tolerance) 
❌ Do not copy CSAM to personal devices 
❌ Do not forward via WhatsApp / email / pen drive 
❌ Do not store multiple duplicates 
❌ Do not display in open court without safeguards 
❌ Do not include images/videos in general case diary 
❌ Do not discuss content informally within unit [10] 
Single violation may attract criminal liability. 
 
4.B.3 CSAM Seizure Memo – Mandatory Clause 
“The seized digital material contains suspected Child Sexual Abuse Material. Access, viewing, 
storage, and analysis shall be strictly limited to lawful investigative purposes and conducted in 
accordance with privacy safeguards and child protection obligations.” [11] 
 
4.B.4 Forensic Examination Instruction (CSAM) 
“Forensic examination shall prioritise identification, source attribution, and offender linkage. 
Unnecessary duplication or extended viewing of CSAM content is expressly prohibited.” [12] 
 
4.B.5 Court Presentation Protocol (CSAM) 
 
Prefer hash-based proof 
 
Use descriptive testimony, not visual replay 
 
Request in-camera proceedings 
 
Avoid screen display unless court insists [13] 
Courts have repeatedly discouraged re-victimisation through repeated display.

This is a reputation-defining area for the organisation.

PART V – ETHICAL UNDERCOVER OPERATIONS & ANTI-ENTRAPMENT 
BOUNDARIES (COVERT CYBER POLICING SOP) 
[[PAGE 682]]
 
5.1 Undercover Cyber Operations: A Necessary but Dangerous Tool 
Undercover cyber operations—including the use of covert online identities, decoy profiles, and 
controlled digital personas—have become indispensable in investigating darknet markets, online 
fraud syndicates, CSAM networks, terror financing, and organised cybercrime. However, these 
operations exist at the outer edge of constitutional permissibility and therefore demand the 
highest degree of ethical restraint and supervisory control [1]. 
Unlike traditional physical undercover work, cyber undercover operations are scalable, 
anonymous, and persistent. These characteristics amplify investigative reach but simultaneously 
increase the risk of entrapment, provocation, privacy violation, and abuse of state power. 
This SOP therefore treats undercover cyber operations as exceptional measures, not routine 
investigative tools [2]. 
 
5.2 Legal Foundation: No Undercover Action Without Lawful Authority 
Every undercover cyber operation must be traceable to a lawful investigative purpose grounded 
in statutory authority. Covert digital presence is not justified merely because an offence is 
suspected. There must exist credible material indicating ongoing or imminent criminal activity 
that cannot be effectively investigated through overt means [3]. 
Courts have repeatedly held that deception by the State is permissible only to the extent 
necessary to detect crime, not to manufacture it. In Ramakant Rai v. Madan Rai, the Supreme 
Court cautioned that investigative techniques must not cross the line into inducement. This 
principle applies with greater force in cyber environments, where manipulation can be subtle yet 
decisive [4]. 
 
5.3 Distinguishing Legitimate Undercover Work from Entrapment 
The most critical boundary in undercover cyber policing is the distinction between detection of 
crime and creation of crime. Legitimate undercover work observes, documents, and intercepts 
criminal conduct that the suspect is already inclined to commit. Entrapment, on the other hand, 
involves inducing or persuading an otherwise unwilling person to commit an offence [5]. 
Indian courts have consistently rejected prosecutions where state agents play an active role in 
instigating the offence. While Indian law does not explicitly codify “entrapment” as a defence, 
courts examine whether the police conduct was fair, reasonable, and non-provocative. Cyber 
operations that cross this boundary risk collapse at the trial stage [6]. 
 
[[PAGE 683]]
5.4 Sock-Puppet Accounts: Permissible Scope and Hard Limits 
The use of sock-puppet accounts—false digital identities created for investigative purposes—is 
permitted only within narrowly defined limits. Such accounts may be used to: 
 
Access closed online groups involved in criminal activity 
 
Observe and document illegal transactions or communications 
 
Respond passively to suspect-initiated contact 
They shall not be used to: 
 
Encourage escalation of criminal conduct 
 
Suggest illegal acts 
 
Offer inducements, discounts, or assurances 
 
Create criminal intent where none existed [7] 
The guiding principle is reactive presence, not proactive provocation. Courts have little 
tolerance for investigative creativity that results in ethical compromise [8]. 
 
5.5 Dark Web Investigations: Special Sensitivity Protocol 
Dark web investigations involve inherently illegal marketplaces and communities. While 
presence within such spaces may require engagement with criminal actors, Investigating Officers 
must ensure that: 
 
Any interaction is limited to intelligence gathering 
 
No illegal transaction is initiated by the officer 
 
No assurances of anonymity, protection, or partnership are offered 
In several jurisdictions, courts have scrutinised dark web stings where law enforcement appeared 
to act as facilitators rather than investigators. Such conduct undermines the legitimacy of the 
prosecution and exposes officers to serious legal risk [9]. 
 
5.6 Financial Interactions: Absolute Prohibition on Inducement 
Under no circumstances shall undercover cyber officers initiate financial transactions that create 
or expand criminal conduct. Controlled purchases, where legally sanctioned, must be: 
 
Specifically authorised 
[[PAGE 684]]
 
Proportionate in value 
 
Closely supervised 
 
Fully documented 
Offering money, crypto assets, or other benefits to induce criminal activity is impermissible. In 
cyber fraud cases, courts have rejected evidence where police participation altered the natural 
course of events [10]. 
 
5.7 Documentation & Transparency: The Shield Against Allegations 
Every undercover cyber operation must be accompanied by meticulous documentation. This 
includes: 
 
Written approval with scope definition 
 
Clear articulation of necessity 
 
Logs of interactions 
 
Preservation of original communications 
 
Exit strategy documentation 
Courts place significant reliance on contemporaneous records to assess investigative fairness. 
Absence of documentation is often interpreted against the prosecution, regardless of officer 
intent [11]. 
 
5.8 Privacy Boundaries During Undercover Engagement 
Even while operating covertly, officers remain bound by privacy constraints. Access to personal 
data encountered incidentally during undercover engagement must be limited to evidentiary 
relevance. Harvesting unrelated personal information, screenshots, or metadata without necessity 
constitutes privacy violation [12]. 
The Supreme Court has consistently held that the means of investigation must be as 
constitutionally sound as the objective. Undercover status does not confer immunity from 
privacy obligations [13]. 
 
5.9 Supervisory Control: Non-Delegable Responsibility 
[[PAGE 685]]
Approval and oversight of undercover cyber operations shall rest with senior supervisory 
officers. SHOs may propose, but ACP/DCP-level officers must authorise and periodically review 
such operations. Passive supervision or blanket approvals are unacceptable [14]. 
Judicial scrutiny increasingly examines whether supervisory officers exercised real oversight or 
merely endorsed proposals mechanically. Accountability flows upward as well as downward 
[15]. 
 
5.10 Hindi Field Instructions (Critical) 
महत्वपूणट क्रनदेश: 
अींडरकवर जाूँच का अथभ अपराध करवाना नहीीं है। 
यकद पुकलस की गकतकवकध से अपराध उत्पन्न हुआ, तो पूरा केस कगर सकता है। 
ऑनलाइन पहचान का उपयोग केवल कनरीिण और प्रमाण सींकलन तक सीकमत रखें [16]. 
 
5.11 Consequences of Ethical Breach 
Ethical breaches in undercover cyber operations carry severe consequences: 
 
Evidence exclusion 
 
Acquittal of accused 
 
Adverse judicial remarks 
 
Departmental action 
 
Personal liability 
No operational success justifies ethical compromise. Institutional credibility once damaged is 
difficult to repair [17]. 
 
5.12 Transition to Intermediary & Platform Engagement SOPs 
With ethical boundaries of undercover operations clearly defined, the next part will address 
Intermediary Requests, Preservation Notices, and Platform Engagement Protocols. 
Improper handling at this stage often nullifies otherwise lawful investigations [18].

PART V – ADDENDUM 
CASE-LAW MAPPING FOR ENTRAPMENT & UNDERCOVER CYBER OPERATIONS 
 
[[PAGE 693]]
A. Foundational Position in Indian Law 
Indian criminal jurisprudence does not formally recognise entrapment as a statutory defence, 
unlike some foreign jurisdictions. However, Indian courts consistently examine police conduct 
under the broader constitutional doctrines of fairness, reasonableness, and due process under 
Article 21. Where police action appears to manufacture crime rather than detect it, courts 
have either disbelieved prosecution evidence or extended benefit of doubt to the accused [1]. 
Therefore, in cyber undercover operations, entrapment arguments succeed indirectly, by 
attacking: 
 
voluntariness of accused conduct 
 
credibility of evidence 
 
fairness of investigation 
This makes anticipatory compliance essential [2]. 
 
B. Core Supreme Court Authorities Relevant to Entrapment Arguments 
5.B.1 Ramakant Rai v. Madan Rai (2003) 
The Supreme Court cautioned that investigative agencies must not induce or provoke 
commission of an offence. Evidence obtained through unfair investigative practices weakens 
prosecution credibility [3]. 
If an undercover cyber officer: 
 
suggests illegal acts, or 
 
encourages escalation, or 
 
reassures safety/anonymity 
the defence may argue that the offence was police-facilitated, not accused-initiated. 
Use only reactive communication, never proactive suggestion. 
 
5.B.2 Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) 
[[PAGE 694]]
The Supreme Court held that investigative techniques violating personal autonomy and mental 
liberty are unconstitutional, even if aimed at crime detection [4]. 
Entrapment arguments often rely on Selvi to show that: 
 
manipulation of will, or 
 
psychological pressure, or 
 
deceptive inducement 
violates Article 21. 
No undercover messaging that nudges intent or pressures compliance. 
 
5.B.3 State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh (1999) 
Procedural safeguards are not technicalities; they are substantive protections. Breach creates 
presumption of unfairness [5]. 
If undercover approval, scope, or documentation is missing, defence may argue procedural 
illegality, indirectly supporting entrapment claims. 
Written approvals, logs, and exit reports are mandatory. 
 
C. High Court Jurisprudence Influencing Entrapment Analysis 
5.C.1 Delhi High Court – Fair Investigation Doctrine 
The Delhi High Court has repeatedly held that investigations must be fair, transparent, and 
non-manipulative, especially in technology-driven cases. Courts examine whether police 
conduct altered the natural course of events [6]. 
Cyber Context: 
If police: 
 
extend conversations unnecessarily 
 
push suspects toward transactions 
[[PAGE 695]]
 
accelerate offence commission 
courts may infer inducement. 
 
5.C.2 Bombay High Court – Decoy Operations Scrutiny 
In multiple cases involving decoy operations (including corruption and cyber stings), the 
Bombay High Court has scrutinised whether the accused was predisposed or artificially 
tempted [7]. 
Cyber Context: 
Undercover profiles offering easy money, anonymity, or technical help are particularly 
vulnerable to challenge. 
 
D. Entrapment Defence: Typical Arguments vs SOP Neutralisers 
Argument 1: “Police created the offence” 
Accused would not have committed the offence but for police interaction. 
 
Document pre-existing criminal indicators 
 
Preserve suspect-initiated messages 
 
Avoid first-move communications [8] 
 
Argument 2: “Police induced or encouraged escalation” 
Police participation expanded the offence. 
 
Maintain minimal engagement 
 
Do not suggest quantities, prices, methods 
 
Log refusal to escalate [9] 
 
Argument 3: “Undercover officer acted as agent provocateur” 
[[PAGE 696]]
Officer crossed from observer to instigator. 
 
Use passive acknowledgements 
 
Avoid reassurance of safety or success 
 
Supervisory monitoring of chats [10] 
 
Argument 4: “Investigation violated fairness under Article 21” 
Even if offence occurred, method was unconstitutional. 
 
Puttaswamy-compliant proportionality 
 
Clear necessity justification 
 
Early judicial oversight where feasible [11] 
 
E. Judicial Test Likely to Be Applied in Cyber Entrapment Claims 
Courts generally assess: 
1. Who initiated the criminal idea? 
2. Was the accused already predisposed? 
3. Did police merely provide opportunity or actively persuade? 
4. Would the offence have occurred anyway? 
Failure on any of these may weaken prosecution [12].

This mapping shall be used in charge-sheet vetting and prosecution briefings [14]. 
 
With ethical limits, flowcharts, and case-law mapping now integrated, PART V stands as a 
complete undercover cyber policing doctrine. 
The next part will govern Intermediary Requests, Preservation Notices & Platform 
Compliance, where even small drafting errors destroy admissibility. 
 
PART VI – INTERMEDIARY REQUESTS, PRESERVATION & PLATFORM 
COMPLIANCE SOPs 
 
6.1 Why Intermediary Handling Decides the Fate of Cyber Prosecutions 
In contemporary cyber investigations, intermediaries—social media platforms, messaging 
services, email providers, cloud hosts, ISPs, payment gateways, and financial institutions—are 
the primary custodians of decisive evidence. However, improper engagement with 
intermediaries is one of the most common reasons for cyber acquittals in India. Evidence is 
frequently rejected not because it is false, but because it was requested, preserved, or obtained 
improperly [1]. 
Courts increasingly treat intermediary-derived data as high-risk evidence, requiring strict proof 
of legality, necessity, proportionality, and chain of custody. This part of the SOP therefore treats 
intermediary engagement as a procedural discipline, not a clerical task [2]. 
 
[[PAGE 698]]
6.2 Legal Architecture Governing Intermediary Engagement 
Intermediary requests by police must be grounded in a clearly identifiable legal framework. The 
principal sources of authority include the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (summons, 
search, seizure, letters of request), the Information Technology Act, 2000 (especially Sections 
67C, 69, 69A, 69B, 72, 79), the Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code Rules, 
2021, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 [3]. 
The Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasised that intermediaries are not extensions of the 
police. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Court underscored that intermediary obligations 
must operate within constitutional limits. This principle applies equally when intermediaries 
cooperate voluntarily; legality cannot be replaced by convenience [4]. 
 
6.3 Preservation Requests: The First and Most Critical Step 
Preservation of digital data is time-sensitive. Logs, IP data, session metadata, and transactional 
records may be deleted automatically due to platform retention policies. Therefore, the first 
lawful step upon identification of an online offence is issuance of a preservation request, not a 
blanket data demand [5]. 
A preservation notice must: 
 
Be offence-specific 
 
Identify the precise account, content, or transaction 
 
Specify the legal basis 
 
Clearly state that only preservation, not disclosure, is sought at that stage 
Courts have looked favourably upon investigations where preservation was sought immediately, 
even if formal disclosure followed later through proper legal process [6]. 
 
6.4 Disclosure Requests: Precision Is Mandatory 
When seeking disclosure from intermediaries, Investigating Officers must abandon generic 
phrases such as “entire account details” or “complete history”. Such requests are increasingly 
rejected by platforms and criticised by courts as disproportionate [7]. 
Disclosure requests must specify: 
 
Exact data categories (subscriber info, IP logs, content) 
 
Defined time windows 
[[PAGE 699]]
 
Clear linkage to the offence under investigation 
In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, the Supreme Court made it clear that 
informational privacy demands minimal intrusion. Courts now read intermediary requests 
through this constitutional lens [8]. 
 
6.5 Content vs Metadata: Understanding the Legal Sensitivity Gradient 
Not all digital data carries the same privacy weight. Content data (messages, images, videos) 
attracts higher constitutional protection than metadata (IP addresses, timestamps). Investigators 
must therefore justify content requests with greater care and necessity [9]. 
Courts have questioned investigations where content was requisitioned even though metadata 
alone could establish attribution or linkage. Overreaching content requests often trigger 
proportionality objections and delay prosecutions [10]. 
 
6.6 Platform-Specific Compliance Realities 
Investigating Officers must understand that global platforms operate under multiple jurisdictions 
and internal compliance protocols. Poorly drafted or legally vague requests are routinely ignored 
or delayed. This is not platform hostility; it is legal risk management [11]. 
Experience shows that: 
 
Narrow, lawful requests receive faster responses 
 
Preservation-first strategy improves cooperation 
 
Clear articulation of Indian legal authority reduces back-and-forth 
Courts are unsympathetic to police explanations blaming platforms for evidentiary gaps when 
requests themselves were defective [12]. 
 
6.7 DPDP Act, 2023: State Exemption Is Not Absolute 
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 recognises lawful state processing of personal 
data for criminal investigation. However, this exemption is conditional, not blanket. Processing 
must still satisfy necessity, proportionality, and safeguards against misuse [13]. 
Intermediary requests that appear excessive or poorly justified may attract objections not only 
from platforms but also from courts examining constitutional compliance. Investigators must 
therefore internalise that DPDP does not dilute privacy obligations; it codifies them [14]. 
[[PAGE 700]]
 
6.8 Chain of Custody for Intermediary-Supplied Data 
Once data is received from an intermediary, the police become its custodian. Courts scrutinise: 
 
Mode of receipt 
 
Integrity verification (hash values, platform certifications) 
 
Storage conditions 
 
Access logs 
Failure to maintain a clear chain of custody may render otherwise authentic data unreliable under 
the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 [15]. 
 
6.9 Avoiding Informal or “Backchannel” Data Access 
Investigating Officers are strictly prohibited from obtaining data through informal means such 
as: 
 
Direct messaging platform employees 
 
Using personal email accounts 
 
Accepting screenshots or dumps without certification 
Such practices are indefensible in court and expose officers to allegations of evidence fabrication 
or unauthorised access under the IT Act, 2000 [16]. 
 
6.10 Supervisory Oversight of Intermediary Engagement 
All major intermediary requests—especially content disclosure—must be reviewed by 
supervisory officers. SHOs may initiate routine requests, but ACP/DCP-level oversight is 
mandatory for: 
 
Content data 
 
Long-duration data 
 
Cross-border requests 
Courts increasingly inquire whether senior officers applied independent mind to privacy-
impacting requests [17]. 
 
[[PAGE 701]]
6.11 Hindi Field Guidance 
मैदानी क्रनदेश: 
इींटरमीकडयरी से डेटा माूँगना साधारण पत्राचार नहीीं है। 
गलत, व्यापक या अस्पष्ट अनुरोध से प्लेटफॉमभ र्ी जवाब नहीीं देता और अदालत र्ी सबूत खाररज कर देती 
है। 
पहले सुरकित रखें, कफर सीकमत और कानूनी तरीके से माूँग करें [18]. 
 
6.12 Transition to Cloud & Cross-Border Evidence 
Having established lawful intermediary engagement within India, the next part will address 
Cloud Data, Remote Servers, and Cross-Border Evidence, including MLATs and letters of 
request. This area carries heightened risks of jurisdictional error and admissibility failure [19].

A. SPECIMEN PRESERVATION REQUEST FORMAT 
6.A.1 Preservation Request (Time-Sensitive Digital Data) 
Subject: Preservation Request – FIR No. ___ / 20__ 
This is to inform that FIR No. ___ / 20__ under Sections ___ (BNS / IT Act / other applicable 
law) is under investigation. 
It has come to notice that the account / identifier listed below may contain data relevant to the 
said investigation: 
 
Account ID / URL: ___ 
 
Registered Email / Phone (if known): ___ 
 
Relevant Period: From ___ to ___ 
In exercise of lawful investigative authority, you are requested to preserve all relevant data 
associated with the above account for a period of not less than 90 days or until further 
lawful process, including but not limited to: 
 
Subscriber information 
 
Login IP logs 
[[PAGE 702]]
 
Session metadata 
 
Relevant content linked to the alleged offence 
This request is limited to preservation only. Formal disclosure, if required, shall follow through 
appropriate legal process. 
Kindly acknowledge preservation at the earliest. 
(Signature) 
Investigating Officer 
Rank / Police Station 
Contact details 
 
Why This Works (Judicial Defence) 
 
Specifies offence 
 
Defines account 
 
Limits temporal scope 
 
Separates preservation from disclosure 
 
Demonstrates proportionality 
Courts view preservation-first strategy as good faith compliance [1]. 
 
B. SPECIMEN DISCLOSURE REQUEST FORMAT (LIMITED & PROPORTIONATE) 
6.B.1 Subscriber & Metadata Disclosure (Lower Intrusion) 
Subject: Lawful Request for Limited Disclosure – FIR No. ___ 
Reference is invited to the preservation communication dated ___ regarding account ID ___ . 
In connection with investigation of offences under Sections ___, you are requested to furnish the 
following limited information: 
1. Subscriber information (name, registered email, phone, creation date) 
2. Login IP logs for period ___ to ___ 
3. Account status and linked identifiers 
This request is confined strictly to the above categories and period, in compliance with 
constitutional standards of legality and proportionality. 
[[PAGE 703]]
Certified copies or digitally signed records may kindly be furnished to ensure evidentiary 
integrity. 
 
6.B.2 Content Disclosure (High Intrusion – Requires Justification) 
Subject: Request for Specific Content Disclosure – Judicially Reviewable 
During investigation of FIR No. ___, it has been established that specific communications dated 
___ between account ID ___ and Victim A are directly relevant to the alleged offence under 
Section ___ . 
Accordingly, you are requested to provide only the following content: 
 
Messages exchanged between ___ and ___ 
 
Limited to dates ___ to ___ 
This request is made after assessment that metadata alone is insufficient to establish evidentiary 
elements of the offence. 
No blanket or historical data beyond this defined scope is sought. 
 
Critical Judicial Safeguard 
Always record in case diary: 
“Content request is necessary as metadata alone is insufficient to establish elements of offence.” 
Failure to record this reasoning weakens proportionality defence [2]. 
 
C. CHAIN OF CUSTODY ENTRY FORMAT (WHEN DATA RECEIVED) 
“On date ___, data received from [Platform Name] via official channel (email / portal / MLAT 
response). Hash verification conducted (if applicable). Data stored in secure digital evidence 
repository. Access restricted to IO and designated forensic personnel.” 
This protects admissibility under BSA, 2023 [3].

PART VII – CLOUD, REMOTE & CROSS-BORDER DATA SOPs 
 
7.1 The Illusion of Territorial Control in the Cloud Era 
In traditional policing, seizure implied physical custody. In cyber investigations, however, 
critical evidence may reside in servers physically located outside Uttar Pradesh, outside India, or 
distributed across multiple jurisdictions simultaneously. Investigating Officers must understand 
that cloud-stored data is not automatically within their legal reach merely because the user 
resides in India [1]. 
Courts increasingly examine whether police respected jurisdictional boundaries while obtaining 
remote data. Evidence collected in disregard of international legal processes may face 
admissibility challenges under both constitutional privacy principles and sovereign cooperation 
frameworks [2]. 
 
7.2 Defining “Cloud Evidence” for Investigative Purposes 
Cloud evidence includes: 
 
Email servers hosted abroad 
 
Social media content stored in foreign data centres 
 
Encrypted messaging platform backups 
 
Cloud drive repositories 
 
SaaS-based financial or enterprise systems 
 
Cryptocurrency wallet logs stored remotely 
Such data may involve foreign legal regimes, cross-border privacy laws, and international 
cooperation treaties. Treating cloud evidence as if it were locally stored digital media is a 
fundamental mistake [3]. 
 
7.3 The Legal Route: Domestic Authority vs International Process 
[[PAGE 708]]
When cloud data is stored on servers outside India, Investigating Officers must determine 
whether: 
1. The intermediary has a legal presence in India and can comply under Indian law; or 
2. The data requires invocation of international legal assistance mechanisms such as Mutual 
Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs), Letters of Request, or other bilateral arrangements 
[4]. 
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 provides procedural mechanisms for letters of 
request in cross-border investigations. Failure to use these routes where necessary may render 
evidence vulnerable to challenge [5]. 
 
7.4 Preservation Before MLAT: A Critical First Step 
Given the often lengthy MLAT timelines, investigators must immediately issue preservation 
requests to foreign platforms with Indian operational presence. Preservation does not equal 
disclosure and is generally less jurisdictionally contentious [6]. 
Courts have recognised that preservation-first action demonstrates diligence and prevents loss of 
volatile data. However, disclosure must follow lawful international channels when required [7]. 
 
7.5 MLAT & Letter of Request: When Mandatory 
Where a foreign entity declines disclosure citing jurisdictional constraints, and no Indian entity 
has custody or control of the data, investigators must initiate: 
 
MLAT request through designated central authority 
 
Letter Rogatory via competent court 
 
International cooperation mechanisms recognised under Indian law 
Circumventing this route through informal channels or unofficial cooperation may expose the 
investigation to evidentiary rejection [8]. 
 
7.6 Chain of Custody for Cloud-Derived Evidence 
Cloud evidence must satisfy three integrity requirements under evidentiary scrutiny: 
1. Authenticity (platform certification, digital signature, hash value) 
2. Integrity (no tampering during transfer) 
[[PAGE 709]]
3. Continuity (documented custody from receipt to production in court) 
Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, electronic records must inspire judicial 
confidence in their reliability. Poor documentation at the cloud transfer stage is a recurring 
weakness in cyber prosecutions [9]. 
 
7.7 Remote Access Without Authorisation: Strict Prohibition 
Investigating Officers are strictly prohibited from: 
 
Logging into accused accounts using seized credentials without lawful authority 
 
Accessing remote accounts through password recovery mechanisms 
 
Using impersonation to bypass jurisdictional barriers 
Even if technically feasible, such actions may violate privacy principles laid down in Justice K.S. 
Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India and may attract judicial criticism or exclusion of evidence 
 
7.8 Encryption & Cross-Border Constraints 
Many cloud platforms operate under end-to-end encryption frameworks. Officers must recognise 
 
Lawful requests may still yield limited data 
 
Metadata may be available even where content is encrypted 
 
Compulsion without legal authority is impermissible 
Courts are unlikely to accept investigative frustration as justification for bypassing legal 
safeguards [11]. 
 
7.9 Proportionality in Cross-Border Data Requests 
Foreign authorities scrutinise requests for overbreadth. Blanket demands for “entire account 
history” or “all data ever stored” are frequently rejected. Precision and narrow tailoring improve 
success rates [12]. 
This aligns with constitutional proportionality requirements under Article 21. International 
cooperation is strengthened—not weakened—by disciplined drafting [13]. 
 
[[PAGE 710]]
7.10 Delay Management & Documentation 
MLAT processes may involve significant delay. Investigators must: 
 
Document each step of international request 
 
Record follow-ups 
 
Inform prosecution regarding timelines 
 
Avoid filing incomplete charge-sheets without disclosure of pending requests 
Courts assess diligence, not merely speed [14]. 
 
7.11 Hindi Operational Summary 
क्लाउर् र्ेटा – महत्वपूणट क्रनदेश: 
 
सवभर कवदेश में हो तो सीधी जब्ती सींर्व नहीीं 
 
 
आवश्यकता होने पर एमएलएटी / न्यायालय मागभ अपनाएूँ 
 
पासवडभ से अनकधकृत लॉकगन न करें 
 
हर कदम कलक्तखत रखें 
 
7.12 Supervisory Oversight in Cross-Border Matters 
All cross-border requests must be reviewed at DCP-level or above. Given diplomatic 
implications and evidentiary sensitivity, lower-level unilateral action is discouraged. Supervisory 
officers must ensure compliance with both Indian law and international legal processes [15]. 
 
7.13 Transition to Institutional Integrity & Accountability Framework 
With cloud and cross-border evidence governance clarified, the next part will address 
Institutional Integrity, Internal Audits & Accountability Mechanisms. Even the most lawful 
SOP fails if not institutionally enforced [16]. 
 
PART VII – ADDENDUM 
MLAT SPECIMEN DRAFT LANGUAGE & CROSS-BORDER TIMELINE MATRIX 
[[PAGE 711]]
 
A. SPECIMEN MLAT / LETTER OF REQUEST DRAFT LANGUAGE 
(To be routed through designated Central Authority under BNSS, 2023 and relevant treaty 
mechanisms) 
 
7.A.1 Covering Narrative (Judicial Submission for Letter of Request) 
In the Court of ________ 
Subject: Letter of Request for International Judicial Assistance 
In connection with FIR No. ___ / 20__, registered under Sections ___ of the Bharatiya Nyaya 
Sanhita / Information Technology Act, 2000, investigation has revealed that material digital 
evidence relevant to the offence is stored on servers located in [Country]. 
The said evidence pertains to account ID ___ hosted by [Platform Name], and is directly 
connected to the alleged commission of offence involving [brief offence description – e.g., 
online financial fraud / CSAM distribution / cyber terrorism]. 
It is respectfully submitted that: 
1. The requested data is necessary to establish essential elements of the offence; 
2. The request is limited to defined data categories and specific time period ___ to ___; 
3. Metadata alone is insufficient, and content disclosure is proportionately required; 
4. The request satisfies constitutional standards of legality, legitimate aim, and 
proportionality. 
This Hon’ble Court may kindly issue a Letter of Request to the competent authority of [Country] 
seeking assistance in obtaining the specified digital records. 
 
7.A.2 Annexure – Data Specification (Precision Format) 
The following limited data is sought: 
 
Subscriber information (name, registration date, linked identifiers) 
 
Login IP logs between ___ and ___ 
 
Content messages exchanged between ___ and ___ during period ___ 
 
Account deletion or modification logs (if applicable) 
[[PAGE 712]]
No blanket or historical data beyond the above scope is sought. 
 
7.A.3 Certification Clause (Chain-of-Custody Conscious) 
It is further requested that the records be certified in accordance with the laws of the requested 
State, including digital authentication or attestation, to enable admissibility before Indian courts. 
 
Why This Drafting Survives Scrutiny 
 
Identifies offence clearly 
 
Demonstrates necessity 
 
Defines temporal limits 
 
Records proportionality reasoning 
 
Avoids vague language 
Foreign authorities often reject overbroad requests. Precision improves compliance [1]. 
 
B. SUPPLEMENTAL MLAT CASE DIARY ENTRY TEMPLATE 
“Today, it was determined that relevant digital evidence is stored outside Indian jurisdiction. 
Direct access being impermissible, international legal assistance process initiated through 
proper channel. Request limited to offence-linked data categories only.” 
This protects against defence arguments of jurisdictional overreach [2].

A. INTERPOL CHANNEL – SPECIMEN DRAFT LANGUAGE 
(To be routed through designated Interpol NCB India / CBI channel, not directly by IO unless 
authorised) 
 
7.A.1 Interpol Assistance Request – Operational Draft 
Subject: Request for International Police Cooperation – Cyber Investigation (FIR No. ___)** 
[[PAGE 716]]
The Cyber Crime Police Station, District _, Uttar Pradesh, India, is investigating FIR No. ___ 
/ 20 registered under Sections ___ of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / Information Technology Act, 
2000. 
Investigation has revealed that digital evidence relevant to the offence is associated with account 
ID ___ hosted by [Platform Name], with suspected linkage to infrastructure located in [Country]. 
It is respectfully requested that the competent law enforcement authority in [Country], through 
INTERPOL cooperation channels, may assist in: 
1. Confirming preservation of specified data categories; 
2. Identifying subscriber details linked to the account; 
3. Facilitating lawful transmission of certified digital records through appropriate judicial 
process. 
The request is strictly limited to data categories essential for the investigation and complies with 
principles of legality, necessity, and proportionality. 
All requested information shall be used solely for the stated investigation and handled in 
accordance with privacy and evidentiary safeguards. 
 
7.A.2 Interpol Use Limitation Clause 
“The requested cooperation does not seek operational intervention within the territory of the 
requested State without lawful authority, and is confined to assistance permissible under 
international police cooperation norms.” 
This clause reduces sovereignty-based objections. 
 
7.A.3 Documentation Requirement 
Case diary must record: 
“Interpol channel invoked due to cross-border digital evidence requirement. MLAT process 
initiated / under consideration. Interpol request limited to identification and preservation 
assistance.” 
Courts scrutinise why Interpol route was chosen over direct judicial request [1]. 
 
B. WHEN TO USE INTERPOL CHANNEL 
Use Interpol where: 
[[PAGE 717]]
 
Immediate intelligence verification required 
 
Suspect infrastructure location unknown 
 
Identity tracing needed before MLAT 
 
Urgent preservation needed 
Do NOT use Interpol to bypass MLAT where formal judicial process is mandatory [2].

PART VII – ADDENDUM III 
INTERNATIONAL EVIDENCE ADMISSIBILITY REBUTTAL NOTES & APPELLATE 
DEFENCE CHECKLIST 
 
A. INTERNATIONAL EVIDENCE ADMISSIBILITY – REBUTTAL NOTES 
[[PAGE 720]]
International digital evidence is frequently challenged at trial. The defence typically raises 
objections based on jurisdiction, privacy, certification, and chain of custody. The following 
rebuttal structure is to be used by IOs and prosecutors. 
 
7.A.1 Objection: “Evidence obtained without jurisdiction” 
Foreign-stored digital evidence was collected without lawful authority; hence inadmissible. 
 
Preservation initiated promptly 
 
MLAT / Letter of Request processed through competent court 
 
Central Authority channel followed 
 
No unauthorised remote access undertaken 
 
Evidence transmitted via lawful cooperation framework 
Courts examine procedural compliance, not geographical distance alone [1]. 
 
7.A.2 Objection: “Violation of privacy / Puttaswamy principles” 
Cross-border data request was disproportionate and violated informational privacy. 
 
Request was narrowly tailored 
 
Time window clearly defined 
 
Data categories restricted to offence-linked content 
 
Case diary records proportionality reasoning 
 
Metadata insufficient; content necessity recorded 
Judicial reasoning under Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India requires documented 
necessity, not abstract justification [2]. 
 
7.A.3 Objection: “Improper certification under BSA, 2023” 
[[PAGE 721]]
Foreign digital records lack proper authentication or certification. 
 
Certification obtained under foreign authority 
 
Digital signature / hash integrity verified 
 
Chain of custody recorded upon receipt 
 
Evidence stored in secure repository 
Courts focus on reliability and integrity, not nationality of server [3]. 
 
7.A.4 Objection: “Delay in MLAT renders evidence unreliable” 
Delay undermines authenticity or credibility. 
 
Preservation requested immediately 
 
Delay attributable to international process 
 
Timeline documented in case diary 
 
Follow-ups recorded 
Judicial assessment often centres on diligence, not speed [4]. 
 
7.A.5 Objection: “Interpol used improperly to bypass judicial route” 
Interpol channel misused to avoid MLAT safeguards. 
 
Interpol invoked only for identification / preservation 
 
Judicial request initiated separately where disclosure required 
 
No operational enforcement conducted abroad without authority 
Clear documentation neutralises sovereignty-based arguments [5]. 
 
[[PAGE 722]]
B. APPELLATE DEFENCE CHECKLIST (CYBER CROSS-BORDER CASES) 
This checklist is to be used before and after conviction to ensure appellate sustainability. 
 
7.B.1 Pre-Judgment Internal Review 
Before trial conclusion, ensure: 
✔ Preservation letters on record 
✔ MLAT acknowledgment available 
✔ Certification compliant with evidentiary law 
✔ Proportionality reasoning documented 
✔ No unauthorised account access 
✔ Chain of custody intact 
Weakness identified at this stage can still be corrected before judgment [6]. 
 
7.B.2 Post-Conviction Appellate Risk Audit 
Immediately after conviction: 
Risk Area 
Audit Question 
Mitigation Prepared? 
Jurisdiction 
Was international route properly followed? Yes / No 
Privacy 
Is proportionality documented? 
Are digital records authenticated? 
Chain of Custody Is transfer log complete? 
Delay 
Is timeline documented? 
Appellate courts focus on procedure more than trial courts [7]. 
 
7.B.3 Anticipating High Court / Supreme Court Scrutiny 
Appellate courts often examine: 
 
Was evidence lawfully acquired? 
 
Was accused prejudiced by irregularity? 
[[PAGE 723]]
 
Did police act fairly? 
 
Was investigation constitutionally compliant? 
The record—not oral explanation—decides these issues [8]. 
 
7.B.4 Standard Appellate Rebuttal Statement (Template) 
“The international digital evidence was obtained through recognised legal channels, with 
documented preservation, judicial request, and certified transmission. The request was limited to 
offence-specific data and satisfies constitutional proportionality standards.” 
 
C. Institutional Appellate Safeguard Directive 
All cross-border cyber convictions must undergo: 
 
DCP-level appellate readiness review 
 
Legal cell documentation audit 
 
Verification of digital evidence certification 
 
Preservation of complete communication trail 
Cyber acquittals at appellate stage frequently arise from procedural complacency, not evidentiary 
weakness [9].
