CHAPTER 24 
 
PART VIII – INSTITUTIONAL INTEGRITY, AUDIT & ACCOUNTABILITY 
FRAMEWORK 
 
8.1 From Policy to Practice: Why Institutional Enforcement Matters 
A privacy-compliant SOP is meaningless unless enforced through institutional mechanisms. 
Courts have repeatedly observed that constitutional compliance is not satisfied by policy 
statements alone; it must be reflected in day-to-day practice. In cyber investigations, procedural 
lapses are often systemic rather than individual. Therefore, this Part establishes a structured 
accountability and audit framework [1]. 
The Supreme Court has consistently emphasised that the State bears positive obligations to 
protect fundamental rights. Institutional indifference to privacy safeguards may attract judicial 
criticism extending beyond individual officers to the department itself [2]. 
 
8.2 Institutional Privacy Governance Structure 
All Cyber Crime Units shall adopt a three-tier privacy compliance structure: 
1. Investigative Level – IO responsibility 
2. Supervisory Level – SHO / ACP oversight 
[[PAGE 725]]
3. Command Level – DCP / SSP review and audit 
This layered structure ensures that privacy compliance is examined at multiple checkpoints, 
reducing risk of oversight failure [3]. 
 
8.3 Mandatory Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) in High-Risk Cases 
For cases involving: 
 
Bulk data seizure 
 
Content-level intermediary disclosure 
 
CSAM investigation 
 
Dark web infiltration 
 
Cross-border MLAT requests 
Investigating Officers must record a brief Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) in the case diary 
addressing: 
 
Nature of data involved 
 
Scope of intrusion 
 
Necessity justification 
 
Safeguards applied 
Courts increasingly examine whether police assessed privacy impact before intrusive action [4]. 
 
8.4 Quarterly Privacy Compliance Audit 
Each district cyber unit shall conduct a Quarterly Privacy Audit, examining: 
 
Random sampling of seizure memos 
 
Intermediary request proportionality 
 
Cloud evidence documentation 
 
CSAM handling compliance 
 
Undercover operation authorisations 
Audit findings must be documented and corrective instructions issued in writing [5]. 
 
[[PAGE 726]]
8.5 Red Flag Indicators Requiring Immediate Review 
The following trigger automatic supervisory scrutiny: 
 
Seizure memos lacking necessity reasoning 
 
Blanket intermediary requests 
 
Full device cloning without justification 
 
CSAM duplication beyond single forensic copy 
 
Unauthorised account access 
 
Missing chain-of-custody documentation 
Such red flags indicate constitutional vulnerability [6]. 
 
8.6 Disciplinary Sensitivity in Privacy Violations 
Privacy violations in cyber investigations are not minor procedural errors. Depending on gravity, 
they may constitute: 
 
Departmental misconduct 
 
Violation of IT Act, 2000 (Section 72) 
 
Contempt of court 
 
Grounds for evidence exclusion 
Supervisory officers must treat such lapses seriously and not shield negligence under operational 
pressure [7]. 
 
8.7 Training & Continuous Legal Updating 
Cyber privacy jurisprudence evolves rapidly. District Cyber Units must conduct: 
 
Annual refresher training on privacy law 
 
Case-law update sessions 
 
Practical drafting workshops 
 
Simulation exercises on proportionality analysis 
Failure to update knowledge is not a defence in court [8]. 
 
[[PAGE 727]]
8.8 Documentation Culture: The Ultimate Institutional Shield 
Courts rarely penalise documented good-faith actions. They consistently penalise undocumented 
discretion. Every major investigative decision impacting privacy must be recorded 
contemporaneously in case diary or supervisory note [9]. 
The constitutional test is not perfection; it is reasonableness backed by record. 
 
8.9 Data Retention & Destruction Protocol 
Institutional integrity requires not only lawful acquisition but lawful retention and destruction. 
Upon completion of trial and exhaustion of appeals: 
 
Sensitive victim data must be securely archived or destroyed as per law 
 
Access logs must be maintained 
 
Unnecessary duplicates must be eliminated 
Retention beyond necessity may itself violate privacy principles [10]. 
 
8.10 Command-Level Accountability 
DCP / SSP-level officers must: 
 
Review quarterly audit reports 
 
Identify systemic patterns of non-compliance 
 
Issue corrective circulars 
 
Escalate repeated violations 
Institutional discipline flows from command example [11].

सींस्थागत स्तर पर ध्यान रखें: 
 
कनजता कनयम केवल कागज़ पर न रहें

With institutional enforcement mechanisms established, the next and final part of this chapter 
will present: 
 
Consolidated operational flowcharts 
 
Field-level quick reference matrices 
 
Constitutional compliance summary grid 
 
Decision-tree models for IOs 
This will convert the entire chapter into a ready-to-use field manual format [12]. 
 
PART VIII – ADDENDUM 
INTERNAL DISCIPLINARY MATRIX & PRIVACY IMPACT ASSESSMENT (PIA) 
TEMPLATE 
 
A. INTERNAL DISCIPLINARY MATRIX FOR SOP VIOLATIONS 
 
8.A.1 Foundational Principle 
Violations of privacy safeguards and procedural boundaries in cyber investigations undermine 
constitutional rights and institutional credibility. Disciplinary response must therefore be 
calibrated, consistent, and documented. Informal warnings without written record are insufficient 
in serious cases [1]. 
 
8.A.2 Categorisation of Violations 
Category I – Minor Procedural Lapse (Correctable) 
 
Omission of proportionality wording in seizure memo 
[[PAGE 729]]
 
Incomplete case diary reasoning 
 
Delayed but not prejudicial documentation 
 
Written advisory 
 
Mandatory corrective entry 
 
Supervisory counselling 
Repeated Category I lapses escalate to Category II [2]. 
 
Category II – Serious Procedural Non-Compliance 
 
Blanket intermediary request without justification 
 
Full device cloning without necessity recording 
 
Failure to initiate preservation leading to data loss 
 
Missing chain-of-custody documentation 
 
Formal explanation sought 
 
Entry in service record 
 
Temporary restriction from handling sensitive digital cases 
 
Mandatory retraining 
Where court criticism is recorded, escalation to Category III review required [3]. 
 
Category III – Gross Privacy or Legal Violation 
 
Unauthorised login to remote account 
 
Informal data acquisition bypassing lawful process 
 
Improper handling or duplication of CSAM 
 
Disclosure of victim identity in violation of law 
[[PAGE 730]]
 
Manipulative undercover conduct creating offence 
 
Immediate supervisory inquiry 
 
Departmental proceedings 
 
Possible suspension pending inquiry 
 
Intimation to legal cell regarding evidentiary risk 
 
Consideration of liability under IT Act, 2000 (Section 72) 
No operational success mitigates Category III misconduct [4]. 
 
8.A.3 Supervisory Responsibility Clause 
Failure of supervisory officers to detect or prevent repeated violations may attract review at 
command level. Accountability is hierarchical and shared [5]. 
 
8.A.4 Documentation Requirement 
All disciplinary actions under this matrix must be recorded in: 
 
District Cyber Compliance Register 
 
Quarterly Audit Report 
 
Command Review Minutes 
Institutional memory prevents recurrence [6]. 
 
B. PRIVACY IMPACT ASSESSMENT (PIA) TEMPLATE – FIELD FORMAT 
 
8.B.1 When PIA Is Mandatory 
PIA must be recorded in case diary when: 
 
Seizing multiple digital devices 
 
Requesting content-level data 
 
Conducting undercover cyber operations 
[[PAGE 731]]
 
Handling CSAM 
 
Initiating cross-border MLAT 
 
Bulk data analytics involved 
PIA is not bureaucratic formality; it is constitutional insurance [7].

Where defence alleges privacy violation, existence of contemporaneous PIA demonstrates: 
 
Conscious constitutional compliance 
 
Application of mind 
 
Absence of arbitrariness 
Courts evaluate intention through documentation [8]. 
 
C. Integration Directive 
All cyber police stations shall: 
 
Maintain PIA annexure files 
 
Digitise PIA into e-Sakshya module 
 
Audit random PIAs quarterly 
 
Include PIA review in supervisory meetings 
PIA culture transforms privacy from theoretical principle into operational habit [9].

Privacy compliance is not an obstacle to cyber investigation. It is its constitutional backbone. 
An investigation that respects legality, necessity, proportionality, victim dignity, and

Survives trial 
 
Survives appeal 
 
Protects officers 


 
Protects the Constitution 
Chapter 24 therefore stands not merely as a policy statement, but as a constitutional shield for 
every cyber investigator in Uttar Pradesh Police [12]. 
CHAPTER 24 – AT A GLANCE 
(Senior Officer Command Brief – UP Police Cyber Crime) 
 
🎯 Core Objective 
To ensure that every cyber investigation: 
 
Complies with Article 21 – Right to Privacy 
 
Satisfies the Puttaswamy three-fold test 
 
Meets admissibility standards under BSA, 2023 
 
Preserves victim dignity 
 
Withstands appellate scrutiny 
Privacy compliance is not optional — it is constitutional obligation + evidentiary survival 
strategy. 
 
[[PAGE 742]]
🔐 1. Constitutional Compliance Framework 
Every digital investigative action must pass: 
✔ Legality – Statutory basis (BNSS / IT Act / Court Order) 
✔ Legitimate Aim – Specific offence-linked purpose 
✔ Proportionality – Least intrusive method 
No verbal approvals. No “practice-based” justification. 
 
📱 2. Digital Seizure Discipline 
 
Possession ≠ relevance 
 
Record necessity in seizure memo 
 
Prefer targeted extraction over full cloning 
 
Apply Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) in high-risk cases 
Failure to document proportionality = trial vulnerability. 
 
🌐 3. Intermediary & Platform Engagement 
Golden Rule: Preserve first, disclose later. 
 
Send preservation notice within 24–48 hrs 
 
Avoid blanket requests 
 
Distinguish metadata vs content 
 
Record proportionality in case diary 
 
Maintain certified chain of custody 
Overbroad requests delay and weaken prosecution. 
 
🕵️ 4. Undercover & Dark Web Operations 
Permitted only when: 
 
Prior criminal activity exists 
 
Written supervisory approval granted 
[[PAGE 743]]
 
Reactive presence maintained 
Absolute Prohibitions: 
❌ Inducement 
❌ Escalation suggestion 
❌ Crime creation 
❌ Informal transactions 
Entrapment collapses prosecutions. 
 
👩⚖️ 5. Victim-Centric Safeguards 
Non-negotiable in cases involving: 
 
Women 
 
Children 
 
CSAM 
 
Intimate content 
Mandatory: 
✔ Redaction 
✔ Access restriction 
✔ Sealed court production 
✔ No training exposure of real victim data 
Victim privacy breach = institutional damage. 
 
🌍 6. Cloud & Cross-Border Evidence 
If server abroad: 
1. Preserve immediately 
2. Determine domestic compliance feasibility 
3. Initiate MLAT / Letter of Request if required 
4. Document timeline 
Never: 
[[PAGE 744]]
❌ Log in using seized credentials 
❌ Use backchannel data access 
Jurisdictional violation invites appellate reversal. 
 
📊 7. Institutional Controls 
Mandatory Mechanisms: 
 
Quarterly Privacy Audit 
 
PIA recording in high-risk cases 
 
Disciplinary matrix enforcement 
 
Supervisory approval tracking 
 
Cross-border evidence register 
Privacy governance must be measurable. 
 
⚖️ 8. Appellate Survivability Check 
Before filing charge-sheet: 
✔ Legality documented 
✔ Proportionality recorded 
✔ Chain of custody intact 
✔ Victim protection ensured 
✔ MLAT steps recorded (if applicable) 
Appellate courts examine procedure first, merits second.





 
CSAM duplication 
 
Informal intermediary communication 
[[PAGE 745]]
 
Unauthorised remote access 
Two or more red flags = constitutionally fragile case.

% cases with PIA recorded 






Institutional maturity reflects constitutional discipline.

Cyber policing strength lies not in data volume but in constitutional precision. 
A legally disciplined investigation:









Chapter 24 transforms privacy from abstract right into operational command responsibility. 
CHAPTER 25 
TRAINING, CAPACITY BUILDING & CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT 
PART I – STRATEGIC VISION: INSTITUTIONAL SUSTAINABILITY IN CYBER 
POLICING 
 
25.1 Introduction: From Reaction to Resilience 
Cybercrime is not merely an extension of conventional crime into the digital domain; it 
represents a structural transformation in the nature of criminal conduct. The anonymity of 
[[PAGE 746]]
networks, velocity of financial transfers, borderless jurisdictional spillover, and algorithm-driven 
deception models have fundamentally altered investigative timelines and evidentiary 
expectations. Uttar Pradesh, being India’s most populous State, experiences this transformation 
at scale, both in terms of victim volume and financial impact. As per consolidated police data, 
more than 87,850 cybercrime cases have been registered in the State since 2017, demonstrating a 
persistent upward trajectory in digital offences.[1] 
The magnitude of the problem is not limited to registration numbers. In 2025 alone, Uttar 
Pradesh Police froze approximately ₹325.25 crores in financial cyber fraud cases, improving the 
recovery rate from 11% in 2024 to 24% in 2025.[2] This measurable improvement was not 
accidental; it was the outcome of improved coordination, timely reporting via NCRP/1930 
helpline, and enhanced technological response capabilities. However, episodic improvement is 
not institutional sustainability. The objective of this Chapter is to convert success stories into 
systemic capacity. 
Institutional sustainability (सींस्थागत स्थाकयत्व) requires that cyber policing must evolve from an 
incident-driven response model to a data-driven, court-defensible, intelligence-integrated 
architecture capable of anticipating and absorbing technological shifts without operational 
paralysis.[3] 
 
25.2 Defining Institutional Sustainability in Cyber Policing 
Institutional sustainability in cyber policing refers to the ability of the police organisation to 
continuously adapt its manpower, infrastructure, forensic capability, legal preparedness, and 
inter-agency coordination mechanisms in response to evolving technological crime vectors—
without degradation in investigative quality or courtroom admissibility.[4] 
Unlike conventional crimes where modus operandi may evolve gradually, cybercrime techniques 
mutate at exponential speed. Phishing has evolved into AI-driven voice cloning scams; sextortion 
has been amplified by deepfake technology; investment fraud now operates through algorithmic 
social engineering campaigns; ransomware groups operate via dark web escrow systems. Static 
training modules cannot address dynamic criminal ecosystems. 
Therefore, sustainability must be anchored on five pillars: 
1. Human Resource Specialization (मानव सींसािन क्रवशेषज्ञता) 
2. Forensic Infrastructure Modernization 
3. Legal-Technical Synchronization 
4. Data-Centric Intelligence Platforms 
5. Continuous Feedback & SOP Revision Mechanism[5] 
[[PAGE 747]]
This Chapter operationalizes these five pillars into measurable protocols. 
 
25.3 The Shift from “Generalist Policing” to “Dedicated Cyber Mandate” 
Historically, cyber investigations were often assigned as an additional responsibility to general 
police stations. However, digital investigation is not a peripheral skill; it is a technical discipline 
requiring uninterrupted attention, log preservation timing awareness, hash verification protocols, 
metadata interpretation, and inter-state financial trail coordination. 
As of recent expansion, the number of Cyber Crime Police Stations in Uttar Pradesh has 
increased from 18 to 75, reflecting structural prioritization of cyber policing.[6] This expansion 
is not merely infrastructural; it marks a policy decision to treat cybercrime as a primary policing 
domain. 
Cyber investigation is inherently time-perishable. The “Golden Hour” principle (स्वकणभम घींटा 
कसद्धाींत) in cyber financial fraud refers to the narrow time window within which fraudulent 
transactions can be frozen before they are layered across mule accounts and converted into 
cryptocurrency or withdrawn in cash. Diversion of Cyber IOs for unrelated law-and-order duties 
during this period results in irreversible financial loss. 
Therefore, exclusive cyber mandate (कवकशष्ट साइबर दाकयत्व) shall be treated as a structural 
doctrine, not an administrative convenience.[7] 
 
25.4 Golden Hour Doctrine in Financial Cyber Frauds 
The Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System (CFCFRMS), integrated 
under I4C, has demonstrated that early reporting and immediate freezing of funds drastically 
improves recovery outcomes. National data reflects that more than ₹7,13 0 crores have been 
saved across India through real-time intervention mechanisms.[8] 
In Uttar Pradesh, measurable improvement in recovery rates correlates directly with prompt 
NCRP/1930 reporting and swift action by Cyber Thanas.[2] This empirical evidence establishes 
that training must prioritize Golden Hour Response Protocols. 
The Golden Hour Doctrine includes: 
 
Immediate acknowledgment of complaint (within 5 minutes). 
 
Real-time entry into NCRP/CFCFRMS. 
 
Simultaneous bank alert and transaction hold request. 
 
Mule account layering trace initiation. 
[[PAGE 748]]
 
Digital evidence preservation (transaction logs, IP logs, device metadata). 
 
Preliminary jurisdiction assessment without delaying freezing action.[9] 
Training modules must simulate Golden Hour drills through live scenario exercises. 
 
25.5 Data-Driven Policing: From FIR to Analytics 
The future of cyber policing lies not only in investigation but in predictive intelligence. 
Platforms such as Samanvaya and Pratibimb under I4C provide interstate linkage analytics and 
mapping of crime infrastructure.[10] 
Institutional sustainability requires that: 
 
Every Cyber Thana must upload structured data. 
 
Crime patterns must be reviewed quarterly. 
 
Repeat IP addresses, mule accounts, and device fingerprints must be centrally tagged. 
 
Suspect Registry integration must be operationalized at district level.[11] 
A case registered in Meerut may share infrastructure overlap with an offence in Hyderabad. 
Without analytics-driven review, such linkages remain undiscovered. 
Cybercrime is modular. Investigation must therefore become modular. 
 
25.6 Legal Defensibility as a Core Objective 
Training must not merely produce arrests; it must produce convictions. The Bharatiya Sakshya 
Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) now explicitly recognizes electronic records and prescribes hash value 
integrity, certification requirements, and admissibility conditions under Sections 61–63.[12] 
Failure to comply with hash documentation, chain of custody, and Certificate requirements leads 
to evidentiary collapse in court. Digital evidence must be collected, preserved, and presented in 
accordance with statutory mandates. 
Similarly, lawful interception procedures must align with Section 5(2) of the Indian Telegraph 
Act, 1885 and Rule 419A, along with Rule 69 of the IT Act framework.[13] 
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 introduces compliance expectations in handling 
personal data, breach notifications, and fiduciary accountability.[14] 
Thus, every IO must be a techno-legal officer. Training architecture must eliminate the historical 
divide between legal officers and technical investigators. 
[[PAGE 749]]
 
25.7 Capacity Building as a Continuous Cycle 
Capacity building (िमता कनमाभण) is not a one-time training event; it is a cyclical institutional 
process. The CyTrain MOOC platform developed under I4C has registered over 1,44,895 
officers nationally and issued more than 1,19,628 certificates.[15] 
However, certification without operational application does not guarantee quality investigation. 
Therefore, Uttar Pradesh shall adopt a Continuous Learning Cycle Model, consisting of: 
1. Training 
2. Field Application 
3. Audit & Review 
4. Feedback Integration 
5. Re-Training / Skill Upgrade[16] 
This closed-loop mechanism ensures knowledge does not stagnate. 
 
25.8 Institutional Flowchart – Strategic Cyber Policing Model 
Below is the foundational model that governs this Chapter: 
Incident Reporting (NCRP/1930) 
        ↓ 
Golden Hour Intervention 
        ↓ 
Digital Evidence Preservation (Hash + Chain of Custody) 
        ↓ 
Data Analytics Integration (Samanvaya/Pratibimb) 
        ↓ 
Specialized Investigation (Dedicated IO) 
        ↓ 
Legal Vetting (BSA/DPDP/Telecom Compliance) 
        ↓ 
[[PAGE 750]]
Court-Ready Charge Sheet 
        ↓ 
Conviction & Recovery 
        ↓ 
Lessons Learned Documentation 
        ↓ 
Training Module Update 
        ↺ (Cycle Repeats) 
This flow ensures that every investigation contributes to institutional memory. 
 
25.9 Objectives of Chapter 25 
The primary objective of this Chapter is to transform Uttar Pradesh Police Cyber Crime units 
into a continuously evolving, specialized institution capable of: 
 
Maintaining optimal Case-to-IO ratios. 
 
Eliminating non-cyber duty diversion of Cyber Thana personnel. 
 
Institutionalizing mandatory technological upskilling. 
 
Establishing Technical and Legal Advisory Desks. 
 
Integrating interstate intelligence frameworks. 
 
Measuring performance through KPI-based evaluation. 
 
Ensuring forensic and legal compliance at every stage. 
 
Embedding continuous improvement doctrine into SOP revision cycles.[17] 
This Chapter therefore shall not be treated as an administrative guideline but as a structural 
blueprint for sustainable cyber governance. 
 
25.10 Strategic Declaration 
Cybercrime will not stabilize. Technology will not slow down. Criminal innovation will not 
pause for institutional adjustment. 
[[PAGE 751]]
Therefore, the Uttar Pradesh Police shall adopt a doctrine of anticipatory institutional 
adaptation. 
Training shall be continuous. Specialization shall be mandatory. Audit shall be structured. Data 
shall guide policy. Legal defensibility shall be non-negotiable. 
Only then can cyber policing evolve from reactive enforcement to strategic resilience. 
 
 
Revised Section 25.6 – Legal Defensibility as a Core Objective 
25.6 Legal Defensibility as a Core Objective 
Training must not merely produce arrests; it must produce sustainable convictions grounded in 
statutory compliance. Cyber investigation today is inseparable from telecom data analysis—Call 
Detail Records (CDRs), Internet Protocol Detail Records (IPDRs), subscriber identity modules, 
traffic data, and telecommunication identifiers. With the enactment of the Telecommunications 
Act, 2023, the legal architecture governing interception, suspension, user identification, and 
spectrum governance has undergone structural consolidation.[3] 
The Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 and the Indian Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933 now stand 
repealed under Section 60 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023.[1] Therefore, investigative 
training shall align exclusively with the new legislative framework. 
 
25.6.1 Interception & Suspension Powers under Telecommunications Act, 2023 
Section 20(2) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 empowers the Central Government or State 
Government, or an officer specially authorised, to intercept, detain, suspend, or disclose 
telecommunication messages in the interest of: 
 
Sovereignty and integrity of India 
 
Defence and security of the State 
 
Friendly relations with foreign States 
 
Public order 
 
Prevention of incitement to commission of an offence[4] 
Unlike the previous regime, the new Act requires: 
 
Recording of reasons in writing 
 
Prescribed procedure and safeguards 
[[PAGE 752]]
 
Time-bound action during public emergency or public safety circumstances[4] 
Therefore, IO training modules must incorporate: 
1. Drafting legally sustainable interception requests. 
2. Maintaining documentation trail for judicial scrutiny. 
3. Ensuring proportionality and necessity principles are recorded. 
4. Strict adherence to authorization hierarchy. 
Failure to comply renders telecom-derived evidence vulnerable to challenge under constitutional 
standards of privacy laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India.[5] 
 
25.6.2 Protection of Telecom Networks & Traffic Data 
Section 22 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 authorizes the Central Government to prescribe 
measures for protection and cyber security of telecommunication networks and services, 
including collection and analysis of traffic data.[6] 
The explanation to Section 22 clarifies that “traffic data” includes data relating to type, routing, 
duration, or time of telecommunication. For cyber investigators, this directly impacts: 
 
IP tracing 
 
Tower dump analysis 
 
Session timing correlation 
 
Mule account SIM mapping 
 
Deepfake call origin traceability 
Training must emphasize lawful requisition formats under Section 44, which empowers specially 
authorized officers to direct authorized telecom entities to furnish information in relation to 
pending or apprehended civil or criminal proceedings.[7] 
This replaces earlier reliance on Telegraph Act mechanisms. 
 
25.6.3 User Protection & SIM Misuse Prevention 
Section 29 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 imposes a statutory duty on users not to furnish 
false particulars or impersonate another person while establishing identity for telecommunication 
services.[8] 
Further, Section 42(3) criminalizes: 
[[PAGE 753]]
 
Possession or use of unauthorized telecom identifiers. 
 
Tampering with telecommunication identifiers. 
 
Fraudulent procurement of SIMs. 
 
Unlawful interception of messages.[9] 
Given the prevalence of mule SIM rackets in financial cyber fraud, IO training must include: 
 
SIM issuance audit trails. 
 
Biometric verification compliance checks under Section 3(7). 
 
Cross-referencing telecommunication identifiers with bank KYC records. 
 
Coordination with telecom compliance cells.[10] 
This integration strengthens charge-sheet sustainability under both cyber fraud and telecom 
offences. 
 
25.6.4 National Security & Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure 
Section 21 empowers the Central Government to issue directions in the interest of national 
security, including suspension or removal of specified telecommunication equipment.[11] 
Section 22(3) ) allows declaration of “Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure” disruption of 
which may have debilitating impact on national security, economy, public health, or safety.[6] 
Cyber forensic training must include identification of cases involving: 
 
Attacks on telecom backbone networks. 
 
SIM box fraud. 
 
Infrastructure sabotage. 
 
Unauthorized spectrum use. 
Because offences under Section 42 are cognizable and non-bailable.[9] 
 
25.6.5 Digital Implementation Doctrine 
Section 53 m mandates that implementation of the Telecommunications Act shall be “digital by 
design.”[12] 
This aligns with the digital transformation of investigation, including: 
[[PAGE 754]]
 
Electronic requisition orders. 
 
Digital documentation of telecom responses. 
 
Integration with NCRP and I4C databases. 
 
Blockchain-based evidence ledgering (future roadmap). 
Investigators must be trained not only in telecom law compliance but also in digital 
documentation workflows to ensure traceability. 
 
25.6.6 Synchronization with Other Digital Statutes 
Telecommunications compliance cannot operate in isolation. Cyber investigation training must 
ensure harmonization with: 
 
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Electronic Evidence Admissibility & Hash 
Integrity)[13] 
 
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Processing & Breach Notification)[14] 
 
Information Technology Act, 2000 (Cyber Offences Framework) 
The Telecommunications Act explicitly provides under Section 52 that its provisions are in 
addition to and not in derogation of other laws.[15] Therefore, multi-statute compliance is 
mandatory. 
 
25.6.7 Institutional Mandate 
Legal defensibility (न्याकयक कटकाऊपन) is not optional; it is foundational. 
Every Cyber IO shall be trained to ensure: 
 
Lawful interception authorization. 
 
Proper telecom data requisition. 
 
Documentation of necessity & proportionality. 
 
Chain of custody for telecom logs. 
 
Statutory alignment with Telecommunications Act, 2023. 
An investigation unsupported by statutory compliance may collapse at trial stage. Sustainable 
conviction requires procedural purity. 
 
[[PAGE 755]]
 
PART II – HUMAN RESOURCE OPTIMIZATION & SPECIALIZED UNITS 
 
25.11 The Structural Imperative: From Manpower Deployment to Manpower Engineering 
Cybercrime investigation is not manpower-intensive in the traditional sense; it is competency-
intensive. A single poorly trained Investigating Officer (IO) handling fifteen simultaneous 
financial fraud cases can cause greater systemic damage than ten vacant posts. Therefore, human 
resource planning in cyber policing must shift from numerical strength to capability density.[1] 
Uttar Pradesh, being the largest State in terms of population, faces disproportionate exposure to 
financial fraud, sextortion, deepfake exploitation, online radicalization and crypto-enabled 
money laundering. The registration of more than 87,850 cybercrime cases since 2017 
demonstrates volume stress on investigative officers.[2] Without structural HR reform, 
institutional fatigue becomes inevitable. 
This Part lays down binding protocols for human resource optimization (मानव सींसाधन अनुकूलन) 
in Cyber Crime Police Stations. 
 
25.12 Case-to-IO Ratio Management Framework 
25.12.1 The Problem of Investigation Saturation 
Cybercrime investigations involve: 
 
Multi-layered bank account analysis. 
 
IP log extraction. 
 
Telecom data requisition. 
 
Digital device seizure & forensic imaging. 
 
Interstate coordination. 
 
Court-bound evidentiary compliance. 
Each of these processes is time-sensitive. Excessive case load results in: 
 
Delayed freezing of funds. 
 
Expiry of log retention periods. 
 
Poorly drafted 65B certifications. 
 
Incomplete charge-sheets. 
[[PAGE 756]]
 
Acquittals due to procedural lapses.[3] 
Therefore, a maximum Active Case-to-IO Ratio must be institutionalized. 
 
25.12.2 Recommended Active Case Threshold 
Based on operational experience and forensic complexity, the following thresholds are 
recommended: 
Case Type 
Maximum Active Cases per IO 
Financial Cyber Fraud (Live Freezing Stage) 
5 
Financial Fraud (Post-Freezing Investigation Stage) 10 
Dark Web / Crypto / Ransomware Cases 
3 
Social Media / Harassment / Sextortion 
12 
Deepfake / AI Manipulation Cases 
4 
An IO handling Golden Hour financial frauds should not be simultaneously burdened with dark 
web crypto tracing. Specialization reduces error margins. 
District SP Cyber shall review case allocation fortnightly. 
 
25.12.3 Expansion from 18 to 75 Cyber Thanas 
The expansion of Cyber Crime Police Stations from 18 to 75 across Uttar Pradesh represents a 
structural decentralization of digital investigation.[4] However, mere physical expansion without 
trained manpower produces administrative shells. 
Each Cyber Thana shall mandatorily include: 
 
1 Inspector (Cyber Ops Lead) 
 
2 Sub-Inspectors (Financial & Technical Stream) 
 
2 Assistant Sub-Inspectors 
 
4 Constables (Digital Support & Data Entry) 
 
1 Technical Consultant (Contractual/Empanelled) 
 
1 Legal Officer (Advisory Desk) 
[[PAGE 757]]
This staffing model shall be non-negotiable. 
 
25.13 Exclusive Cyber Mandate Doctrine (Unit Decoupling Policy) 
25.13.1 The Time-Perishability Principle 
Cyber investigation is inherently time-perishable (समय-सींवेदनशील). The Golden Hour doctrine 
establishes that delay beyond the initial freezing window results in layered fund dispersal across 
mule accounts and crypto conversion.[5] 
Diversion of Cyber IOs to: 
 
Mela duties 
 
VIP escorting 
 
Bandobast deployment 
 
General law & order duties 
directly impacts recovery outcomes. 
Therefore, Cyber Thana personnel shall be exempt from non-cyber duties except in extraordinary 
situations declared by DGP Office. 
 
25.13.2 Operational Justification 
Empirical data indicates recovery rate improvement from 11% to 24% in UP during 2025 due to 
focused intervention.[6] This improvement correlates with dedicated attention to cyber financial 
complaints. 
Diverting IOs during peak fraud season (festivals, financial year-end, exam seasons) is 
operationally counterproductive. 
Hence, Exclusive Cyber Mandate becomes institutional doctrine. 
 
25.14 Unified Command Structure & Review Rationalization 
25.14.1 The Problem of Review Fatigue 
Cyber IOs often attend multiple review meetings at district and range levels, consuming critical 
investigation hours. Non-specialized senior officers sometimes require technical briefings 
unrelated to investigative progress. 
This creates: 
[[PAGE 758]]
 
Documentation overload. 
 
Redundant presentations. 
 
Reduced field time. 
 
Psychological fatigue.[7] 
 
25.14.2 Streamlined Reporting Channel 
To eliminate review fatigue, the following hierarchy shall apply: 
Cyber IO 
   ↓ 
Cyber Thana Inspector 
   ↓ 
SP Cyber (District Level) 
   ↓ 
Range Cyber Nodal Officer 
   ↓ 
State Cyber Crime Coordinator (ADGP/IG Rank) 
IOs shall not be required to present technical case briefings before non-specialized review 
forums unless specifically directed. 
Quarterly review at State HQ shall focus on: 
 
Recovery rate metrics. 
 
Conviction sustainability. 
 
Telecom compliance adherence. 
 
Dark web case mapping. 
 
25.15 Bridging the Seniority–Technology Gap 
25.15.1 Structural Knowledge Lag 
[[PAGE 759]]
Promotion from Sub-Inspector to Inspector typically occurs after 8–10 years of service. During 
this period, digital technology may have transformed entirely—encryption standards evolve, 
cryptocurrency frameworks change, AI tools proliferate. 
This creates a “knowledge lag” (तकनीकी अींतराल) in newly promoted officers. 
Without mandatory re-skilling, supervisory quality deteriorates. 
 
25.15.2 Mandatory 4-Week Advanced Cyber-Ops Bridge Course 
All newly promoted Inspectors posted in Cyber Units must undergo a 4-week Advanced Cyber-
Ops Bridge Program covering: 
1. AI Voice Cloning & Deepfake Forensics 
2. Blockchain & Crypto Tracing Fundamentals 
3. Dark Web Market Monitoring 
4. IoT Device Exploitation Patterns 
5. Telecom Data Analysis under Telecommunications Act, 2023 
6. Electronic Evidence Admissibility under BSA, 2023[8] 
7. DPDP Act, 2023 Compliance in Data Handling[9] 
Certification shall be mandatory before independent supervision.

This ensures investigation becomes “court-ready from day one”.

25.20 Institutional Directive 
Human resource management in cyber policing shall not be treated as routine posting exercise. It

PART III – CYBER LAB INFRASTRUCTURE & FORENSIC STRENGTHENING 
 
25.21 Forensics as the Spine of Cyber Policing 
If human resource optimization is the muscle of cyber policing, digital forensics is its spine. 
Without scientific acquisition, preservation, and analysis of electronic evidence, even the most 
sophisticated investigation collapses at the trial stage. Courts do not convict on suspicion; they 
convict on proof. In cybercrime, proof is technical, traceable, and hash-verifiable.[1] 
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) has formally embedded electronic records 
within admissibility standards, requiring integrity, certification, and demonstrable authenticity.[2] 
Therefore, institutional sustainability demands that every Cyber Thana in Uttar Pradesh be 
supported by structured cyber forensic infrastructure (कडकजटल फोरेंकसक सींरचना), whether at 
district level or through zonal pooling. 
 
25.22 District-Level Cyber Lab Architecture 
25.22.1 Minimum Infrastructure Requirements 
Each district with a Cyber Crime Police Station shall either maintain an in-house Mini Cyber 
Lab or be formally linked to a designated Zonal Cyber Forensic Laboratory. 
The minimum hardware capability shall include: 
 
Write-blockers (SATA/IDE/USB compatible) 
 
Forensic imaging workstation (minimum 32GB RAM, SSD-based) 
 
Dedicated evidence storage server (air-gapped) 
 
Mobile extraction tools (logical + physical extraction capability) 
 
Network traffic analysis suite 
 
Malware sandbox environment 
 
Hash verification tools (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) 
The lab shall maintain environmental controls and access logs. 
[[PAGE 763]]
 
25.22.2 Zonal Digital Forensic Laboratories 
Given cost and specialization constraints, certain high-end capabilities such as: 
 
Chip-off extraction 
 
JTAG recovery 
 
Advanced crypto wallet tracing 
 
AI deepfake artifact detection 
 
Encrypted disk brute-force capability 
may be centralized at Zonal Labs. 
However, Golden Hour investigations cannot wait for distant lab processing. Initial acquisition 
and hash generation must occur at district level. 
 
25.23 Chain of Custody Protocol (साक्ष्य अक्रभरक्षा शींखला) 
25.23.1 Foundational Principle 
Digital evidence is volatile. A single alteration—even unintended—can render it inadmissible. 
Therefore, strict chain-of-custody documentation is mandatory from seizure to court production. 
The Chain of Custody must record: 
1. Date & Time of Seizure 
2. Device Description & Serial Number 
3. Hash Value (at time of imaging) 
4. Officer Conducting Imaging 
5. Storage Location 
6. Transfer Log Entries 
7. Court Production Record 
The BSA 2023 mandates integrity demonstration; without documented chain-of-custody, 
certification under Section 63 equivalent provisions becomes vulnerable.[2] 
 
25.23.2 Hash Integrity Mandate 
[[PAGE 764]]
At the time of forensic imaging: 
 
SHA-256 hash must be generated. 
 
Hash value must be printed and digitally stored. 
 
Re-verification hash must be generated before court submission. 
Mismatch equals evidentiary doubt. 
Investigators shall never analyze original media. Only forensic copies shall be examined. 
 
25.24 Evidence Acquisition SOP 
25.24.1 Mobile Devices 
Procedure: 
 
Photograph device condition. 
 
Isolate from network (Faraday bag / Airplane mode). 
 
Record SIM details. 
 
Generate forensic image. 
 
Extract logical + physical dump where permissible. 
 
Document app-level metadata. 
Particular care must be taken in cases involving encrypted messaging platforms. 
 
25.24.2 Cloud & Platform Data 
Data requisition shall align with: 
 
Telecommunications Act, 2023 (Section 44 – supply of information)[3] 
 
Mutual Legal Assistance procedures where cross-border 
 
DPDP Act compliance principles[4] 
IO must record necessity and proportionality. 
 
25.24.3 Financial Trail Evidence 
Financial cyber fraud cases require: 
[[PAGE 765]]
 
Bank transaction logs 
 
Beneficiary KYC documents 
 
IP login records 
 
Device fingerprint data 
 
ATM CCTV retrieval 
Delay beyond log retention period (often 90–180 days) risks irretrievable loss. 
 
25.25 Cyber Lab Operational Governance 
25.25.1 Access Control 
Only authorized forensic personnel may access lab premises. Biometric entry logs shall be 
maintained. 
25.25.2 Evidence Storage 
Evidence shall be stored: 
 
In sealed tamper-evident packaging. 
 
In temperature-controlled cabinets. 
 
With barcode tagging system. 
25.25.3 Audit Frequency 
Internal forensic audit shall be conducted quarterly. 
External audit by State HQ Cyber Wing annually. 
 
25.26 Deepfake & AI Forensic Capability 
The increasing use of AI-generated voice cloning and synthetic video manipulation necessitates 
specialized detection capabilities. 
Labs must maintain: 
 
Spectral voice analysis software 
 
Frame-level artifact detection tools 
 
Metadata consistency analyzers 
 
Reverse image search capability 
[[PAGE 766]]
IO training shall include recognition of: 
 
GAN-based inconsistencies 
 
Lip-sync mismatch 
 
Lighting anomalies 
 
Synthetic compression artifacts 
These capabilities are essential for emerging sextortion and political misinformation cases. 
 
25.27 Dark Web & Crypto Forensics 
25.27.1 Crypto Tracing 
Bitcoin and Ethereum transaction analysis tools shall be made available at zonal labs. 
Investigators must understand: 
 
Wallet clustering 
 
Exchange tracing 
 
Mixer identification 
 
Layering pattern recognition 
25.27.2 Dark Web Intelligence 
Dedicated terminal (isolated network) for: 
 
Marketplace monitoring 
 
Threat intelligence collection 
 
Ransomware leak site tracking 
Strict logging and supervisory oversight required. 
 
25.28 Forensic Reporting Standards 
Forensic reports must include: 
1. Description of tools used. 
2. Version details of software. 
3. Imaging methodology. 
[[PAGE 767]]
4. Hash values. 
5. Limitations of analysis. 
6. Opinion summary. 
Reports must avoid speculative language. Only technically demonstrable findings shall be 
recorded. 
 
25.29 Integration with Court Processes 
Under BSA 2023, electronic evidence admissibility requires demonstrable authenticity and 
certification.[2] 
 
Forensic officer must prepare certification. 
 
IO must ensure annexures properly indexed. 
 
Screenshots must include metadata context. 
 
Digital exhibits must be submitted in secure storage media. 
Judicial familiarity with cyber evidence varies; therefore clarity in reporting is essential. 
 
25.30 Forensic Quality Assurance Flowchart 
Device Seizure 
     ↓ 
Photographic Documentation 
     ↓ 
Forensic Imaging (Write Blocker) 
     ↓ 
SHA-256 Hash Generation 
     ↓ 
Secure Storage of Original 
     ↓ 
Analysis on Forensic Copy 
[[PAGE 768]]
     ↓ 
Report Drafting 
     ↓ 
Legal Review 
     ↓ 
Certification under BSA 
     ↓ 
Court Submission 
This sequence is non-negotiable. 
 
25.31 Training Modules for Forensic Personnel 
Training shall include: 
 
Advanced Disk Forensics 
 
Memory Forensics 
 
Network Packet Analysis 
 
Malware Reverse Engineering (Basic Level) 
 
Encrypted Chat Artifact Recovery 
 
AI Content Verification 
Certification renewal every 2 years. 
 
25.32 Institutional Directive 
Cyber forensic capacity shall not remain ornamental. Equipment without trained operators is 
institutional illusion. 
Every seized device must produce verifiable evidence. 
Every forensic report must withstand cross-examination. 
Every cyber lab must function under audit discipline. 
Forensic strengthening is not a technical luxury; it is a judicial necessity. 
PART IV – TRAINING ARCHITECTURE & CERTIFICATION FRAMEWORK 
[[PAGE 769]]
 
25.33 Training as a Strategic Weapon, Not an Administrative Ritual 
Training in cyber policing cannot be reduced to occasional workshops or ceremonial 
certifications. The velocity of technological crime demands a permanent training ecosystem 
(स्थायी प्रकशिण पाररतींत्र). What was cutting-edge two years ago is now obsolete. Encryption 
standards change. AI models evolve. Fraud scripts mutate. 
Therefore, training shall be institutionalized as a continuous strategic function, not a peripheral 
activity.[1] 
The Ministry of Home Affairs, through I4C and CyTrain, has already initiated national-level 
digital capacity building.[2] However, Uttar Pradesh must internalize and localize this 
framework through structured state-level training architecture. 
 
25.34 Tiered Training Model (Three-Level Structure) 
To ensure progression-based learning, cyber training shall operate under a three-tier model: 
Level I – Foundational Cyber Policing Certification (Basic Level) 
 
Newly inducted Sub-Inspectors 
 
Constables posted to Cyber Thanas 
 
Basics of Cyber Crime Typologies 
 
Financial Fraud Investigation Workflow 
 
NCRP & CFCFRMS Utilization 
 
Digital Evidence Preservation Basics 
 
Introduction to Telecommunications Act, 2023 
 
Introduction to BSA, 2023 Electronic Evidence[3] 
Duration: 2 Weeks (Residential or Hybrid) 
Certification: Mandatory for Cyber Thana Posting 
 
Level II – Intermediate Investigative Specialization 
[[PAGE 770]]
 
Serving Cyber IOs (2+ years experience) 
 
Advanced Financial Trail Analysis 
 
Telecom Data Interpretation (CDR/IPDR Analytics) 
 
Dark Web Fundamentals 
 
Cryptocurrency Tracing (Introductory Level) 
 
Deepfake Detection Fundamentals 
 
DPDP Act Compliance for Investigators[4] 
Duration: 3 Weeks 
Practical Assessment Required. 
 
Level III – Advanced Cyber-Ops & Supervisory Leadership Program 
 
Inspectors, Deputy SPs, Supervisory Officers 
 
AI Voice Cloning & Synthetic Media Forensics 
 
Blockchain Intelligence Analytics 
 
Ransomware Case Strategy 
 
Legal Vetting & Courtroom Presentation 
 
Inter-State Intelligence Coordination 
 
KPI-based Unit Performance Management 
Duration: 4 Weeks 
Mandatory for supervisory cyber postings. 
 
25.35 Mandatory Re-Skilling Cycle 
Every cyber officer shall undergo refresher certification every 24 months. 
[[PAGE 771]]
Failure to re-certify shall result in: 
 
Temporary suspension from sensitive cyber assignments. 
 
Mandatory remedial training. 
Technology stagnation equals institutional vulnerability. 
 
25.36 Integration with National Platforms 
The CyTrain MOOC platform developed under I4C has already issued more than 1,19,628 
certificates nationally.[2] Uttar Pradesh officers shall mandatorily register and complete specified 
modules annually. 
However, online certification must be supplemented with: 
 
Scenario-based simulation drills. 
 
Mock Golden Hour exercises. 
 
Cross-district fraud tracing simulations. 
 
Courtroom evidence presentation practice. 
Practical exposure transforms theoretical knowledge into investigative competence. 
 
25.37 Specialized Training Streams 
25.37.1 Financial Fraud Response Unit Training 
Modules shall include: 
 
Mule account pattern detection. 
 
ATM cash-out analytics. 
 
SIM swap fraud analysis. 
 
Loan app harassment evidence capture. 
 
Bank compliance communication. 
 
25.37.2 Dark Web & Crypto Intelligence Training 
Officers shall be trained in: 
 
TOR navigation ethics. 
[[PAGE 772]]
 
Wallet tracing tools. 
 
Mixer identification. 
 
Exchange subpoena strategy. 
 
Blockchain analytics dashboard use. 
 
25.37.3 AI & Deepfake Forensics Training 
Modules: 
 
GAN model understanding. 
 
Voice spectral analysis basics. 
 
Video metadata correlation. 
 
Platform-based content reporting protocols. 
 
Court demonstration methods. 
 
25.38 Legal-Technical Synchronization Module 
Investigators must internalize the intersection of: 
 
Telecommunications Act, 2023 (Interception & Data Requisition)[5] 
 
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Admissibility Standards)[3] 
 
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Data Processing Compliance)[4] 
 
Information Technology Act, 2000 (Offence Provisions) 
Case-based workshops shall be conducted where legal and technical instructors jointly evaluate 
mock investigation files. 
This ensures “court-ready investigation from day one”. 
 
25.39 Training for Public Prosecutors & Judicial Interface 
Cyber investigation sustainability does not end with charge-sheet filing. Prosecutors must 
understand: 
 
Hash verification principles. 
 
Chain-of-custody documentation. 
[[PAGE 773]]
 
AI-generated evidence challenges. 
 
Crypto tracing explanation methods. 
Joint training sessions between IOs and Public Prosecutors shall be conducted bi-annually. 
Judicial familiarization workshops may be coordinated through State Judicial Academy, subject 
to administrative approval. 
 
25.40 KPI-Linked Training Evaluation 
Training shall not be evaluated merely by attendance. 
Post-training evaluation shall measure: 
1. Reduction in procedural errors. 
2. Increase in recovery rate. 
3. Reduction in average freezing time. 
4. Improvement in conviction sustainability. 
5. Compliance score under BSA standards. 
Data-driven training impact assessment shall be conducted annually.

       ↓ 
       ↓

       ↓ 
[[PAGE 774]]

       ↺ Cycle Repeats 
This creates institutional muscle memory. 
 
25.42 Faculty Development & Trainer Accreditation 
Cyber instructors must themselves undergo annual upskilling. 
Trainer eligibility criteria: 
 
Minimum 5 years cyber investigation experience. 
 
Advanced certification completion. 
 
Court testimony experience preferred. 
A “Train-the-Trainer” program shall be instituted at State HQ level. 
 
25.43 Documentation & Knowledge Repository 
All training material, case studies, SOP revisions, and anonymized best practices shall be stored 
in a centralized digital repository accessible to cyber officers across the State. 
Lessons learned from major cases shall be converted into micro-modules. 
Institutional memory must outlive individual postings. 
 
25.44 Institutional Directive 
Training is not an event; it is an obligation. 
Every officer must remain technologically literate. 
Every supervisor must remain legally updated. 
Every forensic examiner must remain technically current. 
Continuous learning is the only antidote to exponential cybercrime evolution. 
PART V – INTER-STATE & INTER-AGENCY COORDINATION FRAMEWORK 
 
[[PAGE 775]]
25.45 Cybercrime Is Borderless: Jurisdiction Is Administrative, Not Digital 
Cybercrime does not recognize district boundaries, State borders, or even national jurisdiction. A 
complainant in Lucknow may transfer funds to a mule account in Mewat, layered through 
Kolkata, withdrawn in Bengaluru, and converted into cryptocurrency routed via offshore 
exchanges. The crime scene is fragmented across digital geography. 
Therefore, institutional sustainability in Uttar Pradesh requires structured interstate and inter-
agency coordination (अींतरराज्यीय समन्वय), not ad-hoc communication.[1] 
Without coordinated response, criminals exploit jurisdictional delays, especially during the 
Golden Hour. 
 
25.46 Joint Cybercrime Coordination Teams (JCCT) 
The Ministry of Home Affairs has operationalized Joint Cybercrime Coordination Teams (JCCT) 
to address cybercrime hotspots and regional fraud clusters.[2] 
Uttar Pradesh shall: 
 
Nominate dedicated JCCT liaison officers. 
 
Share actionable intelligence in real-time. 
 
Participate in joint operations targeting mule account syndicates. 
 
Share technical signatures (IP clusters, wallet IDs, SIM patterns). 
JCCT coordination shall not remain ceremonial; monthly review of shared intelligence shall be 
mandatory at State Cyber HQ. 
 
25.47 Samanvaya & Pratibimb Protocols 
25.47.1 Samanvaya Platform Utilization 
The Samanvaya Platform, developed under I4C, functions as a Management Information System 
(MIS) and interstate coordination tool for cybercrime analytics.[3] 
It provides: 
 
Interstate linkage analysis. 
 
Shared suspect registry. 
 
Data-driven crime pattern mapping. 
 
Coordination logs between States. 
[[PAGE 776]]
Every Cyber Thana shall designate a Data Officer responsible for uploading structured 
investigation data into Samanvaya within 48 hours of FIR registration. 
Failure to update deprives the system of analytic intelligence. 
 
25.47.2 Pratibimb Module 
The Pratibimb module maps the geographical concentration of crime infrastructure and suspect 
clusters.[3] 
It allows: 
 
Visualization of mule account clusters. 
 
Mapping of SIM procurement hotspots. 
 
Cross-state criminal footprint tracking. 
Training shall include dashboard interpretation skills. 
Data without interpretation is institutional noise. 
 
25.48 Zero FIR & 24-Hour Digital Handover Protocol 
25.48.1 The Jurisdictional Challenge 
In financial cyber fraud cases, the victim’s location often differs from the suspect’s location. 
Traditionally, physical transfer of case diaries caused delays and loss of Golden Hour response. 
 
25.48.2 Standardized Digital Handover Protocol 
Uttar Pradesh shall adopt a 24-hour Digital Handover Protocol: 
1. Zero FIR registered at complainant location. 
2. Immediate freezing action initiated. 
3. Case file digitized (FIR, complaint, transaction logs). 
4. Uploaded to Samanvaya / Secure State Portal. 
5. Receiving State acknowledges electronically within 24 hours. 
6. Formal transfer recorded in Crime & Criminal Tracking Network (CCTNS). 
No physical presence of IO shall be required for initial jurisdictional transfer. 
[[PAGE 777]]
Golden Hour action shall not be delayed due to territorial technicalities. 
 
25.49 Telecom & Banking Sector Coordination 
Cyber policing effectiveness depends heavily on cooperation with: 
 
Telecom Service Providers (TSPs) 
 
Banks & Payment Aggregators 
 
FinTech Platforms 
 
Social Media Intermediaries 
The Telecommunications Act, 2023 empowers lawful data requisition under Section 44.[4] 
Similarly, banking coordination through CFCFRMS enables real-time fund freezing.[2] 
Uttar Pradesh shall establish: 
 
State-Level Cyber Fraud Mitigation Desk. 
 
Monthly Telecom Compliance Review Meetings. 
 
Bank Nodal Officer Coordination Framework. 
 
Emergency escalation contact matrix. 
Response time from institutions shall be logged and reviewed. 
 
25.50 Integration with Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) 
I4C functions as the national nodal agency for cybercrime coordination.[2] 
UP Police shall: 
 
Participate in “State Connect” and “Thana Connect” sessions. 
 
Share best practices. 
 
Contribute anonymized case studies. 
 
Align SOP revisions with national advisories. 
Institutional isolation breeds inefficiency. 
 
25.51 International Cooperation Protocol 
[[PAGE 778]]
Certain cases—especially involving crypto exchanges, phishing infrastructure, or dark web 
marketplaces—require cross-border cooperation. 
Training shall include: 
 
Basic understanding of MLAT procedures. 
 
Preservation request drafting. 
 
INTERPOL notice coordination. 
 
Data preservation timelines. 
Delay in international requisition often results in data deletion due to retention policies. 
 
25.52 Multi-Agency Investigation Cells 
Complex cases may require coordinated investigation between: 
 
Cyber Crime Unit 
 
Economic Offences Wing 
 
Special Task Force 
 
Anti-Terror Units (where applicable) 
 
CERT-In (technical advisory) 
A Unified Case Coordination Committee (UCCC) may be constituted for large-scale financial 
fraud or ransomware cases exceeding ₹5 Crores. 
Minutes of coordination meetings shall be documented. 
 
25.53 Inter-Agency Data Governance & DPDP Compliance 
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 mandates lawful processing and purpose 
limitation.[5] 
When sharing data across States or agencies: 
 
Data minimization principle shall apply. 
 
Access logs must be maintained. 
 
Sensitive personal data shall be masked unless required. 
 
Confidentiality agreements shall be documented. 
[[PAGE 779]]
Coordination must not violate statutory privacy safeguards.

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

25.55 Performance Metrics for Coordination 
To institutionalize accountability, the following shall be measured: 
1. Average Time for Interstate Acknowledgment. 
2. Recovery Amount through Coordinated Action. 
3. Shared Intelligence Utilization Rate. 
4. Number of Joint Operations Conducted. 
[[PAGE 780]]
5. Conviction Rate in Interstate Cases. 
Quarterly review by State Cyber Crime Coordinator. 
 
25.56 Institutional Directive 
Cybercrime networks are collaborative. Law enforcement must be more collaborative than 
criminals. 
No district shall function in isolation. 
No State shall withhold actionable intelligence. 
No investigation shall stall for procedural ego. 
Institutional sustainability requires synchronized coordination architecture. 
PART VI – AUDIT, COMPLIANCE & CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT MECHANISM 
 
25.57 From Investigation to Institutional Learning 
No organization improves automatically. It improves only when it measures itself, questions 
itself, and corrects itself. Cybercrime evolves exponentially; therefore, the police institution must 
evolve systematically. 
Training without audit becomes complacency. Infrastructure without compliance becomes 
decorative. Recovery without documentation becomes legally fragile. 
Institutional sustainability (सींस्थागत क्तस्थरता) demands a structured audit and feedback 
ecosystem.[1] 
 
25.58 Cyber Investigation Audit Framework (CIAF) 
A formal Cyber Investigation Audit Framework (CIAF) shall be instituted at three levels: 
1. Case-Level Audit 
2. Unit-Level Audit 
3. State-Level Performance Audit 
 
25.58.1 Case-Level Audit 
Every charge-sheet filed in a cyber case shall undergo internal audit checklist verification 
covering: 
[[PAGE 781]]
 
Proper registration under relevant sections. 
 
Golden Hour action documentation. 
 
Telecom requisition compliance under Telecommunications Act, 2023.[2] 
 
Electronic evidence certification under BSA, 2023.[3] 
 
Chain-of-custody integrity. 
 
Proper annexure indexing. 
 
Financial trail mapping clarity. 
Any deficiency shall be flagged and rectified before trial stage wherever possible. 
 
25.58.2 Unit-Level Audit 
Quarterly audit of each Cyber Thana shall assess: 
 
Average Time-to-Freeze (ATF). 
 
Case-to-IO ratio adherence. 
 
Recovery percentage. 
 
Pending forensic reports. 
 
Data upload compliance on Samanvaya. 
 
Refresher training completion rate. 
Audit reports shall be submitted to SP Cyber and Range Cyber Nodal Officer. 
 
25.58.3 State-Level Performance Audit 
Bi-annual review at Cyber Crime Police HQ shall examine: 
 
District performance ranking. 
 
Emerging crime typology trends. 
 
Resource gaps. 
 
Conviction sustainability metrics. 
 
Inter-state coordination responsiveness. 
Performance matrix shall influence budget allocation and manpower deployment. 
[[PAGE 782]]
 
25.59 Digital Evidence Compliance Score (DECS) 
To ensure forensic and legal robustness, each investigation shall be evaluated on a Digital 
Evidence Compliance Score (DECS): 
Parameter 
Score Weight 
Hash Verification Accuracy 
20 
Chain of Custody Integrity 
20 
Telecom Requisition Compliance 15 
Proper 65B/BSA Certification 
15 
Annexure Documentation Quality 10 
Metadata Preservation 
10 
Court Objection Resilience 
10 
Minimum acceptable DECS: 75/100. 
Cases scoring below threshold must undergo supervisory review. 
 
25.60 Recovery Performance Benchmarking 
Recovery percentage is a measurable indicator of operational efficiency in financial cyber fraud 
cases. 
District-wise benchmarking shall include: 
 
Average freezing time. 
 
Percentage of recovered funds. 
 
Amount prevented via Golden Hour intervention. 
 
Number of mule accounts identified. 
Recovery benchmarking shall not overshadow legal compliance; both metrics must move 
together. 
 
25.61 Conviction Sustainability Index (CSI) 
[[PAGE 783]]
Conviction sustainability is not merely about conviction rate; it measures: 
 
Survival of evidence under cross-examination. 
 
Appellate stage sustainability. 
 
Judicial observations regarding procedural compliance. 
CSI shall be reviewed annually in coordination with Public Prosecutor office. 
Acquittals due to procedural lapses shall trigger targeted retraining. 
 
25.62 Lessons-Learned Integration Mechanism 
Every major cyber case (especially those exceeding ₹1 Crore impact or involving new 
technology) shall undergo Post-Investigation Review (PIR). 
PIR shall document: 
 
What worked. 
 
What failed. 
 
Procedural delays. 
 
Legal objections faced. 
 
Technology gaps encountered. 
These findings shall be converted into micro-training modules and SOP updates. 
Institutional memory must not depend on individual recollection. 
 
25.63 SOP Revision Cycle 
Chapter 25 itself shall not remain static. 
Revision mechanism: 
 
Annual review at State Cyber HQ. 
 
Consultation with forensic experts. 
 
Feedback from prosecutors. 
 
Inputs from JCCT liaison officers. 
 
Incorporation of new statutory amendments. 
[[PAGE 784]]
Revised SOP shall be digitally circulated and archived. 
 
25.64 PDCA Model Adapted for Cyber Policing 
The internationally recognized Plan–Do–Check–Act (PDCA) cycle shall be adapted: 
PLAN   → Training + Resource Allocation 
DO     → Investigation & Coordination 
CHECK  → Audit & KPI Review 
ACT    → SOP Update & Re-Training 
   ↺ Continuous Loop 
This ensures continuous institutional evolution. 
 
25.65 Compliance with DPDP Act in Audit Processes 
While auditing investigations, care must be taken to comply with Digital Personal Data 
Protection Act, 2023 principles.[4] 
Audit access shall: 
 
Be role-based. 
 
Maintain access logs. 
 
Avoid unnecessary data duplication. 
 
Mask irrelevant personal identifiers. 
Compliance culture must permeate audit processes. 
 
25.66 Performance Dashboard – State Cyber Analytics Portal 
A centralized digital dashboard shall display: 
 
District ATF. 
 
Recovery percentages. 
 
Pending forensic backlog. 
 
Training certification status. 
[[PAGE 785]]
 
Samanvaya upload compliance. 
 
CSI index. 
Transparency fosters accountability. 
 
25.67 Risk Assessment Matrix 
Annual Cyber Risk Assessment shall identify: 
 
High-incidence districts. 
 
Emerging AI-based fraud patterns. 
 
Telecom misuse hotspots. 
 
Dark web supply networks. 
Resource deployment shall follow risk mapping.

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

Institutional improvement is cyclical, not episodic. 
 
25.69 Institutional Directive 
No cyber investigation shall conclude without institutional learning. 
No acquittal shall be ignored as individual failure; it shall be studied as systemic signal. 
No technological shift shall catch the institution unprepared. 
Audit is not criticism. Audit is institutional self-defense. 
PART VII – KPI METRICS & PERFORMANCE EVALUATION FRAMEWORK 
 
25.70 From Activity-Based Policing to Outcome-Based Policing 
Traditional policing often measures activity — number of FIRs registered, number of arrests 
made, number of raids conducted. Cyber policing must measure outcomes — recovery, 
conviction sustainability, procedural compliance, and technological adaptability. 
Uttar Pradesh has demonstrated that focused intervention can improve recovery rates from 11% 
to 24% in financial cyber fraud cases.[1] This improvement underscores the importance of 
measurable performance benchmarks. 
Therefore, this Part establishes a formal Cyber Performance KPI Framework (CPKF). 
 
25.71 Core KPI Categories 
Cyber policing KPIs shall be divided into five domains: 
1. Operational Efficiency Metrics 
2. Financial Recovery Metrics 
3. Forensic & Legal Compliance Metrics 
4. Inter-State Coordination Metrics 
5. Training & Capacity Metrics 
Each domain shall carry weighted importance in district evaluation. 
 
I. OPERATIONAL EFFICIENCY METRICS 
[[PAGE 787]]
 
25.72 Average Time-to-Freeze (ATF) 
Definition: 
Average time taken between complaint registration and successful transaction freezing under 
CFCFRMS framework.[2] 
Target Benchmarks: 
Target ATF 
Urban District < 2 Hours 
Semi-Urban 
< 4 Hours 
Rural 
< 6 Hours 
Reduction in ATF directly correlates with recovery percentage. 
Districts exceeding threshold shall undergo operational review. 
 
25.73 Golden Hour Response Rate (GHRR) 
Percentage of cases where first action (bank alert / NCRP entry) was initiated within 60 minutes. 
Target: Minimum 75%. 
GHRR below threshold indicates procedural delay. 
 
25.74 Case Backlog Ratio (CBR) 
Formula: 
Pending Cyber Cases ÷ Total Active IOs 
CBR must align with prescribed case-to-IO ratio established in Part II. 
Overloaded IOs produce compromised investigations. 
 
II. FINANCIAL RECOVERY METRICS 
 
25.75 Recovery Percentage Index (RPI) 
[[PAGE 788]]
Formula: 
(Amount Recovered ÷ Total Amount Reported) × 100 
District ranking shall be based on RPI adjusted for case volume. 
High-value urban fraud cases must not skew performance unfairly; normalization mechanism 
shall apply. 
 
25.76 Prevented Loss Index (PLI) 
Measures funds blocked before transfer to second mule account layer. 
This metric recognizes proactive freezing rather than post-loss recovery. 
 
III. FORENSIC & LEGAL COMPLIANCE METRICS 
 
25.77 Digital Evidence Compliance Score (DECS) 
As detailed in Part VI, DECS shall be aggregated district-wise. 
District DECS average must remain above 80/100. 
Below-threshold districts shall undergo forensic retraining. 
 
25.78 Charge-Sheet Timeliness Index (CTI) 
Measures percentage of cyber charge-sheets filed within statutory period under CrPC. 
Delayed filings risk bail and evidentiary decay. 
 
25.79 Conviction Sustainability Index (CSI) 
Measures: 
 
Conviction survival at trial stage. 
 
Survival at appellate stage. 
 
Judicial remarks on procedural compliance. 
CSI shall not be calculated merely on conviction rate; quality of conviction matters. 
[[PAGE 789]]
 
IV. INTER-STATE COORDINATION METRICS 
 
25.80 Interstate Acknowledgment Time (IAT) 
Average time for another State to acknowledge digital transfer under Zero FIR Protocol. 
Target: < 24 Hours.[2] 
 
25.81 Samanvaya Data Compliance Rate (SDCR) 
Percentage of FIRs uploaded to Samanvaya within 48 hours.[2] 
Target: 100%. 
Incomplete uploads reduce interstate intelligence visibility. 
 
25.82 Joint Operation Participation Index (JOPI) 
Number of coordinated operations conducted through JCCT or multi-state collaboration.[2] 
Measures proactive intelligence sharing. 
 
V. TRAINING & CAPACITY METRICS 
 
25.83 Certification Coverage Ratio (CCR) 
Percentage of Cyber Unit personnel holding valid certification under Tiered Training Model. 
Target: 100%. 
Expired certifications shall reflect negatively in district evaluation. 
 
25.84 Refresher Completion Rate (RCR) 
Percentage of personnel completing 24-month mandatory re-skilling cycle. 
 
25.85 Specialized Stream Deployment Index (SSDI) 
[[PAGE 790]]
Measures whether units maintain specialization streams: 
 
Financial Fraud Stream 
 
Technical Forensics Stream 
 
Dark Web Stream 
 
AI Crime Stream 
Generalist-only units shall score lower. 
 
25.86 Composite Cyber Performance Score (CCPS) 
A weighted index combining all domains: 
Domain 
Weightage 
Operational Efficiency 
25% 
Financial Recovery 
25% 
Forensic & Legal Compliance 20% 
Inter-State Coordination 
15% 
Training & Capacity 
15% 
CCPS shall determine: 
 
District Ranking. 
 
Additional Resource Allocation. 
 
Recognition & Incentive Decisions. 
 
Corrective Administrative Action. 
 
25.87 Performance Dashboard Architecture 
A centralized digital dashboard at Cyber Crime HQ shall display: 
 
Real-time ATF. 
 
Recovery amounts. 
 
DECS averages. 
[[PAGE 791]]
 
Training compliance. 
 
Interstate coordination stats. 
Dashboard access shall be role-based and auditable. 
Data transparency reduces administrative ambiguity. 
 
25.88 Incentive & Corrective Framework 
High-performing districts: 
 
Eligible for advanced forensic equipment allocation. 
 
Recognition at State Police Conference. 
 
Priority for specialized training seats. 
Low-performing districts: 
 
Mandatory audit intervention. 
 
Supervisory review. 
 
Focused re-training deployment. 
Performance management shall be constructive, not punitive. 
 
25.89 Risk-Adjusted Performance Analysis 
Districts with: 
 
High population density. 
 
Known cyber fraud hubs. 
 
Interstate proximity risk zones. 
shall be evaluated under risk-adjusted scoring model to ensure fairness. 
Performance must be contextualized.

       ↓ 
[[PAGE 792]]

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

25.91 Institutional Directive 
Cyber policing cannot function on perception; it must function on precision. 
Every hour saved improves recovery. 
Every compliance step strengthens conviction. 
Every trained officer reduces systemic risk. 
Metrics are not bureaucratic burdens. They are institutional safeguards. 
PART VIII – INSTITUTIONAL ROADMAP & CYBER POLICING 2030 VISION 
(UTTAR PRADESH) 
 
25.92 The Imperative of Forward Planning 
Cybercrime does not evolve linearly. It evolves exponentially. Artificial Intelligence systems that 
generate convincing human voices today will generate indistinguishable synthetic personalities 
tomorrow. Crypto tracing tools effective today may be obsolete against privacy-chain 
architectures within three years. 
[[PAGE 793]]
Therefore, institutional sustainability demands anticipatory governance (पूवाटनुमान आिाररत 
शासन) rather than reactive adaptation. 
The Cyber Policing 2030 Vision of Uttar Pradesh is not a document of aspiration; it is a 
structured roadmap with measurable milestones.[1] 
 
25.93 Strategic Objectives for 2030 
By the year 2030, Uttar Pradesh Cyber Police shall aim to: 
1. Maintain ATF (Average Time-to-Freeze) below 90 minutes statewide. 
2. Achieve minimum 35% average recovery rate in financial cyber fraud. 
3. Ensure 100% BSA-compliant digital evidence in charge-sheets. 
4. Establish AI-assisted fraud detection analytics dashboard. 
5. Integrate predictive crime modelling into cyber monitoring. 
6. Achieve statewide forensic lab decentralization coverage. 
7. Develop specialized AI & Crypto Investigation Cells. 
8. Institutionalize annual SOP evolution framework. 
These targets shall be reviewed annually. 
 
25.94 Three-Phase Implementation Roadmap 
 
Phase I (2025–2026): Stabilization & Standardization 
 
Full operationalization of 75 Cyber Thanas.[2] 
 
Enforcement of case-to-IO ratio policy. 
 
Implementation of DECS scoring. 
 
Mandatory Tiered Certification for all cyber personnel. 
 
Statewide integration with Samanvaya platform.[3] 
Deliverable: Uniform baseline operational standards across districts. 
[[PAGE 794]]
 
Phase II (2026–2028): Technological Deepening 
 
Establishment of Zonal AI & Deepfake Forensic Units. 
 
Blockchain Intelligence Node at State HQ. 
 
Automated mule account clustering analytics. 
 
Integration of telecom data dashboards under Telecommunications Act framework.[4] 
 
Launch of AI-driven anomaly detection pilot projects. 
Deliverable: Technologically empowered investigation capability. 
 
Phase III (2028–2030): Predictive & Preventive Cyber Policing 
 
Predictive fraud hotspot mapping. 
 
Real-time financial fraud alert system integration with banks. 
 
Behavioral analytics for repeat offender profiling. 
 
State-level Cyber Intelligence Fusion Centre. 
 
Automated SOP revision engine using case audit data. 
Deliverable: Shift from detection to disruption. 
 
25.95 Establishment of Cyber Intelligence Fusion Centre (CIFC) 
By 2028, Uttar Pradesh shall establish a Cyber Intelligence Fusion Centre (CIFC) integrating: 
 
Crime analytics dashboard. 
 
Telecom metadata pattern recognition. 
 
Crypto tracing feeds. 
 
Dark web intelligence monitoring. 
 
AI anomaly detection systems. 
CIFC shall function as the strategic brain of State Cyber Policing. 
[[PAGE 795]]
 
25.96 AI Integration Roadmap 
AI shall be used responsibly and within statutory safeguards. 
Applications may include: 
 
Fraud pattern clustering. 
 
Voice similarity detection. 
 
Suspicious transaction anomaly scoring. 
 
Automated document indexing for charge-sheets. 
Compliance with DPDP Act, 2023 shall remain mandatory.[5] 
AI shall augment human judgment, not replace it. 
 
25.97 Advanced Specialization Cells 
By 2030, the following dedicated cells shall operate at State HQ: 
1. AI & Deepfake Investigation Cell 
2. Crypto & Blockchain Intelligence Cell 
3. Ransomware Response Cell 
4. Telecom Compliance & Data Analytics Cell 
5. Digital Evidence Litigation Support Cell 
Each cell shall include: 
 
Technical Expert 
 
Legal Officer 
 
Data Analyst 
 
Field Liaison Officer 
Specialization is the future of cyber policing.

To sustain innovation, UP Cyber Police shall collaborate with:







FinTech regulatory bodies.

25.99 Cyber Lab Modernization Roadmap 
By 2030: 


 
Zonal labs shall include AI artifact detection. 
 
Blockchain analytics tools shall be standardized. 


25.100 Human Capital Roadmap

Mandatory advanced training for all Inspectors.

25.102 Citizen-Centric Cyber Protection



Institutional sustainability includes citizen resilience.

Crypto-based money laundering spikes.
